- no , please ! first, the nations of europe are sufficiently different in every respect to be unable to form an optimal currency area. some people here will no doubt say that a superstate with the power to bring about cohesion is all the more necessary. it is true that it would be more necessary, but at the same time it is more impossible. this is the vicious circle in which the eurozone countries will be struggling in the coming years. we could also speak of a race against time: either, in order to make the euro work, its leaders will succeed quickly enough in destroying the nations and building the superstate - and at that point the euro may last, but with a europe and a democracy in what state? the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, although i have adopted a rather critical tone in the explanatory statement of this report, our approach must remain constructive and, despite the late hour, i would recommend that the european parliament give its opinion in favour of ratifying this acp-eu agreement. the signing of the cotonou agreement was not initially a given. while the acp countries have always expressed their willingness to continue their cooperation with the european union, other scenarios were envisaged on the european side. european interests on the international stage have changed, africa has become a marginal continent. no acp country is among the top ten recipients of european aid. we have never really taken a political assessment of lomé, but we are starting from the same starting point for cotonou. we doubt that the cotonou agreement will be able to generate a dynamic of sustainable development without a redefinition of a more balanced international economic order, where developing countries will finally have rights. the structural causes which have impeded the success of the lomé conventions are still present: the burden of debt repayment which is suffocating the budgets of the acp countries and their investment possibilities for sustainable development, the continuing deterioration of the terms of trade to the detriment of the acp countries, the absence of an international system of regulation of trade in basic commodities, a policy of structural adjustment which imposes budgetary restrictions on the acp countries and, finally, an incoherent european policy which, in parallel with its development policy, not only subsidizes its agricultural production and exports its surpluses to developing countries, thus destroying local markets, but also allows industrial fishing vessels to exploit the territorial waters of the acp countries, which undermines the protection of the populations and the livelihood of biodiversity at night. nor should we underestimate the problems of the internal functioning of the acp group, the democratic deficits in some countries and the unproductive use of funds by corrupt regimes. the cotonou agreement is not new. it perpetuates and accentuates the shift towards liberalization begun under lomé iv and continued by the international institutions: trade liberalization, with the abandonment of the system of non-reciprocal trade, as well as stabex and sysmin, in favour of the future trade regime which will probably take the form of aper compatible with wto rules. but can the acp countries withstand global competition? is there any danger that differentiation from the ldcs, which benefit from the 'everything but arms' initiative, will undermine the cohesion of the acp group? economic liberalisation also, in the framework of the general agreement on the marketing of services. the privatisation of this economic sector is a very dangerous process in acp countries where basic public services - education, health, justice - are already fragile or non-existent. similarly, the reference to trips is a danger to the people of the south who risk being deprived of access to their own natural resources. biodiversity is in danger. in fact, the environment is relegated to the background in the cotonou agreement. the aim is simply to limit the environmental impact of development policies, as opposed to a sustainable development strategy. the cotonou agreement does, however, contain some interesting elements which should be put to good use. the recognition of civil society as a partner is a major innovation. its representatives must be involved in the dialogue on development strategies and policies at an early stage, be involved in the implementation of programmes and benefit directly from the funds. we must define this civil society and ensure that it is not exploited by either party. the civil society of each acp country must therefore organise itself at national, but also regional, level in order to participate actively in the development of its country. this process is under way with the establishment of the acp civil society forum. the european union must support this process, as the belgian presidency has done. the joint parliamentary assembly sees its role strengthened at this level, in that it must monitor the participation of civil society and the implementation of democratic processes in particular. but it has no binding instruments to do so. political dialogue is another essential element. it must be reciprocal and effectively implemented. the 'everything but arms' initiative was taken without consulting the acp countries and the sanctions are still variable in geometry. finally, since the european community wants to make considerable investments in a few key sectors, the national indicative programmes should give priority to strengthening public services and administrative and institutional capacity. in reality, it is the implementation of the cotonou agreement that is at stake. for example, the new cotonou agreement provides for a scalable programming of aid, in particular in the light of the performance of the countries. but who's going to define these performance criteria? will we assess the ability of countries to restore their major macroeconomic balances or the impact of aid on poverty reduction? the new distribution of responsibilities between the commission's departments does not seem to be conducive to greater coherence in development policy. to what extent can the directorate-general for trade promote a more favourable trade model for acp countries while defending european trade interests? finally, the fact that the directorate-general for development is gradually being stripped of its prerogatives in this area does not bode well. as for us, the members of the european parliament, and this is my conclusion, mr president, after tomorrow's vote, our task will in theory be completed. since the edf is not budgeted, we are no longer competent for monitoring and achieving the objectives of acp-eu cooperation. this is unacceptable and we must work collectively to implement this agreement so that aid really contributes to the well-being of the people of the acp countries in accordance with their food, health and educational needs.
mr president, i naturally wish mr fischler a speedy recovery and ask the officials present to convey to him our concerns in a scrupulous manner. as the new common fisheries policy is being prepared, i would like to draw the commissioner's attention to three essential points. firstly, the new common fisheries policy must be based on the tac and quota system, which is the best way of reconciling catches and the state of stocks. yes, these quotas must be multiannual. in particular, as the atlantic coast association has asked the commission, in order to avoid erratic variations from one year to the next and to allow fishermen to have the minimum visibility without which no human or economic activity is possible. but these quotas must not be individual and transferable, otherwise we would be witnessing an irreversible concentration and extinction of marine life in most of our coastal regions. we are sticking to our current system of collective management of quotas by member states and professional fishermen's organisations. secondly, the new common fisheries policy must abandon the brutal, unfair, costly and ineffective system of authoritarian reductions in fleet capacity. the commission proposes to tighten up existing fleet renewal arrangements. we are totally against it. the commission has not, because it supported the excessive construction of factory trawlers in europe yesterday, been obliged today, by a kind of symmetry in error, to make impossible the indispensable modernisation of our small-scale fleet, the need for which is sadly demonstrated, in particular, by the tragic increase in accidents due to the ageing of the fleet off our atlantic coasts. the fleet must be managed with flexible and reversible instruments. in this connection, it is essential that aid for modernisation, and above all aid for the first installation, which concerns young people, should be maintained in the long term. thirdly, the new common fisheries policy must establish a sustainable management system which therefore integrates the skills, knowledge and expertise of professionals into the decision-making process. many recent examples, such as the anchovy and the cod, show that it is extremely dangerous to rely exclusively on biologists' estimates and models to justify decisions with particularly serious socioeconomic consequences. in an area where resource evaluation is extremely complex, no source of information should be deprived. i hope that these three concerns, which were strongly emphasized during the consultation process, will inspire the proposals for regulations which the commissioner will present to us shortly. the green paper is a long way off and a lot of work to be done. we ask the commissioner to propose a new common fisheries policy which is essentially forward-looking and no longer sadly palliative, because we believe that fisheries in all our maritime countries are at the heart of the development of coastal regions. we believe in the future of fishing. we would like to have a common fisheries policy which also believes in the future of fisheries.
mr president, we set ourselves a double objective: to guarantee fishing along our coasts while preserving the reproduction of fish. this dual objective is shared by all. we had to make a choice, as did the rapporteur: either change everything, at the risk of destabilising everything, or adapt what could be. the choice was made for the second alternative proposal, which i also prefer. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. these two choices are fundamental and i hope that parliament will endorse them. i would like to mention three of the necessary adjustments which must be undertaken. i remain convinced that it is preferable to make tacs and quotas the central element of the common fisheries policy, since they offer the most guarantees, especially if they are multiannual. the second adaptation is that if pops are still used, as they should be, they must be measured against the safety implications for seafarers. in my own region of brittany, in france, in 2001, 25 people died at sea. i imagine that in your regions, the situation is similar. it is considerable, it is almost inadmissible of course! i believe that we must strengthen maritime safety and enable our sailors to build new ships at all times. the fleet must not be allowed to age, as this increases the risks at sea. finally, the sanctions. a good rule requires that it be applied equally to all. sailors feel that even when two offences are the same, the penalties are different. i think the commission should pay particular attention to these three adjustments.

mr president, the common fisheries policy is one of the most sensitive european policies. it is characteristic of the gap between the general interests of a common policy, which is designed to control a dwindling resource while rationalising a traditional economic activity, and the development objectives of the outermost regions, for which fisheries represent one of the few sectors of activity that generates jobs in the medium and long term. the commission's green paper on the common fisheries policy paints a very bleak picture and i regret that, in general, it does not refer to fishing in the territorial waters of the outermost regions of the european union. the ideas it proposes, and especially the solutions it advocates, are clearly designed to meet the challenge of inland fishing and are not well suited to the outermost regions. these regions have fought to ensure that their differences are respected under article 299 (2) of the treaty of amsterdam and that their specificities are finally taken into account by each of the european union's policies and, a fortiori, by the common fisheries policy. the size of this sector in the outermost regions, its characteristics and, above all, its impact on the whole of european fishing activity should, however, make it all the more justified to envisage concrete measures adapted to the outermost regions, in particular in terms of resource and fleet quotas, support for coastal fishing and aquaculture and public investment ceilings, on which the growth of this sector in these regions depends. an adequate rate would enable them to develop and modernise their fleet and also to ensure greater coherence in the measures proposed by the european commission by reconciling the objectives of financial support for enterprises in writing. - we cannot endorse either the rapporteur's approach or that of the commission. both, under the guise of simplifying and updating existing community legislation on the award of public contracts (the february 1998 directives), create a single european market based on liberal criteria. we cannot accept that the lowest price should be favoured in public procurement and that social, territorial and environmental criteria should be relegated to the background. this approach is a prisoner of the dogma of liberalism. it does not meet the expectations of users or employees, because it is mainly at the expense of quality, safety and employment. the question of the thresholds proposed by the commission above which a public contract would be open to community regulation may seem rather ridiculous. raising them by 50% offers no alternative but only temporarily pushes back the time when private trusts will be able to get their hands on the €1 trillion generated annually by public procurement across the european union (or 14% of gdp). we need a different logic, a logic of public services provided by public companies and controlled by citizens. that is why we voted against the zappalà report.
in writing. - the major political obstacle to the adoption of this report concerns the thresholds for the application of european standards which are of major economic importance for public works undertakings, for the environment, for public finances, for the quality of infrastructure. the political issue is simple: from what value, in millions of euros, should a public contract be subject to community procedures? two opposing theses were therefore put forward: the advocates of high thresholds indicated that this would avoid administrative costs and burdensome bureaucratic procedures for markets that would not attract international competition anyway. they would therefore not allow for an increase in crossborder operations in the field of public procurement. at the same time, however, the local authorities have to bear extremely high costs of tendering. i am, however, in favour of maintaining the thresholds as proposed by the commission. the aim is to create a genuine european single market in this sector. in addition, the increases requested would deplete the directive of its impact and even its purpose. i believe that this increase would risk drastically reducing the number of markets which would actually be open to community competition. most contracts would be awarded according to national or regional procedures. that is why i abstained in the vote in plenary.
in writing. - the second zappalà report on procurement in the water, energy and transport sectors pursues the same objectives as the first zappalà report on procurement. the rapporteur, under the guise of simplifying and updating existing community legislation, wants to see the creation of a genuine liberalised european single market in the water, energy and transport sectors. the preferred criterion is price, to the detriment of social and territorial cohesion, equality and employment. the battle over thresholds and the battle for better consideration of social and environmental aspects is certainly important. we therefore voted in favour of the amendments which go in that direction. but we reject the basic logic of the rapporteur and the commission, namely that of liberalizing these sectors, because it is dangerous for users and for employees. on the contrary, while some governments are considering reversing their policy of liberalizing and privatising their public services, the approach of the rapporteur and the commission appears archaic and dogmatic. that is why we voted against the report.

- mr president, the european council stated at the tampere summit that the legal status of third country nationals should be brought closer to that of nationals of the member states in order to grant them a uniform set of rights as close as possible to those enjoyed by citizens of the european union. the commission proposal has set out in a balanced and very clear way the conditions for acquiring longterm resident status. it's a balanced offer. the criteria include the length of legal residence and sufficient income. furthermore, the person must not pose a threat to public order or national security. but i must say that i am very concerned about some of the amendments, because they go against the tampere objectives. article 7 of the commission proposal on the threat to public order is clear and it seems to me to be worrying and counterproductive to make an amalgamation between immigration and terrorism. on the other hand, we agree that language level is an indicator of a person's integration but in no case can it be considered a condition for obtaining resident status. why would you do that ? well, simply because it is not an objective and precise criterion: there is no causal link between a certain level of language - what level are we talking about? - and integration itself. i personally know people who have been living in my country for ten years and who, as everyone will tell you, are perfectly integrated, even though they still have some difficulties in french. finally, it seems to me dishonest to introduce the requirement of adequate housing as an additional condition to avoid giving status to third country nationals legally residing in the european union. unfortunately, many of these people do not have adequate housing, and yet they are not second-class citizens. everyone wants a decent home. it is essential to create a welcoming society and to recognise that integration is a two-way process requiring adaptation both by the immigrant and by the society that welcomes him or her.
mr president, the two proposals for directives presented by the commission on the conditions of residence and movement of thirdcountry nationals within the european union seem to us to be out of step with the needs of the moment. they are the result of a mentality that we thought was outdated after the attacks of september 11th, and which included putting openness and uncontrolled traffic ahead of the safety of our fellow citizens. sadly, this dangerous attitude is still very much alive. as regards the conditions for the movement of third-country nationals, for example, the proposal for a directive abolishes the obligation to declare which is currently imposed on them, pursuant to article 22 of the schengen convention, when they move from one country of the union to another. member states retain the option of maintaining this obligation individually, but in a reduced form and with a longer reporting period. we think that the opposite should have been done. it would have been necessary to consider how to make this declaration of presence more operational and effective. it is not unknown to anyone here that after 11 september europe was accused of being too easy a base for terrorists because its internal borders are too porous. the commission has already proposed a number of measures to improve the quality of the water. we are also opposed to the introduction of a specific six-month travel authorization which is not provided for in the treaty and which would distort the spirit of the treaty, since, according to him, the common visa policy only covers visas of less than three months. finally, as regards the other proposal for a directive on longterm residents who are nationals of third countries, we believe that the community has no competence to establish, even unanimously, a common statute containing unified principles. article 63 tec only provides that the council will take 'measures' relating to immigration policy in the field of entry and residence conditions, but this cannot be, must not be, a complete statute which would impose a centralised, uniform and rigid solution on all member states. in particular, we do not think it appropriate to give third country nationals, who are entitled to this alleged status, rights which eliminate the differences with national citizens and an almost automatic right of residence in the other member states. those of our colleagues who think that we are here primarily to defend the interests of our respective peoples will vote against these two projects.

- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we naturally welcome the proposal for a council directive which is in line with the treaty of amsterdam and the tampere conclusions, which stressed the need to finally put in place a policy for the integration of third country nationals. however, we could not support this report, because we regret that the proposal only sets out the conditions under which third country nationals can stay and that it does not in any way create a genuine european status for third country nationals comparable to that of union citizens. in the same way, family members should enjoy the same rights as the person they are joining. the right to family life, as it is presented here, is an internationally recognized right which violates certain fundamental rights. if the right to vote has been partially adopted in principle, the conditions of application are not mentioned. political rights are an integral part of any integration policy. fundamental rights are universal and if this universality of rights is to apply without exception, it should also apply to all, whether they are citizens of the union or not. as regards the criteria for assessing resources and stability, would it not be better to give all residents access to the labour market, rather than restrict some to exclusion? in addition, no grounds should be found for excluding students or persons authorized to stay under a subsidiary form of protection from the scope of the proposal. moreover, the concepts of public policy and security, which are grounds for exclusion from the permanent statutes, require a common definition beforehand. however, these concepts are now left to the discretion of the states or the competent authorities, which reveals serious discriminatory practices, particularly in relation to third-country nationals. finally, as regards the procedure, the examination requires a period of six months, which is far too long. in the event of a rejection of the application, a time limit for appeal should be provided for - a time limit with a suspensive effect allowing the blocking of any expulsion in the name of the right of defence - which does not exist. finally, the directive does not concern the millions of third country nationals who are irregular nationals, but for whom a european political solution is urgently needed. the union must therefore assume its responsibilities. in conclusion, this report does not allow for equality between citizens of the union and citizens of third countries. there is no european longterm resident status. we must not therefore endorse such a political approach.
in writing. - we voted against the ludford report, which supports the commission's proposal to introduce a unified status for thirdcountry nationals legally resident for more than five years in one of the countries of the union. we think this is a bad idea in itself, because it will standardize, freeze the existing system and deprive each member state of any room for manoeuvre in an area - the presence of longterm foreign residents on its territory - which must remain primarily a matter for national sovereignty. secondly, this proposal cannot be given a legal basis without distorting the meaning of article 63 (3) and (4) tec, which provides only for 'measures' concerning residence, and not for a 'status' in the full sense of the term. it is true, however, that if the treaty of amsterdam had not been ratified, the loopholes exploited by the commission today would not exist. finally, it is once again clear that in practice the commission is using this idea of status as a lever to give third country nationals with long-term residence (including refugees, for that matter) rights virtually equal to those of national citizens. article 12 of the proposed directive lists the areas where equal treatment would be a requirement, that is to say almost all, except for the right to vote. this systematic equality is not justified: while it is clear that foreigners are entitled to the benefits for which they have paid contributions, the granting of those financed by taxation must be a matter of the free choice of each nation. we wonder whether this unbridled search for indifference is not one of the root causes of the disaffection felt today in our countries towards citizenship.
in writing. - we are in favour of full equality of rights, including political rights, for all those who live and work in the european union, whether they are citizens of a member state or nationals of third countries. the proposal for a council directive has a completely different objective, namely to increase the mobility and flexibility of immigrant labour within the european union. it would nevertheless bring some improvements - which we voted for - to the status of third country nationals residing in the european union. however, even these few improvements, it intends to limit them to longterm residents only, which we cannot approve. we cannot even approve most of the amendments of parliament which restrict the original text even further and have no other purpose than to flatter nationalist, sovereigntist or xenophobic prejudices. we are not voting against the text because of some improvements for certain third country nationals living and working in the european union. but we refuse to endorse the many restrictions it contains. we therefore abstained on the whole, while rejecting those amendments - the majority - which would make the original text even worse.

larger scale and must be a lever in the fight against racism and xenophobia. we're reassured now, the baroness is relieved. the report is therefore presented as a statement of duties. duties reserved, of course, exclusively for european populations. thus, third-country nationals who have resided in a country of the union for more than five years acquire de facto long-term resident status. the administration has limited competence to issue this residence permit. it is valid for 10 years and may be renewed automatically (articles 8 and 9 of the directive). once granted, member states can withdraw it only under very limited and controlled conditions. the legal certainty must be "maximum" for the holder. he can thus be absent for more than two years without losing his longterm resident status. the host state is obliged to grant these third-country nationals and their families, in the context of the right to family reunification, the same rights as those granted to nationals, whether in the field of education, vocational training, social protection, social aids, taxation, etc. they may also benefit from additional social benefits, such as economic or cultural benefits, in order to maximise their integration. to complete the loop, obtaining this status must be able to constitute the first step towards obtaining the nationality of the member state in which they reside. this is in origin, religion, etc. we look forward to the baroness's hastening to welcome on her lands the few thousand refugees from sangatte who are eager to settle in england. home, sweet home!
in writing. - the commission's proposal on the movement of third-country nationals to the countries of the union for stays of less than three months not only harmonises the conditions but also reduces certain controls in the name of 'freedom'. this is the case, for example, with the 'declaration of presence' of foreigners provided for by the schengen convention, which i mentioned yesterday in the debate. even if this reporting obligation was not properly applied, it seems to me that the urgency was rather to strengthen it, not to weaken it. in another area, the commission is also continuing its previous initiative by proposing the introduction of a 'specific travel authorisation' issued by one member state on behalf of all the others, to facilitate the movement of third-country nationals for a period of less than six months. this reform well illustrates the subversive technique of leaning on a small edge to lift a large lid. today, residencies of more than three months are subject to national visas under the sovereignty of each state. the 'travel authorization' proposed by the commission would override this arrangement. to justify this derogation, it invokes, on page 9 of the explanatory statement, the case of certain foreigners who would need to move for six months within the union as 'beneficiaries of services', for example 'tourists' or 'tourists', or even 'musicians', as commissioner vitorino added during the debate. this is a rather light pretext: tourists who spend six months in a row in the union are not very numerous and do not justify the development of a specific directive. the commission's interest lies elsewhere: it is a question of destroying the coherence of a system based on national sovereignty in order to introduce a different kind of mechanism with a supranational purpose. this dogmatic exercise will not bring any more to today's priority, the control of migration flows and security. but it may actually damage it, causing it to be faulty and incoherent.
in writing. - we voted for this report for the sole reason that a possible rejection of the text by the european parliament should not be used as a pretext for further reducing emergency aid following natural disasters in poor countries, which is already shamefully low. the report, however, conceals the appalling lack of resources by denouncing only the problems of coordination. and, far beyond that, the report does not mention the fact that if natural disasters have such dramatic consequences in poor countries, if these countries are totally unable to cope with any of their consequences, it is because they do not have the material and human resources, hospitals, doctors or transport, they are impoverished by the past and present of plunder by the capitalist groups of the great powers. to speak of "lack of international assistance" is scandalous when it comes to great powers who are content with symbolic gestures when it comes to helping a poor country in the face of a natural disaster, but who also spend astronomical sums to drown a poor country like afghanistan (and many others before it) under bombs.
in writing. - the von wogau report on 'comitology' in the context of financial services - that is to say, on the implementation by the commission of implementing measures in this field - raises a number of very interesting questions, without always providing the right answer in our view. the starting point of the discussion is the current wording of article 202 of the tec, which entrusts the council, and it alone, with the task of delegating implementing powers to the commission, something which the european parliament disputes: it believes that in view of the recent extension of its co-decision power, it should now not only co-decide on the rules but also on implementing measures. in the von wogau report, the european parliament has put forward some excellent ideas, such as the systematic insertion in legislative acts of a 'sunset clause' whereby, after four years, any delegation of powers to the commission to take implementing measures would be suspended so that its appropriateness could be reviewed. the european parliament, on the other hand, is out of its proper role when it wants to check all the implementing measures, and even 'participate as an observer in the meetings of the securities committee'. the council has traditionally had a "double-hat" role, executive and legislative. it is because of its executive role that article 202 confers on it a special role in the establishment of implementing measures. the same cannot be said of the european parliament, which has only a 'legislative' role under the treaties and should therefore not interfere in everything. nevertheless, there is clearly a problem of commission control in the establishment of implementing measures. the european parliament's reaction may not be entirely appropriate, but it is triggered by a real cause. the next intergovernmental conference should respond by strengthening the role of the council in the executive committees and by strengthening the democratic control exercised over these committees: control by the european parliament over the commission representatives, perhaps, but also control by sectoral assemblies composed of national parliamentarians, which would be exercised over the council representatives.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the tragic situation in palestine illustrates two political truths which are bitter only to the utopian. first, each nation necessarily aspires to sovereignty, that is to say to the complete disposal of its own territory in which it can organize itself in accordance with its own genius. secondly, it is not the borders that create conflict, but the absence of secure and recognized borders. it's not the division of nations that creates war, it's their confusion. all over the world, multiethnic and multicultural societies have failed in a bloody way, and yet here we find many utopians who would like to turn our european societies into such experimental fields. i very much admire mr cohn-bendit's realism on the middle east, which is in total contradiction to the whims of his friends and his own, for example on the situation in france. the dramatic but partial events - the bloody bombings, the arms trade, the mutual accusations of murder, terrorism, the repeated failures of truces, the unacceptable destruction - are sad effects, which must not be confused with the root causes of the situation. the basic problem is that there will be no peace unless the israelis and the palestinians have a territory with recognized borders and within that territory the possibility of governing themselves freely, without threats, without interference. the state of israel now controls three quarters of the former british mandate of palestine. he must admit that the palestinians must and can live free, in peace, on the last quarter. as sensitive as some places are to the jewish soul and to the souls of other believers, which have a great resonance in religious history, the colonization of the territories occupied since 1967 must be stopped. we must respect the resolutions of the united nations security council and also put an end to a military occupation which has lasted for almost 35 years and which is an absolute record in history. israel is entitled to serious guarantees in return for this withdrawal. these guarantees can be given in the framework of the united nations, and especially by the united states of america. they must be more serious than those which failed to prevent the 1967 conflict. but this isn't 1967. so let israel have the courage to dominate its victories, to withdraw from the occupied territories. only then can peace return to the middle east.

commission. – i realise, not without relief, that i am not the commissioner responsible either for taxation or for monetary union, but merely the commissioner for humble competition policy which, nevertheless, has a role to play and tries to play it vigorously – with the support of parliament, which is apparent once again today. on competition proper, why not be even more liberal and refrain from applying sector-specific rules? well, we have looked into this and a detailed analysis has brought us to the following conclusion. if we did not have specific rules for this industry competition-wise, the industry would fall under the application of the block-exemption regulation on vertical restrictions. that would have two main drawbacks. it would allow the industry to use very similar distribution agreements to those permitted at present, on which our evaluation report was pretty negative. also applying the general regime would not be a satisfactory means of improving competition on the after-sales market. independent repairers could be foreclosed from the market as a result. this is clearly something which could not be accepted. furthermore, all motor vehicles would most likely continue to be distributed through the same type of selective and exclusive distribution systems if no new regulatory regime was introduced. last, but not least, the general regime does not offer provisions which are crucial in the car sector to ensure benefits for the consumer. this is the case with the so-called availability clause, which allows, for instance, a british consumer to buy a right-hand-drive car in a left-hand-drive country. so, although we are in principle against sector-specific rules, as you have seen with the telecom package with my colleague, mr liikanen, we have moved some way towards the adoption of general competition rules. but here the particular nature of the situation has led us to firmly believe that a sector-specific rule would be more appropriate. as for supermarkets, for example, i can only say that, during the lengthy consultation process undertaken by the commission, no supermarket or association speaking on its behalf directly expressed a desire to sell cars on a regular basis. on the other hand, it would not be true to suggest that the draft regulation adopted today gives no business opportunities to supermarkets. a supermarket could become a mono- or multi-brand sales dealer if it satisfied the criteria laid down by the manufacturer. similarly, it may act as an intermediary for consumers. finally, on the two issues which do not relate to competition but have a bearing on prices, tax and the euro, i will not go beyond the answer i gave on the issue of the uk, cars and the euro. as for taxation, the honourable member underlined that this is a national responsibility and it is tempting, but perhaps not entirely consistent, to argue that this is to be jealously guarded as a national prerogative and commission. – regulation 1408/71 and regulation 574/72 protect the social security rights of workers by coordinating the different national social security systems of member states. there are two main rights that workers have through these regulations. firstly they have the right to unemployment benefit; secondly, to look for employment in another member state and to continue to receive unemployment benefit for a maximum period of three months. however, this regulation applies to workers who are community nationals. in 1997 the commission presented a proposal to the council to extend the scope of this regulation to workers who are third-country nationals. the same extension had been included in the larger frame of the commission proposal of 1998 to modernise and simplify regulation 1408/71. there were many discussions over many years. there was a very complicated discussion in the council of ministers. there were many disagreements between the member states. the main obstacles to progress in this regard had been the lack of agreement on the legal base. it is not a legalistic or technical problem, it is a political one. but the difference in the legal base concerned first the commission's proposal, which was based on the implementation of articles 42 and 308, and certain member states which considered that the basis of this proposal could be article 63. the political difference is that under the last article there are some member states that have the right to opt out of the regulation. under the belgian presidency the council of 3 december 2001 unanimously agreed that the basis which must be used is article 63. so the commission will very shortly present a new proposal to extend regulation 1408/71 to third-country nationals using this new basis of article 63. as far as the substance is concerned, i must highlight the commission's agreement with your concept.
- just a comment: these workers are brought to the national territories by their employers, their bosses. they're good at paying taxes, they're good at sweating profits, but they're not good at collecting the bare minimum of what they're entitled to. this is completely unusual.
the agenda calls for the report (a5-0466/2001) by mrs kauppi, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on administrative cooperation in the field of value added tax (com (2001) 294 - c5-0269/2001 - 2001/0133 (cod)) and on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending council directive 77/799/eec on mutual assistance by the competent authorities of the member states in the field of direct and indirect taxation (com (2001) 294 - c5-0270/2001 - 2001/0134 (cod)).
commission. – may i begin by saying that it gives me a great deal of pleasure to be able to discuss with parliament today a proposal for a regulation to strengthen administrative cooperation between member states in order to enhance vat control. i thank mrs kauppi very much for her report. it is extremely constructive. i can only echo what was said by mr karas who referred to mrs kauppi as his "young and effective colleague". she is not my colleague but i should like to echo the appreciative words of mr karas. mrs kauppi, along with other members of parliament, spoke about the legal basis of this proposal. it is about administrative cooperation. it is not about changing the vat regime. i wish the commission could do that. we have wanted to do so for many years but we are not able to do so. but no, it is about administrative cooperation. it is not designed to change in any way the obligations of taxpayers or the rules governing the application of that legislation, but rather to gear administrative cooperation to the challenges of the internal market. that is why the commission is submitting this proposal under article 95 of the treaty. in taking that article as the legal basis the commission is consistent with its proposal for regulation no 218/92 as well as with its proposal to modify the recovery directive. the commission is correct in choosing article 95 as the basis of this proposal. as mr garcía-margallo y marfil said quite clearly, it gives parliament codecision and that is what many members of this parliament want. i take this opportunity to thank mr garcía-margallo y marfil for the kind words he uttered in my direction. i add to that that the commission is extremely pleased that we have settled the matter of the so-called lamfalussy proposal and that we can now continue with the work ahead. more to the point, the commission is of the opinion that this proposal is an important element of the new vat strategy to improve the operation of the vat system within the context of the internal market. it also constitutes a response to the council calling on the commission to present proposals for fighting vat fraud. the intra-community market is today seriously affected by organised vat fraud, where professional fraudsters abuse the exemption mechanism of the vat system. tackling that kind of fraud requires rapid and efficient cooperation between the tax administrations of the different member states. but at present the legal framework is too weak to support really effective cooperation, essentially because it is vague, over-centralised and the exchange of information is not sufficiently intensive. in addition, cooperation is complicated owing to the existence of two legal instruments in this area with different scopes and different rules. this proposal sets up one single legal framework merging, for vat purposes, the regulation and the directive, and modifies the current arrangements in three ways: firstly, the proposal lays down clear and binding rules governing administrative cooperation between member states, for example, for the presence of foreign officials during controls, or for organising multilateral controls; secondly, the proposal devolves cooperation and provides for more direct contacts between tax inspectors of different member states. this is also a point which mrs kauppi drew to our attention. she said that when french and spanish controllers – for example – in a border area want to communicate, at the moment this communication has to pass via madrid and paris. it is obvious that direct communication between inspection staff will make cooperation faster and more effective. thirdly, the proposal aims to intensify the exchange of information between tax administrations in order to combat fraud more effectively. i am very pleased that this proposal gets the support of all speakers this evening, except for mrs doyle, whom i can no longer convince, since she is no longer here. the commission is extremely pleased with this support. i would therefore like to particularly welcome the positive contribution of the rapporteur, mrs. kauppi. but given the fact that examination of this proposal is ongoing in the council, and given the commission’s strong desire to address this issue in a timely manner, i believe that the most appropriate course of action at this time is for the commission not to formally accept the amendments put forward by parliament, but to endeavour to take them on board, as much as possible, during the negotiations in the council. however i fear it will not be possible to take some of these amendments fully into account. in particular, as regards the issue of electronic communication, i would like to stress that much of the information covered by this regulation is not available in electronic format, and therefore, in practice, cannot be exchanged by electronic means. as regards the translations, i share the argument according to which member states should strive as far as possible to waive a translation. but the commission takes the view that the arrangements under which member states should waive translations should be determined in an implementing regulation, binding for all member states, and not individually by each member state. finally, as concerns data protection, the commission takes the view that if directive 95/46/ec is fully applied, fraudsters would be informed that they are under suspicion, and consequently it is to be expected that they would transfer their fraudulent activity and would dispose of the evidence of fraud. that would seriously hamper the fight against vat fraud. i am personally confident that an agreement between the european parliament, the council and the commission will be achieved on these issues. the council has already started to discuss the proposal in detail. it will do its best to achieve an agreement as soon as possible, and we are making good headway. but your support of the proposal is important to achieve that much desired result. i would therefore recommend this proposal most warmly for parliament's approval. i thank parliament for its most constructive intervention.
commissioner, thank you very much. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.

environmentalists and health protectors alike want to contribute to sustainable development, but the goals are the same for all. the public health obligation therefore does not allow for any relaxation of the rules: application of the precautionary principle, the principle of zero tolerance, compliance with the ban on feeding animal meal to animals, destruction of existing stocks of such meal. i recognize that our british colleagues have some difficulties and that they want to find alternative methods to the destruction of whole herds, but all this must not allow us to relax the rigor we want in this monitoring of the bse crisis. i would like to conclude, madam president, by recalling that in this area it is essential that the commission can put in place a number of sanctions and that it ensures the necessary controls with the food and veterinary office. the application of community legislation must be more systematic and must be applied in the same way in all member states. there must be a follow-up to the sanctions, we must be able to guarantee the greatest possible security to consumers so that our citizens can regain confidence in their farmers and their politicians.

- ladies and gentlemen, the first thing we must bear in mind as we open this useful and necessary debate on the follow-up to the bse crisis is the dismay, the distress, the suffering and the anger of the farmers, who are suffering in their markets, in their prices and in their morale in the face of a real earthquake which has upset their world, ruined long-term efforts at selection, good practices where 99% of clinical cases have occurred, measures, which were adopted late and applied effectively even later, are now bearing fruit. the number of bse cases has been steadily declining by 40% a year, falling to below 1000 last year from 36,000 in 1992. in france, where the epidemic is more recent and where systematic testing for the past 18 months initially seemed to increase the number of cases, the decrease has been significant since the end of 2000. other countries with a lower prevalence rate also appear to be in control. now, as you know, it is japan's turn to be infected by the mr president, the european arrest warrant you are proposing is a political, legal and procedural fraud. the framework decision is already prepared and drafted. all this was endorsed at the laeken summit on 14 december 2001. the consultation of our parliament is therefore completely illusory, useless and i would even say almost insulting. the commission has also been asked to provide a report on the implementation of the new financial perspective. in reality, the scope of the future arrest warrant has expanded to thirty-two counts, which means two things. the first is that the aim is to move from an interstate system of extradition, which guarantees individual freedoms, to a single judicial system, without the involvement of the representatives of the peoples. the second is that under the pretext of fighting terrorism, this european mandate will be an opportunity to crack down on the crimes of opinion which are explicitly listed in the list in question. tomorrow, for example, for criticism of immigration policy that will displease a partisan judge, or for calling for national preference in his country, or for expressing an opinion that is considered politically or historically incorrect, a patriot may be torn from his country, arrested, translated into another whose language or law he knows neither. what you are preparing is not the europe of security, which requires many other measures, but the europe of uniformity, of power systems and of ready thinking. big brother is watching you.
acting president of the council. - mr president, after hearing all the speeches, the council presidency would like to share the feeling of satisfaction that a major decision is being taken today, namely the adoption of these two watson reports. i agree with those who have said that this is a great day. i think it's a big step forward in building that space of security, justice and freedom. although it has been said that we could have done it sooner, the reality is that, at least, we are on the way to achieving it. at the same time, mr president, i would also like to say that, in the face of the comments of some members of parliament who have expressed doubts that the implementation of these decisions could endanger fundamental rights, human rights, the concept that all european countries share of the primacy of the rule of law, i would like to say that precisely this primacy and the safeguarding of these fundamental values and human rights are the first considerations that the council and the member states take into account when implementing these anti-terrorist measures. we are convinced - and i believe parliament is too - that the best way to combat the scourge of terrorism is precisely to do so with our own values and the law in hand. and to do so firmly, precisely to safeguard that system of values which terrorism wants to ignore. i therefore want to give every guarantee on behalf of the council that the rights of citizens will never be infringed in the implementation of the decisions taken by the council and supported by parliament in the two watson reports.
commission. - mr president, mr council representative, ladies and gentlemen, the commission is pleased to be able to take part today in this debate, which we consider to be politically important for the future of the area of freedom, security and justice. we have already discussed on several occasions the legal configuration of the european arrest warrant and the framework decision on measures to combat terrorism following the watson report, which was approved by this parliament on 5 september. i would remind you that the commission was already working on these issues more than a year ago, following the request of the tampere european council, and i believe that parliament can attest that the commission has attached the necessary importance to this subject in order to conclude the negotiations within the deadlines set by the extraordinary european council after the events of 11 september. i would like to thank the belgian presidency once again for the efforts it has made to achieve the results we are discussing today. the two texts before you are an important step towards improving the effective capacity of the european union and the member states to combat organised crime in general and terrorism in particular. as we wished, the european arrest warrant procedure will replace extradition in the union as a whole, as requested by the tampere council in october 1999, and reiterated by the extraordinary european council in september 2001. i would also like to stress that the tampere council was not only in favour of using the european arrest warrant in the fight against terrorism, but also of making the european arrest warrant an instrument to replace the entire extradition procedure between member states. the requirement of double criminality - that the surrender of the accused person is possible only if the acts for which the warrant has been issued also constitute an offence in the member state where the arrest warrant is to be executed - is abolished for 32 offences, provided that they are punishable in the member state which issued the warrant by at least three years' imprisonment. this list covers the most serious crime and most of it is taken from the europol convention, which has been ratified by all the member states, which means that it has been submitted to the democratic vote of the national parliaments of the 15 member states. the european arrest warrant will enable the magistrates of europe to work directly together in full independence and with full respect for fundamental rights. we have eliminated the administrative part of extradition, we have eliminated the politicization of the extradition procedure, we have put the procedure entirely under the authority of the magistrates, the judges of the member states, and i believe that this is an essential element in strengthening the area of freedom, security and justice. the text will harmonise the definition of terrorist offences at member state level. the text defines terrorist offences in terms of both the material elements (attacks on the life or physical integrity of persons, kidnappings, taking of hostages, massive destruction of public or private facilities, seizure of aircraft, etc.) and the aim pursued (intimidation of a population, destabilisation of the structures of a country or an international organisation, compulsion of the public authorities to carry out or refrain from carrying out an act). it also establishes a definition of a terrorist group, based on the concept of a criminal organisation established by the joint action of 21 december 1998, and creates specific offences for the leadership of the group and for participation in a terrorist group. in addition, a system to facilitate the cooperation of repentant terrorists with the police and judicial authorities is provided for through a mechanism for the mitigation of punishment. i would like to stress that this definition is particularly important at a time when the european union must have a voice, a single voice, in the negotiations which are under way at the united nations in new york for the adoption of an international convention on terrorism on a global scale. but we have intended to clarify the text, following several speeches by members of the european parliament. i hope you will be pleased to see your views reflected in the text adopted by the council. this is particularly the case with trade union movements and anti-globalisation demonstrations. the framework decision should not, under any circumstances, be used to impugn them, even in the event of occasional overruns. it would therefore be purely demagogic to claim that the purpose of this instrument is to punish such demonstrations. everything is now quite clear and legally established. in addition, a recital and a council statement will confirm that the framework decision cannot apply to the conduct of those who act with the aim of preserving or restoring democratic values. as regards respect for fundamental rights, a point on which this house and the commission are particularly vigilant, i think that both texts are satisfactory. as regards the arrest warrant, it is recalled on several occasions, in particular in article 1, that in the missions and in the execution of the european arrest warrant, member states and judicial authorities must at all times ensure strict compliance with the principles recognised by article 6 of the treaty and reflected in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. we have also insisted that it is impossible to expel or extradite a person to a state where there is a serious risk that he will be subjected to the death penalty, torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
the president-in-office of the council. - mr president, the spanish presidency of the european union is very pleased to be here in this chamber to report on the current state of preparations for the international conference on financing for development, which is scheduled to take place in monterrey, mexico, from 18 to 22 march. in recent months the monterrey conference has come to occupy a prominent place in the so-called development agenda, especially after the attacks of 11 september and the realization that the problems of development in a globalised world require our attention in a comprehensive, immediate and urgent way. this general interest justifies the efforts made by all those attending the fourth meeting of the preparatory committee for the conference, which has just been held in new york and which has concluded with the adoption of a text to be submitted for approval to the heads of state and government who are scheduled to attend the monterrey summit. it is not by chance that this document, which i shall briefly discuss later, is entitled 'the monterrey consensus'. since the holding of the financing for development conference in monterrey is undoubtedly one of the most important events in cooperation during the six months of our presidency, spain wishes to give this event a special priority and this priority is reflected in the level of official representation. i am referring to the fact that the spanish prime minister, who is president of the european council, will be leading the community delegation to the monterrey summit. the preparation of the conference, mr president, has been extremely complex, given its all-embracing nature and the multiplicity of actors involved in the deliberations. i would like to take this opportunity to thank the important effort made by the previous presidencies of the union throughout this process, since it has been a development that has brought us to the present moment. this continued and joint effort now enables the european union to play its rightful leading role in monterrey as the world's largest donor of official development aid. before i mention the characteristics of the text adopted in new york, let me put the monterrey conference in its proper context, mr president, because it is not an isolated process but part of the process initiated by the millennium declaration, adopted by the united nations general assembly in september 2000, in favour of sustainable development and the fight against poverty in the world. we are therefore faced with three independent but closely related processes. firstly, the trade area in the framework of the commitments adopted at the world trade organization conference in doha. secondly, everything that concerns the mobilization of financial resources, the united nations conference on financing for development and, thirdly, the environment, the conference on sustainable development which is scheduled to take place, precisely this year, in september in johannesburg. i shall now briefly refer to the characteristics of the monterrey document, the famous monterrey consensus which i mentioned earlier. this final text, adopted ad referendum, since a formal closing session could not be held in new york, consists of 73 numbered paragraphs and reflects the spirit of consensus in which it was drafted. by not having open elements, since everything is agreed, we hope that the heads of state and government will be able to have a genuine, frank and open political dialogue on the main issues affecting development and its current challenges. the agreement reached establishes that international development cooperation is based on a set of principles shared by donors and recipients, including, in particular, the concept of good governance at all levels, the existence of sound democratic institutions and respect for the rule of law, all in the spirit of partnership, in which developed countries undertake to take a series of measures to speed up the flow of financing to developing countries - with a number of conditions - and, through international cooperation, enable governments to create the internal conditions favourable to economic growth and social development. the developed countries also assume the obligation to promote trade in accordance with the agreements adopted within the world trade organization, which are widely regarded as the main engine of all economic activity. the developed countries, having also noted the decline in official development aid in recent years, are committed to increasing it. this increase in resources is a commitment which concerns all donors, including the united states and japan. the text adopted is in line with the laeken declaration. the role of the private sector as a driver of development and a source of resources is highlighted throughout the document. the need to increase resources to strengthen the institutional capacity of developing countries and the full implementation of the debt relief initiative for the heavily indebted poor countries is also highlighted. as regards the international financial architecture, the autonomy of the existing institutions and the mandate of their governing bodies is maintained and the process currently under way at the international monetary fund and the world bank is supported. at the same time, the principles of coordination, transparency and participation of developing countries in international financial institutions are emphasized. the conference's follow-up mechanisms were also the subject of intense debate, with various follow-up modalities finally agreed at the ecosoc spring meeting, with the bretton woods institutions and the world trade organisation, including also representatives of civil society and the private sector, and at the biennial high-level dialogue of the united nations general assembly. at the same time, within the united nations, the general secretariat is requested to support the full use of the existing mechanisms for coordination of the specialized agencies of the united nations and the preparation of an annual report on the efforts made in this field. the international monitoring conference is also involved, the details of which will be defined before 2005. this set of instruments and mechanisms is intended to ensure that the monterrey process continues to be on the agenda of the main international organisations and institutions, as well as in the forums of the united nations, its programmes and specialised bodies. i would not like to conclude, mr president, without mentioning some of the contributions made by the european union which are mentioned several times in the text. i think that the european parliament should be very conscious, and we should be proud of the firm position that the european union has taken throughout this monterrey process. i would like to list these contributions. firstly, the concept of partnership and the insistence on the need for sound economic policies, good governance and democratic principles, as well as the defence of human rights. at the same time, the european union has insisted on the involvement of civil society in the development process. secondly, i would like to emphasize the european union's position in favour of stressing the need for development to be sustainable and to integrate economic, social and environmental aspects, respecting in any case gender equality and having the fight against poverty as a fundamental objective. in this connection, the presidency regrets that it was not possible to include a specific reference to the innovative concept of global public goods, in the face of opposition, up to the last moment, from both the group of 77 and other donors, but hopes that, given its importance, discussions on its definition and financing will continue in the appropriate forums. thirdly, the european union wanted to emphasize the link between the effectiveness and efficiency of official development assistance and the implementation by the recipients of aid of appropriate policies in the political, economic and social fields. policies focused on helping those most in need, so that this official development assistance can be made the most of. the emphasis is not only on increasing the volume of resources but also on their effective use, with the fight against corruption also playing a prominent role and, moreover, the commitment to continue negotiations on the specific convention within the united nations on this subject. similarly, external debt relief has been linked to the effective use of these resources to achieve sustained economic growth and development that benefits the most disadvantaged sectors in each country participating in these instruments. the european union has naturally worked very actively with other major donors, such as the united states and japan, as well as with the group of 77, to reach a consensus formulation around the 0.7% of gdp development contribution target, which allows for the integration of different views, economic realities and sensitivities. i would like to stress that it is precisely because of this effort that the monterrey consensus has used terminology similar to that adopted at the laeken european council. fourthly, the european union has made efforts, which have been successful, to introduce specific references to multilateral cooperation in the text in the face of the new transnational challenges and threats posed by the financing of terrorism and organised crime. fifthly, the european union has also worked actively to introduce specific references to private banking and the importance of developing this sector in support of small and mediumsized enterprises in developing countries. finally, support measures to increase the institutional capacity of developing countries in trade matters should also be highlighted. in this connection, the presidency looks forward with great interest to the package of concrete measures being prepared by the relevant commission departments to increase the negotiating capacity of the developing countries in the commercial field. in short, after the fourth and final preparatory meeting, the presidency is reasonably optimistic about the forthcoming monterrey conference. despite the doubts that existed until the last moment, a final text was finally adopted on 27 january, almost two months before this important international meeting. the fact that it is the result of consensus - as i have already said - and that all the donors have been involved in it, makes the monterrey consensus a good platform for the future, because it creates the climate of confidence that this complex process requires and also now makes it easier for the round tables planned in monterrey to develop in a positive, constructive and non-confrontational atmosphere. the monterrey conference is a ground-breaking experience, tackling development and the fight against poverty from an all-embracing position, covering the different aspects and encouraging the participation of all actors. this overall vision gives the process as a whole an extraordinary complexity, which we must also tackle in a pragmatic and realistic way, through work whose main objective is the inclusion - and not the exclusion - of all those engaged in development cooperation tasks. we hope that the international campaign for the millennium development goals announced in article 62 of the document will also contribute to this. i can assure this parliament, mr president, that the presidency of the council remains firmly committed to this path and that the success of the conference remains our main objective, especially if we bear in mind that development cooperation policy must be one of the pillars on which the european union's external action is based, and must be in perfect harmony with other pillars such as the common foreign and security policy and the trade policy. in this respect, we are confident that the monterrey conference offers us a historic opportunity for the european union to project and transmit, together with the other participants in the conference, a clear message in defence of the values that are our own. we therefore consider that the defence of democracy, good governance, the strengthening of the institutional capacity of the countries receiving aid, the rule of law, peace and security and human rights are essential elements of all economic and social development. - mr president, we should welcome this international conference on financing for development, which is a major theme in the context of the reduction in aid to developing countries. for more than 20 years, the un has been reminding donor countries that they must devote 0.7% of their gnp to official development assistance, according to oecd standards, but only four countries have met this commitment. overall, aid is declining: the average is 0.2% today. the developing countries are suffering the full brunt of the gradual and structural deterioration of the terms of trade for basic commodities and are being sucked into the vicious cycle of paying back the often illegitimate debt and its interest. how can financial resources be mobilised for the human, economic and social development of their populations in these conditions? the hope is therefore in monterrey, unless the stakes are already high and the american positions prevail at this conference, as was the case in doha. following to the letter the liberal principles of development applied for twenty years by the international institutions and the european commission, the document presented, like the monterrey consensus, never calls into question neoliberal globalisation. yet, the incomes of people in developing countries have been steadily declining over the same period, proving the inefficiency and counterproductivity of such recipes. they fail, but we keep going. i do not know whether the monterrey pre-consensus, which does not propose ambitious objectives, concrete financial measures or a timetable, is definitive. if that were to be the case, and if the conference is limited to beautiful declarations which will never be followed by effects, i believe that it should be cancelled and the millions of euros devoted to its organization redistributed directly to the least developed countries. it would be a pity, because there is much to denounce and criticize, but also much to discuss and propose, concerning the mobilisation of aid, the cancellation of debt, the taxation of capital and the reform of the wto. the european union must seize this opportunity to push for ambitious targets with binding measures to halve poverty by 2015. it must reiterate the commitment made in gothenburg to ask the member states to increase their aid to 0.7%. the governments and parliaments which have accepted the principle of a tobin tax must make its case for the regulation of the stock markets and redistribution to the south. mr president, all the participants must make this summit a success. the european union is responsible.

in writing. - on the occasion of the olsson report on the follow-up to the bse crisis, i would like to stress the scandal of the judgment of the court of justice of 13 december last condemning france for not complying with the commission's request to lift the embargo on imports of british beef. the judgment refers to the higher powers of the commission, which itself refers to the primacy of freedom of movement. the question of principle is: what kind of europe do we want ? a europe in which each people has the right to exercise its fundamental choices, or a europe in which the commission decrees from above the so-called common good? we believe that each people should be sovereign. in the field of public health, for example, if one member country democratically chooses an option, the others must take note of it, even if they do not agree. it must be stressed that the french government has put itself in this impossible position by having the treaty of amsterdam ratified, which gives the community the powers it is now using against us. when will governments stop believing that the laws they sign have no consequences? when will they stop imagining that their actions will never catch up with them? when will they stop blinding themselves and blinding the citizens at the same time? after the judgment of 13 december, the commission will not hesitate to refer the matter to the court of justice for a penalty payment for each day of delay in the implementation of the decision, even though the french government says it will not comply. we will thus have to pay a ransom for the right to use - and again, provisionally - a fundamental competence which we ourselves foolishly abandoned with the amsterdam treaty. of course, this absurd situation will only last for the duration of the french election campaign. once it's over, our future government will probably rush to comply behind closed doors. what we need is a fundamental reform of the treaties to restore national sovereignty.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this own-initiative report. the european union must now take up its responsibilities in this matter. i voted in favour of a reform of the common agricultural policy to take account of the objective of food security. it is important to understand that this is not a matter of opposing farmers and environmentalists. the former want to produce with the highest possible quality, the latter want to regain confidence in products that are safe for their health. those who question this principle bear a heavy responsibility for the future. the precautionary principle must be applied systematically. the principle of 'zero tolerance' must always prevail in all matters relating to the protection of public health. the report considers that existing stocks of animal meal and food containing it should be destroyed and insists on a ban on feeding animal meal to ruminants. moreover, when a confirmed case of bse appears, the removal of the entire herd from the food chain always appears to be the solution with the maximum guarantees for the safety of our fellow citizens. alternative methods to the destruction of the entire herd could only be implemented once their effectiveness has been demonstrated and only if they offer the same level of safety. the greatest caution is required because of the current scientific uncertainties about the modes of contamination. that is why i believe that research into tse and other diseases and contaminations that are still unknown is needed and should be developed. i also think it is essential to ensure that the sanctions and measures taken against member states which do not comply with this legislation are monitored as closely as possible.
in writing. - the question of the french embargo on british beef, which i raised yesterday in the debate on the olsson report, is an example of the profoundly undemocratic nature of the current functioning of the european institutions. the court of justice has condemned france in law for a narrowly uniform conception of the single market, while recognising that, on the substance, it may have had valid reasons to protect its population against the uncertainties surrounding the traceability and labelling of british beef carcasses. the french government announced its intention not to implement the court's judgment. the commission has indicated its willingness to impose heavy fines on france as a result. we are therefore faced with a legal system which obliges member states either to refrain from implementing measures which they consider essential for the protection of the public health of their citizens or to buy the right to do so. the first responsible party for this situation is, of course, the french government, which, after happily transferring food safety to the community's sphere of competence by signing the treaty of amsterdam, discovers with a beautiful inconsistency a few months later the terrible consequences of a decision taken lightly. but more generally, the olsson report should have called into question a whole system that is an attack on democracy: the system that denies a people the right to take the measures it considers necessary to preserve its public health, even if other peoples think differently.
