- mr president, commissioner, from the very beginning europe - or what we call europe, that is to say the quasi-state which makes the law in brussels and a little here, which renders justice in luxembourg and which coins money in frankfurt - has been desperately seeking legitimacy, without which its very existence remains in doubt. the best proof of this lack of legitimacy is that the peoples of europe, when consulted, refer to the europe of the past as its work, as the danish and irish peoples have shown most recently and in succession. president napolitano's report, for which i am grateful, seeks to answer this existential question which sometimes strikes us (and which we could call 'democratic remorse') in a kind of hybrid parliamentarisation, a risky experiment in which national parliaments and the european parliament trade with each other in a kind of democratic no man's land as vague as it is opaque. legitimacy, mr president, commissioner, can only be conferred by the peoples themselves, directly consulted, and not come down as the holy spirit from the reflection of distinguished areopages such as our future convention and a fortiori its praesidium, the last avatar of what was once called enlightened despotism. the construction of europe must involve people and not institutions, otherwise what we will continue to call europe will remain an abstraction increasingly alien to the hearts of europeans, as the latest eurobarometer has shown and has just shown forcefully.
mr president, the napolitano report on relations between the european parliament and national parliaments starts from the correct observation that there is a serious imbalance in the european union between executive bodies with extended powers and parliamentary power which is still too weak. it is also rightly suggesting that there is a risk of a growing democratic deficit. so how do we correct this defect? although mr napolitano has shown a certain openness to the traditional positions of the european parliament, i do not think his report has yet reached the right balance when it calls for the extension of the powers of this assembly and confines the national parliaments to an indirect, often illusory role, drowning the whole thing under the vague term of 'parliamentarisation'. this imbalance is, in our view, due to an omission. nowhere in the report is it said that the european parliament is merely an assembly with powers of delegation and that only the national parliaments have full sovereignty. more importantly, nowhere is it said that this legal inequality is matched by an inequality of political legitimacy in the eyes of the citizens. we cannot carry out any useful reforms in the union by concealing such massive realities. that is why i have attached to the napolitano report a minority opinion stating that there will be no real democratization of the union without a revalorisation of national parliaments and without these acquiring direct power in the european decision-making process. i have detailed the means in a report to the sos democracy intergroup which we will be putting forward at the next convention.
- commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, mr pohjamo's own-initiative report, which i commend for its clarity, once again highlights the objectives to be met by regional policy and the structural funds. they are the result of the failure of previous programmes. how can we not agree with a number of proposals, which are declarations of intent, to make these programmes more effective? the rapporteur. - mr president, almost two years ago we adopted the charter of fundamental rights. the right to know and, therefore, to be able to read, write and count is one of them. the opportunity to learn to read and write should therefore be offered to all as a fundamental right, and parents, teachers, as well as men and women politicians, should recognize their obligation to ensure that this opportunity is taken by all, especially since when one cannot express oneself with words, one often does so with the fists, feeling excluded from school, from the company, or even from the family. but today this right to know is lacking, since on our continent 10 to 20% of the population of the union, and up to 30% of the population if the candidate countries are added, are considered illiterate: 45% in portugal, 35% in italy, 22% in ireland and great britain, 15% in germany and france and, if i add the candidate countries: 42% in slovenia and poland, 33% in hungary, 29% in bulgaria and 20% in lithuania. the problem of illiteracy is creating a growing divide between those who are privileged and in a situation of relative security and those who are disadvantaged and marginalized, who do not have access to employment and who therefore suffer from financial insecurity, psychological isolation and non-participation in social life. from an economic point of view, we all know that illiteracy also has consequences for the life of our enterprises and their modernization: it leads to an increase in the burden of accidents, an increase in the burden of wages and an increase in working hours, due to the need for additional supervision. the commission and our institutions have produced a number of documents, but they have also encountered a number of obstacles: the lack of reliable data, the lack of readability of some of the proposed programmes and the lack of integration of policies. it is therefore necessary to tackle this issue, which i consider to be a serious one, through integrated policies combining, madam commissioner, social objectives with cultural and educational objectives, and it is necessary to engage in political debate to raise awareness of this phenomenon. it is in this spirit that i ask the commission to submit to parliament and the council, as soon as possible, a green paper on illiteracy, with a timetable of concrete achievements, similar to the social agenda, and setting out precisely the measures to be taken at european level. in the same spirit, i ask the commission to draw up, in the framework of the employment guidelines, concrete indicators and benchmarks in the field of illiteracy, in close cooperation with the social partners. i also ask him to submit to us every year a written and numerical report on the achievement of the objectives of combating illiteracy and social exclusion. we must all be aware that this is a major issue for the development and harmony of our societies. we're not always aware of it; i would therefore also like to see a sort of european institute for literacy set up within the european centre for the development of vocational training in thessaloniki, not as an additional observatory, as my group has suggested, particularly in amendment no 5. finally, with regard to the amendments tabled recently, in particular by the green group, i would like to say that i am in favour of amendment green paper on illiteracy and ignorance of numbers), i would call for a vote against it, because i consider that the term 'green paper on illiteracy' obviously includes the question of numbers. in writing. - article 299 (2) of the treaty provides for the possibility of introducing special measures to preserve the vitality of activities in the outermost regions, where economic operators are in urgent need of a climate of legal certainty in order to maintain and develop themselves. the rum sector has a decisive impact on the economy of the french overseas departments, with 40 000 jobs linked to it. the 1995 council decision, which expires at the end of this year, authorizes france to apply a reduced rate of excise duty on 'traditional' rum produced in the french overseas departments. the current revision of the sugar mco and the removal of customs protection in 2003 led france to propose that this tax scheme be maintained beyond 2002, on the grounds that national and community measures would not be sufficient to enable these products from the french overseas departments to reach the same level of competitiveness as products from other regions. in order to maintain a traditional agricultural activity generating employment at all stages of the sugar-cane-rum sector, the current scheme ensures that the production of the french overseas departments is sent to the french market in a strictly limited and controlled manner, so that it can withstand the permanent growth in rum sales from third countries, which are not subject to the same production specifications. in order to ensure the survival of the sector, local rum producers are obliged to source local raw materials, which is a guarantee of quality, but which prevents, for example, guadeloupe rum from being produced from cane from third countries, but also from martinique cane. the dom rum is therefore obliged to participate in the dom rural development policy, which increases its constraints and production costs and places it in a disadvantaged position on the market compared to products from third countries. the derogating tax scheme is therefore intended exclusively to compensate for the obligation on domestic producers to contribute to the survival of the cane-sugar-rum sector. in writing. - the mpf delegation strongly supports the galileo project to set up a european satellite radio navigation system, parallel to the american gps system, autonomous in relation to the latter, but preserving "interoperability", i.e. non-contradiction and the possibility of working together. the galileo project is exemplary for three reasons. from the technical point of view, it will bring many positive benefits to all economic activities and will increase the general productivity of europe, which is in great need of it. from an institutional point of view, it is clear that european cooperation would be justified, as regards subsidiarity, and that the european space agency (esa) could provide the appropriate instrument. finally, from a political and strategic point of view, the galileo project will give europe autonomy vis-à-vis the united states, whereas, on the other hand, acceptance of the gps monopoly would imply a visible dependence, which would be worsened over time. despite these arguments, the final decision on the development of galileo was postponed from council to council, and the last one, held in laeken, did not break the rule. we're already almost out of bounds to make a useful decision. beyond the technical discussions on the precise modalities of involving private partners, the real reason for the delay lies in the reluctance of the united states, which has influenced some european countries. we come to the essential question: is the compulsory passage through community structures not a hindrance, because they are too rigid and the partners are not all in agreement? it is a brake today to launch the project, and it would be a brake tomorrow at every stage of its development, especially if we want to add military or "peacekeeping" applications. on this point, the european parliament is frankly going in the wrong direction by calling for an even greater communityisation of the project, and by considering, for example, in its resolution of 17 january last, that 'the esa, the fruit of cooperation between states, should in the long term join the european union'. the opposite is true: the principle of variable geometry must be applied to galileo, as it was for airbus and ariane, and a structure must be created which brings together the only states which are really interested. it's the best way to get this project out of the rut and moving forward.
in writing. - first of all, i would like to congratulate my colleague mr norbert glante on the substantive and negotiating work he has done on this highly strategic issue. i would also like to make a reminder about the galileo system. we often hear about this project without really knowing its future applications. it is a satellite-based radio navigation system which allows the user of a receiver to pick up signals from several satellites in order to determine his position in time and space. at present, there are two such systems: gps (united states) and glonass (russia). both of these systems were developed on a military basis, unlike galileo. the system will be used in a wide range of practical applications, including transport, fisheries, agriculture, telecommunications, oil exploration, defence and civil protection. for example, in land transport, it will make it possible to anticipate and better manage transport times, to guide vehicles automatically, to reduce traffic jams and the number of road accidents, etc. of course, we're not there yet. the galileo system is to be set up in four phases. we have completed the definition phase. the next step is to launch the development phase (2002-05). during this period, the technical and financial conditions for a rapid deployment of the infrastructure (2006-2007) will need to be established in order to be able to operate the system commercially in 2008. the european commission has made proposals for this second phase of galileo. our itre committee felt that what was being proposed in terms of structures was not appropriate. the model envisaged by the european commission would allow private companies to participate fully in the setting up of a joint venture. i agree with the rapporteur that a conflict of interest would arise if these companies were directly involved in the creation of such a company, since they would then have to respond to calls for tenders published by the same company. it therefore seems desirable that only the founding members, the european communities and the european space agency, should join this joint venture. the eib could also join in the future. in writing. - (de) i consider that the establishment of a european satellite navigation programme is, in general, useful and desirable. however, i voted against the glante report today because i cannot agree with the rapporteur in the solution he proposes. the economic success of galileo, which is competing with gps - which has held a monopoly position up to now - cannot be considered assured. i therefore believe that the financial risk should be borne equally by the public sector and the private sector. the rapporteur wishes to allow industry to enter the galileo funding system via a promotional company, rather than, as the commission had envisaged, involving it in the joint venture. on the one hand, the security policy concerns of the member states must be addressed and, on the other hand, it is necessary to prevent private commercial undertakings, which are part of the joint undertaking, from gaining competitive advantages in the tendering procedures for the construction and operation of galileo. i am afraid, however, that this purely optional solution of financial participation will ultimately lead to the public sector being the only one to provide the necessary investments for galileo. the industry will only take the train when galileo proves to be profitable and dividend-bearing. this would mean investing taxpayer money as venture capital before the high dividends of the private economy. that's not the use i'm looking for for taxpayer money. i am not convinced by the argument of conflict of interest in tenders either. in the municipalities, for example, it is common practice for municipal enterprises to compete with private commercial enterprises in tendering procedures, without this leading to unequal treatment. as far as the security policy argument is concerned, my concerns are of a very different nature. the commission and the council leave no doubt that they regard galileo as a central element of the independence of european defence policy. the european parliament could not bring itself to oppose a clear refusal to the military use of galileo. however, i am generally opposed to the military use of satellite navigation systems.
in writing. - the mpf delegation in the european parliament supported mr glante's report in order to support the implementation of the galileo programme, but they would like to express their disagreement with the mixed approach, both community and intergovernmental, which has been adopted. this project is a perfect example of one of the areas in which european cooperation is indispensable. the common interest is obvious and clearly defined. the galileo system is vital to ensure the independence of the member states of the european union in the strategic field of satellite positioning, since it will enable them to be free from the dependence on gps, which the americans control in a discretionary manner. on the other hand, the idea of running the project as a 'joint venture' of which the commission would be one of the two pillars, with the esa, risks paralysing its implementation, leading to disagreements, bureaucracy, delays, the impossibility of calling on outside expertise from the union... the only effective way seems to us to be through a specific esa programme, the mechanisms of which have proved to be flexible and effective. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the system.

in writing. - we live in a world of unprecedented global wealth. but this wealth has never been so poorly distributed. global inequality has reached unbearable and scandalous proportions. in 1960, the 20 percent of the world's population living in the richest countries had incomes 30 times greater than the 20 percent of the poorest. in 1995, their income was 82 times higher. at the other end of the scale, nearly three billion people live on less than two dollars a day. nearly 800 million people are hungry. in september 2001, in the "millennium declaration", the international community committed itself to halving poverty by 2015. the international community must now move from intention to action. europe must take the lead in this mobilization. the european union must take the initiative in making concrete proposals and setting a precise timetable for meeting this commitment at the world summit on sustainable development in monterrey in march and then in johannesburg in september. this offensive for development and against poverty must be organized around four ideas. first, to increase public aid to a considerable extent, reaching - finally! - the target of 0.7% of the wealth of the nordic countries set more than 30 years ago. an important step in this direction was taken by the last development council, which put this objective back on the agenda and asked the commission to set the deadlines with the member states. it is now necessary to set a precise and binding timetable. secondly, to provide new answers to the debt problem of the poor countries. this requires a greater number of debt conversion operations to the basic education and health sectors, as in the case of the "debt reduction and development contracts" (c2d) introduced by france. we must go beyond the hipc initiative ('highly indebted poor countries') and embark on a broad programme of debt cancellation for developing countries. we must begin to consider the conditions under which developing countries can access international financing, in accordance with the guidelines set out by the french prime minister. in writing. - the napolitano report reflects the traditional view of the european parliament on relations with national parliaments: the latter are locked, with consolation, into the secondary role of defenders of national interests. it is obvious that we are forgetting that the most vital democratic level is that of the nation, and that to want to go beyond it too much is to go beyond democracy. the european common good is not decreed from above, from a european democracy too weak to be anything but a screen for technocracy, but is defined by the peaceful dialogue between the interests and aspirations of the various national democracies. there is one point, however, on which the napolitano report claims to bring, in the words of the explanatory statement, 'a major innovation': it is the proposal for a kind of 'shared constituent power'. it is a question of removing from national parliaments the exclusive right to ratify the european treaties and thus to define the union's sovereign powers. this new 'constituent power' would be exercised jointly by the national parliaments and the european parliament, and, as paragraph 21 of the resolution states, by the commission and the governments of the member states, which is truly unprecedented from a democratic point of view. such a reform would be a serious step backwards: the power to revise the treaties (and a fortiori the 'constituent power') belongs to the people alone, and certainly not to national or european executives; the people may delegate this power in certain cases to assemblies elected for that purpose (such as the french parliament in the cases provided for in article 89 of the constitution), but the european parliament is not part of it, since no constituent power, or even only the power to revise the treaties, is provided for in the very specific powers of attribution that the people have conferred on it.
in writing. - first of all, i would like to thank both our rapporteur in the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, mr francesco musotto, and the whole of this committee for the quality of the work they have presented to us. the vote on this report is, first of all, my way of emphasizing that the principle of cohesion and, therefore, of solidarity and integration of the peoples and territories of the union is enshrined in the treaties and that as such it is essential to defend it. the report also stresses the diversity of the progress made and, above all, the persistence of intolerable regional disparities, which lead to the marginalisation of the regions lagging behind, in order to call on the states to support the efforts of regional economic convergence at european level. the authors of the report - who rightly believe that it is essential to ensure a maximum degree of coherence between the action taken at european level, under cohesion policy, and the internal development support policies in the member states - thus invite the member states to support, in accordance with the principles of additionality and subsidiarity, this effort at european level to achieve regional economic convergence, in particular through an appropriate investment policy. this effort is all the more vital as we have to meet the challenge of enlargement. cohesion must therefore be strengthened even further if we are to avoid any catastrophic increase in disparities and disparities between regions as a result of enlargement. finally, i will fully support amendment no 49, which stresses that 0.45% of community gdp is not enough for cohesion policy if we want to have an effective cohesion policy that is truly solidarity-based.
in writing. - i believe that there is a fundamental contradiction between the so-called cohesion policy and the neo-liberal orientations which prevail in europe; the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to take part in the negotiations on the future of the european union. this would involve the provision of funds to ensure the necessary transfers and equalisation, which would thus introduce positive distortions in relation to pure market phenomena and the blind pursuit of profitability. these funds could be fed by a unified tax on capital gains. the musotto report acknowledges this contradiction in its own way, for example by stressing 'the need to adapt competition policy and tax policy'. but he immediately felt the need to apologize by extolling the merits of a public-private partnership. the report's suggestions, although timid, are still in the right direction: by calling for a better assessment of the effects of enlargement; or by considering as a floor the proportion of 0.45% of community gdp devoted to cohesion policy. that is why i did not vote against this report, even though it falls far short of what a genuine policy of solidarity and equality at european level would require.
in writing. - one of the greatest achievements of europe in its construction was its decision in 1975 to establish the solidarity and cohesion needed to bring economic levels closer together between all the regions and all the constituent states of the european union. we can now say that the way in which we adapt our community cohesion policy to the prospects of enlargement will determine the qualitative path the union will take in the future. the european parliament has long maintained, and rightly so, that a proper policy of economic and social cohesion cannot be reduced to taking from some what we would like to redistribute to others. it is the analysis of real needs, amplified by the prospect of enlargement, which must be considered first, and not a fixed reference to the envelopes fixed in the past, for different situations. as the european commission points out, enlargement will increase the development gap between the central regions and the peripheral and outermost regions. i would therefore ask that the outermost regions continue to be given priority in regional and cohesion policy, through further progress in the implementation of article 299 (2) of the treaty. in addition, there is a need to adapt competition policy (in particular regional state aid) and fiscal policy in order to strengthen regional and cohesion policy, given that the structural funds alone are not sufficient to offset the handicaps and development delays accumulated over several decades. the adaptation of the common agricultural policy and rural development policy should also be considered in order to better coordinate the urban and rural dimensions of regional development. finally, i believe that there is an urgent need to set up a european observatory on territorial cohesion. the agenda calls for the report (a5-0010/2002) by mr koukiadis, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the commission report: progress in the transposition of council directive 93/104/ec of 23 november 1993 concerning certain aspects of the organisation of working time (the working time directive) (com (2000) 787 - c5-0147/2001 - 2001/2073 (cos)).
the commission. - mr president, i would like to congratulate mr koukiades on his excellent report on the implementation of the working time directive and to agree with the last speaker who noted that there are gaps in the working time directive. but gaps that are filled in over time. i would like to remind you that in the last two years we have had important developments, both in terms of the working hours of doctors and of those working in the fisheries sector, and recently in the directive on transport workers. the commission's report on the implementation of the working time directive gives an overview of the way in which the member states are implementing the directive. the commission was not obliged to publish it, but we felt politically that this would help to increase transparency and openness. this means that, as mr koukiadis has rightly pointed out, the transposition of the directive varies greatly from one member state to another. and here we must see that there is always a need for compromise and agreement between economies and societies with very different cultures and habits, which is why the framework agreed is flexible, so as not to promote uniform and rigid solutions, which would be impossible to achieve, and the framework agreement would be very difficult to achieve. the member states were given considerable latitude to transpose the directive. the directive allows for certain derogations on the basis of legislation or collective agreements, allowing for the flexibility of the national authorities i mentioned above. the commission also recognises this diversity and does not seek to promote uniform solutions in this area. i would like to make a few specific recommendations to the commission. the report calls on the commission to monitor the shipment and to take the necessary measures in the event of a wrong shipment. we agree with this and, for the points of non-compliance identified, the procedure for infringement of community directives has already been initiated or, in some cases, is about to be initiated. as regards the definition of working time and the consequences of the judgment of the european court of justice in simap, which held that the on-call time of medical staff serving in first aid teams must be regarded as working time in its entirety. in this case the commission is looking at the consequences, a meeting has already taken place between the national authorities and the commission services, and the commission is going to launch a study of the legal situation and the consequences of this decision for health systems and other sectors. the european parliament's report also asks the commission to clarify the situations in which derogations based on labour agreements are justified. there is a clear reference to this condition in article 18 (1), which allows member states to circumvent the 48-hour limit provided that the worker agrees to work more hours. and here i should note that there are also safety barriers so that there are no measures and consequences for the worker who will not accept it. the only state to have made use of this derogation is the united kingdom. the same directive provides that the council, on a proposal from the commission accompanied by an evaluation report, is to review this provision. i would like to assure you that the commission will submit this evaluation report. i would also like to stress that in 2002 each member state will submit a national report, to be submitted by the national authorities, analysing the practical application of this directive. and on the basis of these national reports, a synthesis report by the commission on the application of the directive in the member states will be produced, which will give us a clearer picture. i would like to conclude with my report on the new working models. it is certainly difficult to have the application of classical working time to new forms of work, as is the great debate on lifelong learning and the clustering of time. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the social partners, their discussions and agreements on the role of lifelong learning, on the principles of teleworking, the agreements already reached in specific areas, show that in a first phase, individual agreements at european level can create the conditions for moving further, if necessary, into a legislative framework.
thank you, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place at 6.30 p.m.
the agenda calls for the oral question (b5-0003/02) on behalf of the group of the european people's party (christian democrats) and european democrats to the commission on promoting access to the internet.
the commission. - i would like to thank the honourable member very much, because it is indeed an excellent subject, which is a top priority, not only in the european parliament and the commission, but also in each of the portfolios, since the electronic europe is a priority for all of us. the request at the lisbon summit was for cheap, high-speed networks to provide internet access. and this, for reasons which you yourself have explained, is a cornerstone of the european knowledge economy, it is a cornerstone of the policies of justice, equality and non-exclusion in europe. as mentioned in the question, internet access pricing is also an important tool. there is a question of charging access with a flat rate. i would like to say that i have a problem with the vocabulary and translation of terms in all languages, and i have to say that i recognised some words in english but not in greek on the basis of a one-way connection, from internet service providers and from newcomers to the telecommunications networks of the former monopoly operators. the national regulatory authorities of four member states, the united kingdom, the netherlands, spain and france, have required established ex-monopolists to provide wholesale internet access service to market participants. this is the principle known as friaco, or single-ended internet access call initiation. the service is to be installed and soon to be provided in italy. the industry argues that friaco results in increased internet use and also that since there is no time-bar, users spend more time on the internet and become familiar with the relevant commercial and cultural pages. it is also argued that all these services together increase consumer demand for broadband access and services in the free market. the commission welcomes the decisions of the regulatory authorities of the member states, which i have mentioned before, and encourages the use of this model in other states. this encouragement and support from the commission was expressed in the following ways: firstly, in the open network provision committee in the enr, the forum chaired by the european union, where the regulatory authorities and ministries of the member states are represented in their advisory and regulatory capacity. this issue will be put back on the agenda of the open network provision committee on 20 february 2002. secondly, in the seventh edition on the implementation of the telecommunications regulatory package, submitted to the european parliament and the council in december 2001, where again the commission provides specific support for single-ended narrowband internet access as a gateway to broadband access. the commission has already taken a number of decisions on the basis of the commission's proposal, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. the commission is thus ensuring that the local loop unbundling (llu) regulation is properly implemented. unbundled access to the local loop provides first-time entrants with the opportunity to compete with established operators by offering high-speed data services and continuous internet access based on digital hotline technology. the commission also referred to this aspect of high speed internet in the 7th edition, along with the provision of equal access to the retail offers of the incumbent for high speed internet access. the commission also encourages the provision of fair and cost-effective short-haul leasing conditions, which is another form of internet access and is particularly important for small businesses and companies using data services from newcomer telecoms operators. it is therefore clear that the commission operates on two levels. the first concerns the strengthening of specific political cooperation, the support for the implementation of models which are already successful, and i have indicated how, and the second is to act at the level of monitoring the implementation of binding decisions such as regulations, which of course play a very important role. on the issue of the spread and adoption of broadband technology, the commission recognises in its report to the barcelona european council that the deployment and exploitation of this technology is not currently taking place at the rates we would expect from member states. in this context, the commission proposed to the european council that broadband technologies be widely available throughout the european union by 2005.
thank you, commissioner.

mr president, i was really perplexed by the oral questions from the socialist and liberal groups on the obstacles to rail traffic in the channel tunnel caused by refugees trying to enter britain illegally. the main, if not the only, problem which arises from these oral questions is that of the disruption of the free movement of goods in the channel and therefore the damage caused to railway undertakings, which is doubled, horresco referens, by a distortion of competition between the different modes of transport to the detriment of the railway. i am very sorry, as are my colleagues, for the damage suffered by the railway companies concerned and i would even add that i find it illogical that the french state, whose responsibility is assumed by its socialist government, should not be severely condemned, morally and financially, for its inability to maintain public order. but let me also say, ladies and gentlemen, that this case raises much broader and more serious social problems than a simple inequality of competition between private operators. i would therefore add a series of supplementary questions to the questions put by the socialist and liberal groups. firstly, some of the people who are trying to enter britain illegally are asylum seekers, but others are illegal immigrants, even in france. how can illegal immigrants arrive in large numbers in the heart of europe after crossing several internal borders without ever being detected? the commission. - mr president, it is obvious that we are facing a difficulty in implementing one of the fundamental principles of freedom in europe, the free movement of goods. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the possibility of using articles of the treaty, of the commission intervening in order to put pressure on the french government to take more rapid measures. the current law of the european union allows the commission to initiate infringement proceedings against a member state when obstacles to the free movement of goods are observed. however, such action is subject to strict criteria when the obstacle is created by individual individuals and the commission can only act when the authorities concerned fail to take the necessary appropriate measures. that is clearly not the case here. the commission has already made a very important effort, and the contacts between the commission and the french government have proved useful, and we will continue in this direction. the french government has already closed the site, the study and the first attempt to install the necessary technology have been made, but of course the degree of policing, the number of police officers required, the installation of the high-tech equipment needed, is something that depends on the french government. the second point i would like to make is the substance of the problem. why are there these traffic interruptions? why is there this constant difficulty in moving the trains through the tunnel? why is there an undesirable presence of illegal immigrants at various points used by rail freight companies? i would therefore say that the essence of the problem, as put forward by several members, is a european policy on common principles, a common asylum policy, to avoid the phenomenon of migrants trying to reach specific member states. the commission has already put forward a number of proposals on the procedures and rules for granting refugee status and on the minimum common conditions for the reception of asylum seekers. another proposal lays down criteria and mechanisms for determining the member state responsible for examining an asylum application. these proposals stipulate that a long stay in a member state implies that the member state responsible for examining an asylum application is that member state. in this case, therefore, and under this system, asylum seekers cannot obtain refugee status in britain after a long stay in france. i would therefore say that, as far as the immediate solution of a problem which has a significant impact on certain areas, and particularly on the remote areas of great britain, the area of scotland, but also on the european continent itself and on trade relations with great britain, is concerned, the french government alone is responsible. it must move as quickly as possible to complete this plan which it has put forward, and in this direction there is cooperation with the british government and the commission. as regards the long-term solution to the problem, because as many members have said today it is found on the french-british border, tomorrow we may see it in other parts of europe, a rapid decision on a common asylum policy at european level is needed.

- mr president, in view of the barcelona council, the commission has just presented an action plan for the mobility of people in europe which seems to us to be questionable in more than one respect. some proposals, it is true, are obviously sensible, such as lifelong learning, better coordination of social security schemes or the transferability of pension rights. but the commission is putting its initiative in a strange perspective. it states at the outset that geographical mobility in europe is five times lower than in the united states. as if the intention was to make the nations of europe identical with the states of america. that would be a serious misunderstanding. our real objective, the one that the majority of our fellow citizens want, is respect for the nations and also for the living conditions, cultures and languages to which they are rightfully attached. let's not subtly reverse priorities. that would be a truly totalitarian approach. the commission has also included in this action plan calls for a common immigration policy which have nothing to do with it. that is another matter. the member states should not be forced to adopt guidelines which they are not fully aware of.
mr president, the theme of the spanish presidency, more europe, is a priori an ambition which we could support. the whole question is: which europe ? the european union needs strong economic and social momentum, and the need to respond to the aspirations of citizens, and the barcelona summit is being heralded as a decisive step towards the implementation of the accelerated liberalisation of public services which the president-in-office has just described as the 'network' industry. liberalisation is the magic answer. yet expectations are growing for more ambitious and high-quality public services. is it national selfishness? i think that need is universal. the considerable inequalities between countries in terms of access to these services justify the development of common european standards which could allow harmonisation from above. it is not less public services that should be on the agenda, but more and better with their development, their democratization, their modernization. public services, or services of general interest, are still considered in the union as a derogation from the competition rules. on the contrary, they must become the heart of european social cohesion, the key to action for a europe of progress, and one of its benchmarks and values. as we are now presented with the progress report on the cohesion of the union, will we continue to undo on the one hand what we are trying to build on the other? the barcelona summit is not, of course, limited to this issue, but the basic problems are the same: the economic situation, the fight against terrorism, enlargement, the need for more democratic institutions - all subjects which call for fresh reflection on the meaning of the union and its ambitions, as the first meeting of the convention opens tomorrow. the formal reference to more social europe, as well as to the need to bring people closer together, is no longer sufficient. we need strong signs, concrete actions. the answers announced for the summit so far are not going in the right direction, quite the opposite. behind the 'more europe' banner is a more liberal europe, the credo of the market. the citizens expect other things. they'll say it loud and clear at the demonstrations on the eve of the summit. it is urgent that we hear them.
- mr president, two years after the lisbon summit, the most optimistic and willing europeans are still holding out hope for a new paradigm: to make the union the most competitive knowledge-based economy in the world, accompanied by greater social cohesion. this strategy, completed in gothenburg, became a strategy for sustainable development in the environmental and social fields. we wanted to believe in it, we would like to believe in it, we still want to believe in it, but in reality this integration of the economic, social and environmental dimensions is still only a deception. the spanish presidency is not pretending. she's very forthright. for her, the union's sustainable development is the efficiency of markets, goods, services, capital and labour. can we pretend to believe it? we are being sold the idea of accelerated liberalization of markets, transport, electricity and gas, when we know that this will result in a weakening of the capacity of the services to act in the fight against poverty, for social protection, less territorial cohesion, less quality employment, as all the studies show. the flexibility of the labour market and the mobility of employees are being organised in place of a real policy of job creation. mr bullmann's report is trying to do the impossible. he'd want the butter and he'd want the butter money. respect for the commitments of the stability pact and investments in education, research, the environment and networks. quality of employment and market flexibility. no, for us the real priorities for barcelona are: development of the social and solidarity economy, income autonomy, including for young people whose poverty is increasing greatly, real definition of services of general interest, reduction of working time, investment in the environment and living conditions. these are the priorities for us at the barcelona summit.

the council has already made a number of recommendations to the council, and i am sure that the council will make a number of recommendations to the council. since the signing of the association agreement in 1963, through its formal application for accession in 1987 and the customs union achieved in 1996, relations have come a long way, not always easy, marked by mutual interest, rapprochement and at the same time by the clear european demand for compliance with certain essential requirements for any candidate for accession to the union. the copenhagen european council set out the political criteria which the candidate countries should meet, namely achieving institutional stability guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law, the defence of human rights and respect for and protection of minorities. the european council in helsinki later formally recognised turkey's candidacy for membership of the union, concluding that turkey is a candidate country destined to join the union on the basis of fulfilling the new criteria governing the other candidate countries. turkey would then benefit from the same accession partnership strategy as the other candidate countries, which should serve as a stimulus and support for its reforms. the conclusions of the laeken european council indicate that turkey has made progress in respect of the political criteria for accession, in particular through the recent amendment of its constitution. the prospect of opening accession negotiations with turkey has thus become closer. the european council encouraged turkey to continue to make progress towards respecting the copenhagen criteria, both economic and political, especially with regard to human rights, and recognised turkey's participation on an equal footing with the other candidates in something as momentous as the convention on the future of europe, which is to be opened tomorrow in this parliament. the progress 2000 report said that turkey had initiated a very positive debate on the political reforms needed for accession, including the signing of some international human rights instruments. the year 2001 saw one of the most important changes in turkey's democratization process: the adoption of a package of 34 constitutional amendments, the most significant change to the basic law since it came into force in 1982. the most important new developments include the recognition of freedom of thought and expression, measures to prevent torture and the strengthening of civil authority vis-à-vis military authority, and major reforms in the prison sector. these reforms have undoubtedly been helped by the fact that turkey has been recognised as a candidate and has the prospect of future membership of the union. in addition, at the end of january 2002, another important step was taken when the turkish government decided to withdraw its reservation to article 5 of the european convention on human rights, concerning the right to liberty and security in relation to maximum periods of detention before judicial release. the secretary-general of the council of europe welcomed this decision, stating that it marks a step forward in the protection of the rights of persons in detention. i think it is also worth mentioning the decision to set up a committee, which would include the ministers of justice and the interior and the minister for human rights, to monitor the situation in the field of human rights protection and take any necessary measures. the same applies to the entry into force in turkey of the new civil code, which marks a significant step forward in the recognition of non-discrimination on grounds of sex, in the field of family law and also in the field of succession law. the amendment to the national security council law, which is about to be adopted by parliament, is also worth mentioning in order to adapt it to the new wording of article 118 of the constitution and which increases the number of civilian members of the national security council, more clearly proclaiming its consultative nature. it is also positive that the council of ministers has approved the decree which will allow amnesty international to legally open an office in turkey. but if the constitutional amendments are a great hope for the democratic process - even though they omit some important points, such as not having completely abolished the death penalty, which will continue to be applied in case of war or to punish especially serious crimes, such as terrorism - the legislative development of these constitutional precepts has been clearly insufficient. although the legislative mini-package for the development of constitutional reforms contains a more restrictive definition of the crime of apology for terrorism and grants greater guarantees to detainees before they are put at the disposal of the judiciary, concepts of great vagueness are introduced at the same time and even, in some cases, the scope of punishable actions is extended, such as continuing to place limitations on the rights of association and demonstration, which is totally incompatible with the practices in force in the european union. the same can be said of the reform of the civil code. the amendment of the legal person regime does not solve the problem of legal barriers to the right of association or the foundations law, recently ratified by the supreme court, which prohibits the acquisition of real estate by foundations of non-muslim religious minorities in turkey. it should be recalled in this connection that one of the priorities of the accession partnership document is non-discrimination on religious grounds. another important element to consider is the practical implementation of the reforms. it is not enough to simply pass laws; their provisions must be put into effect. turkey can be said to have the basic characteristics of a democratic system, but the implementation of the reforms necessary to guarantee democracy and the rule of law is very slow. the situation of torture and ill-treatment has hardly improved, especially in the south-east, mainly due to the difficulties in prosecuting the members of the security forces responsible for these acts. the independence of the judiciary is limited in practice, due among other reasons to the fact that the supreme council of judges and prosecutors is chaired by the minister of justice, which prevents the separation of the competences of the executive and the judiciary in practice. the criminal procedure law continues to prevent the review of contested judgments or any action to redress violations of the european convention on human rights. the action plan for the south-east remains unpublished and turkey has not signed the council of europe's framework convention for the protection of national minorities. all this is without prejudice to important limitations presented by the judicial system itself. despite legislative reforms, effective improvement in this area will depend on the correct application and interpretation of development legislation. in practice, it has already become clear that acts which have ceased to be criminal offences under the recent reform of the criminal code do not prevent them from being regarded as a crime under another article of the criminal legislation and punished, in some cases, even more harshly. an essential element in the turkish democratization process is the so-called national programme for the incorporation of the deer, presented by the turkish government shortly after the council of the european union approved the association document for accession in march 2001. it is a step in the right direction, but it is insufficient because it has some shortcomings which could jeopardise the objective of fully meeting the priorities and objectives demanded by the union. in some respects, this national programme for the incorporation of the deer has been drafted in vague terms, so it will present difficulties of interpretation before it goes ahead. in particular, mention should be made of the abolition of the death penalty, the subordination of the armed forces to civilian authority, the eradication of corruption, the socioeconomic situation in the south-east of the country with a predominantly kurdish population and the lifting of the state of emergency in the south-east. the plan also makes no commitment to eliminating legal obstacles to radio and television broadcasts in the mother tongue or to ensuring the cultural rights of turkish minorities. in this process of reform and progress in the recognition of the cultural rights of minorities, turkey still has shortcomings. the recent reform of the constitution has led to the amendment of articles 26 and 28 and the corresponding disappearance of the prohibition on the use of other languages. however, the recent demonstrations by university students and parents demanding the inclusion of kurdish language courses in the academic curriculum have been harshly repressed by the security forces, claiming that the kurdish language does not exist as such, that the only national language of the republic is turkish and that the detainees who have remained in detention have been arrested for their alleged support for the terrorist organization of the kurdistan workers' party, better known by the acronym pkk. the council also called on the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the eu's external relations are not jeopardised by the threat of a nuclear war. another problem that cannot be ignored in the legislative process of democratization in turkey is that it affects the recognition of the right of association, in particular the outlawing and closure of political parties. in 1994 the people's democratic party (hadep) was created to replace the defunct democratic party (dep), which was accused of having links with the terrorist organization of the kurdistan workers' party. former dep members who wanted to become hadep members had to apply for express permission from the government, which only allowed membership to those who had no criminal record or on whom no accusation existed. since its creation, hadep has been the first political force in the southeast of the country, controlling most of the mayorships of the cities in this area; but also, since its creation, the threat of its closure hangs over hadep. the june 2001 decision of the constitutional court to close down the fazilet islamist party highlighted the problems with freedom of expression and association. now, the constitutional court has before it the decision of the hadep case. the prosecutor has requested its closure for its alleged relationship with the terrorist and leader of the kurdistan workers' party, abdullah ocalan, he is accused of having used the party congresses to make propaganda in favor of ocalan and incite hatred against the constitutional order and the indissoluble unity of the turkish republic. thousands of cases of hadep detainees have occurred and while most have been released after a short period of detention, the detainees were released as alleged members of the pkk terrorist organisation and were accused of involvement in terrorist activities. no one was arrested and sentenced for the mere fact of belonging to the party. this does not prevent us from saying that in turkey any mention of kurdistan, its flag, the demand for education in the kurdish language is considered collaboration or support for terrorist activity. but it is also true that, as long as it is not closed down, hadep is a legally recognised party in turkey and no one can be arrested for the mere fact of belonging to it. its illegalization would mark a step backwards in turkey's progress towards accession and would raise the need for the european union to take a joint position expressing its concern about the negative impact on freedom of expression, association and political pluralism, on the understanding that respect for the cultural rights of the turkish population of kurdish origin is one of the objectives set out in the accession partnership document. mr president, it is undeniable that turkey has made progress in meeting the political criteria for accession and that the prospect of opening negotiations has therefore become closer. however, these advances are not yet sufficient to start accession talks. one of the main obstacles is the protection of the cultural rights of all turks, regardless of their ethnic origin. recently, the secretary-general for european union affairs, volkan vural, announced that a second package of legislative reforms is being prepared. this gives us hope today of seeing a new step in the democratization process in turkey, which will open the way to a more fluid relationship and, perhaps in the future, to negotiations for its future accession to the union. mr president, the common position adopted by the council on 15 october on the opening up of the postal services of the member states to competition represents a good compromise, our rapporteur tells us, and the governments, including the french socialist government, are all committed to supporting it. however, this text seems to us to be based on a series of ambiguities which can conceal many dangers. firstly, the french state secretary in charge of the file, mr piret, claims that less than 10% of the turnover of the post office will be subject to competition in 2009, whereas commissioner bolkestein, for his part, estimates this share at 50% of the european market as of 2006. who's right? the first one concerns france and the second the union as a whole, but the enormity of the gap suggests that there is some misunderstanding or concealment. second ambiguity: we are told that the new directive will make it possible to achieve a gradual and controlled opening-up. but if we look closely at the proposed methods, we may have doubts about the quality of this control. the interim stage of 1 january 2006, which will see the weight of the mail reduced from 100 to 50 grams, and thus the weight of the mail split in half, will be an automatic step already decided on in today's text without any real and serious assessment of its impact. in these circumstances, the prospective study, which is planned to be carried out from 2006 onwards, may conclude that the essential decisions have already been taken, that they will already be behind us and, once again, we will have moved forward in the fog without knowing exactly when and under what conditions we will have crossed the essential markers. this will be a new example of the monnet method on a smaller scale. in conclusion, we are in favour of an opening which would allow the postal services to be stimulated, but we do not want to throw the baby out with the bath water. we do not want to risk that this poorly controlled opening up will destroy the universal service, which would be even more disastrous for the user, especially in a country like france, where vast rural areas could see their postal service deteriorate. we therefore believe that the 2006 stage should not be automatic, but should be preceded by a serious and contradictory impact assessment and clarification of the public service obligations to be imposed on all operators. and, even better, we would like to see it enacted, mr president, that each of the public services, as a whole falling within the competence of each member state, will remain free from the final organization of its postal service.

postal services contributes to the performance of national economies and of certain sectors, in particular the banking, insurance or distance selling sectors. at a time when we are completing the sectors for improved services and reduced costs of postal services. a certain degree of competition, together with increased requirements on the quality of services, promotes cost transparency and contributes to the competitiveness of activities consuming or using postal services by opening up potential markets for them. i remain, however, firmly opposed to any form of total liberalisation, because services of general economic interest play a role in the economic, social and territorial cohesion of the union. the european charter of fundamental rights recognises the principle of access to an economic service of general interest as provided for by national laws and practices. the challenge of access to postal services is not the same in a country with 17 000 post offices or in a country with barely a thousand. it is therefore necessary to ensure that the opening up to competition will not have a negative impact on access to postal services in the most isolated and remote regions. in other words, it seems to me that the modernisation of postal services under the impetus of competition is now necessary for the development of these services and, more generally, for the competitiveness of our companies. but this liberalisation must be gradual and controlled in order to preserve adaptability, economic viability and guarantee access to the universal postal service throughout the union. i think that the compromise we are discussing here meets this dual objective, and that is why i shall be voting on it tomorrow.
- mr president, commissioner, at the end of the common position we must congratulate ourselves that parliament's first democratic expression has led to the commission and the council retaining some of its proposals such as the special services, the gradual opening with a new passage before parliament in 2009, or the maintenance of direct mail in the public service. however, it must be noted that two things are missing today and we are dealing with one of the few liberalization directives which does not specify them. the first is the financing of universal service. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it's not the least of it. secondly, the conditions for access to the networks. is it known whether the french postal networks are available to the german postal service and its major competitors and vice versa? it is also one of the few liberalisation directives which does not specifically lay down this aspect. i would like to regret that the commission and, finally, parliament, have not wanted to go into these debates and these questions in depth. the commission says that it wants transparency in all areas. it refuses to give us an assessment of what has happened in sweden or the netherlands, for example, where a weak market has led to higher prices for average consumers. the commission is denying us the truth about costs, and that truth is that serving everyone in greece is not the same as serving in the netherlands. in total, we have demonized the debate, we have made it seem as if conciliation is a bad thing. i think we could have gone to the end of this debate to reach a more balanced position.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, all the member states have decided to create a single market for electricity and gas. it's a good choice, but the whole problem is, how do we build this market? in its new directive, the commission aims at regulated competition. is there a balance between competition and regulation, i.e. taking account of fundamental rights to public services, environmental quality and energy security? this is the central criterion for evaluating our work. in the committee on industry, many colleagues have fallen short of the commission's proposals. their only objective mr president, today we are voting on the acceleration of the liberalization of the energy sector. after air transport, telecommunications, rail transport and the postal service, this sector will now be subject to market dictatorship through the total opening up to competition, in 2003 for electricity and in 2004 for gas. however, overall the opening up of public enterprises to capital was not conclusive. there have been no expected productivity gains. for the user, the dismantling of the utilities has reduced the quality of service and safety and has increased prices by 30% for gas and 5% for electricity. as regards employees, there have been significant reductions in the number of employees: 300 000 jobs have already been eliminated in this sector in europe. for the population, inequalities have increased. only a handful of shareholders and speculators have an interest in this deregulation. today, however, a new energy policy must be promoted. the need for coordination of public services at european level is greater than ever.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i have the pleasure of presenting the report on biodiversity. let me take this opportunity to thank all the colleagues present and those who have worked with me to produce and present this resolution to you today. i would also like to thank the rapporteurs for the opinions of the committees on agriculture, fisheries and development, who all support the proposal that your rapporteur has put forward on the preservation of biodiversity. finally, i would also like to thank the ngos who have really worked hard on this report. we know that they are excellent observers who are well aware of the state of biodiversity around the world. the situation is not very bright, mr president, and i would like to answer a question which is not really asked but which is often overlooked in the speeches of some of our colleagues: what is the real purpose of biodiversity, or, in simpler terms, why preserve nature when there are so many other issues of concern? i would remind you that biodiversity is an element of our own survival and that while nature does not need humans to survive, we humans need it to live. our responsibility as elected officials is to preserve the richness of biodiversity. they contain the assets of the development of future generations. every living species that disappears from the planet is a net and irreversible loss, and if we allow biodiversity to be destroyed we are gradually destroying ourselves. we can measure this destruction every day. the brazilian congress is therefore due to vote soon on a bill authorizing the exploitation of 50% of the amazon forest, of which we know what genetic reservoir it represents. it is not that man is destroying or threatening biodiversity out of selflessness. quite the contrary. it's really about self-interest. this is because of the huge financial interests involved, from the valuable timber to the illegal trade in endangered species, the intensive exploitation of land, the overexploitation of fish stocks, and the looting of the ancestral knowledge of indigenous peoples. to stop this slaughter, the convention for the preservation of biological diversity was signed at the earth summit in rio. ten years later, it is still the poor relative: the states that signed the convention have not kept their commitments and no country has, at present, included biodiversity in its priorities for the september summit in johannesburg. with only a few days to go until the hague conference of the parties to the convention on biological diversity, the european parliament, through our resolution, must take up its responsibilities and send a strong and clear message. we ask that the union put the issue of biodiversity on the agenda of the johannesburg summit and that the commission present an action plan there, as it does for the european union. we must recall the fundamental role of biodiversity as a cornerstone of sustainable development and the importance of full implementation of the convention and its provisions. we also call on the union to implement an ambitious policy to preserve its own biodiversity. the action plans presented by the commission in the fields of natural resources, agriculture, development and fisheries, which are the subject of this report, can of course be regarded as a first step, but they are not sufficient. additional action plans are needed, for example for forestry and transport, because all these community policies have had or are having a negative impact on biodiversity. and while the commission has the ambition to reverse the current trend, it is fully aware of the challenge it is facing. i quote the report: 'during the past two decades, the rate of decline and loss of biodiversity in europe and the world has accelerated dramatically and the measures taken have proved insufficient to reverse the trend.' i would add to this the new threats posed by the introduction of certain gmos and the conflicts over the ownership of living things, which reflect new greed. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to combat this problem. the union still has to provide itself with the political and financial means to hope to achieve this. we already have the birds and habitats directives, which help to preserve some of our biodiversity. we demand that they be applied throughout the union, including in the candidate countries and in the outermost regions, and in particular in areas such as the coral reef. we must find ways to preserve these areas. the second way to achieve results in the implementation of environmentally sustainable development, as the gothenburg summit has also agreed, is to have effective measuring instruments to assess the integration of the environment into the policies of the union. the spring european council in barcelona is expected to adopt six environmental indicators. it's too little. indeed, we hear nothing about biodiversity. we also ask the commission to present a specific indicator for biodiversity by 2003. if we want to achieve results in terms of biodiversity, we know that this issue must be imposed on the union's policies immediately and every day. this will begin with the forthcoming reform of the common agricultural policy, the common fisheries policy, the transport policy and the cotonou agreements for development. while there is consensus among the various groups in this parliament on the means of preserving biodiversity, there is still some disagreement among some members on the impact of gmos on biodiversity. and here, as the author of the report, i would like to see the references to the environmental responsibility of gmos for the pollution of rural areas retained. in conclusion, mr president, i would like to assume that it would not occur to anyone to plan to demolish a cathedral or a listed monument to make way for a motorway. we must have the same reflexes to preserve natural heritage and biological diversity.

in writing. - the history of the european directives on the opening up of postal services to competition shows clearly the commission's method: by using force and concealment, it skillfully uses the weapons given to it by the treaty, in particular the monopoly of initiative, to impose its theses and gradually push back its opponents, including in this case the european parliament, which in this case was rather in favour of moderation. it is all the more regrettable that, as is often the case, the commission's position is fundamentally completely unilateral and questionable. it has not shown that full competition in postal distribution would be profitable overall in a country such as france. but it is to this objective that it is actually leading us. and by what right ? it would seem justifiable for the commission to take care of the transnational distribution of mail, but it seems to us that internal distribution should be the responsibility of each state. however, the commission does not consider that such distinctions exist. commissioner bolkestein has just explained to this house that we should 'move towards the completion of the internal market for postal services'. is there no such internal market today?
