in writing. - first of all, i would like to thank both our rapporteur in the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, mr markus ferber, and the whole of this committee for the work they have proposed to us. the compromise amendment by the rapporteur, mr ferber, is unsatisfactory, if not unacceptable. unsatisfactory, because this amendment calls for a unilateral assessment by the commission alone and not, as i would have wished, a contradictory assessment by all the parties involved. unacceptable, because by rejecting parliament's initial proposal to limit the next stage of liberalization to 150g and 4 times the price, no guarantee is given to maintain a high level of social cohesion. this is unacceptable, because this amendment refuses to raise the question of the conditions for access to the networks of new operators. finally, it is unacceptable because this amendment refuses to raise the question of the financing of the universal service. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. nevertheless, i shall vote for the common position by default, because to try to amend the text again is to risk the common position being rejected; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the postal services are not subject to any new regulations. it is therefore more a concern for security than a genuine enthusiasm for this text which, in my opinion, is far too cynically liberal that leads me to vote in favour of this common position.
in writing. - on 14 december 2000, when voting at first reading, we were a handful of members who rejected the 'gradual and controlled' liberalisation of postal services. we had tried to convince those who, although in favour of public service, explained to us that the essential had been preserved. this was not to be confused with the commission's and governments' firm determination to liberalise and then privatise all public services. there is no compromise on the timing or scope of liberalization. that is why we voted against the common position and will continue to defend the postal service as a public service. this is the only way to ensure that quality is maintained for users and that access is free for all, especially for people in rural areas and working-class neighbourhoods. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competition' in the context of the directive. against the liberal dogma of commodifying our needs and our fundamental rights, it is time to mobilize the populations, the workers and their organizations to impose a public postal service coordinated at european level and placed under the control of the populations.
in writing. - the compromise reached at the council meeting on 15 october on the opening up of the member states' postal services to competition, supported by the french socialist government among others, seems to us to be based on a series of ambiguities which may conceal many dangers. in the name of the french exception and the precautionary principle for the maintenance of equality for our fellow citizens, i did not support this fraudulent compromise which is nothing more than a blank cheque given to the commission to complete, by 2006, the dismantling of the french postal service. the economic dimension must not be the sole guiding principle of european policy. france has chosen a quality service, distributed throughout its territory, accessible to all and at a single price. that's our idea of public service. it is our will to maintain our system at all costs. i would like to see it stated that, since the public services as a whole are the responsibility of each member state, each member state will remain free to decide on the final organisation of its postal service.
in writing. - each member state must retain full control over the organisation of its public services. it is up to the council, and it alone, to define the areas and the procedures of this organization. it is perhaps necessary to ensure that these services, in order to meet the needs of the population, cannot be paralysed by purely corporatist concerns. but it is not acceptable that in the name of a broad conception of the competence which has been transferred to it in competition matters, the commission arrogates to itself the right to define the nature of public services which a people may or may not benefit from. we reject the application of the monnet method, today to the postal services and tomorrow to other public services. the monnet method, that is to say, in this case, the adventure of a general deregulation in stages without any serious study having been carried out beforehand on the consequences of such a policy. the commission, as the internal market progresses, is prepared to take the risk that the social function of postal services will not be taken into account in the future, that the territorial coverage of our countries will be reduced, that the quality of the services provided will be reduced and that costs will rise considerably. the impact assessment will be carried out, as usual, when everything is in play and there is no going back. it is because we are opposed to this logic of the fait accompli that we voted against the ferber report and against the joint proposal of the council and the commission, which i note is actively supported by one component of the french government and fiercely opposed by its other two components.
in writing. - the malmström report on the presentation to the european parliament of the commission's annual work programme offers a sympathetic side at first sight: it ends up, without saying so, by undermining the college's monopoly of initiative and exposing its unilateral and undemocratic character. but on the other hand, it omits the essential point: it says nothing about the council's right to approve this same work programme. the malmström report shows first of all that, as the european parliament grows in strength, the commission's monopoly of initiative weighs heavier and heavier on it. so he tries to impose his priorities. this desire had caused some tension last december when the commission presented its programme for 2002. the commission/european parliament agreement which has just been approved provides for a timetable for the joint preparation of the work programme for year n during year n-1. it's a good move. but it raises another question: where is the equivalent timetable for dialogue with the council? such a timetable would be even more justified for three reasons: 1) the council is the european institution with the deepest democratic roots, since it is based on national parliaments; (2) it already has, in theory, unlike the european parliament, a real power to give impetus and direction to the work of the commission, pursuant to article 4 teu; 3) finally, the council has an overview of the work to be done at european level in the three pillars of the treaty, including the initiatives of the member states in the intergovernmental pillar. in the absence of any clarification on this point, the malmström report therefore appears above all as a manoeuvre by the two old accomplices, the commission and the european parliament, to trap the council's fundamental rights.
in writing. - we are in favour of anything that would bring national legislation closer together, particularly in this area, if it means an improvement for consumers. but here the rapporteur and the authors of most of the amendments are not inspired by that: they are primarily, if not exclusively, the interests of the capitalist groups producing food supplements. it is so obvious that, for example, the french employers' union in this sector sent a fax to all members of the european parliament with the headline which is quite cynical, since it says: 'the french food supplement industry thanks in advance its representatives in the european parliament for voting in favour of the directive'. well, let those who are the representatives of these people vote on this report and the directive! we voted for only one amendment, rejecting the text as a whole.
in writing. - many european citizens take vitamin and mineral supplements. in the context of a european consumer policy, it is therefore necessary to avoid any diversion from the use of these substances and to ensure the quality of the products offered to consumers. this recommendation responds to these wishes, in particular by proposing an adequate european legal framework which does not impede the free movement of these products while guaranteeing the consumer greater protection of his health and the guarantee of correct and appropriate information on the products available. one of the determining factors for the safety of these products is the maximum level of minerals they contain. the establishment of maximum levels of vitamins and minerals allowed in food supplements is therefore important for the measured use of these products. scientific advice shows that taking in excessive amounts of certain vitamins and minerals can produce adverse or harmful effects. in addition, the list of these substances should not be fixed because other products with a nutritional or physiological effect could be incorporated into this device. in the light of experience gained in this field, i would like the commission to submit to the european parliament and the council supplementary proposals with appropriate legal measures on other nutrients and substances which may have effects comparable to those of food supplements.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report by mrs emilia franziska müller and i would like to emphasize the quality of the work carried out by our rapporteur. i am glad that our assembly is finally taking a decision on such an important matter. the aim is to ensure that the products concerned do not present any health risks by ensuring that labelling allows european consumers to obtain clear, correct and appropriate information on the products. it is desirable to set a minimum amount of vitamins and minerals that these products should contain in order to ensure that food supplements contain a sufficient amount of them to justify the declared purpose of the product. once the principles governing the setting of maximum and minimum limits have been agreed, the adoption of specific limits for each nutrient, on the basis of the opinion of the scientific committee for food, is a technical matter. it should be borne in mind that the intake of certain vitamins and minerals in excess can produce adverse or harmful effects. hence the need to ensure the safety of these products, in particular by means of a labelling containing precise instructions on the use of the product, and in particular on the quantity that can be consumed. this will enable european citizens to choose vitamins and mineral supplements from the wide range of products currently available on the market without having to worry about their health.
in writing. - i've always been a health and consumer protection advocate. i would like to make two main points on the points i have been fighting for in the committee. the decisions of the european union must be consistent. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. by laying down rules for the prevention, control and eradication of transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, regulation (ec) no 999/2001 already subjects animal by-products from ruminant slaughterhouses and ruminant meat boning plants to strict and controlled health rules. it is therefore unnecessary, for reasons of consistency and proper application, to include those establishments in the scope of a second regulation pursuing the same objectives. the european union must also take the relevant decisions. however, we know that the treatment and destruction (incineration or landfill) capacities cannot allow for the application, at community level, of measures which can be implemented in too short a time when they concern effluents produced by slaughterhouse wastewater treatment plants, which are often common wastewater treatment plants - whether they are classified as category 1 or category 2. these shortcomings were particularly apparent when animal meal was banned from animal feed, which forced member states to store such flour in large quantities pending incineration. adding several million tonnes of products to be destroyed or treated before recovery would impose new storage constraints, as there is no possibility of treatment or incineration in the open stream. we know that storage can be a health and environmental hazard. it is therefore necessary to establish an adequate timetable for sound, safe and environmentally friendly community management.
in writing. - by establishing the single market, as it claims, the report on crossborder trade in electricity aims first and foremost to open up the electricity market to competition and, in fact, although it does not admit it openly, to its privatization. in other words, the responsibility for providing electricity to more than 300 million europeans has been handed over to the interests of large private groups. the rapporteur is not satisfied with this, but in perfect harmony with this approach, he recommends that the burden of this opening up of national networks to private operators be passed on to consumers throughout the european union. we are firmly opposed to the privatization of electricity production and supply, just as we are against all privatizations of public services by national governments and the european institutions, because this policy can only be carried out to the detriment of the interests of both the workers in the sectors concerned and the broad mass of consumers. we condemn this policy of dismantling public services, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the capitalists' appetite for profit, whether it is admitted as such in the mombaur report or whether it is badly concealed under ecological considerations, as in the turmes-rapkay report. we therefore voted against both reports.
in writing. - energy is not a commodity like other commodities! how many times have i said it and repeated it... the security of supply and the burden of investment it entails must be taken into account. the necessary public service and its importance in terms of spatial planning must be integrated. nevertheless, following the lisbon european council and the call to undertake work on completing the internal market in gas and electricity as quickly as possible, the european commission presented a communication, a proposal for a regulation and a proposal for a directive aimed at accelerating the liberalisation of the gas and electricity market with full opening planned for 2005. at the stockholm summit, the member states approved this acceleration, with the exception of france, which strongly opposed this date. the commission wants to speed up the opening up of the electricity sector with the possibility for all non-residential consumers to choose their supplier freely by 01/01/2003 and for all consumers to benefit from this possibility by the beginning of january 2005 at the latest. for gas: for non-residential customers 01/01/2004 and for all consumers at the beginning of january 2005. it's totally irresponsible and unacceptable. it is the caricature of an ultra-liberal europe that i am fighting against. the struggle is difficult, given the balance of power in the european parliament and in europe. that is why i supported a compromise amendment with p. herzog and g. savary to amend article 19 on the dates and conditions of opening up to competition by stressing the need for equalisation to guarantee equal rates for residential customers. that is why i voted against the report in the final vote. france should support this position at the barcelona council.
in writing. - the izquierdo rojo report on 'women and fundamentalism', which has just been adopted by a small majority despite our vote against it, shows a good idea that has been completely perverted in the course of the discussions. the original aim was to affirm our determination to ensure that women's rights are strictly respected in the territories of all the member states, at a time when the flows of dense and unassimilated immigration tend to implant conceptions that degrade women, or that amount to cruel torture, such as female genital mutilation. unfortunately, the european parliament has finally given up on naming the evil we suffer from - unassimilated immigration, often from countries with an islamic culture. in these circumstances, he has resorted to sanitized statements or, worse still, to general condemnations which seem to apply to all europeans without distinction and which falsely blame everyone. the same is true of the very notion of "fundamentalism": it blends the rigorous practice of a religion that places the individual at the centre of society, christianity, with the rigorous practice of another, which subjects the individual to the community, islam. it's not the same thing. the european parliament also called for the adoption of a directive on the right of asylum, which would allow women from all over the world who are "suffering from fundamentalist persecution" to be granted asylum. in order to be consistent, we should have called for the abolition of the fiscal stability pact at the same time!
in writing. - the report has the merit of denouncing one of the most odious aspects of the oppression of women in the world, by speaking out against religious fundamentalism and the regimes that practice it. we voted for the paragraphs of denunciation and measures to make things easier for women who are forced to flee from countries where misogyny is rampant. we have, however, abstained on the whole. the text rightly denounces islamist fundamentalism, but it is much more discreet about the various forms of fundamentalism, particularly catholic fundamentalism, which women are victims of, even in countries that are members of the european union, such as ireland and portugal or certain länder in germany. to deny women the right to terminate a pregnancy, that is, the right to control their own bodies, is already misogynistic and oppressive. and the european union would be more credible in its good resolutions towards misogyny and islamist regimes if it started by sweeping up on its doorstep by banning its member states from discriminatory practices against women. the european institutions have arrogated to themselves the right, with the complicity of european governments, to impose a measure as backward as women's night work. why do they refuse to impose on the whole of europe this basic right of women to self-determination, including that of the ivg?

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it is now nine months since the economic and monetary affairs committee considered the european commission's proposal for a directive on this highly technical and yet very topical subject. as early as last spring, the bursting of the e-economics bubble had reminded us that banking is a high-risk industry. in the autumn, the september 11 attacks, together with the steady rise in industrial accidents and natural accidents related to the greenhouse effect, reminded us that insurance is also a high-risk activity. it will be more and more. for years, the european union, like the rest of the world, has standardized the prudential rules for these branches and the forms of supervision by the competent authorities. the work for the financial groups in both banking and insurance must now be completed. this work is particularly urgent in europe, the continent that pioneered the banking-insurance business. this is all the more urgent as the development of life insurance and all forms of funded retirement savings is putting our society at a major risk. what would happen if the long-term savings of future retirees were swallowed up in the crash of risky investments? that is what this directive is about. its rapid adoption aims at nothing less than making europe the safest financial area in the world, decisively improving its competitiveness through the geographical factor of the rating agencies. i do not conceal the fact that at the beginning of our discussions some colleagues were reluctant to impose new prudential requirements on the financial industry. there was discussion, arguing here and there, of the opportunity for europe to display its own rules before the completion of the basel negotiations on the same subject in 2004. but one event shattered that reluctance: the bankruptcy of the enron conglomerate in the united states due to failures in compliance with prudential rules and failures in supervision. by adopting the directive, europe would become the 'enron-proof' continent. so the last of the reluctance melted away. yes, the directive is urgent. no, it must not be watered down either as regards its scope or as regards the rigor and transparency of the prudential rules which the authorities will have to monitor. during these nine eventful months our committee was able to meet with representatives of the profession and to take into account to a large extent those of their arguments which were in accordance with common sense and the public interest. i am thinking in particular of two groups of amendments: those relating to the choice of accounting method and the appointment of the coordinator of supervisors and those relating to the relaxation of the capital requirements for groups which are not yet conglomerates. finally, your rapporteur was able to work with the commission and the belgian and then the spanish presidencies of the council throughout his work. both institutions should be warmly thanked for this. we have shown that the three institutions of the union are able to move forward together very quickly when the public interest and the interest of the european union are at stake. at the moment i am speaking, at 5.15 p.m., i have been able to finalise a handful of compromise amendments, which include the bulk of the amendments tabled last week and which seem to me to be capable of forging a consensus between most of the groups and of anticipating by a large margin the necessary compromise with the council. i therefore believe that our assembly is in a position to adopt a text, almost unanimously, very close to the one which the council will adopt. in these circumstances, i believe that at first reading, or at one and a half readings, if you wish, we can get this directive ratified, and i would be very pleased to see that. we will avoid europe having to deal with enron again and at the same time we will have legislation which will enable us to deepen the basle discussions by proposing to the world the rules which europe has set for itself and by immediately reaping the dividends of a better valuation of our financial activities.

mr president, the granting of legal personality to the european union, in addition to the european communities which already have it, would really do little, at least if we consider this amendment in isolation. in order to change the institutions in depth, it would actually have to be combined, as mr carnero gonzález' report suggests on several occasions, with several other, much more important reforms: the merging of the pillars, the power to conclude treaties on its own, the general communitization of decision-making, the adoption of a supranational constitution. the report is therefore, in a sense, correct in saying that this reform would not in itself involve transfers of powers to the union. it is true that a mere association of states acting unanimously could have legal personality. but it is wrong to say that it alone would provide the consistency, unity of representation and visibility which the report attributes to it. in other words, this reform is nothing, or if it is something, it is that it is accompanied by the fusion of the pillars, communitization and constitutionalization that would be the distinctive signs, call it what you will, of a super-state or something that would strongly resemble it. that is why i have drawn up a minority opinion which is annexed to the report. and that's why i'm offering a deal to mr. carnero gonzález. i am prepared to accept the legal personality of the union if, in return, you, mr carnero gonzález, agree that a possible european constitution, should it come into being, should give priority to the supremacy of national constitutions, the freedom of choice of the member states on the world stage and the unanimous decision or variable geometry within the framework of the third pillar. if you were to say all that, mr carnero gonzález, i might vote for your report, but you will not say that, because your report is not what it says it is.

- the next item is the report (a5-0050/2002) by mrs carlotti, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on the work of the acp-eu joint parliamentary assembly in 2001 (2001/2012 (ini)).
the rapporteur. - mr president, every year the european parliament presents a report on the activities of the acp-eu joint assembly. since 2000, however, the cotonou agreement has introduced a new reality which profoundly changes the very nature of this relationship. the cotonou agreement introduced a profound change in the objectives of cooperation, with the new ambition of a renewed, more balanced and more efficient partnership. this requires a change in the app's rules of the game. more than changes to the rules of the game, it requires a real cultural change. where are we in that process? the joint parliamentary assembly is in the middle of the ford. following on from the year 2000 which had raised high hopes for a new era in eu-acp relations, 2001 did not deliver on its promises. the working group has indeed initiated a vast process of adapting working methods, but many obstacles and resistance have still hindered progress. three examples: first, the inertia of the european states in the ratification process. only three countries have ratified it: denmark, sweden, the united kingdom, and then we, here in the european union. and although we know that the procedures are lengthy in many european countries, the acp see in this a political message and a negative sign. by the end of 2002, all europeans should have ratified it. second example: the untimely use of separate collegiate voting in the assembly. it is an attack on parliamentary character. i propose limited use, and above all a moratorium on european use. the question of voting rights is a fundamental one, and the debate on article 2 of the rules of procedure has been a source of much controversy. the principle of exclusive representation of members must be vigorously reaffirmed and the compromise reached by the working party, which specifies only the cases in which a non-member may be prevented from voting, is the last position we can accept here. we have to get past this bad time. this report offers some clues. i will mention only a few of them, as a concrete instrument in the service of democracy: the democratic bonus, financial or material aid to improve the functioning of democratically elected parliaments and better representation of the opposition. on the acp side, the principle is one country, one vote. in fact, each country speaks with one voice. it is impossible for acp parliamentarians from the opposition to make themselves heard. to remedy this, we will need to have an open, unbiased reflection on a re-weighting of the votes. and for the time being, the proposal of three delegates per country, put forward by my colleague mr martinez last year, is going in the right direction. this raises the question of funding. after a rigorous financial analysis by the commission, a special fund would be set aside for the travel of acp parliamentarians and the organization of sessions. more generally, the app is the only assembly that does not have a budget. the commission must be given new powers to exercise financial and political control over the financing of cooperation. finally, the european parliament should pay particular attention to the work of the acp countries in a wide-ranging debate, at least once a year, here in the european parliament, on the various aspects of cooperation.
- mr president, the year 2001 was marked for the acp countries by the entry into force of the cotonou agreement. the ratification by the european parliament last january will encourage member states to follow suit, thus enabling the financial component. the joint parliamentary assembly has adapted its work to the new role it has been given, in particular the promotion of democratic processes. as a forum for the expression of the will of the people and of democratic values, it has a central role to play. but his powers are limited. it remains a mere forum for political expression, without decision-making or executive powers. it must therefore be given new powers, both political and financial and operational, and the logistical means to go with them. a working group should be set up to monitor the evaluation of civil society involvement in the partnership. similarly, parliamentarians should be involved in the forthcoming negotiations on the future acp-eu trade regime. we will therefore vote with conviction for mrs carlotti's report, which makes excellent proposals on the other points, as she said earlier, recalling that democratization in the acp countries requires democratization of the joint institutions and of development cooperation in general.

- doc. a5-0049/2002 by mrs carrilho, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation extending and amending regulation (ec) no 1659/98 on decentralised cooperation (com (2001) 576 - c5-0509/2001 - 2001/0243 (cod)).
- mr president, the european parliament was the originator of the creation of a budget line for decentralised cooperation in the 1990s. the lomé iv convention also incorporated this idea, thus derogating from the principle of state-to-state cooperation. today, the concept, in the commission's words, has made its way and proved its validity, its effectiveness. the commission therefore proposes to extend its application for two years. we can only approve this proposal, with reservations, however, about the form. the regulation, apart from the fact that it is transitional, remains vague. it's a little bit of everything: decentralized cooperation, civil society, ngos. is there no strategy on the part of the commission in this area? similarly, the cotonou agreement enshrines the participation of acp civil society in the partnership, to the detriment of decentralised cooperation, which has disappeared. the communication on civil society in developing countries, which the commission has been promising for several months, should clarify these concepts and develop the european union's coordinated approach to the matter, but it is still awaited. the two themes of 'support for decentralised cooperation' and 'support for civil society' go hand in hand. in both cases, the aim is to support local dynamics by avoiding the burdensome and sometimes non-transparent implementation of national programmes. the commission seems to have understood this, since it is planning to merge these two budget lines, but the one-off adjustments which are being made without consulting the european parliament are not enough. the transfer of funds from one budget line to another shows the absence of an overall perspective and shows little regard for the budgetary authority. we are, of course, in favour of direct aid to projects on the ground. but we're a little annoyed by the last-minute actions. this budgetary revision can only be achieved if the concept of decentralized cooperation and relations with ngos in the north and south are really put to the test. the two additional years should therefore be devoted to a substantive reflection on the european union's cooperation with local actors in developing countries and their contribution to sustainable development. we must ask ourselves what is meant by decentralized cooperation, cooperation between subnational entities in the north and the south, or aid to local and regional authorities in developing countries. what is civil society? this question is becoming more pressing with the implementation of the cotonou agreement. in reality, it is the broader question of governance and democracy that is being asked. the development of the countries of the south necessarily requires their democratization, that is, the involvement of the citizens in the orientations of the country. but these citizens can participate in many ways: by voting for local, regional, national governments. in this sense, support for elections and institutional capacity building at the various levels of decision-making and administration are essential. they also play the role of economic and social actors in enterprises or in the associative sector. direct aid to ngos and smes is therefore also important. these two aspects are not contradictory but are in fact complementary. the commission must continue the debate, must continue to speed up the debate, because it is high time to give the local people the means of their development.

- madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission is taking the opportunity to change prices and guarantee thresholds for the period 2002-2004, to make a disastrous change for producers and for the social and economic balance of entire regions. the aim is to lay the foundations for a cessation of tobacco production without any alternative. tobacco is a crop that is valued in difficult territories and in many small and medium-sized farms. the labour force it employs supports the economic activity of rural areas. the european union produces 5% of the world's tobacco and imports 70% of its needs. if we do not produce it, europe will be dependent on imports. moreover, the impact on consumption will be absolutely zero. tobacco is a public health issue that must be treated as such. prevention through training, especially among young people, must be a priority. the producers are also helping to prevent this by financing the community fund, which should have been used to inform consumers and also to advance research into the harmfulness of products. unfortunately, no tender has been issued since 1997. by maintaining european production, we are giving ourselves the means to control the quality of tobacco production and processing. we also provide the means to develop less harmful varieties. farmers will not accept that the levies on premiums are increased to finance their own demise. our group can only reject recital 5 of the commission proposal which in fact condemns small and mediumsized farms which contribute to the maintenance of agriculture throughout the territory.
- mr commissioner, we obviously share the commission's concerns - which are those of everyone - about the dangers of smoking to public health. but given the european union's tobacco deficit, it is obviously the demand that must be addressed, not the supply. let us recall two figures: 800 000 tonnes of raw tobacco consumed, 250 000 tonnes produced in the european union. europe imports 70% of its raw tobacco needs, the european union is by far the world's largest importer. it is therefore obvious that any action to reduce production would only increase our dependence on imports. but i am particularly concerned about the social effects of such measures. it is important to remember that the very labour-intensive tobacco industry is made up of 130 000 farms and 400 000 seasonal workers, which means more than 500 000 jobs. it is worth mentioning that the first processing employs 18 000 permanent and 40 000 seasonal workers in rural areas. it is worth recalling that tobacco is grown on small family farms with between one and two hectares of tobacco, where tobacco accounts for on average 60% of the family income. it is important to remember that most of these farms are located in disadvantaged areas, where there is a rural exodus, desertification and problems of occupying the rural space of dormant villages. it is worth recalling that tobacco growing, which provides stable incomes, now makes a major contribution to the maintenance of the agricultural population and thus to trade and public service activities. that is why we must approach the architecture of the tobacco cmo with the utmost caution. when the tobacco reform of the wto was adopted in 1998, the parliament and the council planned an evaluation of the reform by the end of 2002. only this evaluation will be able to provide a basis for relevant reflection on the future of european tobacco. i therefore agree with our rapporteur that no decision on the future of the current tobacco regime can be taken until mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, let me remind you that the system of compensation for the extra costs incurred by the outermost regions in the disposal of certain fishery products - wrongly called 'poseidom fisheries' - is based on a simple principle: it consists in supporting the disposal of the species most affected by marketing activity abroad, under conditions comparable to those in which economic operators established on the european continent operate. i welcome the work done by the rapporteur, which corresponds to the expectations of the representatives of the outermost regions of the european union. however, as a fictitious rapporteur, i would like to make two additional remarks. in the exhaustive overview of the advantages facing the outermost regions, the rapporteur omits to mention a difficulty which, however, seems to me to be paramount, namely the problems of access to these areas, which result from the modes of connection between these regions and the continent and the tariffs applied in this respect. and for us in remote areas, this obstacle can go as far as increasing costs by about 30%. i would also like to point out that the rapporteur bases his report - and i welcome this - on article 299 (2) of the treaty of amsterdam, which recommends that the specific features of remote regions be taken into account in all the policies of the european union, especially in the case of fisheries. however, i think it would have been more logical to refer to article 37 of the treaty, which is the very basis of the fisheries and agricultural policies, if that article had not shown its shortcomings when we talk about the outermost regions of the union. it is totally inadequate as it stands, since it takes account exclusively of continental fishing conditions, without taking account of situations linked to the outermost regions. finally, i strongly support the rapporteur's proposal that the commission should send the european parliament a copy of the study it has commissioned from external consultants on the impact of community measures adopted so far in the fisheries sector on the outermost regions. the content of this document would certainly enable us to take account more accurately of the specific situations of these very remote regions of the union.

in writing. - the proposed directive introduces prudential rules (capital requirements and supplementary supervision) for financial conglomerates. our project is the socialisation of these sectors (credit, insurance, investment) because the functions these rules fulfil fall within the logic of public service. in a rational economy, credit should be allocated according to the social utility of investments, and insurance integrated into social investment and social protection funds. the directive is a timid attempt to regulate financial markets, whose chaotic functioning is now recognised as the cause of financial crises and social disasters around the world, as illustrated by the enron affair. i voted for it with no illusions, if only to put a brake on the ultra-liberalism that is in the air and because we are not in favour of the worst-case policy of waiting for the dysfunctions of capitalism to lead to its final crisis. only social mobilisation can put an end to the vagaries of an uncontrollable system.
in writing. - the directive proposes to reduce certain forms of financial crime, and we welcome this noble project. but we will be careful not to be naive. firstly, because, as the rapporteur points out, 'a community regulation would have been preferable. but the treaty doesn't allow it". the fact that criminal sanctions are the responsibility of the states opens the floodgates wide and, as in the case of taxation, encourages the setting up of operations involving several countries. secondly, we do not believe that capitalism can operate in a transparent and fair manner. capitalist competition is a form of warfare that uses all the means at its disposal, agreements, lobbying, arranged accounts and rigged audits, as the news shows us. it is not unusual for institutions that serve capital to suddenly want to control its methods. as for the insiders, it is difficult to see how they could be deterred by declarations of intent, even if they are called directives, since the directive does not provide for any really binding scale of sanctions. despite these reservations, i voted for the directive so as not to impede the minimum measures it contains.
in writing. - i voted for this report. it is clear that the rate of decline and loss of biodiversity in europe and worldwide is accelerating. the measures in place do not seem to be sufficient to reverse current trends, including the decline in the number of species and their habitat, ecosystems and genes. it is up to europe to play a special role of initiative and leadership in this area and not to be content with making wishes which will not be followed by action. as a first step, europe must ensure that environmental legislation is applied. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be given the possibility of adopting the new directive on the protection of the environment. actions in the field of agriculture and fisheries are also to be carried out. agriculture must play a central role, and the new cap cannot afford to ignore reforms which take account of the requirements of sustainable development. as regards fisheries, it is essential to provide for coherent measures in the short and medium term in order to preserve or restore biological diversity where it is threatened. finally, preserving biological diversity does not mean stopping research and the development of knowledge. in the field of gmos, for example, if the precautionary principle is to be applied, then objective scientific validation of these experiments, step by step, should be supported.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report. the european union, and in particular the european parliament, is very much committed to the protection of citizens, their environment, their daily lives and their health. often, balanced texts in these areas are agreed at community level. however, we are aware that the transposition of a number of directives by the member states is unduly delayed. the urban waste water directive is an example of this misapplication. adopted in 1991, it aims to protect the environment from the effects of urban wastewater and biodegradable wastewater discharges from the food industry. when implemented, the directive has led to a significant improvement in water quality. the main obligation of the member states is to set up waste water collection and treatment systems and to respect a pre-established timetable. not only are some member states late in providing all the information necessary for an objective assessment of this directive, but, worse still, others do not provide any information at all. this is totally unacceptable! i therefore ask that the delay in the member states should not be made worse, that all the information be sent to the commission as required by the directive adopted by the council at the appropriate time. i have spoken in favour of the commission initiating infringement procedures in cases where the criteria for identifying sensitive areas have not been respected or taken into account.
in writing. - it is regrettable that the united states has introduced a tax on imported steel, which is detrimental to european interests and apparently breaks free from the rules of the wto. however, on the contrary, we were astonished by the confidence and good conscience with which commissioner lamy was lecturing the americans in this house yesterday on free trade morality. we should recall some of the realities that are being forgotten, and which should lead to greater discretion. firstly, the us surcharge, which could amount to up to 30%, roughly corresponds to the depreciation of the euro since its entry into force, which imposes a real 'monetary dumping' on our trading partners. of course, nobody in europe is talking about it because, unexpected as it is, this depreciation is good for us commercially. it is a very serious problem for our partners. the united states wanted a strong dollar, but it did not want a dollar that was too strong, severely penalizing its own industries. in the steel case, the united states invoked the need for safeguard measures to avoid internal unrest. in this case, they are probably deviating from the wto rules which they themselves have adopted and which are trapping them. but they are a real problem. instead of overwhelming them, should we not instead take the plunge and propose to open a debate on the legitimate exceptions to free trade, for developed countries and even more for underdeveloped countries? europe in particular would do well to think about this if it wants to save its agricultural model in the future. it is also questionable whether commissioner lamy's blistering statements attacking the 'unilateralism' of the us measures will not, beyond the present case, lead (or are not intended) to reinforce the multilateral discipline of simplistic free trade, as it was adopted, by manipulation of public opinion, at the end of the uruguay round. and we shall find out tomorrow that these reinforced disciplines are holding us captive, in turn, to other subjects that are vital to us, such as agriculture. the manipulation continues.
in writing. - the attitude and decisions of the united states aimed at shamelessly protecting their steel industry to the detriment of europe perfectly illustrate that, beyond the great speeches and great liberal declarations, what dominates the world today is the law of the strongest, which is supported, in this case, by george w. bush (read the fable of the fountain "the wolf and the lamb"). that is why europe must react vigorously through the legal means provided for in the wto framework, but also through all the other means of pressure available at a time when the united states is continuing to call for other forms of solidarity in its fight against terrorism. this situation demonstrates the true nature of globalization "by the american way". it reduces to its proper level the talk about the benefits of free competition without rules. it is a comfort to those who think that we need a political europe which can exist and then have a say in the management of world affairs!
in writing. - transatlantic relations are going through a turbulent time. the us government's offensive is at the root of this, taking advantage of its military victory in afghanistan to strengthen and consolidate its superpower. however, the american quest for global supremacy also generates conflict and tension with the ruling classes of the center and periphery of the world. the current dispute over the us import tax on steel is a clear example of this. us imperialism is ready to impose "global deregulation", but does not refuse protectionist measures when it feels its interests are threatened. i did not, however, vote for this joint resolution. this opposition by the eu is only a way of supporting european multinationals in a ruthless economic war. we stand in solidarity with the workers of the world, including those of the united states. we do not support the interests of multinational corporations against others. the more the eu seems to 'fight' the us, the more it adopts its policy. the 'lisbon process', which aims to transform the eu into 'the most competitive economy in the world', is designed to undermine the living conditions of the working world in europe and the third world through liberalisation, privatisation and over-commercialisation.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report. this recommendation is based on a realistic and modern vision of the european economy. the slowdown in economic activity in the united states is having an impact on the european union. this is not, however, sufficient to explain the mixed results recorded by many member states. there are indeed internal problems that need to be solved. structural reforms are expected. every european consumer must be able to choose freely his service provider. the european union is therefore developing an innovative competition policy that rejects all dominant positions. this approach must be supported, including by involving all the parties concerned for greater personal and collective efficiency. it is not a question of reforming against the actors, but of developing these sectors in consultation with them. determined action in the field of education, training and research development is also a key element if we are to maintain a high level of employee competence and ensure optimum competitiveness for our enterprises. the report also proposes raising the retirement age for workers who wish to remain in employment. today, the widespread introduction of compulsory retirement represents a huge waste of skills, talent and experience. these experienced people are still useful in our companies. finally, analysts show that the economic downturn we are experiencing could have been more severe without the existence of monetary union. so those who today, motivated by domestic political considerations, advocate a return to the past are mistaken for centuries, confusing self-interest with the common good.
in writing. - the report by the former trade unionist trentin opens with a line which is clear: "priorities must be to reduce labour costs". he added that the eu should be able to reduce its tax burden and social security contributions while guaranteeing the "integrity of pensions and health services". the report does not understand the reasons for the 1997-2001 recovery and the recent economic reversal, but it is unfazed by the suggestions that strict application of the inapplicable stability pact can only lead to an increase in the current recession. the report emphasizes training and r & d efforts as if, in terms of employment, these expenditures could replace sustained wage demand and widespread reduction in working time. he dares to speak of 'social cohesion' when the reduction of taxes and social contributions he advocates can only lead to a deepening of inequalities. i therefore voted without reservation against this indignitous and hypocritical report, which should put its authors to shame.
in writing. - the title of this report makes its objective clear from the outset: to provide the union with a harmonized tax policy. it is therefore disturbing that the della vedova report opens with a kind of half-hearted admission that tax policy must remain a matter for the member states. the rest of the text, however, advocates the means by which the union can claim the same prerogative. we've come a long way, you know. the text voted in the commission has considerably improved the rapporteur's proposal, which saw a european tax as an opportunity to affirm the federal principle of european integration. the majority of this parliament thought it more prudent to erase this excess of frankness and replace it with a text which, in the end, hides behind a certain form of liberalism, advocating lower taxes and finally calling for the transfer of the instruments of fiscal policy under the control of the community authorities, the commission and parliament itself. in its usual strategy of small steps, this house is making progress, but it is not making progress. and yet she only goes halfway. the proposals on vat are not bold enough. it would have been necessary, on the one hand, to affirm that each nation is sovereign in this matter and, on the other hand, to make proposals that are broader than those aimed at exempting ngos from vat and include, for example, all cultural events produced by non-profit-making associations. a report which clearly affirms the national character of tax policy and recommends improved coordination between member states in this area could have won my vote. i'm afraid i haven't read anything like that.
in writing. - if there was any doubt about the scope of the carnero gonzález report - which calls for the european union to have legal personality - it was removed by yesterday's debate. the speakers attacked with federalist zeal, thus demolishing all the cautious demonstrations which the rapporteur had constructed to prove that his reform was entirely innocent. giorgio napolitano spoke of the establishment of a "supranational entity". andrew duff spoke of the need for the union to become a full-fledged 'contracting party' on the international scene. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the european parliament, the council and the commission. finally, the commission said that this was a 'substantial' reform and that it was committed to supporting the project. it is therefore clear that the purpose of granting the european union legal personality, in addition to the communities, is to create a new actor with full capacity on the international scene, which will in particular use all the potential of article 24 teu (especially as revised after nice) to gradually remove the autonomy of the member states in their foreign policy. europe would then have entered, without the citizens having clearly decided so, the era of the superstate. on the contrary, we believe, as we have said in the minority opinion attached to the report, that the european union must remain an organisation sui generis of major and responsible states - that is to say, major and responsible national democracies - organised in a network. it will be the job of the convention, when it meets in the coming months, to find the combination which best promotes voluntary synergy without killing the freedom of choice of the peoples.

- mr president, tunisia has committed itself to respecting human rights and this is an essential element of the association agreement between the european union and tunisia. but these commitments, which were reiterated at the association council meeting on 29 january, now appear to us to have been violated by the way in which hamma hammami and his friends are being treated by the tunisian government. voluntarily released from the clandestine conditions in which they had been forced to take refuge after the infamous trials of 1997-1998, they were again sentenced on 2 february at first instance and their sentence was confirmed in a sham court hearing which unfortunately confirms the serious failures of the rule of law observed for several years in this country. two hundred lawyers had gathered for the defense. they were harassed by the police while the prisoners were subjected to violence. hamma hammami began a hunger strike on february 26 to protest his current conditions of detention. he was assigned to the death row section of the tunis prison while a political prisoner. this is incompatible with respect for the treaties, in particular with regard to article 2 of the association agreement with the european union on respect for human rights. the urgent need today, a few weeks before the opening of the conference on foreign affairs (barcelona v) to be held in valencia on 22 and 23 april, is to show that we, the members of parliament, are calling on the tunisian authorities to release hamma hammami and his friends. this is a first and essential step towards respecting the rule of law in tunisia. we also ask the commission to demand that tunisia comply with international law and to instruct its parliamentary delegation to take a more firm approach to this matter with the tunisian authorities.
mr president, once again our assembly must take a decision on the violations of human rights in tunisia. today we are talking about the sentencing of three pcot activists. after four years of hiding, the three activists decided to appear in court freely to challenge their conviction in court. the trial on 2 february, as other colleagues have pointed out, was a travesty. they were taken from their seats, abducted by the police in the middle of the court, and in a matter of seconds were sentenced to heavy prison terms: nine years and three years for hamma hammami, without being given the opportunity to speak and without being able to benefit from the assistance of their lawyers. all this happened in front of many tunisian and foreign observers and advocates. they are being held in civilian prison under scandalous conditions. this trial is a travesty of justice. in view of this situation, the council of the tunisian bar association has called for a strike. hamma hammami and abdel jabarmadouri have decided to go on a hunger strike to protest their detention conditions and demand the right to visit their lawyers. these events are part of a continuing campaign of intimidation and repression targeting political opponents, human rights defenders, journalists, trade unionists, students, lawyers and judges. once again we see that the association agreement between the european community and tunisia, which stipulates that relations between the two parties are based on respect for democratic principles and human rights, is being flouted. we call for an extraordinary meeting of the eu-tunisia association council to be held as soon as possible on the issue of human rights. our parliament must demand the release of hamma hammami and his comrades and the respect of article 2 of the agreement. the council and the commission must use all the means provided for in this agreement to ensure respect for democratic freedoms and human rights in tunisia.

mr president, the commission is today presenting a proposal for a directive which requires member states to impose criminal penalties for a number of particularly serious infringements of community environmental law. there is no denying that a more and more degraded environment needs to be protected and that strict enforcement measures are unavoidable. but what is problematic in our view is the commission's intention to use the community instrument of the directive based on article 175 tec for this purpose. this article provides for a number of common actions to be undertaken in the field of the environment, but it fully respects, in accordance with the general philosophy of the treaties, the autonomy of the member states in matters of criminal law. it would be quite specious to claim that the right to impose criminal penalties is implicitly contained in the community's competence to protect the environment, because it is indispensable to its implementation and therefore inseparable from it. if criminal sanctions are implicitly contained in article 175-1, why not also in all the other articles of the treaty which authorise the adoption of community standards in a particular field? this would be tantamount to denying a fundamental principle of the treaty: national jurisdiction over criminal law. and by denying this principle, we would be moving a little further towards the concept of a centralised union which is not what we want. this does not mean that nothing should be done. no , it 's not . the danish presidency had presented a draft framework decision on the protection of the environment through criminal law, which encouraged tougher penalties while better respecting the freedom of states by establishing its legal basis on the third pillar, i.e. on the purely intergovernmental part of the treaty. this way is much better. that is the one, mr president, we should follow.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there are in fact a great many european directives and regulations designed to protect the environment in all its various aspects. but we all know that many of these texts remain dead letters in the absence of effective sanctions. in most cases, the application of financial or material penalties by applying the polluter-pays principle is considered insufficient by a public opinion fully aware of the lack of dissuasiveness of these penalties in view of the considerable profits generated by the activities which are the source of the greatest pollution. we also know that some environmental damage is quite irreversible and therefore not likely to be physically repaired. these considerations therefore justify the adoption by the member states of provisions designed to penalise non-compliance with european environmental requirements. that is why i - together with my fellow socialists - fully support the commission's initiative. however, we must not overlook the main difficulty which we are faced with here, namely the problem of the legal basis. i am of the opinion that the question before us does indeed fall within the powers conferred on the union under the first pillar and therefore requires the adoption of a framework directive by this house. this is the sense of the recommendation voted by our parliament in november 2001. the council should be reminded that if it had finalised its draft framework decision under the third pillar, it would certainly have done so against the political will of the european parliament. in addition, and because we are committed to strengthening environmental legislation by means of effective, proportionate and dissuasive criminal sanctions, we must adopt a solid text that is beyond any legal challenge and is not liable to be sanctioned by the court of justice. this means that we must be particularly vigilant with regard to the principle of subsidiarity and the rules of jurisdiction laid down in the treaty. while the community has the power to require member states to adopt criminal sanctions in the event of infringement of community substantive standards, it does not have the power to define the types and levels of sanctions applicable. we must therefore be particularly careful about references to concepts such as extradition, which refer to a level of seriousness of offences and penalties. i am, however, reassured by the wording adopted more recently by our rapporteur, mrs oomen-ruijten. similarly, the community does not have the power to adopt provisions which result in the approximation of national criminal provisions. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. it is with these observations in mind that i would like to reiterate my full support for the adoption of this text and my congratulations to the rapporteur, mrs oomen-ruijten. this text is a strong political signal to us in relation to a form of crime which is increasingly being misunderstood by our fellow citizens.
commission. – mr president, i wish to thank mrs oomen-ruijten and mr di lello finuoli for their excellent work on two texts that cover the same subject: the proposal for a directive and a draft framework decision on the protection of the environment through criminal law. both reports contribute significantly to an important european-union-level debate. the extraordinary european council meeting in tampere in 1999 agreed in that common definitions, common incriminations and common sanctions should be established in a limited number of sectors of particular importance, and among those sectors it highlighted the environmental crime issue. as the house will recall – and several members referred to it – in 2000, denmark presented an initiative for a framework decision on combating serious environmental crime. this framework decision is based on the rules of the treaty on european union and therefore belongs to the third pillar. in 2001 the commission adopted a proposal for a directive on the same subject, which is based on article 175 of the european community treaty. both proposals pursue the same objective. they seek to improve the implementation of community environmental law and have the same starting point: we all recognise that there is a lack of effectiveness in the protection of the environment in our member states. nevertheless, the commission has taken a more ambitious approach by proposing a directive. the commission has pursued this line for a number of reasons. the community has, within given competence parameters, the power to regulate behaviours in order to achieve a community objective. the commission has never contested that, as regards concrete criminal sanctions, the community cannot purport to act in the criminal area in isolation. however, to the extent that this is necessary for the achievement of community objectives, the commission is convinced that the community can oblige member states to provide for criminal sanctions where criminal law guarantees that community law is enforced effectively. the commission believes that the sanctions currently established by member states are not enough and that they do not guarantee full compliance with european union law. the commission is not seeking an interinstitutional conflict. the key aim of our proposal is to create an additional guarantee of impartiality and to give authorities greater scope for cross-border investigations of environmental crimes. mr blokland, this is the reason why it is necessary to have a framework decision together with the directive. we can provide for the provision of criminal sanctions in the directive, but the concrete scope of those criminal sanctions must be included in the framework decision. the framework decision has the leverage to allow the judicial authorities of the member states to pursue cross-border investigations on environmental crimes. whether measures concerning criminal law should be based on the rules of the european union treaty or of the european community treaty, is not just an interesting legal question for european lawyers, it is of fundamental institutional importance, in particular as regards the role and powers of the european parliament, the jurisdiction of the court of justice and the legal effects of european legislation in this area. i can fully subscribe to the arguments that have been put forward by mrs oomen-ruijten. i would like to inform you that the commission has never called into question the fact that matters of judicial cooperation belong to the third pillar. the draft framework decision is therefore to be seen as a complementary text to the directive. all the amendments tabled seek to transform the draft framework decision into a complementary instrument to the commission proposal for a directive. all the fundamental aspects of the issue are covered by the commission proposal for a directive. the council framework decision will deal with three relevant matters: liability of legal persons, jurisdictional competence and issues concerning extradition and prosecution. we respect subsidiarity because the framework decision put forward by denmark very closely follows the council of europe convention concerning environmental crime. to date, nobody has accused the council of europe convention of being against the principle of subsidiarity. the reports by mrs oomen-ruijten and mr di lello finuoli follow exactly this same line. on behalf of the commission, i therefore welcome the opinion on the draft framework decision by legal affairs and the internal market, for their valuable input and support, especially as they all had to work within very tight time limits on a very complex matter. i hope that the reports will in writing. - i voted against the oomen-ruijten report which supports the commission's claim to include the principle of criminal sanctions against offenders in the community's environmental protection powers. as i said in yesterday's debate, we must instead follow the wise approach of the danish presidency, which is urging the member states to tighten up sanctions in this area, but within an intergovernmental framework, and without removing this aspect of criminal law from national competence. in fact, the oomen-ruijten report and the commission proposal which it supports show how, by a short-sighted logic, where each step seems to be the natural consequence of the previous one, but without any attempt to take a global view, europe is gradually drifting towards an increasingly uniform model. officially, no one wants the ultimate consequences of this model that would make the nations disappear. but in every concrete case, in every small step that has to be taken, it is the standard solution that is always presented as the most rational. this is how the practical europe is gradually diverging from the europe of intentions, much to the discomfort of the citizens.
in writing. - the standoff between the commission directive and the council framework decision to 'penalise' article 174 of the treaty raises the question: who is doing what in europe? while the convention deals with the division of competences between the eu and the member states, this project entails an extension of community law beyond the letter of the treaties. until 2004, let us apply the principle of institutional precaution. should environmental crime be made part of the community acquis and should we say that this objective will be better achieved at union level? in the framework of the amsterdam treaty, this issue falls under the third pillar (judicial cooperation in criminal matters). the aim of punishing all breaches of environmental legislation is an unrealistic goal, which is intended to satisfy the demands of a few powerful but unrepresentative environmental lobbies. i also do not share the view of the di lello finuoli report which calls on the council not to take any action on criminal environmental law until the draft directive on environmental protection has been adopted. each member state must be able, under its national law, to classify as criminal offences those listed in the framework decision. penalising certain offences is appropriate, provided that only the most serious offences are punishable and that they are of a cross-border nature. the battle must be fought on an international scale. in writing. - the argo programme is a good programme, designed to promote cooperation between national administrations in the implementation of common rules on external border control, visas, asylum and immigration. it is not a question of defining this policy - on which we would have much to say - but only of training the administrations to work effectively, which is obviously a very desirable objective. we have two reservations, however, which led us to vote against the oostlander report. - the argo programme is organised in partnership between the commission and the member states, but this partnership appears to be unbalanced. in particular, if the actions to be taken are proposed by the national administrations, the commission alone has the right to select the actions selected, after hearing, for a simple "consultation", a committee of national representatives. the european parliament has further strengthened the commission's prerogatives by its amendments, and this has gone beyond what the commission itself wanted. - an amendment was voted which calls for the status of refugee to be recognised from now on for persons who are the subject of 'persecution by any state or by any other state'. this extremely broad wording would open the door to asylum to a host of new immigrants. this is a very irresponsible measure and has nothing to do with the original subject of the report.
in writing. - we are today presented with a proposal for a council regulation laying down the conditions for determining the member state responsible for examining an application for asylum. this regulation builds upon and improves the existing provisions of the dublin convention. we welcome it, because it is the result of a serious approach, the commission having worked closely with the national experts. the basic principle that the member state of first entry is responsible for processing the asylum application is maintained, but a corollary principle is added: each member state is responsible vis-à-vis all the others for its action in relation to the entry and residence of third-country nationals, and must bear the consequences in a spirit of solidarity and loyal cooperation. in particular, when illegal immigrants apply for asylum in one member state, while they have previously been staying illegally in another, the latter must process the asylum application and cannot reject it. it is clear that these provisions will apply exactly to the case of france, which is knowingly allowing illegal immigrants to gather in sangatte and its surroundings and then seek asylum in britain. many amendments to this proposal for a regulation have been put forward by the very active group of far-left pro-immigration meps. most of them were fortunately rejected. however, some questionable amendments were passed, which justify our reservations about the marinho report.
in writing. - this proposal for a regulation will suffer from the same shortcomings as the dublin convention, since the basic principles remain basically the same. the heaviest burden is shifted to the countries in the east and south which have to take in the most asylum seekers. however, this report does allow us to make some progress and it contains positive points which should not be overlooked and that is why we voted for it. only one member state is responsible for the asylum application and the concern for family reunification is given greater weight, and personal data concerning asylum seekers and their family members are relatively protected. the replacement of the convention by a regulation therefore depends on the interpretation and review of the court of justice and the commission; the european union is therefore taking a further step towards the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice.
in writing. - we abstained on the von boetticher report on amendments to the procedure for crossborder surveillance (article 40 of the convention implementing the schengen agreement of 14 june 1985) because, as i said in yesterday's debate, it tends to turn this right of follow-up in surveillance into a right of wider intervention which can lead to a great confusion of responsibilities in a europe without internal frontiers. in addition, it also tends to make crossborder surveillance a kind of one-off palliative for the dysfunctions of the police services of certain states, in which their neighbours could intervene more easily. for example, the explanatory statement of the european parliament is somewhat surprised to read the following comments from the german ministry of the interior (i quote without changing a word): 'a neighbouring member state continues to insist officially that it be entrusted with border surveillance. problems arise when the observers concerned interrupt the observation due to national provisions restricting working hours beyond a certain observation period, and/or do not resume the next day due to a lack of staff.' i hope the name of this mysterious state bordering germany doesn't start with the letter "f". in any case, the solution to the problem cannot be found in a wider police intervention in each other's homes.
- mr president-in-office of the council, mr president, commissioners, we must not pay for words. the sad fact is that despite some positive signs, such as the decisions to implement the galileo satellite positioning programme and to build the a 400 m military transport aircraft by 2008 after endless and laborious negotiations, european defence has not been able to be structured in concrete terms and has mostly remained at the semantic or comitology stage. the reason why european defence is not doing well is that the method of variable geometry is not clearly applied, which would allow the states which are determined to act to define common strategic interests and to deduce the means to implement them. the result of this error of method is that we still lack the essential elements which meet our common defence needs. we still do not have a european arms agency. the european union is not only a member of the european union but also a member of the european union, and it is also a member of the european union. we have no missile defence programme: denouncing the american project is the policy of the europeans in this field. finally, defence spending is falling everywhere except in the united kingdom. over the last ten years, defence budgets have been the adjustment variable for most of our governments: the decline in both volume and percentage is impressive. the shock of the events of 11 september and the obvious need to wage a permanent battle against terrorism have not, strangely enough, given the fact that we are equally exposed, given european leaders the necessary start. it is time, however, to abandon once and for all the false rhetoric of the peace dividend. to meet the new threats, our countries will not spare a substantial increase in their defence effort. the task will be all the more difficult as we have become accustomed to certain facilities in europe;
