- mr president, the community patent should not be a missed opportunity. everybody wants it, but nobody can get it done. two dates mark this cross-border project: 1975 and 1989, both unsuccessful attempts. in lisbon, the heads of state and government made it a priority. the community patent was due to be issued by the end of 2001. the need and urgency of this were stressed at the feira, stockholm and gothenburg councils. what about today? the council has not reached an agreement. parliament, through its committee on legal affairs, which is responsible for the substance of the matter, is proposing a political compromise which i congratulate mrs de palacio on, but which does not seem to me to meet the expectations of future users, because it does not bring about any major improvement over the existing system. the industrialists and inventors are asking for a reduction in the cost of patents, so that they can become competitive. they also want to ensure that legal certainty is respected in the most equitable manner. the european commission's proposal is a pragmatic response to these aspirations. it concerns cost reductions, in particular through the linguistic regime for the three working languages of the european office, which, by ensuring the threshold of international competitiveness, is compatible with our linguistic specificity, the recognition of the privileged role of the national offices for the specific tasks of information and technical assistance to inventors and smes and, finally, a judicial system guaranteeing the unitary character of the court by the establishment of a community intellectual property court. these three main points were supported by the professionals. they're the ones waiting for the patent. let us not take the risk of creating a community patent which they will not use because it is too far removed from their concerns. that is the signal we must send to the council with our vote tomorrow.

mr president, the debate on the evolution of pension systems is taking place against the backdrop of the new demographic context in europe, a real challenge, indeed posed by the constant increase in the number of people reaching retirement age, an increase linked to the increase in longevity. in this context, it is in the name of respect for the stability pact and the fight against public deficits that the commission and the council have often pushed for this reform of the pension system. if national competences in the field of pensions are not called into question, it is the open method of coordination, an integrated approach to national strategies to ensure safe and sustainable pensions, which is proposed to us and which was the subject of mr fatuzzo's report. the question is what is the meaning of such cooperation, and how can the objective of secure and sustainable pensions be achieved? the questions of the age of retirement, the guarantee of rights, remuneration and, in short, retirement conditions, are all the more sensitive because they arise at the end of a whole professional and human career and are the guarantee of a positive and solidary link between generations. it is good that mr fatuzzo's report recognises that the pension debate must not be limited to funding issues but that rights must be guaranteed. it is also good that it proposes to strengthen the open method of coordination through democratic will by bringing together ngos, social partners, candidate countries and the european parliament to define effective indicators and monitoring mechanisms for the evaluation of reforms and modernisation. but the report still supports the commission's broad lines for a universal pension scheme, even if it introduces a caveat by calling for the preference of collective funded pension schemes over individual pension and savings schemes. i do not know whether this will help to clarify mrs van lancker's question, but in substance the report supports the commission's intention to strengthen the ad hoc reserve pension funds and not to touch on public expenditure in the context of compliance with the stability pact. we all have in mind, however, the barcelona european council which mentioned the objective of extending the retirement age in the countries of the union by five years by 2010. of course, there is the question of funding. the development of the distribution system in the new demographic context cannot be envisaged without an increase in funds. it would be irresponsible. new resources are therefore to be found. in our view, two directions should be given more consideration: the effort to develop and implement employment, quality employment for new contributors, and at the same time the contribution of financial income at the same rate as wages, which is the subject of an amendment by my group.
- mr president, i too would like to thank mr fatuzzo for his report, which, as always, is presented with great passion and is in line with the demographic context, as the secretary-general of the united nations has just emphasized at the second world assembly on ageing, which is currently taking place in madrid. he reminded us that by 2040 there will be more people over 60 than under 15 in the world. the prospects for european demographic change are even more significant, as 40% of the european population will be 65 years or older by 2025, according to eurostat. the consequences of this ageing population - filtering systems, the installation of walled gardens, portals where operators guarantee the quality of the sites to which they give access. the community action plan for safer internet use also application of the recommendation by radio and television broadcasters, all member states now have systems in place which precede programmes which may harm minors with an audible warning or accompany the programme with a visual symbol. we know very well that "closed" hours for children no longer make sense today because our children are very good at recording broadcasts while they are quietly sleeping. in addition, the filtering systems are only used with digital television. so it will be easier to filter when digital tv is in place, but for now, it is very gradual. the commission commissioned a study in 1999 on parental control of television programmes, which advocates leaving a large margin for self-regulation while ensuring that filtering devices are available to families at an affordable price. i agree with all the members who support self-regulation on the condition that it is based on legislation. this is the direction we must work in the future. let me conclude, mr president, by answering a few specific questions put by members. first of all, i would like to say to the rapporteur that it would be premature to present a new report by the end of 2002, but we will take all the comments made by parliament into account in the context of the review. we will continue our work but the report will probably not be ready by the end of 2002. secondly, as regards the classification system: a new study on classification was launched by my departments in january and is due to be completed by the second half of 2002. it will be sent to parliament, we will discuss it and draw the consequences. thirdly, as regards media education: as i have said many times, this is one of my prerogatives, one of my objectives. our children learn to read and write and do arithmetic, more or less well, but they never learn to read and control this society of images around them. that's why we started the first pilot projects for image education. this is why the next net-days in november 2002, which will bring together hundreds of thousands of school classes in most member states and beyond in other parts of the world, will also be devoted to image education and image analysis this year. so our approach is very concrete. i would like to draw your attention to the fact that a commissioner, parliament or the commission alone cannot deal with all these matters. the proposals will therefore be studied in liaison with all the commissioners responsible for the areas which affect this issue, as well as with the institutions other than the commission with responsibilities in this area, such as europol. we need a concerted effort. we will continue to implement it.

- the next item is the report (a5-0035/2002) by mrs de sarnez, on behalf of the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, on the communication from the commission to the european parliament and the council on the strengthening of cooperation with third countries in the field of higher education (com (2001) 385 - c5-0538/2001 - 2001/2217 (cos)).
mr president, i would like to thank all the members who have contributed to the improvement of this text by their amendments, and the rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, who has drawn up a very good opinion. the report i am presenting to you aims to examine, on the basis of the commission's communication, the means to be employed to improve the competitiveness and attractiveness of the member states on the international training market. we all know that training is a major issue for the years to come. students from all over the world are increasingly looking beyond their own borders for the education that offers them the best opportunities. this is the beginning of a truly international training market. however, the presence of students from third countries is lower in europe than in the united states, australia or canada, to name a few examples. we therefore have a considerable backlog to fill and that is why my report makes a number of proposals. firstly, we must have a precise record of the locations of international student mobility, which is not the case at present. it would therefore be useful for the european commission, through eurostat, to work closely with unesco and the oecd to give us a clear and precise picture of the situation of international students in terms of mobility and i think it is finally time to propose a harmonised definition of what qualifies as a foreign student. secondly, we must move towards harmonizing the quality of higher education and the recognition of diplomas and degrees. the european union must be able to offer quality education, regardless of the university or the host country. it is essential that students can start a course of study in one member state and finish it in another with the guarantee that their knowledge gained is validated by a diploma recognised in all member states. i therefore propose that the commission continue to improve its promotion of the system of validation of academic achievement known as ects and to draw inspiration from it in developing new mobility programmes. the creation of joint study programmes between the universities of the member states should also be promoted, with the aim of achieving, as far as possible, the award of joint degrees. thirdly, i propose that a european university label be set up for training modules taught in higher education institutions which are renowned for the quality of their teaching and for the welcome they offer to students from third countries. this university label would not be so much about the quality of the university as an institution as about the modules taught. i am sure that this will help to promote european higher education and send a clear signal to foreign students. fourthly, we must also encourage the promotion of language learning. language learning is an undeniable factor in mobility and it is therefore desirable that the member states systematically introduce foreign language teaching in the form of modules in all higher education courses, but also that foreign students are offered the language of the host country. fifthly, we must also ensure that the reception is of a high quality. universities must now concentrate their efforts on providing this quality welcome for foreign students. the administrative procedures which they will have to face must be facilitated. we must promote their access to housing and to scholarships. this quality of reception will be one of the criteria for the award of the european university label. sixthly, we must build on existing and proven cooperation programmes such as the alpha programme. the future programmes should take into account the development of joint study programmes, the development of a system of mutual recognition of courses and diplomas, and partnerships with companies, local authorities or multilateral organisations. the report i am presenting to you therefore seeks to call on the european union and the member states to mobilize to make european higher education more dynamic, competitive and attractive. this competitiveness, this attractiveness of our european higher education will of course have to begin to take shape first in the member states. the ministers of education of the member states are aware of this and remind each education council of this. i am sure that the european commission and parliament are now ready to do everything possible to achieve the creation of an attractive and competitive european knowledge area, which will finally be able to compete in the international arena. in writing. - the fatuzzo report on the sustainability of pension systems in the european union shows in a fascinating way how brussels manages to take over an issue, as if it were its own responsibility, when not a word of the treaty refers to pensions, which are legally, it is undeniable, a purely national responsibility. as usual, it all begins with cautious communications from the commission, which are intended to show that the sustainability of pensions affects some european competences in a more or less direct way. at the same time, the conclusions of various european councils (lisbon, stockholm, gothenburg, laeken) have included "little phrases" which legitimize the commission's approach. then, to the surprise of many, the barcelona council (march 2002) called for an increase of five years in the average retirement age. we are close to european interference, pure and simple, without any democratic debate. yet, in the background, the ideas expressed are more in the right direction. but this is an essential aspect of the snacking method: for the transfer of competence to be invisible or painless, the policy expressed must first be unquestionable.

the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. i should like to begin by thanking mr hernández mollar for his efforts to reach agreement on his report and the additional amendments to the proposal for a directive under discussion today. the council could reach a final agreement on the proposal today in luxembourg, taking into account the amendments adopted by parliament. the commission will, however, be somewhat dissatisfied with the outcome of the council. the text before the council contains provisions which have watered down the system we are seeking in some areas. despite this negative comment, however, i must say that we still regard the adoption of this proposal as a milestone on the road to a common european asylum policy. the only directive in this field is a directive which provides only temporary protection. this system is only applied in exceptional cases, in the event of a mass influx of displaced persons into the territory of the european union. the directive on the reception of asylum seekers will be the first binding regulation to deal with asylum flows in the union. i should now like to make a few comments on the report and on the amendments to the proposal for a directive which are being discussed today. the changes can be divided into three main categories. firstly, legal amendments which improve the text and which the commission can therefore accept. secondly, substantive changes which are quite reasonable and which will be incorporated in the final version of the directive as it will be adopted. these are amendments deleting any reference to asylum procedures and those aimed at preventing differentiation of reception conditions according to the asylum procedure in force. thirdly, substantive changes which are not problematic for the commission but which will not be passed by the council because they are contrary to the fundamental interests of one or more member states, for example changes which remove any reference to the possibility for member states to apply a voucher scheme. amendments extending the scope of the directive to other forms of protection not based on the geneva convention on refugees fall only partly into this category. the commission has always supported a solution such as that proposed in these amendments, at least as the objective for the second phase of the common european asylum system. in the present proposal, however, the commission had decided to leave the decision on the extension of the scope of application to the member states for the time being. the council remains open as to how to ensure that the relevant provisions of this directive are adapted after the adoption of the directives on subsidiary protection and asylum procedures. i said at the beginning that the commission sees the adoption of the proposal as a milestone towards a common european asylum system. it is also extremely important that the other three pillars of the common asylum system are quickly implemented: the directive on the granting of refugee status and subsidiary protection, the regulation on the member state responsible for examining an asylum application and the amended directive on asylum procedures. these three will be presented again by the commission shortly and are intended to complete the first phase in the establishment of the common european asylum system, as envisaged in the tampere conclusions. in several member states, citizens are already expressing fears in the face of the flows of migrants and asylum seekers. extremist political movements are gaining ground, calling for the unconditional rejection of these people. it is therefore high time that we agreed on a uniform european regulation in this area in order to channel the flows of migrants and asylum seekers in an orderly way. i believe that this is the best way of overcoming these fears, while fully respecting our international human rights obligations and the humanitarian tradition of our member states. in conclusion, let me also express our deep regret, also on the part of the commission, for the accident reported earlier. realise the tremendous potential offered by tourism. i welcome the commission's efforts in its communication to propose an operational framework for european tourism and a series of measures and actions to be implemented by the various actors concerned. the commission stresses the complexity of this sector, given its diversity and its transversal nature, which gives it little political visibility and little representation of its real economic and social importance. but the commission is lacking in ambition: its proposal cannot be a genuine stimulus since it does not envisage a real strategic framework to support an industry with great potential but which is fragile in its growth. i agree with all the recommendations contained in mrs torres marques' excellent report, in particular the inclusion of tourism in the convention for the future of europe, and i believe that joint action is not incompatible with national promotional actions. employment in tourism is often highly seasonal and precarious, which is an obstacle to sustainable development. i therefore ask the commission to make proposals as soon as possible to include catering, and possibly other tourist services which are not yet eligible for this measure, in the list of sectors of activity which can benefit, on a permanent basis, from the application of a reduced rate of vat in order to develop employment in this field, to modernise these professions, to better position european tourism in the face of international competition. in addition, there is an urgent need to acquire and disseminate management and technological know-how in order to promote new production methods and to promote a tourist offer that responds as closely as possible to market developments. tourism is also a decisive element in the economic development of the least favoured regions, in particular the outermost regions, where it is the largest industry in terms of revenue, and contributes to a large extent to the efforts to bring their economies closer to the average rate of development in the community. developing well in the long term: tourism must be a sustainable source of income for local economies while safeguarding and enhancing the richness of the landscape, culture, history and environment. finally, i would like to stress the key role that the european union should play in promoting new forms of tourism in new places, in particular by introducing continental europeans to the attractiveness of the most remote european destinations.
mr president, the commission communication and the european parliament's report on tourism show how european powers can be extended in defiance of any subsidiarity. the starting point: the treaty does not provide for community competence in the field of tourism, since it contains only a specific reference to article 2, which cannot serve as a legal basis. this is a common sense position: tourists who visit a region are attracted by the local specificities and therefore, in the member states, this is a local or regional competence, strictly national. while international cooperation may be desirable, it must remain flexible between public and private partners, without being necessarily confined to the administrative rigidities of the community system. the european parliament and the commission are obviously not listening to it. they want to integrate tourism into community policies and create a framework programme with an appropriate budget line (see paragraph 12 of the draft resolution) with community administrative means (see paragraph 44) and even, one might say, a kind of planning. what are their reasons? tourism is important for growth. it can be a tool for development or a creator of jobs: it is already indirectly affected, directly or indirectly, by several community policies. the report submitted to us even adds that the attacks of 11 september have in turn affected tourism, and that a european tourism policy has become necessary to respond to the shock. these arguments are interesting, but none of them is decisive for deciding whether such a policy should be pursued at community level. in fact, article 5 tec has only one criterion. will the proposed action be carried out more effectively if it is dealt with in brussels? the argument presented in the report seems to be very weak or even non-existent on this point. our committee on industry, in its opinion, had a revealing phrase. after correctly pointing out that there is a lack of clarity as to what would be covered by a community policy on tourism, she added, 'the fact remains that there are common needs which need to be identified'. in other words, you don't know what you need, but you need it. in conclusion, it is clear from this report that the commission and the european parliament are able to demonstrate that anything and everything falls within their competence. if we let them do that, the extension would be infinite. it is therefore essential that the next intergovernmental conference establishes a genuine subsidiarity control, that is to say, an external control of the community institutions.

- madam president, immigration into our countries was originally mainly labour immigration. it was a relationship between the immigrant and the host country, where each was responsible for the other. then came a period of uncertainty and compromise in aid immigration. finally, in recent years, it has become a real immigration of slaves: illegal workers, prostitutes and slaves as we see them by the hundreds in the streets of all our capitals. this situation, where we see immigrants and host countries falling victim to the advocates of uncontrolled immigration, is obviously intolerable. it is the result of thirty years of european left wing evangelicalism, whose good feelings are matched only by disastrous results. it is certainly a good thing to talk about it here, but in conclusion, i will tell you that all this must be handled with the utmost care. we cannot decide for the people whose surnames they will bear, whose neighbours they will be. these are essential things and to go too far and risk killing nations, you would also - perhaps you will pay more attention to this - risk killing europe.
the council has already taken a number of decisions on the basis of the commission's proposals. i am not going to make any personal comments, but the first comment i am going to make does, but i am doing it because i feel that i agree with a good number of my colleagues in the council on it. immigration is, without any doubt, the most important phenomenon that has occurred, is occurring and will continue to occur in the european union in the coming years. it is a phenomenon which is likely to bring about changes far greater than the creation of the eu itself and the progress made in shaping it. it is therefore a matter in which we must act with the necessary finesse, with sufficient balance and with prudence in what we say and, above all - and this is much more important - in what we do. i think we must work to bring the positions of all the countries of the union closer together in this area, because, among other things, we are already, at the very least, an area of free movement of people, goods, etc. the ideas on which i believe we have been working in recent times are the following: firstly, europe can be - indeed it is, it has been and it can continue to be in the future - a host country, because there are people who can certainly earn a decent living here and because, moreover - let us not be mistaken - there is a great deal of activity by many people who contribute to the economic growth of our countries. but - and this is the second point i wanted to make here - immigration must be done legally and it must be made clear that it cannot be infinite, for, among other reasons, infinite immigration generates infinite marginality. in this respect, we must make an effort to act with the greatest possible responsibility. thirdly, we must make an effort to integrate people who come from outside and those who live in the european union. the public administrations of the countries of the union and their own societies are undoubtedly making and should make this effort to integrate, but it is also appropriate to require all those who come from outside to accept the basic rules of coexistence that we have in the countries of the european union, which are our constitutions, our principles and our values, because this affects us all. immigrants certainly have rights, but they must also have obligations, just as we have as nationals of the countries of the european union. the fourth idea is that illegal immigration must be fought vigorously. indeed, by improving our police systems, visas and border controls. i believe that the action plan against illegal immigration is a good way forward and that it must lead to many rules which will help us to be more effective in the future, but i would also like to point out, as i said at the beginning of my speech - and this is an aspect on which i want to place particular emphasis - that we must make immigration policy the basic axis of the european union's foreign policy, which - i think - is pure common sense if we admit, as i think we almost all admit today, that immigration is the most important phenomenon of our times. those were my opening remarks. i would also like to clarify some of the subjective sense it can be radically anti-objective, but in any case, if it is of any use to those who support this thesis, i would remind them to make a comparison with what has happened in the past: it is not wrong to remember that the area of security, justice and freedom is born, practically, in amsterdam, which comes into force in 1999, and that there is a very important part of the union, the economic part, which has existed for years but which had to pass almost fifty years before we had the euro and today there are still many member states which, by their legitimate right, do not have because everyone wanted it, but we have also emphasized active policies, such as integration policies and policies to promote legality. we have discussed a general approach in the council on the proposal for a directive on the reception of asylum seekers. the action plan to combat illegal immigration has very important preventive measures. we have launched a series of dialogues with the countries of origin and transit, including the asian countries. we have made progress in the directives on illegal immigration which contain integration measures and we have made progress in the action plans of the union itself, so i do not think that such statements are fair. the council has already adopted a general approach to the directive on the conditions of asylum seekers on the same day as parliament's opinion, but we are now going to work on fifteen and we are going to take account of the various suggestions that are made to us from this parliament, as we have always done. as regards the european police - another of the issues that have been raised with me - we will be presenting a feasibility study on the 30th in rome. it is a study led by the italian government and in which three or four other countries of the european union, including spain, are collaborating. as for the green paper, i think it is appropriate and that it is necessary to make progress in european repatriation policies. i think we would be making a huge mistake if, in the fight against illegal immigration, we did not make a cooperative effort with the countries from which immigrants come. it is true that this effort must be accompanied by policies of cooperation. that's why i said it was basic that immigration policy be considered as a key policy in our foreign policy. but how can we not support the green paper which the commission has put forward! finally, with regard to some of the comments made on racism and xenophobia, i would like to say that at the last meeting of the jha council in april, after a communication from various countries of the european union and also from the current presidency, we adopted a declaration against racism and xenophobia. the fact is that statements against racism and xenophobia can be adopted - and they should be adopted, because fortunately we are part of one of the most civilized and most respectful spaces for the rights and freedoms of people all over the world - but such approval is perfectly compatible with the observance of the law and with the fight against illegal actions that, in the matter of immigration, we see occurring every day as well. i think that is the council's position on this matter. these are the lines we are working on and will continue to work on until the end. i am grateful for the words and the efforts of the commission, which undoubtedly guides all the council's actions, and i am also grateful for the suggestions, comments, opinions and criticisms which members have expressed here and i thank the president for her patience in allowing me to use the floor for longer than i should have. - the joint debate on - the statements by the council and the commission on the eu-russia summit of 28 may 2002 and - the report (a5-0156/2002) by mrs hoff, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, on the commission communication to the council on the european union and kaliningrad (com (2001) 26 - c5-0099/2001 - 2001/2046 (cos))
the european union, aware of the role russia plays on the international scene, has given this country a prominent place in the field of its external relations. the european union has also been involved in the negotiations with the united states, which have been a major factor in the success of the negotiations. in june 1999, the european union adopted a common strategy with regard to russia, the ultimate aim of which was to strengthen the strategic partnership between the two parties. it is primarily intended to promote the consolidation of democracy, the rule of law and a market economy in russia and to strengthen stability in europe, promoting global security and addressing common challenges on the european continent through enhanced cooperation. on 29 may, the 9th eu-russia summit will be held in moscow, and we will take stock of our relations in the various areas, building on the results achieved after the previous summit, which took place in brussels last october. the progress made since then will be noted and new objectives will be set for our relations. the european union and russia have held numerous meetings since the last brussels summit. the partnership and cooperation agreement, the contractual basis of our relations, has proved to be a highly effective instrument for a fluid dialogue in its various aspects. the guidelines, moreover, set out by the laeken european council, have set out concrete guidelines for the union's policy towards russia. the first eu-russia cooperation council, held in luxembourg on 16 april, was an important contribution to the preparations for the summit, whose agenda is being finalised in these days. the formal preparations for the summit began with a series of working meetings held in brussels by the presidency, the commission and the general secretariat of the council with the russian side on 29 april and 13 may. on 23 april, in brussels, president prodi, accompanied of course by the commissioner responsible for external relations, mr patten, and the russian prime minister, mr kassianov, also met in preparation for the summit. on 27 may, also in moscow, on the eve of this meeting, mr rato, the second vice-president of the spanish government, will present the euro to the russian financial sector, together with mr solbes, the union's commissioner for economic affairs. on the same day, a conference on the integration of the european union and russia in the 21st century will be held in moscow, with the participation of various representatives of the russian government, also of the commission and myself on behalf of the presidency. it is important to note that the eu-russia summit will take place a few days after the russia-us summit, with president bush in moscow. this meeting between russia and the united states will take place from 24 to 26 may. and just one day after the nato/russia summit, we will have our summit with russia on 29 may. so there is a sequence where, from 24 to 26 may, russia will have the summit with the united states, then on 28 may the agreement with nato will be signed in rome and then the eu/russia summit will take place in moscow. with regard to the development of the summit and to date, the european union and russia have agreed on a draft agenda covering the following items: latest developments in the russian federation and the european union, security issues and joint fight against terrorism, eu/russia relations and international issues relating to different regions of the world. i'll allow myself to develop some of these points. firstly, as regards the latest developments in the russian federation, the summit will address the whole process of reforms under way. secondly, in the section on developments in the european union, the community side will report on the state of the enlargement negotiations, the development of the discussions within the framework of the european convention and developments in security and defence policy. on security and the joint fight against terrorism, russia intends to report on the results of the russia/united states and russia/nato summits - today, after the announcement of the reduction of nuclear warheads, this consultation is particularly important. the situation of cooperation in the fight against terrorism will also be reviewed. this issue, as you can well understand, is a priority for both the union and the russian federation. relations between the european union and russia are logically to be seen in several points on the agenda. a joint statement, to be issued at the end of the summit, will contain the conclusions of the parties on the many points covering the chapters of relations between russia and the european union. the declaration will follow the same structure as the last brussels summit and will deal with foreign policy, security and defence, cooperation in the fields of justice and home affairs, kaliningrad, the common european economic area, trade and investment, energy dialogue, the environment and nuclear safety, and cooperation in science, technology and space. i shall deal briefly with all these points later. as regards international issues of mutual interest, the middle east, afghanistan and the balkans have been identified by both sides as priority issues where the exchange of information is particularly useful, as both the european union and the russian federation share concerns and responsibilities in these areas. the european union also has a particular interest in working with the russian federation in conflict prevention in areas of common interest, such as moldova, particularly with regard to the transdniester conflict. as regards foreign policy, security and defence, we hope to agree at the next eu-russia summit on an ad hoc declaration on strengthening dialogue and cooperation in political and security matters. the declaration should reflect the progress made in the implementation of the new cooperation mechanisms agreed at the brussels summit. the declaration shall also refer to the document expected to be adopted at the seville european council on modalities of consultation and cooperation between the european union and russia in the field of crisis management. this important document will be a development and a concrete expression of the general principles on cooperation between the european union and russia in this field, which were adopted at the previous summits in paris, moscow and brussels, and at the european council in nice. as regards cooperation in the field of justice and home affairs, a result has already been achieved which the summit will recognise, namely the holding, on the initiative of the union presidency, of a ministerial meeting of the ministers of justice and home affairs of the russian federation and of the union ministers on 25 april. this was the first time that the union and the russian federation ministers met to discuss common issues, mainly those relating to organized crime, immigration and the fight against terrorism. the results of this ministerial meeting highlight the adoption of the joint resolution on the designation of central contact points for the exchange of information on organised crime in the framework of the action plan against organised crime in russia. the ministers also discussed the situation in kaliningrad, which is of particular interest to russia. i shall refer to this in the following, because the situation in the kaliningrad enclave is of particular importance for relations between russia and the european union. in the very near future, this russian enclave, which is currently surrounded by lithuania and poland, will be, when these two countries join the union, an enclave within the territory of the community. it is therefore one of russia's priorities in its relations with the european union to be able to find a satisfactory solution, above all, to the problems of free movement of persons. this essential problem of movement and transit of persons lies in transit between the enclave and the rest of the territory of the russian federation during the period between the accession of the candidate countries to the union and the full implementation of the schengen acquis by them. the question was discussed between the fifteen and russia at the justice and home affairs ministerial meeting, which i have already mentioned, and the russian federation delivered a memorandum on the matter. this issue was also raised during the recent visit of prime minister kassianov to the european commission. of course, russia's positions do not entirely coincide with what the member states have agreed, and we as the presidency have made considerable efforts to establish a common position, taking into account the interests of poland and lithuania, as future partners of the union, which have been kept informed of the progress of the discussions with russia on this subject. this common line has been confirmed by coreper and has been conveyed to the russian side. for socioeconomic problems, various activities in the project and implementation phases will involve the allocation of some eur 40 million from the union under the tacis programme, for a package of measures aimed at developing various activities within the enclave. to this amount must be added the bilateral contributions of the member states. the european union is certainly open to exploring with the russian side other forms of financing which will allow the living standards of the inhabitants of kaliningrad to be placed in the context of the general economic level of the surrounding area, mainly the two member states, poland and lithuania, which we hope will soon be able to become members of our union. as regards the common european economic area, which is another major theme of this bilateral relationship, the high-level group for the development of the concept of a common european economic area was formally set up on 6 march 2002 and met on 26 march. in december 2001, a first informal meeting took place. the summit will hear an interim report on this issue, which will form the basis for the ad hoc declaration suggested by the russian side. the union would like to see russia declare its intention to adopt european standards by approximating its legislation to the community acquis. at the commission meeting with prime minister kassianov, to which i referred earlier, the russian prime minister said that he was aware that the most important part of the legislative approximation task lies with russia and that the results of the high-level group will be presented at the summit in autumn 2003. i now turn to russia's accession to the world trade organisation. the negotiations on accession to the european union are continuing, following the considerable momentum given to them since last autumn. the main differences at present lie in the agriculture, services and telecommunications sectors. at the meeting with prime minister kassianov, mr lamy, the commissioner responsible for trade, said that russia's declaration on energy prices would also be a condition for progress in the wto negotiations. it does not appear that substantial progress will be made between now and the summit. it will show the impetus for the process with a high frequency of meetings. the view of russia as a market economy is somewhat related to this issue. this is one of russia's main priorities in its relations with the european union and at the recent meeting between commissioner patten, who is here, and commissioner lamy, mr kassianov was shown the commission's willingness to consider granting russia market economy status. it is important to note that the presidency has identified, in its exchanges with the member states, certain difficulties and constraints both in terms of the internal sensitivities within the industrial sectors of the union and in the negotiations with the russian side, which, as i said, are still ongoing. the presidency hopes to reach at least a mutually acceptable solution in principle before the summit. in relation to these two aspects - the wto and the market economy consideration - one of the most important points in the relationship between the european union and russia is the energy dialogue. the main russian concerns in this area include the possible negative consequences of enlargement for its energy exports to the new member states and the attention to the capital from the european union needed for the modernisation of its infrastructure. the union, for its part, insists on the need to create more favourable conditions for foreign investment. another of the constant demands of the community is that russia ratify the treaty we negotiated many years ago, the so-called energy charter and the transit protocol. it is expected that a declaration on energy dialogue will be adopted at this summit, as proposed by the russian side. on this question of the environment and nuclear safety, the community side has told russia that one of the results we would like to see at the summit would be russia's commitment to ratify the text of the kyoto protocol as soon as possible. to this end, the presidents of the council and the commission, mr aznar and mr prodi, respectively, addressed a letter to president puttin prior to the barcelona european council. in relation to nuclear safety, our interest is that russia should sign the agreement called the multilateral nuclear and environmental program in the russian federation. although at the fifth eu-russia cooperation council in luxembourg on 16 april, russian foreign minister ivanov announced that the outstanding issues for the signing of this agreement had been resolved, inconveniences have recently arisen on the russian side which could delay its signing. the importance of environmental aspects in the implementation of the northern dimension action plan is also worth noting. another issue is cooperation in science and technology. since the entry into force of the cooperation agreement with russia in science and technology last may, cooperation relations in this area have progressed. this instrument, together with the international iter agreement, forms the current basis of our joint work. russia may put forward its idea of establishing a joint research and technology centre in the arctic. in principle, the idea may fit within the framework of our scientific and technological cooperation, but we must know precisely what the russian proposals are. as the arctic is an important source of energy supplies for the european union, the possibility of including, where appropriate, the arctic in the energy dialogue should be considered. in conclusion, the ninth summit will serve to take stock of the various aspects of our relations with russia and to set new cooperation objectives for the future. the eu and russia are also expected to strengthen the already important political dialogue and exchange views on key international issues. the union's strategic partnership with russia will thus be strengthened, based on a set of values shared by both countries, of which democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights are essential components.
commission. – i am delighted that we are able to hold this debate in the presence of mrs hoff, whose excellent report i will return to a little later. i am sure that everyone is extremely pleased that she is with us this afternoon. i would like to focus first on the wider issue of the eu-russia summit in moscow at the end of the month. as the presidency has said, this summit will mark the culmination of an intense schedule of high-level meetings between the european union and the russian federation and it comes at a historic moment in relations between russia and the west, with the russia-nato summit in rome at the end of the month. i will not repeat all the important meetings which the presidency has referred to, but we welcomed in particular prime minister kasyanov's visit to the commission on 24 april, and the meeting of european union ministers of justice and home affairs with their russian counterparts was exceptionally important. a special cooperation committee is taking place in kaliningrad this week precisely to discuss all the kaliningrad-related issues. and we continue to hold discussions on crisis management and conflict resolution on a monthly basis with the russian ambassador to the european union. but what about content? is the intense programme of eu-russia meetings making progress? my answer is yes, albeit slowly. there is still a lot that both we and russia need to do to become reliable strategic partners. but we can also welcome many changes that are taking place in russia radically to reform the legal system, the economy, the military and the administration. allow me to comment briefly – i will not cover all the ground covered by the presidency – on the main issues that will be discussed at the summit. we are satisfied with the way relations are developing in the field of esdp, in which russia is a natural key partner. our message to russia, however, is that security and defence policy needs to be seen as part of our broader political dialogue that also covers some of the present "frozen conflicts" in europe, notably transdniestria, which is a source of tremendous instability for moldova, a future european union neighbour. as regards the world trade organisation, we will reaffirm our political support for russia’s accession. but we will not be shy in defending our interests, as in any trade negotiation. as russia’s main trading partner, the european union will play a key role in defining the entry standards in the geneva negotiations. from our perspective, the partnership and cooperation agreement is the point of departure, and russia must, at least, go beyond the concessions already made in it. turning to the related issue of russia’s demand to be treated as a market economy in anti-dumping procedures, the commission has already submitted a proposal to the council that will improve the position of russian companies, and we are looking at whether there is more we can do to meet their concerns. as the presidency said, it was a subject that we were able to discuss with mr kasyanov. we hope that in return russia will be able to respond to our proposals, notably concerning double energy pricing, and the adoption of a conciliation system under the partnership and cooperation agreement to help ensure trade disputes are tackled in an objective, efficient and non-politicised manner. the summit will also examine a progress report from the high level group on a common european economic space. this long-term initiative is meant to underpin russia’s ongoing economic reforms and should help russian companies to take advantage of the prosperity that european union enlargement will bring. against the backdrop of accession to the world trade organisation, cooperation with russia should promote coherence between our respective legislative standards based on studies of the likely benefits for russian industries. the summit will also look at a progress report on the energy dialogue, which moved into a more concrete phase at the brussels summit last october. the presidency referred to the importance of the environment in our dialogue. we will, among other things, be pressing russia to ratify the kyoto protocol, ideally before the un johannesburg summit on sustainable development in september. let me to turn now to the question of kaliningrad, which is rightly high on parliament’s agenda, as demonstrated by mrs hoff’s excellent report and the visit on the ground by the parliamentary delegation for russia in april last year. we will also take careful account of the opinion of the committee on citizens' freedoms and rights drafted by mr oostlander. we share parliament’s view that, as part of russia, kaliningrad is essentially a russian responsibility. we also believe that european union enlargement is an opportunity from which kaliningrad can greatly benefit, rather than a threat. the commission has made huge efforts to work with russia on kaliningrad, addressing both the impact of enlargement and future development policy as part of a comprehensive approach. we have made clear our willingness to increase financial and technical help to deal with the challenges faced by kaliningrad, to facilitate cooperation between customs and immigration authorities in russia, lithuania and poland, and to address the movement of persons and transit issues by exploring the flexibility permitted by the schengen acquis. under excellent leadership from the spanish presidency, member states have recently confirmed that we cannot derogate from the schengen acquis, nor undermine the enlargement negotiations themselves. visa-free transit corridors are not acceptable to the applicant countries. i hope russia will accept this and work with us to make border crossing – which is the real impediment to progress – quicker and easier. efforts are needed from both sides since we need to agree on how to take forward some key issues before further assistance can be offered. in this context, we shall be looking for progress on a readmission agreement and improved cooperation on border management. we also hope that russia will make easier the establishment of consulates in kaliningrad and in mainland russia, and ensure that those who live in kaliningrad are issued with passports that conform with international standards. we hope that the special meeting of the cooperation committee tomorrow in kaliningrad can make further progress on these issues with a view to the moscow summit. i would also like to say a few words on human rights and democratic principles where we continue to have concerns regarding the rule of law and media freedom. the summit will provide a further opportunity to underline the benefits for russia of improving her image in these areas and our willingness to support the development of democratic institutions through tacis. the situation in chechnya remains hugely worrying and reports of human rights violations during so-called "mopping up" operations have not, unfortunately, stopped. our position remains simple and clear. we condemn terrorism world-wide, including in chechnya. our calls for a political solution which, without prejudice to the territorial integrity of the russian federation, satisfies the majority of the chechen people, does not undermine our support for the fight against terrorism everywhere. we will also continue to raise with russia the issue of operating conditions for the delivery of humanitarian aid. in spite of difficult security conditions on the ground, we demand concrete improvements to facilitate the conduct of humanitarian operations according to basic safety and efficiency standards. in parallel, we will insist that any repatriation of chechen displaced persons should only take place on a voluntary and unconditional basis. finally, we also intend to make progress in the field of crisis management and conflict prevention. against the background of our efforts to establish closer political and economic relations, the european union has made clear to russia that it expects her to act in full accordance with the values she committed herself to respect when entering the council of europe and the osce. these basic principles constitute an integral part of the strategic partnership that we are trying to build together. this is a defining period in anchoring russia firmly in the community of democratic nations. against the backdrop of russia’s accession to the world trade organisation and the agreement on a new format for cooperation between russia and nato, we are confident that the eu-russia summit in moscow will bring our bilateral partnership one step forward, rendering our cooperation more concrete and effective. the commission is ready to continue to play an active part in this process. i am confident that the european parliament will continue to make a very valuable contribution as well. i want to make one final, simple point. we share so much with russia: much geography and, in some respects, too much history. the only sensible option for both of us is to make our relationship work as successfully as possible: economically, socially and politically. this is a really significant strategic partnership – a partnership enhanced by enlargement. perhaps we still have some of the ghosts of the past to lay to rest; ancient suspicions to bury once and for all. but the view of the commission is that we should do all we can to make this partnership work and work well. there is no other sensible option. but a partnership involves traffic in both directions: it involves give and take and understanding the other side’s point of view. we understand that, and i am sure our russian colleagues will come to understand that as well. - the european parliament, in contrast to the council and the commission representing governments, is supposed to be the democratic expression of the entire population. but the trentin report shows that if parliament is elected by everyone, the interests it represents are those of the employers' circles alone in opposition to those of the working classes in the union. the amendments requested by the rapporteur of the european parliament all go in the same direction: worsening the condition of the employees. the report calls for flexibility in employment. he advocates what he has the gall to call active ageing, that is, working longer and delaying retirement age. if he speaks of social policy, it is to assert with cynical brutality that it must be a productive factor. for example, if it is considering a policy of continuing training, it is to provide employers with a mobile and skilled workforce according to their needs. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's social policy is not distorted by the introduction of new forms of unemployment. the only social measure in this report is therefore that workers must be warned that they will be made redundant. we shall vote against this text which is designed for the employers.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to concentrate my remarks on the report by mr bruno trentin, first of all to thank him very much for the quality of the contribution which the european parliament will thus make to the elaboration of the broad guidelines of economic policy. i shall deal with two points. firstly, after the commission and the council, the european parliament attaches great importance to the elaboration of the broad economic policy guidelines. simply, if this is to remain an academic exercise, we are wasting our time. these broad economic policy guidelines are only meaningful if, downstream, they make it possible to involve the national parliaments, which, when drawing up the budgets of the member states, will bear these broad economic policy guidelines in mind. they only make sense if, downstream, governments - particularly those in the euro area - agree to coordinate their economic policies more closely, whether in the budgetary, fiscal or structural policy fields. otherwise, what we're doing here is useless. and we wake up when it is almost too late, when the commission is obliged to put in place alert mechanisms. we have a great tool, let's use it to improve coordination. in the same spirit, my second point will be on the contribution that this european parliament can make to the elaboration of the broad economic policy guidelines. we hope that, perhaps through the convention, but also through some practice, the amendments which this parliament is drawing up will be taken more widely into account when the broad economic policy guidelines are finally drawn up. and in this connection i should like to stress three of the amendments which your committee has tabled. the first, amendment no 6, concerns the role of the social partners and the macroeconomic dialogue in order to promote an employment policy. it is, i believe, absolutely essential. the second is amendment no 7, and i would invite some member states to look at it closely when it comes to reducing taxes, a reduction which can only be envisaged in the context of a harmonious balance with the reduction of debt and the rebalancing in favour of public investment. the third amendment will not surprise you: it is in fact two amendments, amendments nos 16 and 18, which very rightly emphasize the importance we must attach to services of general interest as a contribution to the social and territorial cohesion of the union and to the capacity to create jobs.
the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. - the kindermann report is vitally important and it is regrettable that this regulation, like the other four commission proposals, does not fall within the scope of codecision. the proposal for a regulation is based on article 37 of the treaty, which deals with the common agricultural policy. the aim is to introduce more rational rules to prevent the contamination of farm animals by products of animal origin containing pathogens. we all remember the recent foot-and-mouth disease epidemic in europe and the agricultural crisis it has caused, mainly in the united kingdom. initial investigations confirm that the contamination is due to food of animal origin from third countries which has been fed to pigs. as regards the animal health conditions applicable to the production and marketing of community products, the health status of the producing regions should be monitored closely and periodically. national and community controls must be carried out on an ad hoc basis. in order to have adequate resources, we must think - as mr kindermann said - about the number of veterinarians needed in the member states and in the european food safety authority in dublin. in addition, our legal system must take account of the applicant countries. it is necessary to make the penalties uniform. the same provisions as for community countries must be applied to imports from third countries. however, too strict hygiene measures should not be seen as barriers to trade. if this is the case, adjustments should be possible, while keeping the original objective of the regulation in mind. we support the report by mr kindermann, which provides the necessary clarifications to the commission's proposal.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, in reforming community legislation on food hygiene rules - 17 directives are involved here - the commission applies the principle of the responsibility of food business operators. that this principle applies to the agri-food industry, which feeds millions of consumers, i fully agree with. but the directive targets all primary production - products of the soil, livestock, hunting and fishing - on which a compulsory traceability system is to be imposed. how can you take personal responsibility for a mushroom picked in the forest or a fish caught in the river? that seems pretty unrealistic. article 1 of the 'scope of application' regulation states that these provisions do not apply to the primary production of food for private use or to the domestic preparation of food for private consumption. this measure should be extended to the supply of local markets and the marketing of natural products from primary production. these products - berries and mushrooms - contribute to the regions' brand image, reinforce their identity and gastronomic reputation and promote green tourism, which is essential for the rural economy. traditional jobs and practices are at stake. as regards game and game meat, which are delivered directly from the hunter to the consumer or retailer, they must be considered as traditional food production, which must benefit from specific marketing methods. for spiralis, amendment no 92 seems excessive to us, freezing or cooking at more than 65°c eliminates the presence of the parasite. the competent authorities within each member state are best placed to assess the situation and to issue the prescriptions which will ensure adequate consumer protection. let us return to reason by favouring flexibility, taking into account the diversity of geographical and climatic situations, rather than being locked into rigid regulations, which can only lead to deadlock and strong discontent.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this debate is a first. since the treaty of rome, governments and european institutions have never considered it useful to take stock of the distribution of roles within the union. the text before you is the fruit of genuine collective work which goes far beyond the rapporteur or the opinion of a political group. this is the culmination of fifteen months of work. the draft adopted by your committee on constitutional affairs took into account the main suggestions of the committee of the regions and the four committees whose opinions were requested, as well as 170 amendments from some 30 different authors, belonging to all the groups. we have not sought to rewrite the treaties but to set the guidelines for the necessary rewrite. this is based on a few strong political choices. first, it is clear that the text of treaties was written by diplomats for their own use, much as an automobile would have been built by mechanics and for mechanics only. our first objective is therefore to make the text accessible to all citizens, that is to say, to rewrite the treaties in the spirit of a constitution which is clearer, shorter and more coherent. paragraphs of the treaties which are not incorporated into the constitution would remain applicable but would no longer be primary law. secondly, a general framework of competences would be built around three categories: firstly, the member states have the principle of competence. no list of exclusive competences of the states is proposed. the statement of principle of jurisdiction seemed to us stronger in the silence of the constitution. secondly, the union has its own competences. in its fields it may act alone, as in the case of customs or currency; it may have primary responsibility, as in the case of the internal market, competition or cohesion policies. finally, third, there are shared competences: this is by far the longest list. the constitution will have to specify the objective and scope of the union's action in each case, applying the principle of subsidiarity. in essence, we propose to return to the existing distribution between these headings, but with two important policy changes: first, to distinguish between political and technical competence, this is what is known as the hierarchy of standards; secondly, and above all, to transfer to the union the primary responsibility for foreign and defence policy on the one hand and for the area of freedom and security on the other. in these two essential areas, ten years of application of the maastricht treaty have confirmed both the absolute necessity for joint action and, unfortunately, the ineffectiveness of intergovernmental procedures. thirdly, it seems important to safeguard the possibility of adapting this framework without resorting to the overly burdensome and exceptional procedure of constitutional revision. to this end, it is proposed to maintain a mechanism such as article 308, but to make it work in both directions: transfer to the union or return to the states of subjects for which the national dimension would again become predominant. fourthly, in the case of disputes of jurisdiction, we propose the formula of the judge rather than that of the political body. the aim is to transform the court of justice into a constitutional court; the commission has also proposed that the court of justice should be able to rule on the interpretation of the provisions of the treaty on european union, in particular article 177 of the treaty on european union, and to adopt a special procedure for the interpretation of the provisions of the treaty on european union. finally, fifthly, the constitutional committee has long debated the problem of the regions and other territorial authorities. the compromise text, which was finally adopted, calls on the member states to make proposals to the union to ensure that their local and regional authorities are better involved in the union's activities. mr president, the timetable for parliament's work is particularly well chosen: the european convention will be dealing with the subject next week. our resolution will therefore be the first and, indeed, the only working document of the convention on this vital subject. if a large majority, representing the main political groups and all the countries, emerges in our parliament, this will give our resolution considerable political authority. you should be thankful. - mr president, mr lamassoure's report is very interesting. i share his ambition: to give the union more powers so that it can meet its duties and meet its expectations. i particularly welcome his efforts on foreign policy, defence and security. however, i have a few objections. the objectives, which are the foundations of the constitution of the union, must be rewritten and this is what will fully justify progress in skills for the citizens. what goals ? market, currency, freedom of movement, that is not enough. we have to go beyond that. europe is committed to effective multilateralism in the world; it bases its security on dialogue, poverty eradication and the links of development; it chooses full employment and the advancement of human capabilities; it combats exclusion and strengthens cohesion by sharing common goods and, finally, it provides a public space for the exercise of pluralistic and transnational community citizenship and democracy. these choices are identical. they must be constitutionalized and the subject of an annual and multiannual political agenda. the balance of rules and the definition of competences are then aimed at achieving these objectives. in this respect, the report lacks ambition on the essential renewal of the social and growth model: a major issue for citizens, a subject which divides us. the rules of competition must be balanced by common rules and tasks in the fields of safety, public services and industrial policy. the union must have its own competence in economic policy, a redefined framework for the coordination of national policies and fiscal harmonization of budgetary and fiscal instruments. as regards the exercise of these powers, the democratic challenge and the requirement of efficiency, the report is too short and several amendments improve it. as regards the nature of the union's acts, i cannot accept the rapporteur's assumption that the union can only manage exceptionally. a political union which does not manage at all would, in fact, be largely irresponsible. finally, the distinction and sharing of competences should not be based on the principle of subsidiarity alone. in addition to the rule of competition, it does not legitimize a community; it must be combined with a second principle, that of solidarity. let's try to decline it. civil society actors must be directly engaged and must be able to pool resources to carry out projects of community interest. let us therefore have the audacity to form a society in europe.
- mr president, i have only one minute to speak, so i will be very direct. we will not approve the lamassoure report for two main reasons. firstly, it hardly deals with the question, which is of paramount importance to us, of democratic control of powers: nothing about the control of subsidiarity by national democracies, nothing or almost nothing about the exercise of european powers by national parliaments, in particular by the creation of an interparliamentary pillar. secondly, this report deals with the distribution of powers from an abstract technical point of view, without ever mentioning the sovereignty of national democracies. this bias towards abstract techniques leads to erroneous federalist solutions, which are bad for democracy. that is why the members of the socialist group have tabled a minority opinion which is annexed to the report. that is why the french mpf members also drew up a counter-report, in the form of answers to the convention's questionnaire on the union's tasks, 'europe, what to do with it?' this counter-report will be distributed by e-mail to all members of parliament, members of the convention and to anyone who requests it.
mr president, the concept of sustainable development reflects a correct intuition, namely that there are fundamental balances on the planet which must be respected. however, one must beware of the risk of this concept being perverted by ideological, tentacular and enchanting logomachy and supported by questionable technical proposals. the extremely wide range of fields of activity covered by the lannoye report underlines this risk of misunderstanding. however, to be operational, the concept of sustainable development must apply to clearly defined priorities. the first of these, as the rapporteur rightly points out, is the need not to resign ourselves to the persistence or even the increase of poverty, the eradication of which must remain an absolute and lasting priority of our action. to this end, we must help to define the right balance between public aid, which is still essential, and the development of international trade, which must not be portrayed as a systematic scarecrow. it is not a question of considering oda as a substitute but as a necessary complement to international trade. the latter cannot, under present conditions, be the sole engine of development, for the simple reason that economies and states which do not have the same production cost structure cannot compete. it is essential to avoid the development of perverse mechanisms, such as the disappearance of food crops due to cheap agricultural imports, and, as a corollary, the orientation of developing countries towards the export of cash crops which do not generate local development or raw materials on which it is extremely difficult to base sustainable development because of the great variability of their prices. if it is considered essential not to rely on international trade alone to reduce poverty, it is therefore essential to halt the erosion of oda. the european countries have a special mission to fulfil here, both jointly and separately. the member states must guard against the temptation to rely exclusively on community aid, by abandoning bilateral cooperation, the own contribution and specific expertise of which are of irreplaceable value. it is not enough, however, to halt the decline in oda by relying on global considerations of rate developments. it is essential to refocus this aid on strengthening the national state structures of the developing countries, which in many cases remain fragile, and on rural development, which must be given the highest priority. public aid has a crucial role to play in halting the scourge of rural exodus and the impoverishment of these populations in the big cities, which then fuels an emigration of despair. the development of subsistence agriculture, together with the development of basic public services, particularly in the fields of health, education and social protection, is the surest way to reduce poverty by creating employment in rural areas. within this public aid, a special role must be given to decentralised cooperation, that of local authorities such as municipalities, departments or regions. these communities have expertise in the field, they adapt projects to real needs, they ensure rigorous monitoring of actions, they create warm and lasting human relations between northern and southern countries. this form of cooperation should therefore be strongly encouraged. in the midst of all the issues raised by the lannoye report, these seem to me, mr president, to be the priorities that must be set if the concept of sustainable development is to make a real contribution to poverty reduction in our world today.
- mr president, we can only subscribe to the expectations of this report, which, by the facts it cites, is an indictment of the present economic system. what is this economic organization that forces half the world's population to live on less than two dollars a day? an economic system which, on the one hand, subsidizes food waste, destroys or stores food to keep prices up, and, on the other, leaves 826 million people undernourished and 16 million of them starving to death, is a criminal system in itself. but the ferocious realism of the report only underscores the absurdity of the conclusions, and especially of the proposed solutions. while the big private interests are plundering the planet, taking advantage of the poorest, widening the gap between a minority of the rich and a majority of the poor, the european parliament is voting impotent resolutions, knowing full well that summits like those in rio, monterrey or johannesburg will change nothing. the european parliament, like all representative institutions, is reduced to the role of a vine leaf covering up the infamy caused by the pursuit of profit on a world scale. the report also calls for the establishment of a european union-wide network of information and communication networks, which will be able to provide a common platform for the exchange of information and experience between the member states and the commission. for to remain silent on the causes of the damage caused by a profit-based economic system, to remain silent on the responsibility of the big industrial, commercial and financial groups for the poverty, hunger and impoverishment of the majority of the planet, is to remain a passive spectator of crimes against humanity, and thus, to be an accomplice to them.
