- madam president, commissioner, the problem of hunger in the world which we are discussing today cannot leave any human being indifferent and, as it always arises with great acuteness, it calls for us to show greater political will, particularly in the context of the next food summit. it is therefore essential that the european union, at the next summit, take its full part in this fight, which requires the right to food to be recognised as a fundamental human right. true, the problem of hunger may appear to be a misallocation of food between countries of over- and undernutrition. however, its solution does not generally lead to better trade between regions of abundance and those of poverty. the priority is to find and promote solutions where the problem exists, if only to keep pace with the food culture of the people concerned and to consolidate their rural economy. in this context, the fight against hunger and poverty certainly requires debt cancellation, support for education and vocational training, the strengthening of technical assistance, and the encouragement of investment in these backward countries. it also undoubtedly requires the proper use of water and the preservation of biodiversity, which is expected to be declared a "global public good" by the international community. but in the main, we cannot forget that it requires in particular the exploitation of fisheries and the promotion of the development of subsistence agriculture in a sustainable way. in this sense, the promotion of locally adapted agricultural practices, the processing of local products, the development of local markets and the freedom of choice of developing countries in the face of new technologies are all priorities to be implemented in hunger-stricken regions and call for a strengthening of the special and differentiated treatment of the wto. i therefore ask our commissioner to defend the ideas contained in parliament's joint resolution at the forthcoming world food summit.
- of course, i welcome the adoption of a european parliament resolution in preparation for the fao world food summit. it was my group that had asked for it. five years after the first summit, it is clear that the progress made - minus 40 million of the 800 million hungry - is very small compared to the target of halving the number of undernourished people by 2015. this resolution contains interesting paragraphs, such as the necessary refocusing of the new round of wto negotiations on development and food security, the concomitant reforms of the cap and the common fisheries policy. but overall, this compromise is still very weak: it does not recognise the supremacy of the right to food, food sovereignty, nor does it address the structural causes of food insecurity. it is well known that it is not the amount of food available on the planet that is lacking but the distribution of it among its inhabitants. and new reproductive technologies, including genetically modified organisms, will not change that. seeds and genetic engineering are putting small farmers and the people of the south even more at the mercy of multinational companies. not only do they strengthen their hold on farmers by selling their magic seeds, but they also encourage them to produce food for the consumers of the north at the expense of their own needs. for example, three quarters of the hungry people in developing countries are small farmers. it is time to put an end to unfair trade rules and practices in agricultural trade. the european union should abolish its export subsidies now. it is not enough to talk about the coherence of community policies, it must also be put into practice. the millennium development goal is to halve poverty by 2015, not to protect our farmers, our fishing fleets and our agro-food industries; we are therefore asking you to support our amendments. the best way to fight hunger is to give the people of the south back access to their land, to their water, to their genetic resources and to protect their farmers and their own markets.
- the right to adequate and healthy food for all everywhere should be recognized and respected effectively throughout the world. this is a basic human right. the preparations for the world food summit should make it possible not only to affirm this but also to put it into practice for all time. because this is no longer the time for wishes and declarations, followed by too little action, when 826 million people in the world continue to suffer from hunger, including nearly 800 million in developing countries, and 2 billion people are undernourished. it is not unknown that the most vulnerable people are women and children. while the commitment six years ago was to halve the number of hungry people by 2015, a quick calculation shows that the current rate of an average reduction of 8 million per year will not achieve this goal. so it is urgent to act on the consequences of this tragedy, of course, by providing financial aid, contributions, programmes, but it is also essential to tackle the causes of this situation. the liberalization policies promoted by the wto and the opening up of the markets of developing countries are dangerously threatening already vulnerable populations, as is the still pressing reality of debt. the wars, the policies of hegemony and the search, at any price, for markets for the products of the north, the search for profit, and even the privatization of the natural resources of the south, put the food security of the peoples at risk. the priority given to trade over development can only widen the gap between the very rich and the very poor and take the south further away from the possibility of obtaining and enforcing its food sovereignty. each country has the right to choose freely how it will supply its food. access to adequate food and means of production, access to resources are safe means that can guarantee and concretely realize the right to food. a trade policy which respects local production, the incomes of small farmers, the needs mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the plan for the euthanasia of european small-scale fishing which commissioner fischler has just calmly presented to us must be rejected as a whole in its general philosophy and in its technical approach. this plan is characteristic first of all of a detestable supranational method, that of technocratic laziness and arrogance which, after extensive consultation with the professional world, is capable of decreeing the outright condemnation of a sector based on an abusive generalization of fragmentary and contested, partial and partial technical expertise, often false - i refer you to the anchovy and the black spot of the atlantic. this plan is absurd and contradictory, since, while it claims to preserve fish, it actually condemns the most regulated fisheries, the ones most concerned with preserving the sustainability of the resource, to the benefit of third-party fleets, the least respectful of conservation, which, if we follow mr fischler, will be called upon to supply almost exclusively a rapidly expanding european fish market. this plan is dangerous because it is impractical. it is based on a central concept, the rate of fishing effort, which cannot be measured by any reliable indicator, by any reliable statistical instrument - and you know that, commissioner. the plan also reflects the growing contradictions in the union and the danger posed to european assets by the adoption of uniform solutions. in the name of what would the member states which have sacrificed their artisanal fishing to industrial fishing prevent those who wish to keep a living artisanal fishing as a fundamental element of identity and land use from doing so? in writing. - we voted against the european parliament's recommendation on the 'integration of europol into the institutional system of the european union', because it seeks to remove europol from the strictly intergovernmental sphere, where it is placed by its convention, to attract it to the ambiguous status of the third pillar, intergovernmental with community aspects, which would constitute a stepping stone towards a more complete communitization at a later date. this is a very reprehensible legal move: the european parliament is suggesting that the council should substitute for the convention (which is a specific treaty) the legal basis of article 34 (2) (c) which is internal to the treaty and allows the use of qualified majority voting in certain cases. but this change of nature and legal effect is not possible without the ratification of the peoples. the result is that the manoeuvre is also politically deplorable: on such a fundamental point - and on no other - we have no right to change the decision of the people behind their backs. this kind of behaviour on the part of the european parliament does not bode well for its respect for the peoples if more powers were given to it.

in writing. - it must be remembered that coal and steel are the foundations of the construction of europe. at the end of the war, the six founding states decided to pool their steel and coal production. the european coal and steel community (ecsc treaty) was thus established on 18 april 1951. the ecsc treaty was concluded for a period of 50 years from the date of its entry into force; it will therefore expire on 23 july 2002. it was foreseen that after the expiry of the treaty, steel and coal would be considered as any other industrial product, particularly in the context of competition policy. however, it is clear that without financial support measures, the vast majority of the european coal industry would be doomed to disappear in the very short term. most of the community's coal production is, and should remain, non-competitive with imports from third countries. the green paper on the security of energy supply took account of this. it is envisaged to maintain a minimum production capacity as coal remains an important indigenous source of energy, available in the long term, stable and safe. in writing. - commissioner fischler has just told this house that the european initiative to accept duty-free imports of products from the least developed countries - the so-called 'everything but arms' initiative - is likely to include the acceptance of imports of gmo agricultural products. in fact, he said, these countries would be obliged to produce gmos to increase their productivity, they could not do otherwise, and we, on our part, would be obliged to buy and eat them to help development! if this were the case, the danger is clear: development aid would be used as a pretext to get us to import gmos and to undermine the protections which the european peoples have tried to give themselves in respect of them. and secondly, it would probably be argued from these derogating imports that, for the sake of consistency, we must abolish all our bans on the cultivation and marketing of gmos. we have known this kind of manoeuvre from the commission for a long time. these manoeuvres are being directed by who knows what interests, but in any case we know who will be the victims: the peoples of europe.
in writing. - i would like to stress how much i think the reaction expressed in this debate by commissioner fischler to the american farm bill is contrary to the interests of european agriculture. fundamentally, although it does entail trade distortions that need to be examined, the farm bill reflects a major shift in the us position, which now recognizes that the sustainability of agriculture cannot be ensured by free trade rules alone. a responsible european attitude would have been to take note of this recognition by the united states of the specific nature of agriculture, the impossibility of assimilating it to industry or services, and to propose to them to draw the consequences of this common observation by studying together how to translate this right to national or regional protection of the agricultural model chosen by the peoples concerned at world level: revision of the wto rules to exclude agriculture, creation of a specific world organisation for agriculture... instead, commissioner fischler is playing the role of free trade herald and advocating that europe should take the place of the united states as the unconditional defender of global agricultural openness, a principle which will be invoked against our interests tomorrow and which, if left unchecked, will end up destroying our agriculture.
in writing. - article 20 of the text we have just voted for calls for the impact of active substances on domestic bee populations and the comments of professional beekeepers' organisations to be taken into account in the approval procedure. this is not a problem for the future alone, but a very current problem: in fact, in western and central france, for several years now, and this year with a doubled intensity in the south-west, the extremely serious consequences for the populations of domestic bees of several systemic insecticides used in the treatment of certain seeds of large crops, sunflower and maize in particular, have been observed. it has now been demonstrated that these products, the active substances of which are imidacloprid and fipronil, have a devastating effect on the nervous system of insect predators, not only for the crop whose seed has been treated, but also for the following crops in the rotation, as these systemic products have a retention of several years in the crop residues buried in the soil and then in the humus. the beekeeping industry is a major industry, and tens of thousands of hives are lost every year. in writing. - i fully support the approach advocated by the committee on employment and social affairs in the area of corporate social responsibility. it seems to me that the social and environmental practices of european companies should be subject to controls comparable to those applied to competition practices. this is essential for the creation of a genuine social europe, which goes hand in hand with the internal market, where competition plays a major role. this must be seen as a primary objective of a future-oriented enterprise policy, as a guiding principle of european socio-economic policies. ideally, companies, large investors, would have a strategy that goes beyond their short-term profit horizon, they would combine economic expansion, social progress and sustainable development... the race for profit in the globalised economy requires us to adopt pragmatic measures to ensure that the social principles developed at political level do not remain a dead letter. we must therefore demand that we can control the application of this concept, which is admittedly still a little vague, of corporate social responsibility. one suggestion is that the commission should make a proposal, in the framework of the appropriate directive, to oblige companies to produce social and environmental reports just as they do in financial matters. mr president, the corbett report on the revision of the rules of procedure of this house makes some technical improvements, but it follows three general political guidelines which we do not share. firstly, it would like to give the european parliament new powers which the treaty does not grant it. this is the case in particular with amendments nos 14, 29, 33, 45, 48, 49, 52, 53 and 56. for example, in amendment no 56 we see that the european parliament gives itself the right to ask the council to implement article 7 teu on possible violations of human rights. as you know, and as the court of justice of the european communities has already pointed out, the european parliament cannot do this because it is not a fully sovereign assembly. it has only the powers of attribution which the treaty confers on it. second misconception: many of the amendments assume that ratification of the treaty of nice - which is still hypothetical - will be necessary for it to enter into force. this is the case, for example, with proposals 8, 9, 41 and 58. i am sure you will tell me that if the treaty of nice is not ratified at a later date, these amendments will not enter into force and there will be no legal problems. i think there is a problem of political behaviour here, however: our approval of these amendments in advance would be a certain disregard for the irish people. finally, the third negative trend: this report reveals a certain tendency in this parliament to silence minorities, something which mr corbett has just aptly called the simplification of procedures. this regrettable tendency is particularly apparent in proposals 6, 59, 63, 68, 74, 85 and 101. proposition 59 in particular makes it more difficult for minorities to table amendments to a text in plenary if they have not obtained more than 10% of the votes in committee. and everything is in order. we can see, mr president, that in our opinion this report is not in a position to be adopted.

mr president, the duff report seeks to streamline the procedure for waiving the parliamentary immunity of a member of the european parliament and at the same time to introduce additional safeguards against arbitrariness, which is in our interests. however, in our opinion it does not solve the specific technical question which initially gave rise to all this thinking, namely how to determine the national authority competent to forward to the european parliament the request for the waiver of the immunity of one of its members. the common political sense suggests that it is up to the member state concerned to designate this authority itself. in fact, the lamassoure report, which was voted on at our last part-session, states that where a competence has not been explicitly attributed to the european institutions, it is deemed to belong to the member states. but the duff report, in paragraph 13 of article 6a, confuses the problem and succeeds in obscuring this simple rule. of course, we cannot accept that, mr president, as i will say in my explanation of vote.

in writing. - the new rule 6a (13) of the rules of procedure of this house, as voted on following the duff report, states: 'after consulting the member states, the committee (competent for the european parliament) may draw up an indicative list of the authorities of the member states empowered to submit a request for the waiver of the immunity of a member.' as i said yesterday, this confused wording has a purpose: not to clearly recognize a national competence which is a hindrance to the european parliament. to avoid admitting this, we begin by saying that the european parliament has the right to draw up a list. but as this right is purely invented, it is hastily added that the list is "indicative". thirdly, since this reduction in the number of members of the european parliament is still unpleasant, it is stated that the member states are 'consulted', which seems to mean that they do not decide. nor is it clear what they are consulted on - the principle of a list or its contents. this is one of the european institutions' classic methods of appropriating national powers: first, they confuse everything, then they say that the situation is too complicated and that in order to simplify it, the power must be given to brussels.

- madam president, in my group's view, while the rapporteur's resolution is undoubtedly satisfactory, the council's text is still mediocre. it is true that we have made progress on gibraltar. we are happy for our british and spanish friends, as well as those in gibraltar. however, how can the citizens understand that european political families exist unless some of the members of this parliament are elected on a transnational basis? this concept means that, in effect, by dividing up the electoral territory, one can very well arrive at lists of two or three members per constituency, which implies that the electoral threshold rises to 20 or 30%. it is certainly going to make the debates in this house extraordinarily simple, but it will be at the expense of representativeness. proportionality is only of interest if it guarantees the representativeness of citizens. that is why we have tried to combat this threshold effect in the recitals which have been voted on, and i thank our rapporteur and the committee on constitutional affairs formally for this, while hoping that the council will support this position. that is why, in view of this poor copy, my group reserves its final vote on the assent for the time being.
- madam president, mr rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, this report does not seem to me to be very timely, because although there is no uniform electoral procedure, the fact remains that since 1999 european elections have been organised on the basis of very broadly common principles. so why this report on a subject which has been debated many times if not to try to revive an integration process which seems to me more moribund than ever! it is a matter of considerable debate whether a procedure which arbitrarily imposes proportional representation and - even more controversially - the territorialisation of constituencies in the most populous member states, by means of community law, is justified. i would like to stress that there is nothing to show, except for a simplistic and erroneous reasoning, that this measure would bring elected officials closer to the electorate, and since this is one of the objectives pursued, that it would increase participation in the european elections. single or regionalised constituencies, proportional or majority voting: since 1979 all the formulas have been used, in vain. it must therefore be admitted that it is not by tinkering with electoral laws that a feeling of belonging to the european union will be artificially created and that this colossal abstention which affects the legitimacy of parliament will be reduced. that being said, i would like to stress two points in particular which i find unacceptable. first of all, there is the ridiculous idea of a single european constituency for the election of 10% of the seats in parliament, a proposal which was fortunately rejected by the council but which the rapporteur nevertheless revisits. not only is this project in total contradiction with the objective of territorialisation - the single european constituency would distance its members from their constituents, whereas territorialisation aims to bring them closer together - but it also ignores article 189 of the treaty on the european communities. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the second point on which i completely disagree is the considerations on the role of european political parties, which the rapporteur calls on to propose a candidate for the presidency of the commission during the election campaign. i would point out that such an initiative is a further breach of the treaty, which reserves to the governments of the member states the power to designate the person they intend to appoint as president of the commission. i also believe that this absurd idea is dangerous and even perverse, because by usurping a prerogative reserved to the states it introduces, at european level, the party system and its inevitable corollary, parliamentary government. the participation of european parties in the vote is at best conceivable, but their interference in the functioning of the community institutions must be firmly opposed. i therefore regret that i cannot join in the praise that has been paid to our rapporteur - without in any way criticising his personality - and i therefore conclude that this report must be rejected.

the rapporteur. mr president, i shall now present the non-nuclear part of the report on the joint research centre (jrc), which represents two thirds of the budget. in the sixth framework programme, the joint research centre will refocus its activities in order to strengthen its organisation and to participate effectively in the european research area. this work programme has three characteristics: concentration, openness and networking, and a 'client' approach. to this end, the joint research centre has refocused its non-nuclear activities on two core areas, supported by vertical competences: food, chemicals and health, environment and sustainable development. these areas will be supplemented by horizontal activities: technological foresight, reference materials and measurement method, public security and anti-fraud. the total budget allocated to the jrc's activities is eur 760 million. the new strategy adopted by the latter and the restructuring of its services are based on a report published last year by a high-level group chaired by étienne davignon. these changes are designed to better adapt the joint research centre to the needs of policy makers and privileged users: council, commission directorates-general and parliament. the jrc will also play a driving role in the european research area and the sixth framework programme. its action will focus on the establishment of a community system for harmonizing measures and on participation in european and global networks. the jrc will be a major player in the implementation of the sixth framework programme, both in terms of its participation in the networks of excellence and in integrated projects. it will be able to actively contribute to the development of the new european citizenship by providing a common knowledge base for scientific and technological references and by facilitating dialogue between scientists and policy-makers. it must also help with the 'operational' implementation of the new tools, including, of course, excellence in its fields of competence and the integration of research into local development. in certain areas, the proposals of the joint research centre seem indispensable to clarify the calls for tenders that may be made, for example, in the field of sustainable development. this sector contains all questions on ecosystems. the jrc has, for example, worked for over a year and a half on the definition of the criteria for ecosites. it will contribute to the establishment of a european network, including food safety issues, with the establishment of a reference and standardisation system; the same is true of the protection of privacy in information and communication technologies. the joint research centre should be given a high priority in its advisory role on european policies. it improves networking and cooperation with public and private institutions in the member states. it also develops a human resources development and mobility plan, including training young scientists and organising exchanges with national research institutes. it is not a question of making it a competing centre on scientific subjects existing in several european states, but it must make it possible to ensure a link between these centres in the application of results concerning the implementation of european directives, just as the commission must be able to contact it for a response as quickly as possible. it therefore needs to have teams that can adapt easily to demand and respond immediately. to this end, they must always benefit from the knowledge of the subjects chosen and keep abreast of the research upstream, or even carry out complementary research when certain areas are not covered by the national institutes. the jrc has an important role to play in the context of the extension of the programme to the applicant countries and to the mediterranean countries and those concerned with international cooperation, which fall under the meda and tacis programmes. the role of the joint research centre as a risk mediator should also be borne in mind: risk exposure, impact assessment, repair, nuclear safety problems and waste, in synergy with the eur-opa major risks programmes. the centre's activities should be extended to the operational implementation of concrete projects on energy saving, particularly in the building sector, and renewable energies. its achievements must not be confined to research on photovoltaic energy, but must also promote demonstration projects in other fields such as wind energy. it could also monitor the evaluation of the fuel cell deployment. given the growing popularity of organic and locally produced food, the jrc will develop methods to ensure its authenticity and quality. it will also study how to optimise their impact on the environment and local development. finally, in order to be able to guide and possibly reorient certain studies in the light of political developments at the scientific level, i think it would be desirable to set up a monitoring committee, in liaison with parliament, which would thus be kept informed of these activities more regularly, which would allow the development of fruitful exchanges to continue. in conclusion, the main objectives of the joint research centre will therefore be to remain close to its users, the european parliament and the commission, to develop its role as a recognised centre of excellence on safety, health and environmental issues, and to develop its activities as a research network operator. the joint research centre will thus succeed in its reform and justify its unique position within the services of the european commission, and i thank commissioner busquin and his services for their full cooperation in the preparation of this report and in the conclusions we are presenting.

mr president, president cox has apologized to me for having asked for a recall to the rules of procedure which was not followed. i think we have indeed broken our rules. it is quite legitimate that a fifth of our colleagues are calling for a secret ballot, even if i agree with mrs beres that this was not at all appropriate. however, article 136 (4) provides for a precise procedure for such secret bulletins. the results of any secret ballot are counted by two to six members drawn by lot from among the members. this means that we are dealing with a solemn procedure, a heavy procedure, which is precisely intended to avoid untimely requests for a secret vote. you don't vote by secret ballot like you change a tie. i note that in the corbett report on which we have just voted, article 136 has not been amended. so the president was wrong not to apply the procedure provided for in article 4, which is specifically designed to avoid the use of secret ballot for tactical purposes.
in writing. - the european parliament has just once again opposed the friday morning sitting in the weeks of the plenary session in strasbourg. he has no right to do so, since he has to obey the treaty. but he violates it in two ways. first, as the court of justice pointed out in 1997, when the treaty refers to 'the twelve periods of monthly plenary sessions', it refers to the existing practice of one-week periods. secondly, the additional plenary sessions which may be held in brussels are intended to provide a complement when working time in strasbourg is saturated. it is therefore not possible to empty the weeks in strasbourg and at the same time add mini-sessions in brussels. it is not even right to plan the sessions in brussels a year in advance without knowing whether or not the agenda in strasbourg will be saturated. i regret that the previous french government did not take the matter to the court of justice when the strasbourg fridays were abolished in 2000 and 2001, and i hope that the next government will do better.

in writing. - the uen group and the french delegation of the rpf oppose any attempt to shorten the duration of the plenary sessions in strasbourg. in order to correct the unfortunate precedent set last year - the abolition, under the presidency of mrs fontaine, of friday in the calendar of plenary sessions - i asked on behalf of my group for the reintroduction of the five-day week in strasbourg. we know very well that the plenary session reduced to four days does not allow us to work properly. but, apart from this technical aspect, which is already not insignificant, i reject, for major political reasons, the amputation of the strasbourg session for one day (monday or friday) and, at the same time, the unfair increase in the number and duration of the extraordinary sessions in brussels. these practices conceal a clear intention to permanently transfer the seat of parliament from strasbourg to brussels, in defiance of the letter of the treaties. strasbourg must not be reduced to a mere annex of brussels. strasbourg is and must remain the seat of the european parliament.
in writing. - once again, the anti-strasbourg lobby is running amok in an attempt to shorten and devalue the strasbourg sessions and eventually abolish them. so everything is fine, from the use of secret ballot to the threat of legionnaires' disease. i would like to remind you that it is not for an assembly to decide for itself where to sit. it is not for members of parliament to decide for whatever reason on the comfort, mood or gastronomic orientation of the place where they legislate. can we imagine for a moment that the european parliament decides, because it is more pleasant, to sit in courmayeur in winter and in saint-tropez in summer? an assembly can only submit to what the governments, and therefore the peoples, have established through the fundamental texts. in this case, what the texts have fixed for the european parliament is that its seat is in strasbourg, this seat cannot be made virtual by the lobby of the compulsory water zoo.
in writing. - the revision of the regulation proposed by the corbett report will, under the pretext of simplifying and lightening procedures, strengthen the duopoly of the 'large groups' with a federalist majority in the european parliament. the conditions for the formation of groups are tightened, which makes the creation of small groups more complicated. at the same time, parliamentary life will be made more difficult for minorities and the unenrolled. until now, the latter could find an outlet in the written explanations of vote. but the traditional tolerance for the length of these explanations was revoked by the administration without any clear justification being given. this reversal actually penalizes minorities and the unregistered far more than others. the aim of the operation is clear: it is a quiet, discreet witch hunt against everything that is not labeled federalist. finally, as i said in the debate, this revision of the rules of procedure extends the rights of the european parliament beyond what is permitted by the treaty, without any apparent concern on the part of any member state.

mr president, the logic of enlargement must naturally translate itself, for agriculture as in other areas, into the application of identical rules of the game in the old and new member states, while preserving the necessary transitions to avoid, in both, the destabilising consequences of the practical implementation of this historic political imperative. two particularly delicate problems arise in the agricultural sector. firstly, the opening up of western markets to eastern products. this opening up must be done on a sector by sector and country by country basis as producers are able to bring to market products which meet the same quality and safety standards as those which we already impose on our own producers. the second question is that of the so-called first pillar of the cap, namely market support and compensatory aid. the principles governing the cap, aid and support which are justified by the environmental, social and health constraints and requirements on our farmers, must apply without discrimination to the old and new member states, provided that the latter respect the same constraints. how long before they're able to do that? in other words, how long should the transition phase last? the commission proposes a transitional phase which would be totally uniform for all countries in terms of timing and procedures, and would initially involve extremely brutal and painful restructuring for countries with a large number of farms. on the contrary, we believe that this question should be answered on a country-by-country basis, taking into account the particular situation and structure of agriculture in each country, the social impact of their transition to the cap, and the desirable, desirable and sustainable pace for each of their agriculture. to approach this problem from the standpoint of accounting logic alone, as some member states, such as germany and the netherlands, are now doing, is a narrow approach that is dangerous for the future of the union, because these are essential issues for the future and the balance of the societies of the candidate countries. the enemy of the great europe of tomorrow, mr president, is the desire for uniformity.

the commission. - mr president, various comments have been made on the structural funds. i have been able to participate in this debate with my colleague barnier, so to speak, and i should like to say a few words about the remarks on the structural funds. the outflow of funds is unsatisfactory at the moment, but it is not quite right to say that there are major delays here, but it is just that the member states are waiting, as it were, for the last deadline allowed to them by the legislator for the implementation of the programmes. parliament was involved in the arrangements. in the context of the debate on the financial framework for enlargement, let me stress once again as budget commissioner that the commission has been guided in its proposals by the principle that there must be a good balance of interests between the present member states and the new member states. i think we have succeeded in this balancing of interests. the new member states initially complained after the proposals were presented that they were treated unequally. on the one hand, we have provided for a phasing-out of direct payments, but on the other hand the commission's proposal also includes the fact that in 2006 the financial commitments to be made to the new member states will be the same per capita as those in the present member states, so that there will be equal treatment. does the commission's proposal place too much financial burden on the present member states? i would like to point out that we have strictly adhered to the limits of agenda 2000. and we have also proposed as the commission, and this has been accepted by the council, that the new member states should pay contributions to the ec budget from the outset, and this means that the net costs for the current member states are even lower than what was decided in agenda 2000 as the maximum burden of enlargement. i think it's important to record that. let me emphasize one more thing: in the current reporting and debate, it sometimes seems as if only the current net contributors are paying the cost of enlargement. that's not right. all the present member states pay the same relative amount for enlargement, that is, except for the specific arrangement for the united kingdom. but here, the same solidarity is required. this means, of course, in absolute terms, given the different size of the social product and the different sizes of the member states, that in fact 80% of the cost of enlargement is borne by the five largest member states: germany, the united kingdom, italy, france and spain. but it is a joint, solidarity-based achievement, and of course the financial aspect is of great importance in the public debate and also in the debate in parliament, the council and the commission. but we must not forget that this debate is not about whether or not to build a section of motorway, but about the unification of europe. it is a question of stabilizing democracy, the rule of law and peace in europe. these are values of inestimable value. in writing. - to improve the functioning of taxation systems on the european market, the garcía-margallo y marfil report intends in particular to 'support the vat strategy adopted by the commission in 2000'. the rapporteur is 'convinced' that 'the european union must continue to work towards the adoption of the definitive vat system'. we voted against this report because we do not see why european taxpayers' money should be spent on training civil servants to generalize and standardize one of the most unfair tax systems. the fact is that consumers, rich or poor, pay the same amount of tax on products (almost 20% on the budget of most products in france). it therefore weighs relatively heavier on those with the lowest incomes. the predominant role of vat in the budget revenue of a state such as france, and more generally in europe, reflects the fact that it is the popular classes that finance the bulk of state expenditure. only the abolition of indirect taxes would be in the interests of the majority of the population. state expenditure should be ensured by a high taxation of corporate profits and by direct income taxation, based on a single, highly progressive scale, which is mainly charged to the top brackets of the tax.
in writing. - we vote against the report by mr konstantinos alyssandrakis on the nuclear energy research and training programme. this report supports the european commission's position in this area and is in line with the euratom treaty: an obsolete treaty whose very official function is to promote the use of the atom and whose very foundations must be called into question. the funds are thus primarily allocated to research on nuclear fusion, which the industrial establishment now uses to the same extent as nuclear fission, with the results we know. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. but they will not be conducted in the same way depending on the political perspective adopted. by emphasizing the burial of nuclear material deep in the earth, the proposed programme seeks to make it socially acceptable to continue nuclear production by avoiding the object in question. the first urgent measure to tackle the problem is to stop producing this waste and then to focus research on its management in situ with a view to phasing out nuclear energy.
in writing. - under the pretext of preserving fish stocks in eu waters, the commission wants to reduce fishing capacity, which will result in the loss of 28 000 direct jobs by 2006. the report stresses that the studies on which the commission relies are unreliable. however, it does not call into question a process in which the biggest polluters are not the payers, in particular the discharges from polluting industries and large industrial fishing units, which cause more damage to the oceans than small-scale fishing. although we voted for the few tentative measures to help the sector's wage-earners and the safety of the crews, we abstained on the whole report. the future of the world's fisheries depends on the conservation of the world's fish stocks. however, by refusing to tackle the real perpetrators of the threat and, moreover, an anarchic economic system in which competition and the pursuit of private profit make any rational planning project illusory, the problem is not solved, and the problem is simply made to pay for by the artisanal fishermen, which is unacceptable.
in writing. - while it seems obvious to me that a reform of the common fisheries policy is necessary and must be implemented quickly, and while i recognize that the stocks covered by this draft regulation are in a vulnerable situation, i nevertheless believe that this reform, as envisaged here, is unbalanced and risks making us forget that the necessary protection of fish resources must not be at the expense of fishermen. it seems to me that this report does not give enough credit to the men and women who, aware that the survival of their profession depends above all on the management and conservation of the resource, have already made enormous efforts in this direction. i think that this report is a sort of trojan horse for the future common fisheries policy as it is currently being presented by the european commissioner responsible, mr fischler. i shall therefore vote against this motion for a resolution, which, without taking account of the human factor, proposes measures with traumatic and brutal consequences for the fishing industry.
in writing. - the handling of the cod and hake issue is characteristic of autistic behaviour on the part of a european commission which makes bad diagnoses, because it is cut off from reality, and consequently takes bad decisions. misdiagnosis: although cod stocks are in a poor state in some fishing areas, it is wrong to attribute the problem solely to overfishing, as many other factors are involved. the situation for hake is specific and different: the biological cycles are much shorter, the recovery is already under way and the measures proposed by the commission will be completely counter-cyclical. bad decisions: the management of tacs in a multiannual framework is a good measure, which we have been calling for for a long time, but it must be translated into annual variations limited to rates that are acceptable to the trades concerned. the structural measures proposed ignore the economic and social consequences for the various occupations concerned and reflect the same malthusian spirit as the proposal for reform of the cfp: they are totally unacceptable.
in writing. - in its resolution on the preparations for the european council in seville (21-22 june 2002), the european parliament has just called for a european immigration policy 'communitarianised' on the basis of the provisions of the treaty of amsterdam. there's been a serious misunderstanding about this. the situation on the immigration front in europe is not deteriorating because of the absence of a supranational policy. this is because for a long time neither the member states nor the commission have wanted to give the highest priority to the safety of citizens and to controlling immigration, which necessarily implies the fight against illegal immigration and the regulation of legal flows. on the contrary, the member states and the commission have given priority to uncontrolled movement, to the abolition of internal borders, to the acceptance of asylum seekers, even those who are clearly abusive, to the belief that mass immigration will solve our problems of dynamism and demography. the result is now in evidence. but the solution is not supranational integration of immigration policy based on wrong priorities. the first solution is to change priorities. but we are still far from that.

in writing. - discussing the european summits is a simple exercise in style. it is precisely in these large gatherings, to which the elected representatives are not invited, let alone the citizens, that the future of 380 million people is being discussed in the utmost secrecy. the seville summit, like those in genoa, nice and brussels, are a new and sad illustration of the democratic bankruptcy which characterizes the construction of europe. the summit will be marked politically and ideologically by the liberal right and the extreme right. the latter, on the strength of its recent electoral successes in france and the netherlands, has been able to impose its populism and xenophobic demagogy on the fifteen, particularly in the field of immigration and the right of asylum. the only question is to strengthen the fortress europe, whereas the urgent need is to combat trafficking, mafias and illegal activities through a policy of opening up borders, regulating the undocumented and ensuring equal civil and social rights for nationals and foreigners. immigrants and asylum seekers are being used as scapegoats for the people who are victims of liberalism and capitalist globalisation. the anti-immigrant hysteria organized by the heads of state finally masks the real orientations of the seville summit, those of the antisocial summit in barcelona, and those of the neocolonial summit in madrid. the joint resolution is part of this approach.
in writing. - the brok report urges the member states and candidate countries to make the necessary efforts to conclude accession negotiations by the end of this year, with a view to signing the accession treaties by april 2003, with a view to the entry of ten new member states in 2004. we warmly welcome this. the berlin council in 1999 had foreseen that six candidate countries would join the union in 2002. now we're in it, and no one's been in. we can't go on like this. we must break down the last barriers, but we must be realistic, as i shall explain in my explanation of vote on the böge report. in any case, there is at least one false problem: the non-ratification of the treaty of nice by the irish people. if it were to reject this bad treaty again in a second referendum (despite the deception being prepared by the seville council, with a declaration in disguise showing respect for irish military neutrality), enlargement would not be compromised: it would be enough to include the corresponding parts of the treaty of nice in the future accession treaty. we could use this time to review them, which would be good.
in writing. - the dismantling of public services; industrial restructuring leading to an explosion in unemployment, particularly in the czech republic, slovakia, lithuania and poland; ongoing or planned closure of energy sources in lithuania, estonia and bulgaria, with dramatic social and economic implications; the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the spread of the disease, and it is therefore proposing to extend the measures to include the following: the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the effects of the crisis on the community's agricultural production. this is a disastrous record for these countries, and even more so for their workers in towns and villages. but this is a welcome development for eu authorities, as europe's leading tobacco producer, bulgartabak, is to be privatised, and privatisation of banks, insurance companies, telecommunications and industry is progressing alongside foreign direct investment. in other words, this is the systematic reduction of the countries of central and eastern europe by big capital, especially western european capital. the eu consortium of rich countries is thus motivated first and foremost by the desire to extend the range of profits offered to their industrial and financial trusts. our vote is not a vote against the accession of these countries to the european union, but a protest against the way it is done, namely under the aegis of big capital.
in writing. - we voted against the brok report on enlargement. of course, we are not opposed to the integration of new countries into the union. however, we have reservations about the current course of the negotiations. we are also concerned about the burden of transposing the acquis communautaire, which varies, depending on the translation, between 70 000 and 90 000 pages of text, for the applicant countries. agriculture, health and the environment are facing enormous challenges. it is also unfair to make the entry of these countries conditional on strict compliance with legislation on the protection of biodiversity: let us not forget that these countries come to us to consolidate peace on the european continent, to develop their infrastructures and to catch up with their considerable economic backwardness. let's not forget that.
in writing. - the financial perspective for 2000-2006 agreed in berlin in 1999 provided for the entry of six new members in this period, starting in 2002. in reality, there may well be 10 but only in 2004, so that the savings on attendance would offset the additional membership burden. we welcome this balancing, which will keep the budgetary ceiling of 1.27% of the member states' gdp below the present level. we can also accept the gradual adjustment of agricultural policy payments to the new member states, as envisaged in the böge report, knowing that the reasoning here is one of constant policy. but we would also like to see this policy reformed to make it a 'sustainable cap' (see my explanation of vote on the olsson report). we are, however, disappointed at the lack of effort on the part of the member states which are now receiving structural and cohesion funds, and which should understand better the need to shift these funds eastwards. it is clear that the current cohesion fund, which was intended to facilitate access to the single currency for these countries, has to be abolished.
in writing. - the situation in the applicant countries of central and eastern europe is rather bleak, despite the self-congratulations of the eu's governing bodies. in this report, if we are told that there is a 'substantial gap in prosperity (which) could be in the range of 1 to 10' between regions on either side of the line of the next enlargement, this unfortunately realistic observation serves a purpose that does not even bother to hide. the commission has already agreed to provide large subsidies to these regions and their businesses in particular, explaining that after enlargement, the regions currently bordering the eu will inevitably attract poor labour from newly admitted countries. the rapporteur adds that this is "just a drop in the ocean of needs", not of the impoverished people of central and eastern europe, certainly not, but of the rich regions and their businesses. the commission is also proposing to increase subsidies to these countries, while approving the so-called transitional measures which, even after enlargement, will impede the free movement of workers from the newly admitted countries within the eu. these new countries are only integrated into the union with restrictions that make them second-class citizens. we have therefore naturally voted against this report.
in writing. - (de) my group supports the report by mrs sommer, because it deals with the specific problem of the situation of 23 border regions of the european union, with 33 million inhabitants, after the accession of the countries of central and eastern europe. we also welcome the fact that a number of the gue/ngl group's proposals relating to the report have been accepted, such as the emphasis on the need to provide more financial resources for the promotion of smes, or the requirement to increase the eu's co-financing share to take account of the radical development differential. we share the general view of the rapporteur that the amounts made available by the european commission to the tune of eur 195 million are far from sufficient, and we strongly support the need for additional financial resources. this is all the more so as the funds currently available are in the form of budgetary redeployments, while at the same time the finance ministers of different countries can look forward to the non-use, and thus the reimbursement, of amounts of up to several billion euros from the structural and regional funds. we regret that it has not been possible to impose a legal basis of its own for support for border regions, because this deprives itself of the possibility of financing measures over a long period. on the other hand, we welcome the move towards greater consideration of the link between regional transport and transeuropean networks. (explanation of vote abbreviated pursuant to rule 137 (1) of the rules of procedure)
in writing. - (de) my group approves the report by mr turco, who has done a good job. the structural and cohesion funds are essential instruments available to the european union to bring the eu's lagging regions up to the level of development of prosperous regions. we believe that among the various aspects of eu policy, it is these instruments of european aid policy which have the most important and visible immediate repercussions on the different areas of people's lives and which must therefore at all costs remain a part of future policies after enlargement. the solidarity shown by strong regions to weaker ones, across borders, is a symbol of european unification. we therefore reject any discussion of renationalizing, even partially, regional and structural policies, because the principle of solidarity would be weakened and we cannot know where such a policy would lead. we are naturally aware of the serious problems encountered in the implementation of regional and structural policy, and we believe that in this area the european commission as well as the member states have a responsibility. the low rates of implementation and the continuing increase in commitments remaining to be settled (rals), which in 2000 amounted to an astonishing €112 billion, raise the question of a thorough review of the procedures and structures in place. (explanation of vote abbreviated pursuant to rule 137 (1) of the rules of procedure)
in writing. - the olsson report and the commission propose to extend the current common agricultural policy gradually to the new member states for 10 years after their accession, while at the same time considering a new cap applicable to all, which for financial and technical reasons could not come into force before 2006. it seems difficult to do otherwise in the immediate future: the rules in force in the union cannot be applied immediately to everyone, because that would be financially unsustainable, nor can a two-speed cap be accepted on a lasting basis, because that would be politically unacceptable. but at the same time we should avoid that, under the pretext of taking unavoidable transitional measures, we end up with a continent-wide administrative and financial gas factory. let us therefore affirm the future principles of a new cap: the pursuit of quality, respect for nature, support for multi-functionality, the maintenance of social balance in rural areas, in short, the defence of the european agricultural model, assumed by border protection, and thus financed by the consumer, rather than by an infinitely expanding community budget, financed by the taxpayer.
in writing. - the first reason why i support this report is the balance between the necessarily provisional nature of the voluntary commitment of the european automobile industry to improve the chances of survival of pedestrians and cyclists in the event of a collision and the coming community legislation, stricter and more robust legislation which will replace the voluntary commitment. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the protection of pedestrians and cyclists are respected. a framework directive with a precise and realistic timetable seems to me the appropriate way to achieve a truly serious road policy. the voluntary agreement does not seem to be able to provide the guarantees needed for a serious road safety policy. in addition to the fact that such an agreement is not only ineffective if one of the partners decides to withdraw, and suffers from a lack of openness and transparency, it also has the major drawback of not being truly binding. these are all reasons for a framework directive to establish a genuine policy to protect pedestrians and cyclists, and these are all reasons why i support this report calling on the commission to propose this directive.
in writing. - we voted against this text, another plea for the european institutions to be put even more at the service of private capital, for capital to be unhindered in europe and for the opening up of markets to become a reality in the sectors where privatisation is not yet complete: telecommunications, energy, postal services, transport. the report does not concern users who risk seeing the quality of public services deteriorate if these privatisations are eventually imposed. he is interested in the 'dynamic of investment and entrepreneurship' which he intends to promote by reducing the 'tax burden' and by 'access to finance', in particular for so-called small and medium-sized enterprises. he is calling for the european union to give them more attention and help. and while its explanatory memorandum provides information on the situation of 'small enterprises' in europe, it conceals the fact that the vast majority of these enterprises belong to large groups of which they are subsidiaries. in practice, this means that the eu's aid will mainly increase the weight of the larger companies. the elected representatives of the universal suffrage are therefore invited to give their democratic guarantee to the private interests of the small minority of capital owners by their votes.
in writing. - the commission's communication 'meeting commitments, accelerating the pace' has provided a comprehensive overview of the 'special provisions of the lisbon strategy in the field of entrepreneurship' and highlighted the remaining shortcomings in relation to small businesses and the craft sector. much progress remains to be made in supporting and developing learning, which is suffering from a poor image in many european countries. it is time to promote apprenticeship as a modern and dynamic form of training. i am therefore pleased that the european parliament, by adopting mrs vlasto's report, is offering, through the measures i have proposed in various amendments, to put in place a genuine policy in favour of apprenticeship: an erasmus-type exchange programme to encourage the mobility of apprentices; the european status of the apprentice and training exchange grants between apprentices and entrepreneurs; a policy of support for small businesses and craftsmen in the context of the 'european pathways' which i have promoted; the aim of the project is to develop a network of training courses in the framework of these "courses" to serve as a relays to lifelong vocational training.

commission. – mr president, the commission shares the concerns expressed about the use of child labour in the football industry. it condemns all forms of child exploitation, as well as the worst forms of child labour. it supports the calls on fifa and the sporting goods companies to make sure that no children are employed in the production of fifa licensed sportswear and footballs. the commission has not had any contact so far with fifa on this issue. it is ready to support ngos which work with local partners for the elimination of child labour. it has already financed several initiatives to combat child labour, especially in africa. the commission considers that assistance for and protection of vulnerable children should be seen in the wider context of poverty eradication and therefore in the framework of the community framework development cooperation. children are an important focal group in the community's external aid, particularly in sectoral policies such as education and health. the community is committed to applying the ilo core labour standards and has agreed to implement those standards in the framework of bilateral and multilateral agreements with developing countries. a good example is article 50 of the cotonou convention. in that article the community and the acp countries have reaffirmed their commitment to ilo core labour standards, including the fight against the worst forms of child labour. the community is increasing its support to universal and compulsory primary education in all developing countries as part of its commitments to the "education for all" framework and the millennium development goals for education and gender equality. it sees this as one of the most efficient means currently at its disposal for rescuing children from the vicious circle of exploitation. assistance for, and protection of, children is channelled through a number of commission programmes, including the european initiative for human rights and democracy. the promotion of children's rights was one of the priorities for funding in 2001 and will be mainstreamed in funding for the period 2002 to 2004. furthermore, the commission has also made children a cross-cutting priority for humanitarian assistance. in its communication on the promotion of core labour standards and social governance, the commission presented a comprehensive strategy proposing actions at european and international level. this should, in the medium term, ensure better implementation of the ilo core labour standards through institutional support and capacity building and trading in developing countries. as regards trade, in december 2001 the council adopted a revised gsp scheme by which additional trade preferences are granted to countries that respect core labour standards. this includes an improved social incentive scheme and extends the base for withdrawal of gsps to cover serious infringements of all ilo core conventions. finally, the commission played an active role in the un general assembly special session on children. in this context, the eu considers a rights-based approach as fundamental to the promotion of the interest of children, given that the un convention on the rights of the child is the most ratified international treaty in the world and provides an already agreed normative framework. the plan of action agreed at this special session contains strong elements aimed at combating child labour.

- equatorial guinea is currently the scene of unacceptable violations of fundamental human rights. dozens of opponents of president teodoro obiang's regime have been arbitrarily arrested and brought to trial on charges of conspiracy, incitement to rebellion and attempted assassination of the president. in reality, the trial that started on may 23 is only meant to leave the opposition leaders out of the picture. they and their families are held in inhuman conditions and subjected to brutal torture. freedom of expression and the press are systematically violated and independent journalists are subjected to insidious daily pressures. a repressive and brutal policy is being pursued against all citizens with a contrary ideology. the 68 opposition leaders were sentenced to prison terms in an unfair trial that violated the most basic rights of the defence, some even facing the death penalty. equatorial guinea must respect its commitments within the international community and the european union and embark on a genuine process of democratization, including free elections and full respect for human rights. a dialogue must be established between the forces of the opposition, with a view to guaranteeing political rights, democracy and pluralism. in view of this, the trial must be cancelled and the political prisoners released immediately. the press, on the other hand, must be able to report freely and safely. it is essential that the acp-eu joint parliamentary assembly urgently raise the problem of equatorial guinea in its assembly and that the council and the commission show the utmost firmness in their relations with the government of equatorial guinea. in order to ensure a swift restoration of the rule of law and respect for human rights, a consultation procedure between the government of guinea and the european union should be established as soon as possible, in accordance with article 96 of the cotonou agreement. we cannot, as europeans, remain indifferent to what is happening in equatorial guinea and to the attacks on human rights.

the rapporteur. - mr. president, i'm sorry i'm late. - i'm not sure i can do this. i thought i was scheduled later, but my colleague karla peijs was extremely convincing and i thank her and congratulate her on her contribution. this is an extremely difficult report. it is already very familiar to all the members of the committee on transport, having already failed twice. we are faced with a division which is not entirely ordinary, which is more geographical than political, between countries on the periphery who want to move and countries in the centre and transit who want to ban movement. i have been afraid for some time that we would be moving towards a contradictory consensus, where everyone would reject this directive, some because they want freedom of movement, others because they want freedom of prohibition. i think that a good balance has finally been reached, thanks to a commission proposal which is already a compromise after years of work. the only question that remains between us, between some who want to reject this draft directive and others, is whether we should legislate on this matter. i personally believe that. the present situation is indeed totally anarchic. it creates spontaneous difficulties in almost every country, and particularly at the borders. the dates of the ban exist for only seven out of eight countries, they are not coordinated, they create wild parking lots on the highways, and sometimes even on the motorway parking lots. the result is that lorry drivers are very often kept away from their homes because of the difficulties of scheduling, and, finally, they make it very difficult for transport operators and transport economists to organise the supply chain. i think that this legislation is relevant in every respect. firstly, because i think we have the necessary legal basis. it would be extremely paradoxical if road transport, which was the first sector of transport in europe to be established, now seems to be becoming subsidiary again. the ep would send a very bad message if it said: after all, the title 'transport' of the ec treaty does not apply to roads. how, then, can we ensure that it will apply to rail, to shipping and to all other sectors in the future? i personally strongly believe that transport europe should be implemented and that it should lead us to a policy which was foreshadowed by the white paper, and i think that is a good reason. however, there is another, even more important reason: there is no legal certainty today as regards these weekend driving bans and countries - i say this to those who want to reject the proposal - which would unilaterally tighten this proposal would be exposed to prosecutions and possible remedies based solely on the principles of free movement and non-discrimination and which would very likely threaten a number of existing bans, as well as the so-called 'fraise' regulation of 1998, which has just been imposed on france to allow lorries to drive under the mont blanc tunnel. i therefore consider this to be a guarantee of security for all the countries which have introduced bans. i would also remind you that the commission's proposal is a proposal which legalises the most severe bans currently in force, namely those in austria and germany, and which ensures that other countries can choose to comply with them. in reality, it is a system of convergence towards the german and austrian prohibitions with notified or not very important derogations, in short an exemption system, and i will personally support mrs peijs in calling for the introduction of an exemption for fresh horticultural products and flowers, because i believe these are products which do not keep well. in short, there is both a great deal of flexibility and a great deal of security in the prohibition of heavy goods vehicles on weekends. and i, who am in a region where there is a great deal of pressure from heavy goods vehicles, find it difficult to explain to my people that the european parliament does not want a ban on heavy goods vehicles on weekends, which would of course be a very serious setback. i am pleased that the committee on transport has finally succeeded in finding a modus vivendi. tomorrow we shall have to consider 21 amendments which have been voted on in committee and 18 new amendments. i believe that the text should not be too destabilised and i personally would call for the amendments tabled by the edd group (30, 28 and 31) to be rejected, which propose to return to the commission's draft, rejected in 1998: 'only on sundays' is too short. secondly, i would propose that amendments nos 22 and 23, tabled by the eldr group, should also be rejected, since they would, on the contrary, and quite legitimately, have the effect of giving the commission greater powers than are provided for in the text. finally, i agree with mrs peijs that some amendments distort the text and that we should not therefore venture into this area.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i have just arrived and i am pleased to be addressing the issue of biofuels, on which i worked for the committee on agriculture and rural development. it seems that this debate on biofuels has put the cart before the horse in the sense that it is primarily an agricultural problem and that it would have been wiser to wait until the evaluation of the berlin agenda is completed, that is to say until the mid-term review has been completed, before deciding in what direction biofuels policy should be directed. the first thing to remember about the quality of biofuel production is that it is the way in which agriculture is managed that determines the quality of production. the biofuels in question can be produced in a productivist way, with gmos, with inputs per hectare: but then the overall ecological balance would be negative. on the other hand, if we follow the guiding logic which has been the common agricultural policy for some time, that is to say, if we practice greater crop rotation and if we actually respect the environment, then biofuels and their production could become a positive complement to direct production for farmers. it is better to produce pure biodiesel, pure oil or use biomass to create hydrogen than to follow the logic of introducing a small percentage of fuel of agricultural origin into fuels which are still fossil fuels and therefore still highly polluting products at production. this opens the way to a direction which seems to us to be in the right direction. and since the proposed guidelines seem satisfactory, let us examine in detail what will be decided in the end.
- mr president, commissioner, i take the floor again on behalf of my colleague, dominique souchet, who was the other rapporteur for the opinion on the tax aspect in the committee on agriculture. i shall not go into the political arguments, but as you know, the market laws mean that, for two main reasons, biofuels cannot now develop spontaneously in the european union. the first reason is that the price of fossil fuels does not include the external costs of using a non-renewable resource - oil - and of massive greenhouse gas emissions. the second reason is that the oil industries benefit from a century of industrial experience, which has made it possible to optimise industrial costs to a great extent. it is therefore perfectly legitimate for the member states to apply differentiated taxation, a term which seems to us more appropriate than taxation, taxation which would promote the competitiveness of renewable fuels of plant origin and which does not contribute to the greenhouse effect. the aim is therefore to shift the excise duty on motor fuels towards a kind of eco-tax which hits fossil fuels more heavily than renewable fuels because of their negative externality. the commission's tax proposal should help the european union to achieve the green paper's target on the security of energy supply: 20% of alternative fuels in the road transport sector by 2020. the amendments adopted by the agriculture committee aim to make the directive more effective by emphasising that biofuels produced in the european union produce, as co-products, plant-based protein-rich material which can be used in animal feed. by removing the totally arbitrary limit of 50% to the tax differential; by removing the time limit - 31 december 2010 - since the externalities of oil sectors are permanent; allowing the total de-leaching of fuels used for the production of biofuels as is already the case for the production of petroleum products; specifying that the tax exemption can only apply to biofuels produced in the european union, otherwise the european union would not benefit from the greenhouse gas emission reductions or from the co-production of feed proteins.
