the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i would first of all like to thank the rapporteurs, mr trakatellis and mrs scheele, but i would also like to thank them for a lively and interesting debate. the proposals we are discussing today are linked to many important and general questions. the public is very concerned about the way gmos are being handled. it is our duty as legislators to ensure that the health and safety of consumers are guaranteed and that the environment and biodiversity are protected. we must also ensure that our citizens are given the opportunity to choose what they want to consume on the basis of reliable information. the marketing of genetically modified products must therefore be regulated in such a way as to achieve a high level of safety, transparency and reliability. the 2001/18 directive, the novel food regulation and the proposal on genetically modified food and feed have all been developed in response to these needs. the authorisation of the placing on the market of genetically modified products must therefore, in accordance with this legislation and in accordance with the precautionary principle, provide a high level of protection for human health and the environment. the eu system includes the requirement of a comprehensive risk assessment prior to placing on the market. traceability facilitates action after a product has been placed on the market, such as monitoring or recall. it also facilitates the provision of accurate information to all actors in the production and distribution chain. this proposal provides for the monitoring of genetically modified products at all stages of placing them on the market. it also provides that products containing genetically modified organisms must be labelled at all stages of their placing on the market. the ultimate aim is to enable consumers and the public to make their own choices. we believe that these measures are an important step towards restoring consumer and public confidence. the proposal provides for a number of clear obligations for operators without creating an unnecessary or unreasonable burden for operators or control authorities. the amendments tabled by the european parliament have addressed a number of important issues. this is the case, for example, with the scope. the question of whether products produced from animals fed genetically modified feed should be covered by the proposal will be discussed in more detail by my colleague david byrne. i would point out, however, that the commission has given this matter very careful consideration in the preparation of the proposal. after much discussion and consultation we came to the conclusion that it would be unworkable and incompatible with existing community legislation. the commission cannot therefore support the amendments in this respect. there are also a number of amendments aimed at limiting the commission's proposal. these proposals limit the traceability requirements to products only where dna and proteins are detectable. this would allow for the relevant labelling of products produced from gmos, but which no longer contain modified dna or protein. however, this approach has a number of limitations, which have been highlighted in our preparatory work. the main objection is that this would not ensure that consumers are able to make an informed choice. the commission cannot therefore accept these amendments. as regards the purpose, it is important to bear in mind that although traceability facilitates the implementation of security measures, where necessary, it cannot be considered as a security measure in itself. the precautionary principle can therefore be applied to legislation on risk-based authorisation, but not to the implementation of a traceability system in the context of this proposal. the commission cannot therefore support amendments nos 2 and 6 which link the precautionary principle to the proposal. i would also point out that traceability is not a tool for dealing with the question of coexistence. in the communication on life sciences and biotechnology adopted in january this year, the commission undertook to address the question of the coexistence of organic, conventional and genetically modified crops. this proposal deals only with the issue of traceability and labelling of genetically modified organisms. such traceability and labelling cannot serve as instruments for dealing with coexistence, as this issue presupposes decisions regarding the agricultural production system. the commission cannot therefore accept amendments nos 27 in full and 3 in part on this issue. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'commercial vehicle' to cover vehicles with a maximum mass of less than 100 tonnes. as regards the information to be provided to ensure traceability, it is important to bear in mind that the purpose of traceability of genetically modified organisms is different from that of products produced from genetically modified organisms. it is important to be able to identify genetically modified organisms that are to be deliberately released into the environment for cultivation, as such products contain viable genetically modified organisms that can reproduce and spread. the proposal therefore provides that operators must be able to indicate exactly which genetically modified organisms are in the products and that they must forward this information to the operator receiving the products. however, the potential risks to the environment of products containing genetically modified organisms intended for direct use in food, feed or processing are limited, as these organisms will not be cultivated. the commission therefore considers it both appropriate and sufficient that products containing gmos for food, feed or processing, including in bulk, are accompanied by documentation indicating this together with a list of the unique codes of the gmos that may be included in the product or in the shipment. these information provisions are in line with the provisions on cross-border shipments in the biosafety protocol. the commission believes that we should go no further than the provisions of the biosafety protocol in order to guarantee harmonized and consistent procedures in trade with third countries. the commission cannot therefore accept amendments nos 16 and 41, which require operators to indicate precisely which genetically modified organisms are in a consignment by indicating their unique codes. the commission also considers that the retention of information and documentation for traceability purposes should be limited to five years. there is no practical reason for extending this period from five to ten years. this would impose unnecessary additional burdens on operators. the commission cannot therefore accept the amendments seeking to extend this period to 10 years, namely amendments nos 17 and 22. the commission agrees with the european parliament that the provisions of this proposal are compatible with the provisions of directive 2001/18 and do not in any way restrict them. in this context, it is necessary to repeal article 4 (6) of the directive, which provides that member states are to take measures to ensure traceability at all stages of the placing on the market of genetically modified organisms. if article 4 (6) is not repealed, it is clear that national measures could run parallel to those covered by the proposal, which would disrupt the internal market and lead to legal uncertainty. the commission cannot therefore accept amendments nos 28 and 33 as they retain the traceability requirements of that directive. the commission also rejects amendment no 32 which prohibits new authorisations until the genetically modified organisms are assigned unique codes in accordance with this proposal. the current community authorisation framework already includes a number of conditions for authorisation of genetically modified organisms and genetically modified food, including that they must not cause harmful effects on human health and the environment. if the current authorisation criteria were extended to the unique codes under this proposal, an element of uncertainty would be introduced as to how community legislation is to be implemented, which the commission cannot accept. finally, i would like to say a few words about accidental occurrence and thresholds. an important issue is the unintended but technically unavoidable presence of genetically modified material in conventional products. today, over 50 million hectares of genetically modified crops are grown around the world. this means that genetically modified material is inadvertently and inevitably present in imported products, in particular bulk grain for food, animal feed and processing. it is now a reality that can hardly be avoided. a further freeze on authorization in the eu will only make the situation worse, as we would see evidence of an increased number of non-eu authorized genetically modified organisms. community legislation already provides for the labelling of accidental occurrence thresholds. it is therefore logical that accidental occurrence should be excluded, under specific conditions, from the labelling and tracing rules also in this proposal. the setting of thresholds is a multifaceted task and the commission considers that the most effective solution is achieved by a sectoral approach. the commission cannot therefore accept amendments nos 45 and 56, which propose to transfer the competence for the establishment of thresholds for food, feed or processing from the proposal on food and feed products. i repeat that the commission fully supports the principle of establishing thresholds for inadvertent occurrence, as proposed in a number of amendments. however, the proposal to include an article establishing such thresholds is more relevant to the proposal on genetically modified food and feed. madam president, i would like to thank you. to facilitate the handling of the matter, i have compiled the detailed position of the commission on all the amendments. this summary will be attached to the full minutes of the negotiations the commission's position: see the annex. finally, i would like to stress that it is in the interest of all of us, including the european citizens, that this proposal should come into force as soon as possible. comprehensive systems for traceability and labelling of genetically modified organisms are needed not only to facilitate the adoption of protective measures if necessary, but also to restore consumer and public confidence.
commission. – may i first express my thanks for all the work that has taken place in the different committees in relation to this proposal for a regulation on gm food and feed and also to thank the rapporteurs for their hard work – also the commission staff in both dgs, who have worked hard over the last couple of years to bring forward this proposal. the issues raised under this banner are complex and sensitive, and often give rise to strong emotional reactions and divided opinions. the vote in the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy frequently resulted in amendments being rejected or adopted by a very low margin. this highlights the difficulty of the subject – but also, in my opinion, serves to show that the commission proposal strikes a good, sensible and balanced compromise between the differing views. i do not intend to address each and every amendment, but instead would like to focus on four major issues. the first is the scope of the proposal. amendments propose to extend the scope of the proposal to processing aids and animal products from animals fed on gm feed and also to restrict the scope of the proposal to products derived from gmos which contain detectable modified dna or protein. in drawing up the proposal, the commission carefully considered which products should be included within its scope. we decided only to include products that are produced from a gmo. processing aids are not covered by the novel food regulation, as these are not considered to be food ingredients. that is also the reason why, in respect of community law, processing aids do not have to be labelled on the final product. for consistency reasons the commission believes it would be inappropriate to require authorisation and labelling of gm processing aids, without having the same requirements for conventional processing aids. for the first time the commission proposal specifically covers gm feed. however, to extend its scope to products such as milk, eggs and meat from animals fed on gm feed would radically depart from existing food legislation concerning animal products. the commission does not believe that including products from animals fed on gm feed in the scope of the regulation is either feasible or practicable. the commission therefore firmly rejects amendments to that effect. allow me now to address the amendments, tabled last week, that aim to restrict the scope of the proposal, both in respect of authorisation and in respect of labelling. the commission proposes to expand the current labelling requirements, and to require the mandatory labelling of food, food ingredients and feed produced from a gmo, even when modified dna or protein is not present – that is, not detectable in the food, feed, or in the ingredient. the classic example is table oil directly derived from gm maize, gm soya beans, or gm rapeseed. through the refinement process, all transgenic material has been removed. the question therefore arises – should it be labelled as gm or not? safety is not the issue here. this is dealt with in the authorisation process. labelling serves the purpose of informing consumers and users and allowing them to exercise choice. what is abundantly clear to me is that the gm origin of products is something that really matters to a large number of consumers. we also know that many of the member states want the mandatory labelling of gm derivatives. a number of them have clearly indicated that they would not support the authorisation of new gmos if labelling and traceability of gm derivatives was not required. those who argue against mandatory labelling of all gm derivatives, irrespective of the presence of modified dna or protein, take the view that control of this obligation is unworkable and that it would lead to massive fraud. let me state very clearly that i cannot accept this argument. i cannot accept that legal requirements are not enforceable if compliance cannot be checked through analytical methods. the reality is that a great number of regulatory requirements and legal rights, from mandatory labelling of the geographic origin of products to intellectual property rights, are enforced without any recourse to physical checks. none of the practical difficulties predicted in connection with gm labelling has proven insurmountable in these contexts. indeed, the very requirement that we are discussing today is already in effect in many parts of the community, albeit imposed by companies within the food chain rather than through community legislation. i have yet to meet a business operator who would admit that he or she does not know the origin of the ingredients he or she is using. there is a good reason for this. admitting that you do not know whether your input is gm or not is also admitting, by the same token, that you do not know whether or not you are perhaps using a non-authorised gm. it is probably for this very reason that those who oppose the mandatory labelling of products not containing modified dna or protein also propose to exempt these products from authorisation. this, i am afraid, would be totally unacceptable to the commission. it would turn the clock back more than five years, before the adoption of the novel foods regulation, at the very time that international consensus is emerging, particularly in codex alimentarius, that all foods produced from gmos should be subject to a pre-marketing approval process. the message to our consumers would be unacceptable. currently, the message is: “sorry, we cannot tell you whether this table oil is gm or not”. if these amendments were adopted, we would have to add: “...and, sorry again, if it is gm, we cannot tell you whether the gm from which it is originating was authorised or not”. finally, i would like to address the issue of gmo-free labelling. you have already understood that the commission cannot accept gmo-free or non-gm as an alternative to the mandatory labelling of gm-derivatives. however, i do not believe that the amendment that has been tabled to the proposed regulation in relation to a voluntary gm regime is appropriate. but let us look at this again at second reading. i also take up the point that the public will be misled by the proposal that we are putting forward in suggesting that there should be a gmo-free regime. there is an overwhelming risk that the public would be misled by a gmo-free labelling regime because of the fact that such guarantees cannot be given to the public and to try to do so by a mandatory labelling regime, supported by the law of the community, would, in my view, run the risk of bringing the law into disrepute. therefore, having put this objective into the white paper on food safety two years ago, we thought long and hard about this. i have to say to you, mrs flemming, that having considered this, we came to the conclusion that this was not the way forward, for the reasons i have identified. that is why we have come forward with this particular proposal. concerning environmental risk assessment, a series of amendments challenge the suggestion that the european food safety authority should carry out the environmental risk assessment as part of the overall assessment of a gm food or feed. in fact, these amendments would effectively deny the proposed regulation the status of sectoral legislation within the meaning of directive 2001/18. mrs doyle asked earlier why we bring forward two pieces of legislation and add to the confusion. the piece of legislation that commissioner wallström is in charge of is a horizontal piece of legislation as is directive 2001/18. in directive 2001/18 it was envisaged that there would be sectoral legislation, brought forward in due course. that is the piece of legislation that i am promoting – the food and feed legislation. it was a requirement that this house voted on in 2001/18, calling for sectoral legislation. that is what the commission is doing. that has been the objective from the beginning. that is what parliament has already voted for. the commission considers that these requirements are fully provided for by the proposed gm food and feed regulation. equally, it would also deny the application of the “one door, one key” principle. this would result in the need for companies to file more than one application for the same gmo even though the applications would contain much of the same information. in my view, the "one door, one key" proposal is fundamental and a huge advantage not only to the applicants but also to consumers. the commission cannot therefore accept the amendments requiring the environmental risk assessment for gmos covered by the food and feed proposal to be carried out only under directive 2001/18. a number of amendments have been put forward with the intention of strengthening the information requirements of the proposal. the commission would be prepared to accept some of the amendments to increase further the level of public availability of information, but i do not consider it appropriate or reasonable to try to amend general comitology rules through this instrument. it is also important that we do not forget the intellectual property rights of companies. in this regard i would draw attention to article 31 of the proposal which, in my opinion, provides the right balance between protecting such legitimate rights and the interests of transparency. a number of amendments suggest that very small trace amounts of unauthorised gmos and gm material should not be accepted in food or feed. it would simply not be feasible or practicable if the proposals did not provide for any tolerance – under certain conditions – for small traces of food and feed of gmos or gm material. indeed, even when an operator makes an effort to avoid using gmos or gm material, traces may be technically unavoidable during cultivation, harvest, transport and processing. i have said it before and i will say it again. whether we like it or not, this has become a reality. we have to live in the real world. this is not just a problem that is exclusive to gmos. in the production of food, feed and seed, it is practically impossible to achieve end products that are 100% pure and totally free from foreign substances. in the eu, the scientific committees have already assessed a number of gmos and concluded that they do not pose a risk to the environment or to human health. however, some of these gmos have been awaiting final approval for some time. i therefore consider it sensible that the proposal allows for these gmos and gm material, which have been found safe in terms of a complete positive risk assessment from the eu scientific committee, to be present in food or feed up to a maximum of 1%. this is provided that the gm presence is adventitious or technically unavoidable. it was suggested earlier by mr lannoye that we were allowing for the presence of up to 1% of unauthorised gm material. that is not correct. we must make a clear distinction between unauthorised gm material for which an application has never been made and gm material for which an application has been made, a scientific assessment has been made by the scientific committee, a risk assessment has been positive in favour of that application, but no authorisation has yet been granted because of the existence of the moratorium. they are two different situations. it is the latter type, for which we are allowing the presence of up to 1%, not the former. it is an important distinction that i would like parliament to take note of. other amendments suggest that a maximum labelling threshold for adventitious presence of authorised gm material should be established at one half of one percent (0.5%). i believe that we should follow the principle established in directive 2001/18, which provides for thresholds to be fixed in comitology procedure in order to take into account technological and scientific progress. i believe that is the right way to go about this because the response can be made more quickly in the comitology or secondary legislation procedure, rather than putting this into a piece of legislation as has been suggested in the amendment. if we ever need to amend, we will have to do so by the normal procedures that we are used to, which may very well take more than a year or two to do. i repeat that the commission considers that the two proposals together strike a good and balanced compromise between the differing views. furthermore, i firmly believe that they also provide the right approach to foster public confidence and social acceptance of the application of biotechnology in agri-food production. i hope that parliament understands the reasoning behind the decision to reject or to accept in part only some of the amendments put forward. a full list of the commission's position on each of the amendments is being provided to parliament. i do not propose to read them out one by one, but i trust that this will be included in the minutes of this sitting see annex – position of the commission.
- the joint discussion is over. the vote will take place tomorrow at noon.
- the next item is the report (a5-0234/2002) by mr trakatellis, on behalf of the parliament's delegation to the conciliation committee, on the joint text approved by the conciliation committee for a european parliament and council decision adopting a programme of community action in the field of public health (2003-2008) (pe-cons 3627/2002 - 5-0204/2002 - 2000/0119 (cod)).
commission. – madam president, i am very grateful to parliament for its efforts in developing with us and with the council this ambitious new programme. throughout the course of the codecision process, you have put in an enormous amount of work – by analysing the various issues and by putting forward new ideas and approaches. there is no doubt that as a result the programme has been significantly strengthened and that it will provide a firm basis for the development of the community’s health strategy, including new areas of work, such as developing a vaccination strategy and responding to the threat of bio-terrorism. your efforts have further reinforced the three objectives that the commission set out from the very beginning in its proposal. these are: improving health information; - the next item is the report (a5-0243/2002) by mr lisi, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending council directive 96/82/ec of 9 december 1996 on the control of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances (com (2001) 624 - c5-0668/2001 - 2001/0257 (cod)).
- madam president, commissioner, mr rapporteur, we all remember the recent industrial disasters which have caused great mourning in europe. these accidents have occurred despite the legislation in the sites, their structure and geographical location and, finally, on the people, both on the employees as a whole and on the population living or working near the industrial sites. as regards authorities should be given the possibility of requesting that such studies carried out by the company may be examined by a third party in case of doubt. training efforts are necessary for staff as this is a means of better accident prevention. the training must also be aimed at the staff of the subcontracting companies working on the site, as these staff are proving to be increasingly numerous. mobilization inside the companies, but also outside, is essential because in the event of an accident it is secondarily the people living near the sites who are also victims. it is therefore necessary to involve them in the implementation of the external emergency plans by allowing representatives of the population to be part of the advisory committees and also by informing the entire population commission. – madam president, firstly i would like to thank the rapporteurs, mr lisi and also mrs corbey, for their hard work. i know also that they are very interested in this important issue. on 3 october last year i made a declaration here in parliament on the toulouse accident. i proposed that we should move forward with this amendment. in the meantime we have been able to incorporate some conclusions from the toulouse accident into the amendment proposal. however, i remain convinced that it is not because of deficiencies in the seveso ii directive that the toulouse accident happened. nor am i of the opinion that legislation is the only means to ensure industrial safety. safety consists of a mosaic of factors, but the responsibility lies first and foremost with the operators of hazardous facilities. thereafter it is the task of the public authorities to control the operators and to inspect the sites. in my opinion – and i do not seem to be the only one to have this opinion – toulouse was much more a problem of practical application of the legislation than a problem of legislation being deficient. as long as we face problems of enforcement, we should rather concentrate our efforts on good cooperation, both within industry and public authorities, in order to improve safety in practice and not by the letter of the law. so the commission proposal did not aim at a major overhaul of the seveso ii directive. as you are aware, the seveso ii directive has replaced the original seveso directive of 1982 that had been in force for more than 15 years. seveso ii itself represented a major revision of the european major hazards legislation and has only been applicable for three years. i therefore stress that the commission does not intend to move from seveso ii to seveso iii at this point in time. having said this, i regret to say that only a few of the 55 amendments proposed actually address issues raised in the commission proposal itself. the majority of the other amendments seem to have been developed under the cloud of the tragic accident in toulouse and address issues unrelated to the scope of the directive. i would like to draw your attention to the fact that the azf site in toulouse was fully covered by the seveso ii directive unlike baia mare and enschede. it has been repeatedly stated, including in the report of the inquiry commission set up by the french assemblée nationale, that the seveso ii directive contributes significantly to improving safety. moreover, some of the suggested changes will actually increase red tape with no direct impact on safety. i will give you some examples. nevertheless, the commission has had a careful look at all amendments proposed with a view to accepting as many as possible. so we have taken a very positive approach. let me make some detailed comments on some of the proposed amendments. firstly as regards mining, the commission cannot agree to deleting the words "chemical and thermal" as proposed in amendment no 6. in this context we also reject amendment no 43 proposing to make references to the water framework and hazardous waste directives. in our opinion the seveso ii directive should only apply when chemical processes are involved and chemical substances are stored. it is not meant to be mining legislation or waste legislation and the future directive on mining waste management should cover safety aspects of disposal facilities. secondly, as regards explosives, the definition of the two new categories for explosives are the result of a multi-stakeholder consultation aimed at reinforcing the directive while not placing undue burdens on industry. the commission therefore rejects amendment no 49. member states have the possibility to make use of article 176 of the ec treaty to introduce lower threshold levels at national level as the netherlands has done. regarding ammonium nitrate, the commission can accept amendment no 39, in principle amendment no 48, and in part amendment no 53. i can also inform you that the council's position on ammonium nitrate is almost identical to the amendments proposed and this is a sign of good cooperation between council, parliament and the commission and will greatly facilitate an agreement. as regards land-use planning, i acknowledge parliament's strong wish to reinforce article 12 of the seveso ii directive. the commission will therefore accept amendment no 13, and amendment no 54 in part, but reject amendments nos 51 and 55. furthermore, the commission is of the opinion that the development of schemes of incentives and/or funding for the relocation of establishments is a task to be performed by member states and cannot therefore accept amendment no 31 either. there are more things to be said about land use and i understand how important parliament thinks this is. we will definitely follow up this matter and we have also had european workshops on land-use planning. as a result, it was decided to re-establish a european working group on land-use planning involving stakeholders from all interested parties and at all levels in order to develop harmonised guidance on technical advice, taking into account industrial risks in land use planning. this is what parliament is asking for in amendment no 30. there are other amendments that the commission cannot accept. i shall give you a couple of examples. amendment no 35 suggests introducing a new article on training of staff, which would compel industrial operators to provide competent authorities with a training report every two years. however, the issue of training is appropriately addressed in annex iii and annex iv. moreover, as the safety report has to demonstrate that the aspect of safety management has been put into effect it must necessarily contain the information on training of staff. we do not advocate the duplication of effort that would be involved in producing a separate report on training. last, but not least, several amendments even aim at regulating how the public should be informed – newspapers, mail, internet – and go as far as imposing certain obligations on the mayors of municipalities. this raises not only the issue of subsidiarity, but also the following question: should the provision of information be a one-way street or do we believe that responsible citizens should also actively exercise their right to know by requesting information? one of the core novelties of the seveso ii directive is that it gives more rights to the public, but it also strikes a fine balance between active and passive information, thus imposing equal responsibilities on industrial operators, public authorities and citizens. let me confirm the commission's position on the amendments. the commission is able to accept amendments nos 1, 2, 8, 27, 32, 37, 39, 40, 42 and 45. the commission can accept in principle amendments nos 9, 13, 16, 18, 23, 24, 46 and 48 and in part amendments nos 7, 17, 25, 26, 30, 50, 53 and 54. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 3 to 6, 10 to 12, 14, 15, 19 to 22, 28, 29, 31, 33 to 36, 38, 41, 43, 44, 47, 49, 51, 52 and 55. so by way of conclusion, and excuse me for speaking for so long, i would like to emphasise that it is in our common interest – the interest of european citizens – to have this proposal adopted and enforced rapidly. i would therefore ask you to accept the commission's view – which is largely shared by the council – not to consider the present proposal as an opportunity for a major revision of the seveso ii treaty. as you can see, i have already made an effort to accept as many amendments as possible, thus already going beyond our initial intention. i promise that within the timespan of the sixth environmental action programme the commission will undertake to gather all the experience gained with the application of the present directive and present a new proposal for a more comprehensive review of seveso ii as necessary. thank you for the debate. commission. – i am pleased to have been afforded the opportunity to speak, on behalf of the european commission, at the conclusion of the plenary debate on this report. ms van lancker’s report addresses a range of important issues which are amongst the most sensitive and significant health and ethical issues facing our societies today. at the outset, let me acknowledge the efforts that have been made by the rapporteur to respond to the legal order of the european union. as the rapporteur rightly acknowledges, the european union does not have competence to engage in health care delivery. this is clear from the treaty. the treaty sets out in article 152(5) that “community action in the field of public health shall fully respect the responsibilities of the member states for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care.” therefore, i would underline, as does the report, that the delivery of health care falls within the responsibility of member states. this also applies to the policy of delivery of sexual and reproductive health services. in this regard i note, as ms van lancker has said, that the vast majority of recommendations in the report are directed to member states and accession countries. it will be a matter for them to consider how to respond most appropriately in line with their own constitutional and legal frameworks. let me avail of this opportunity to underline that the commission has no ambition to become engaged in health care delivery systems or medical care. at present we do not have the power to do so. i do not envisage this situation changing in the future. subsidiarity is the underlying principle in the delivery of health services and this should be respected. let me be clear. the commission will not be making any proposals in areas relating to the delivery of health services. this is the responsibility of member states. so whilst a full and frank debate about key health issues is essential, we must also respect the distinction between member states' and community competences when we begin to consider general recommendations in sensitive areas. clearly, there are important cultural, ethnic, ethical and religious differences between our citizens on such matters. in highlighting the importance of sexual and reproductive health and rights, sensitivity needs to be shown to the divergent attitudes on issues such as abortion in our member states. sexual and reproductive health issues are core topics of social and public health debate in europe today. these issues touch the lives of our citizens in a way that other issues never could. for this reason they are issues best decided as close as possible to those affected. but in the context of developing a public health policy, there are a number of issues which require careful consideration and analysis. and reports, such as the one under discussion tonight, provide insight into the complex issues affecting today’s policymakers. in all aspects of sexual and reproductive health, the more informed and the better educated the individual, the greater is the chance that they will avoid pitfalls, by taking responsibility for their health and wellbeing. of course, in often very difficult real life situations, individuals must move from absorbing information to developing a holistic understanding of how these issues impact upon their lives. naturally, in this debate, there is significant attention addressed to the responsibility and rights of women in dealing with their health and wellbeing. i believe however, that greater attention needs to be brought to bear on the responsibilities of men in this domain. too often we overlook the importance of improving men’s education so as to change behaviour, attitudes and involvement. i hope that our member states will place a greater emphasis on the education and information of men in this important area. the 1997 commission report on the state of women’s health in the european community also provided some useful analysis. it drew attention to the fact that sexual and reproductive health issues are vital questions for women of reproductive age. work on public health indicators is ongoing within the european commission. experts are developing indicators, which will provide the basis for gathering and analysing health information in europe. these will include a range of indicators addressing various aspects of reproductive and sexual health. the commission is prepared to compile and undertake statistical, epidemiological investigations on the basis of collected data. i must stress, however, that the quality of such work will depend on the quality and compatibility of the data provided by the member states. within the new public health programme, the third strand will address health determinants through disease prevention and health promotion. this applies also to sexual and reproductive health. as with the health promotion programme, accession countries can participate. however, the local health promotion and disease prevention strategy is the responsibility of the member states. this would include school health education and promotion projects which can draw on the scientific data generated by this analysis. in relation to the "mexico city policy" of the us administration referred to in the report, the european commission does not see itself in a position to comment or react. this issue is a matter for the us administration to decide. i have therefore restricted my comments today to those areas for which the commission has competence. may i conclude by underlining the importance and sensitivity of the issues under discussion today which have been raised and explored as a result of the work of ms van lancker.

- mr president, commissioner, madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, the green group/european free alliance has been very keen to see the implementation of the framework programme simplified and, to put it mildly, humanized. the report by mrs quisthoudt-rowohl, whom i would like to thank most sincerely for her availability and for the sensible provisions she has made on the rules of participation, sets us on the right track. i would stress that for the first time in the framework programme, the applicant countries will have rights equivalent to those of the member states, and european scientific cooperation organisations and associated countries will be able to participate on the same basis as entities established in the member states. i am also pleased to see that organisations from third countries will be able to participate fully in the actions of the framework programme. this is particularly important for our group, which wants to intensify research with developing countries and those in the mediterranean and latin american regions. in view of the new management arrangements - brought about in particular by the new tools - it will certainly be necessary to optimise the operation during the implementation of this programme, while avoiding the use of formal conciliation procedures. in this connection, we thank the council, in the person of mr marimon, who has devoted much attention to this matter, for accepting our proposal to speed things up. we will therefore be happy to maintain regular contacts with parliament and the commission, which will be entirely possible thanks to mr busquin's benevolent expertise, and in particular for a possible update during the mid-term evaluations in 2004.
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, together with the decision on the framework programme itself and the specific programmes, the rules on participation and dissemination constitute the third element of the mechanism for implementing the research framework programme. that's not the least of it. the rules of participation establish the legal and financial framework governing the implementation and financing of the research activities of the sixth framework programme. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs quisthoudt-rowohl, very warmly for the very thorough work she has done on the proposal for these rules, in close cooperation with the intervention areas. i also thank the rapporteurs for their opinions, mr linkohr, mrs plooij-van gorsel, mr piétrasanta and mr alyssandrakis, and the president of the commission, mr westendorp, for the excellent atmosphere they have created in these discussions. and you are right, mrs quisthoudt-rowohl, to point out that this agreement was achieved thanks to intensive work in fruitful discussions in which everyone was involved. i would like to stress, as you do, the role of the spanish presidency, particularly in the case of mr marimon, and i believe that the result achieved confirms our common desire to simplify and lighten the burden of the previous programme, while maintaining the necessary rigour. the new model is based on a principle of greater autonomy for consortia, which will be reinforced by more flexible rules and contracts and a substantial reduction in administrative burdens on them. the intention was to make the rules simpler, lighter and easier to use, more readable and understandable for the participants, and more flexible without losing their rigorousness. you are also right, mrs quisthoudt-rowohl, to say that it was only an impression to think that the commission was going to discharge all its prerogatives and therefore all its responsibilities, particularly in relation to the evaluation and selection of proposals to be financed, the selection of participants to receive community funds and the establishment of an effective system for monitoring the projects financed and the decision on the payments to be made. as you have rightly pointed out, the whole process of solidarity must be understood in this context. of course, the rules have also been adapted from those which prevail today to take account of the new developments which have emerged with the sixth framework programme, starting with the introduction of new financial support instruments. among the main changes, some of which were initiated by parliament, is the fact that participation in a research project - except in special cases - is open to any legal entity and not only to legal entities with a specific research activity. the same applies to the conditions for participation of the organisations of the candidate countries and the eu member states - a strong political signal at a time when enlargement is being discussed. the opening up of participation and funding to legal entities established in third countries covered by international cooperation activities also broadens the scope of the european research area. these include the introduction of full participation for international organisations of european interest, the reduction in the number of standard contracts and a new procedure for the entry into force of contracts, the simplification of the funding systems, the budget grant and the integration grant for integrated projects and networks of excellence respectively, the use of audit certificates to justify the expenditure of participants for greater financial security under conditions involving fewer procedures and, finally, the simplification of the rules on intellectual property with the principle of single definition of an overall framework and general principles to be respected, the detailed provisions of which may vary according to the types of action. on all these and many other points, the extensive and sustained discussions between the european parliament, the council and the commission have led to agreement. the commission can therefore formally accept the single compromise amendment which embodies this agreement, and i think the council has expressed the same sentiment. among the points of compromise i would like to highlight, i would mention in particular: the increase in the minimum number of compulsory participants from two to three, the introduction of the possibility of an evaluation of the proposals received in two stages, the limitation to certain specific cases of the use of anonymity for the evaluation of proposals, the mention of a richer set of criteria for the evaluation of proposals, mandatory or optional criteria such as activities, as mrs mcnally has stressed, aimed at increasing the role of women in research and creating synergies with education at all levels, including a clarification of how the responsibility of participants is to be exercised, the definition of the method of calculating the financial contribution of the community to research projects in networks of excellence - this is a question which has given rise to much discussion - and the introduction of the notion of consortium or the establishment of a consortium agreement as a key element. a word about the rules of euratom participation. they are broadly similar to those defined for the framework programme and are therefore acceptable. the only amendment not covered by the compromise is a rate of funding for merger associations which unfortunately cannot be envisaged at this level, within the limits of the budget. the commission cannot accept it, but we will try to find a compromise. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, despite the difficulties, thanks to the efforts and the will of the rapporteur, the rules for participation in the sixth framework programme will, i hope, be adopted tomorrow at first reading. we can only rejoice in this. for the scientific community and for business, this is an essential element in the implementation of this framework programme, which is an instrument of the european research area. i think the scientific community has already partially gotten the message. over fifteen thousand expressions of interest have been received and will be made public. this will enable us to prepare as well as possible for the implementation of the framework programme by the end of the year. once again, i thank parliament for its more than constructive action.

in writing. - consumer protection requires clear and precise information on traceability and labelling of products. we are against the setting of a threshold for the accidental presence of unauthorised gmos, on the basis that consumers must be able to have access to non-gmos. the 1% threshold supported by the ppe and the 0.5% threshold proposed by the pse are unacceptable. for gmos not authorised in the union, zero tolerance should be applied. consumers would not understand that banned gmos are tolerated, even in infinitesimal quantities. the principle of strict traceability should apply in the same way to products from third countries. the import of products must not lead to the fraudulent introduction into the member states of transgenic foodstuffs which we do not allow to be grown. we support the amendments which closely involve the food authorities of the member states and the local and regional authorities responsible for food and health matters in the formulation of the opinions of the european food authority. in this and other sensitive areas, we must not allow excessive centralisation to take citizens away from the decisions affecting their daily lives.
in writing. - the trakatellis and scheele reports refer to two interlocking proposals for regulations which deal with overlapping issues of authorization, traceability and labelling of genetically modified organisms. this presentation, which makes the subject even more difficult to understand, seems to be due only to competence rivalries within the commission. for citizens who already have difficulty understanding europe, this method is intolerable and should have justified the rejection of these texts. the european parliament has not had that dignity and has therefore been reduced to voting in a certain confusion. the idea is to provide certain guarantees of rigor in the authorization and labelling of gmos. on the whole, i supported the amendments to tighten the text, which have often been adopted, so that from this point of view the result does not look bad. unfortunately, the commission has inserted into both regulations a method of voting and decision-making which will wipe out the free choice of the states. i shall explain this in my explanation of vote on the scheele report. that is why i abstained on both reports.
in writing. - this report rightly denounces the fragmented and inadequate nature of community legislation on gmos. but how could it be otherwise ? the big agro-food, chemical and biotechnology companies are obviously not interested in too stringent regulation, let alone in any real control, especially in a context of justified consumer fears. it would of course be possible to impose a coherent system of obligations on them and above all to allow the community to control the companies in question. however, the european institutions are too closely tied to the employers and their interests to be able to impose any real constraints on them in any field. we do not want to follow in the footsteps of those who want to make gmos a modern-day scarecrow, but because we have no confidence in the choices of capitalists who are not guided by the precautionary principle but by the pursuit of profit alone, we are voting for this report. although the proposed measures are part of the competition war between european and american trusts, they could lead to a little more transparency, or even safety for consumers. it is for the same reasons and with the same reservations, particularly on the respect for confidential data which only benefits employers, that we voted for the scheele report.
in writing. - the scheele report endorses a highly questionable centralised european procedure for authorising gmos, in line with the commission proposal com (2001) 425 final. the proposal vaguely refers to decision 1999/468/ec on comitology, according to which: (2) if the committee does not agree, the matter is referred back to the council itself; however, if the council does not adopt the commission's proposal (by a qualified majority) or does not oppose it (unanimously), the decision is taken by the commission alone. thus, a gmo may be authorised against the wishes of a minority of member states and even, in some cases, against the wishes of a majority. there is no national safeguard clause at this level even if, for example, a country expresses its opposition to a gmo in a referendum. this procedure is clearly intended to leave the commission free to give authorizations which governments will then say 'we can't do anything about it, it is the european rule'. that is the way democracy works in brussels.
in writing. - the european parliament has just taken a major step forward in responding to the demand of european citizens concerned about the impact of the presence of gmos in their diet. in voting on mrs scheele's report, parliament has made a clear statement to call for all products containing gmos (including, for example, chocolate) to be labelled. the green group regrets, however, that while animal products are required to be labelled, the final product, meat, is not. that's the only negative thing about this report. while the farmer can choose non-gm feed for his animals, the consumer cannot know whether the feed contains gmos or not. it is regrettable that parliament has not gone all the way. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of genetically modified organisms (gmos) in foodstuffs.
in writing. - the commission presents a directive on the authorisation and labelling of genetically modified food and feed intended for animals. in many ways, this project reflects pressure from the agro-food lobby. it is particularly important to propose an acceptable threshold for the presence of gmos in marketed products, which are banned because they are considered to be dangerous! as karin scheele points out in her report to parliament, such a measure would 'empty the whole of the union's provisions on biosafety'. as regards the gmos currently authorised, the commission proposes a very high threshold below which it would not be necessary to inform the consumer of their presence by means of mandatory labelling. we therefore support the rapporteur's proposal to reduce this threshold from 1% to 0.5%. we will also support any amendment strengthening the directive on the authorization procedure and the right of the public to information. behind the technical appearance of the issues (labelling, traceability) are hidden the essential political and democratic issues that are, in france, a particular resonance at the time when josé bové, leader of the peasant confederation, is imprisoned for his fight for a food respectful of the rights of producers, the health of the population and the quality of the environment.
in writing. - in addition to the commission's proposals, the lisi report calls for a much more stringent revision of the seveso directive. the main advances are: lowering of the thresholds for explosive substances, inclusion of new carcinogenic substances or certain mining activities, taking into account storage as a potential hazard for certain substances. the report stresses the need to integrate company staff, their practical and professional experience, and their training in order to move towards greater safety. the desire for transparency and public information and for the involvement of local populations in all aspects of security is another very positive element of the report. however, the health and safety committees are still not taken into account in the preparation of safety plans. for subcontracting, the report recommends associating staff and training them. however, the logic of subcontracting is not called into question. the objective of maximum profitability pursued by management, which is reflected in the massive use of subcontracting, runs counter to the search for a maximum level of safety. the report also does not stress enough the responsibility of the management of the companies concerned. in spite of these remarks, and for the reasons i have mentioned above, i shall vote in favour of this report.
in writing. - the successive disasters of the enschede in the netherlands, the baia mare in romania, the donaña in spain and the azf in toulouse have led the council and the european parliament to legislate to tighten the rules on the use of dangerous substances. better late than never, though. however, even if the report is adopted, as we hope, the legislation will still be insufficiently binding and will not allow for greater responsibility to be imposed on employers towards the community. it must be remembered that this irresponsibility represents a serious danger for the inhabitants of the neighbourhood and beyond, but also, in the first place, for the workers of these dangerous enterprises. it is significant, however, that in the explanatory memorandum the author of this report argues against "an extreme interpretation of the precautionary principle" which could "unnecessarily penalize the industries". this complacency towards employers, even in a text intended in principle to strengthen "the control of the dangers associated with major accidents", heralds other major accidents due not to the dangerousness of the substances but to the search for maximum profit by companies.
in writing. - i am pleased to see the legislative package for fp6 'closed' today. we have kept our commitments by adopting the report on fp6 as such in may 2002, the reports on the specific programmes in june 2002 and, finally, the rules on participation in july 2002 which provide the legal and financial framework for the implementation of the research guidelines until 2006. i welcome the work done by mrs quisthoudt-rowohl at this stage. it has done everything in its power to ensure that the three institutions can reach compromises which will allow adoption at first reading. the commission pursues various objectives which we have supported from the outset: to introduce simpler rules, to allow for faster and lighter management, to strengthen the protection of the community's financial interests. however, several pitfalls soon appeared. i can only address the question of joint responsibility. the commission proposal provided for joint and several liability of the participants for grants from the community budget, including funds managed by other participants. the limitations of this concept soon became apparent. after several informal trilogues, it was decided to make each participant responsible for his or her share of the community funds. in writing. - in the introduction to the european central bank's 2001 annual report, wim duisenberg gives an interesting personal view of integration. he believes that it will be given a new impetus, as the single currency will encourage citizens to demand "the removal of the remaining barriers between their countries". he concludes: "european integration in the future could be more about a bottom-up process, initiated by european citizens, than a top-up process, driven by politicians and experts". the text contains two admissions: first, the current institutional set-up is unstable; secondly, until now, the construction of europe has been a matter for 'politicians and experts'. however, the idea that european citizens might, because of the single currency, demand more integration seems to us to be questionable. this is probably what the eurocrats want, they want the citizens to tell them that they were right all along. but that's not what we're seeing on the ground at the moment. the process described by mr duisenberg is not really spontaneous, but rather remote-controlled from above, through the existence of the single currency. always the manipulation.

in writing. (fr) fortunately, the van lancker report, which the european parliament has just adopted (despite the fact that i voted against it), has no legal significance. in their efforts to provide advice on gender equality and the legalization of abortion, the authors of the report do not hesitate to interfere with the competence of the member states and even the candidate countries. the text is a typical example of the eu's method of extending its powers. commissioner byrne explained last night that 'sexual and reproductive rights' are not, of course, included in the treaties in a narrow sense, but that on the other hand 'reproductive health' can be linked to public health in general, in which the commission has some additional powers. in any case, in the absence of effective supervision of the subsidiarity principle, the eu institutions are free to say whatever they like. the substance of the van lancker report is that it treats the sensitive subject of abortion too lightly. each country must be able to appeal to its own values and its own trends. in any case, it must be admitted that the state cannot prevent it, but it is difficult to recommend that it be given a happy green light.

the rapporteur. - mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the commission communication has indeed - as you have said, mr president - drawn up a strategy to promote basic labour standards in the context of globalisation. what are we talking about ? it should be noted at the outset that the fundamental standards in question are those identified in the 1998 declaration at the copenhagen summit and enshrined in eight ilo conventions: freedom of association and the right to collective bargaining, the elimination of all forms of forced or compulsory labour, the effective abolition of child labour, and the elimination of discrimination in employment and occupation. while the international labour organisation (ilo) is the body competent to define and negotiate labour standards, the european council of october 1999 recalled that the union should provide strong support for the protection of fundamental labour rights. the role of the european union in the wto was thus particularly emphasised. it is clear, however, that the difficulties, if not the inability, of enforcing these basic rights on a world scale are real. at the same time, voices are being raised all over the world to denounce economic development which is not in harmony with social development, and the communication itself notes that 'market governance has taken precedence over social governance'. are we going to stand by that ? i would first of all like to welcome the communication and the proposals attached to it and to note the interest and the opportunity to launch a debate within our institutions on this relationship between globalisation and labour law and social governance. the communication thus acknowledges that while market mechanisms and trade liberalization are essential for development, they cannot in themselves ensure development for all people on this planet. as regards the basic labour standards, this globalisation must involve the implementation of public regulations as effectively as those implemented in the market area. the wto cannot ignore these standards. nor can it be the only space for these global regulations. nor can it be the one which dominates all the other institutions. on the basis of these considerations, we are submitting this opinion to you, which is intended to complement the commission's proposals. it is based on some of the key ideas developed in the report. i would like to mention three elements which i consider to be fundamental. firstly, the necessary definition and clarification of relations between the european union, the ilo and the wto. the major difficulty in enforcing core labour standards at global level is highlighted by the lack of coherence in the approaches taken by various institutions and the weakness of the global governance system, its architecture not adapted to today's realities, and the lack of a common hierarchy of standards between these different global regulations. the report calls for, among other things, that the partnership between the european union and the ilo be reviewed and corrected - but this is being done and we welcome it - that the ilo be granted observer status in the wto, that the ilo's decisions, including the results of its inspections, be published and that the union really take account of this in its relations with third countries. the second line of action concerns development policies. the european union must develop an integrated approach to its policies and encourage coordinated assistance to promote basic labour standards. let us take just one example: what is the point of promoting child non-work if, at the same time, we do not act on educational policies? what about the right of workers to express themselves in a country that is not a democracy or a state of law? so, in the context of incentive clauses rather than sanctions, clauses which are not only linked to trade agreements, we ask the european union to systematically integrate into all agreements to be concluded with third countries, regardless of the field, the clause mentioning basic labour standards. commissioner, i have taken up a very popular phrase of the feminists who said that what is not named is non-existent. i believe that if the basic standards of work are not named, they are forgotten, they no longer exist. the third point concerns the development of european action in the field of regional action and the new regulatory areas that are being created around the world to better adapt to local realities. the ilo is working towards this and a real synergy effect could be found in this respect. the debate on this issue should be open to representatives of developing countries with the aim of identifying realistic and progressive action plans. this communication, madam commissioner, represents a step forward for us and should herald a change in the working methods which the european union must develop with third countries, in particular on a basis which is more respectful of their realities. we also hope, madam commissioner, that the council will deal with this matter as soon as possible and we ask the danish presidency to consider it at the next social affairs council. finally, mr president, i would like to thank all my colleagues most sincerely, especially those who, in the four committees, have been so kind as to take up the views which we have tried to incorporate as best we can in this report, and which i believe have enriched it and will also, i hope, help to achieve a broad consensus.

in writing. - this report requires that the certification of machines and lifts be based on criteria of greater safety for the users. we have therefore voted for it, even though the measures proposed will apply only to new machines and will only exceptionally affect old machines. while the obligation to maintain aircraft in good working order is emphasized, the realization of such a wish may be questioned. recently, the press reported on a series of elevator accidents in france that resulted in the deaths of several people in public housing units (hlm). the cgt elevators union has long been concerned about the chronic understaffing of maintenance technicians who are responsible for the maintenance of two to three times as many appliances as 20 years ago. in addition, the hlm building stock is ageing, as are its facilities, and is increasingly being neglected by the public authorities. the report's desire to raise safety to the highest level, which we share, should therefore be accompanied by binding measures to prevent unsafe machinery from being placed on the market and by the obligation to allocate sufficient technical and human resources to the maintenance of such equipment and to its replacement as soon as necessary.
in writing. - the proposal for a framework decision on the fight against racism and xenophobia, presented by the commission, seems to us to lack a legal basis from a two-fold point of view. 1. the it seeks to approximate the rules of criminal law, and in particular penalties, between the member states, on the basis of articles 29, 31 and 34 (2) of the treaty on european union. but these articles do not give such competence for the fight against racism. 2. the although the police and judicial cooperation in title vi of the teu is intended, among other things, to combat 'racism and xenophobia', the commission proposal extends the definition of these words by adding to the definition of 'race or national origin' the definition of 'religion or belief' (article 3). if it were enough to change the meaning of words a posteriori to extend the powers covered by the treaty, it would be a little too easy, and it would be known. finally, this attempt to extend the definition of racism to an unreasonable extent raises the fear of a police of thought at european level, and for this reason too it must be rejected.

in writing. - once again, the results of a european summit, in this case the one in seville, demonstrate the impasse in which community construction continues to be engaged. while the 1990s saw an acceleration of integration along federal lines, the voice of the nations seems to be being heard again since the treaty of nice. the conclusions of the seville summit confirm this: most of the major issues have been postponed because of disagreements between nations concerned with their sovereignty and interests. on immigration, the sanctions regime against the countries of origin of illegal immigrants, which some governments wanted, was fortunately not adopted. led by france, several countries have rejected such measures, contrary to their strong and long-standing tradition of welcoming refugees. these measures would have undermined their historical links with the countries of origin of the illegal migrants. similarly, no concrete reforms have been introduced in the way the cap and the council of ministers operate. all this proves that the member states have divergent interests and demonstrates, if need be, that the construction of europe can no longer be pursued in the ignorance of these realities.
