- mr president, allow me to turn to the french approach to packaging, which is more familiar to me than to others. in france, manufacturers have implemented a policy of reducing packaging at source by means of the procedure for certifying compliance with the prevention standard 13428. compliance with this standard is compulsory only in france and great britain. the amendments i tabled in the committee on the environment were intended to extend this procedure to all member states. my colleagues did not accept my proposal, but they were nonetheless receptive to it, since the report rightly points out in amendment no 16 to paragraph 5 of the relevant provision that the commission will assess before the end of 2004 the introduction of the cen en 13428 standard on prevention in all the member states. i would draw the attention of my colleagues to the need to reject the amendment to article 4 (1) (a) introduced by amendment no 16, because an arbitrary limitation of the quantity of packaging takes no account of economic growth or sociological developments. indeed, unit sales are rising rapidly in a world where people are living more and more alone. it is by respecting the cen en 13428 standard on prevention that the volume of packaging, its total tonnage, will decrease, as the french example shows. that is the challenge we must face. i would also draw your attention to the dangers that would result from the adoption of an environmental indicator for packaging, as proposed in the amendment to article 4 (3a) introduced by amendment no 16. such an additional indicator for packaging is not justified, as a standardisation tool already exists but needs to be implemented more by the industry. in addition, its complex definition should take into account all relevant criteria, such as the nature of the product, the raw material needs, the manufacturing processes and the collection and recycling systems available. the differences between countries may have led to unrepresentative results. finally, as regards reuse, this type of recovery should not be systematically encouraged, as the environmental impact of reusable packaging is not necessarily better than that of single-use packaging. various studies have shown this, particularly in the bottled beverage sector, and i shall not go into the action brought by the commission against certain member states which have caused distortions of competition through compulsory storage. i therefore call on my colleagues to vote against amendment no 17. we live in a society that operates at a pace worthy of chaplin's modern times machine: produce, pack, discard and, increasingly, thankfully, recycle, value. but we must not forget that packaging is not just a subtle avatar of our consumer society. it's not just there to make the customer look good or attract them; packaging has a very important function. the solution to the problem we are concerned with is to subject this product to effective environmental requirements and to consider it in its entire life cycle.
- we are here today to talk once again about waste and to note that the 1994 directive has had its effects, even though the results vary from one country to another, from one region to another, from the urban environment to the rural environment. the progress made is visible. the commission's proposal to improve the objectives of this directive nevertheless seems to me very timely. i can therefore only support this approach because, in view of the difficulties encountered on the ground in the treatment of waste, and in particular packaging waste, it seems premature to want to undertake a more thorough revision of this text. the only essential requirement of this parliament in this respect must be realism, because our aim is to make the treatment of packaging waste as easy as possible and to provide, even before it is placed on the market, for packaging that is as harmless as possible to our environment. products and their packaging must therefore be the subject of an integrated policy. we also have to find out where to dispose of our waste. recycling is often a problem and therefore the principle of prevention and limitation of packaging is necessary. our legislation simply needs to incorporate more prevention but also be simpler and more flexible. some definitions used in this directive are also clarified; the main problem at european level, however, remains the harmonization of definitions. this was clearly felt in parliament during the debate on the texts. beyond the problem of packaging waste, it is essential to carry out a thorough reform and to answer this simple question: what is waste? the waste problem in europe is a crucial one: for the community institutions, for national governments, for local authorities, for businesses and for our fellow citizens, whose role is essential. perhaps we should have a framework directive on waste.
commission. – mr president, the commission very much welcomes mr deva's report on trade and development for poverty eradication and food security. the report is timely because of the world summit on sustainable development, which is taking place at this moment in johannesburg. it should also be seen in the context of the commitments made at the doha ministerial conference last november and the monterrey conference on financing for development last march. it is also timely as negotiations on economic partnership agreements will be launched with the african, caribbean and pacific states at the end of this month. the european union, as the largest trade bloc in the world and the largest source of foreign direct investment and official development assistance, has an important role to play. i am pleased to note that the union's imports from developing countries have been rising by 15% per year over the past seven years. this is much faster than the imports from other countries. at the same time, i am aware that many developing countries, particularly the least-developed countries, have not fully shared in this growth. much more needs to be done. the motion for a resolution and mr deva's report are broad in scope – and rightly so. the commission welcomes the overall thrust of the analysis and recommendations. indeed, while there is no doubt that trade can potentially contribute to development, poverty eradication and food security, the actual contribution depends on enabling policies and institutions being in place. i can assure you that the commission will pay close attention to honouring the negotiating commitments made towards the developing countries in doha. the doha development agenda will address the improvement of market access, new trade rules that take into account the needs of developing countries and the further mainstreaming of trade matters into development and cooperation. as to access, and the area of agriculture which is of particular interest to many developing countries, the doha declaration states that 'building on the work carried out to date and without prejudging the outcome of negotiations we commit ourselves to comprehensive negotiations aimed at substantial improvements in market access; reductions of, with a view to phasing out, all forms of export subsidies; and substantial reductions in trade-distorting domestic support.' for non-agricultural products, the doha declaration foresees: '... negotiations which shall aim ... to reduce or as appropriate eliminate tariffs, including the reduction or elimination of tariff peaks, high tariffs and tariff escalation, as well as non-tariff barriers, in particular on products of export interest to developing countries.' needless to say, this is an ambitious negotiating agenda, but one of great relevance for developing countries. as regards rule-making, several subjects of great importance for developing countries will be covered: intellectual property, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade, competition, trade facilitation, government procurement and investment. the provisions applying to regional trade agreements are another subject of negotiation. these negotiations will need to take into account the developmental aspects of regional trade agreements. furthermore, the provisions for special and differential treatment in favour of developing countries will be reviewed with a view to strengthening them and making them more precise, effective and operational. i am convinced that the doha negotiations will make a great contribution towards making the multilateral trading system and its rules more development-friendly. in relation to the third aspect – mainstreaming trade in development cooperation – the european union has already made important progress over the past few years. the community's development policy, based on the commission's communication of april 2000, identified trade as one of six priorities for its development assistance. i would also like to draw your attention to the commission's communication in february of this year on a global partnership for sustainable development. furthermore the commission is at present working on a communication on trade and development, which will describe how mainstreaming trade should go well beyond technical assistance and embrace capacity building, training, institutional support, the preparation of fiscal reform and assistance for adjustment on the supply side. the involvement of civil society and the private sector, including large corporations, which figures prominently in mr deva's report, is also essential. i am pleased to say that over the past years around eur 640 million were allocated by the union for trade-related assistance, of which about 61% went to the acp group, 14% to latin america and 12% to the mediterranean. for the current acp programming exercise for the ninth edf, between 40 and 50% of the regional indicative programmes – eur 280 to 350 million – is earmarked for trade-related assistance in the broad sense. in addition, up to eur 50 million have been pledged for new programmes with acp-wide scope. the union is also the main provider of funds for the global trust fund created for technical assistance provided by the world trade organisation in support of the doha development agenda. for the commission, regional integration is very much part and parcel of a strategy of opening the economy and taking advantage of trading opportunities. regional integration initiatives among developing countries, south-south integration, can contribute to their effective integration into the global economy and to the multilateral system, provided that they are outwardly oriented and lead to lower external barriers. therefore the union is committed to continuing its support for realistic south-south integration. at the same time it is stepping up its efforts to use north-south integration to stimulate deeper and more effective integration within the south. this approach should be reflected in the economic partnership agreements between acp regional groupings and the union. among the industrial countries, the european union took a lead last year with the everything but arms initiative. all exports from the least-developed countries, except arms, can enter the eu market without restriction. only for three products – rice, sugar and bananas – is there a transition period. the benefits of this initiative for the least-developed countries would be greatly enhanced if the other industrial countries, as well as the larger trading nations among the developing countries, were to make a similar gesture. in conclusion, i should like to say that mr deva's report makes a constructive and far-reaching contribution in helping to define strategies to allow developing countries to take advantage of trade and globalisation in order to attain the fundamental development objectives of poverty eradication and food security. the commission can benefit from this analysis and assessment during the forthcoming multilateral and regional negotiations. a regular dialogue on this with parliament is most welcome.
mr president, the 1990s saw a near-generalization of openness to world trade, at the same time as the increase in absolute poverty in the world, with the exception of china. the number of countries classified as "least developed" has increased, while poverty remains widespread in many high-growth countries. the relationship between trade, development and poverty is therefore complex and prejudice must be avoided. my report to the committee on industry, which was adopted unanimously, contains proposals on this subject, some of which are included in the deva report. i'll just take two axes here. firstly, aid, and particularly technical assistance, is a key problem. there is very little information on this subject, but it seems that there are many horror stories. what is crucial is the ability of the countries concerned to identify their needs and communicate them to international agencies by committing to targets. this is what needs to be done, by ensuring a wider participation of civil society and local businesses. we must break with the approach of setting a priori conditions which are in fact in the interests of the dominant countries. the priority of the aid should be to build local capacity for diversified supply. the formation of a trade administration must be based on the scale of regional common markets. the report also calls on the wto to work on social measures to enable vulnerable populations to consider new prospects in the face of the shock of liberalisation. it also seeks to include the issue of migrant workers in the negotiation of services. the committee also called for aid to compensate for the loss of customs revenue in the least developed countries. secondly, the report considers that the place of anti-poverty objectives at the very heart of unilateral trade rules remains to be explored. i am afraid that the commission is frankly sceptical about special and differential treatment. not us, who want to redefine it. as for the forthcoming investment negotiations, they may be fruitful, but we must be careful: direct investment goes very little to the poorest countries, and when it does, it is in return for tax benefits, of which these countries are the first victims. without cooperation between the wto and other major agencies, without tackling financial fragility, the investment negotiations would be unlikely to produce fruitful results for all those suffering from poverty in the world.
mr president, it is not the mention of the extreme poverty of the developing world that is indecent but the guilty deafness of the rich countries which, despite the horror of this reality, continue to follow the same path. it is in this context that the increasingly mixed notions of trade and development are being discussed, including here in the committee on development. the fight against poverty and food insecurity cannot be won by "any business". it must address the structural causes of the impoverishment of the people in developing countries. the priority is to restructure their economies to increase their share of manufactured and diversified products, including in the agricultural sector. this is why it is essential to promote equitable access to land, water and biodiversity resources, as well as a policy of local support for small farms. to do so, three factors need to be considered. firstly, new international commitments are necessary and must above all be respected. i just came from johannesburg. after the disappointing summits in monterrey and johannesburg on food, this is a new opportunity for the leaders of the northern states to reiterate the importance of helping the people of the south, but also to give themselves the real means to do so. i'll take it! but when are strong commitments really followed by concrete action? secondly, the approach to multilateral trade negotiations may well need to be reviewed in depth. in the wto, these negotiations are not conducted with a view to achieving the priorities set by the united nations, but are dominated by the 'who-gives-who-gets-what' logic. moreover, the pace and methods of negotiation de facto exclude many developing countries. why refuse the protections that have enabled the developed countries themselves to ensure their own industrialisation? mr president, the role of the oilseed protein sector in europe is not only an agricultural problem, it is in many respects a social issue. first of all, it is a question of food security. the european consumer rightly demands traceability of all elements of the food chain. in the case of the animal protein needed for our livestock production, europe cannot be satisfied with being dependent on outside sources for more than three quarters of its requirements. it is essential that community producers regain a dominant share of this market in order to exclude the risks associated with the presence of residues, contaminants or gmos. the union has decided to apply a moratorium on the use of new gmos in food and feed. it is known that the majority of soybean exporting countries grow gmos. the second challenge is the quantitative security of the world market. the supply of forage protein is concentrated in a very small number of countries, the united states being the most important, accounting for 45% of world production and 90% of the crushing being carried out by four industrial groups. if there are climatic hazards, europe will be very vulnerable. it is also a market growing by 5% a year and it would be all the more foolish to accept that europe should remain outside this growth, since the internal demand of the union, including the demand of the future member states, where meat consumption will increase with their entry into the european union, is expected to grow steadily. it is also a major environmental issue. it should be remembered that the development of oleoprotein crops promotes biodiversity, improves soil structure, counters the trend towards cereal monoculture and reduces the use of inputs. the growing protein deficit in the union should therefore be a very high priority concern for the commission. but it is not. in the face of these challenges and in order to replace animal flour, the commission is proposing nothing but to resign ourselves to seeing a growing part of our consumption dependent on imports whose prices, production conditions and compliance with the social and environmental specifications we impose on our own farmers would not be controlled by us. this is simply unacceptable. that is why our committee on agriculture has adopted a much more dynamic strategy in adopting the stevenson report, which aims to instill a little bit of voluntarism in the commission's pale communication. the amendments we tabled in committee underline the contrast between the seriousness of the european situation and the substantial aid that the in writing. - the report, in its explanatory statement, is presented as trying to satisfy everyone: the commission, which is implementing deregulation; the member states, which are left - for the time being - with the task of ensuring safety; the large airlines, which are not required to impose regulations which are too restrictive, and above all too costly; the low-cost airlines, which would like to be subject to certain minimum standards, but without these affecting their profits... this is perhaps an example of what the european authorities can do in this area: they set standards for work, rest and presence on board for crews and commercial personnel. these standards, which are common to the eu, perhaps offer a minimum of guarantees to staff and that is why we did not vote against this report. but this minimum is so low that it is the maximum that can be expected from the european authorities, who do not want to cause any inconvenience to the employers in the airline industry.
in writing. - we voted in favour of this report because, of course, we are not against european aid to palestinian refugees. but there is no point in boasting when we see the increase in the amount of aid. given the number of palestinian refugees in the middle east, the maximum amount proposed is only around €40 per year. moreover, there is no guarantee that all this money will go directly to refugees, without spilling over to european businesses and suppliers. above all, how can we fail to see the hypocrisy of the report which laments that 'the living conditions of refugees are becoming increasingly difficult', and which cynically blames this on 'the high population growth', without saying a word about the war waged by the state of israel against the palestinian people and without denouncing the fact that if thousands of palestinians are forced to live in refugee camps, it is because the state of israel, with the support of the great powers, including europe, is opposed to their being able to return to the lands from which they were expelled?
in writing. - each year, the european union produces more than 60 million tonnes of packaging waste. the stabilization objective of the fifth action programme and the fact that waste prevention is a top priority of european environmental policy do not change much: the amount of packaging continues to increase in the european union. with this growing mountain of waste, it is high time to develop an ambitious strategy. the latter necessarily involves strengthening the commission's modest proposal, i.e. by integrating prevention and producer responsibility. the european parliament has already called for higher recycling targets and improved prevention through the introduction of producer responsibility. the commission is not taking this into account. prevention is a real priority in waste management. it should even become the cornerstone of european environmental policy. we have a real chance here of making progress in the area of integrated product policy and the thematic strategy of the sixth environmental action programme. i will support this report, which also has the merit of emphasizing two central ideas of a successful environmental policy: the necessary cooperation of all and the fact that environmental impact must always guide our action in the future.
in writing. - i voted against the single sky initiative, which looks more like a manoeuvre by the commission to increase its power (with the unconditional support of the european parliament, as usual) than an operation really intended to strengthen air safety and increase traffic flow. in the debate yesterday i already stressed one major, unresolved difficulty, namely relations with eurocontrol. another point should be added: relations with the military. the commission intends, as soon as it has the powers conferred by the single sky, to change the division of airspace between civil and military uses. the aim is clear: to encroach on military zones, or sometimes to suppress them, to facilitate civilian traffic. this method shocks us doubly. in the background, it seems to assume that military uses would be less important in europe today, which in turn assumes that we are in lasting peace. that is dangerous naivete. on the procedural side, it should be noted that the commission has no military competence (a good thing, as we can see here). this is a matter for sovereign states. the community procedures have nothing to do with this.
in writing. - while we cannot deny that some progress has been made in the field of air traffic control rules, the commissioner responsible for this matter's reiterated desire to speed up the introduction of competition in air transport services carries with it dangers which the trade unionists in the office have strongly expressed. unfortunately, they have not been sufficiently listened to, let alone heard, except by a few left-wing members of parliament! and yet we cannot believe that liberalisation has only positive effects. it is enough to note the bitter deterioration of rail transport services since they were liberalised in some member states! what was originally proposed was to introduce competition by separating the function of providers (operators) from the regulatory function (establishment and compliance with the rules). under pressure, the commission has fortunately had to revise its copy, which remains mediocre and dangerous. this will put air navigation services in competition with each other, and with real risks to safety! the commission proposes, as part of the process of harmonization at community level, the introduction of a system of authorization for the provision of air navigation services. (explanation of vote abbreviated pursuant to rule 137 (1) of the rules of procedure)
in writing. - i can only give my final support to this report which underlines the importance of the commission's proposal to create a single european sky by 31 december 2004 at the latest. the creation of a single european sky seems to be essential not only for better use of existing airspace, the establishment of increased safety conditions, and the efficient and safe management of the expected increase in air traffic, but also for the creation of conditions enabling european airlines to compete with non-european airlines. this proposal, which is intended to allow for some harmonization and interoperability of air navigation systems, does not, however, go without raising some problems. the definition of cooperation between eurocontrol and the community is one of them, as is that of cooperation between civil and military authorities. i am therefore in favour of the report, and i am in favour of the report, but i am also in favour of the report, and i am in favour of the report, and i am in favour of the report.
in writing. - under the guise of creating 'an integrated airspace governed by single principles and rules', the council, the commission and the fava report actually propose the establishment of a mode of air transport management in europe based on economic criteria: a single market in the skies. does the air disaster in germany last july foreshadow the single european sky? the air traffic control company skyguide was a private company. it operated in a functional airlock where operator and regulator were separate. skyguide lacked human and material resources at the expense of security. is this the path we should follow as recommended by the commission? in any event, this accident should encourage parliament to exercise the utmost caution while awaiting the results of the investigations, also taking into account the consequences of the effective liberalization of other modes of transport such as rail in england. this was the message of the major european air traffic controllers' strike of 19 june 2002. instead of relying on the market, cooperation should be given priority, as in the case of the eurocontrol organisation for aviation safety. we should put public service and safety first. we should think globally about intermodality in transport. (explanation of vote abbreviated pursuant to rule 137 (1) of the rules of procedure)
in writing. - through these regulations, the commission proposes to disintegrate existing systems in order to better serve economic interests. it involves cutting the sky into functional blocks that will be sold separately to service providers. all services will be competitive (control, radio, radar, rescue and weather). this 'single market in the sky' runs counter to common sense and the principles of safety and public service. the british railway has proved this. the competition between service providers and the multiplicity of operators have not been conducive to investment in maintenance operations, in improving safety and in improving the working conditions of personnel. quite the opposite. more cooperation between air navigation services and safety through integrated systems would be needed. more public control of air transport across the continent is needed, paving the way for intermodal freight and passenger schemes. the commission's proposals and the report under consideration do not go in that direction. that is why we voted against it.
in writing. - we are, of course, for maximum air safety. but we abstained on this report because it only deals with this issue from the point of view of the interests of airlines and airport managing bodies. the rapporteur also points out that it is significant that the directive does not envisage any measures concerning the safety of people living near airports. the main aim is for the council and the european parliament to develop a unified system to exclude less safe aircraft from european union airports and also to avoid that certain member states are tempted, for commercial or other reasons, to be less strict on the necessary checks. that's good. the rapporteur, however, believes that this is about restoring the feeling of safety among passengers, a recovery from which airlines will benefit first and foremost. at the same time, the european authorities are preparing to take serious security risks with their single sky project. these same european authorities can take whatever measures they want, it may put african, latin american or eastern european airlines at a disadvantage, but with the single sky and its privatisation plans, it is the european sky that will come close to the conditions faced by the third world.
in writing. - the maes report should actually be called the committee report. we cannot see the rapporteur's work. i do not think that this report deserves to be called maes. the committee has the full credit for the amendments, the consistency and the seriousness of the work. i therefore voted in favour of all the amendments tabled by the committee (logical, adequate) and did not take part in the final votes. that would be giving credit to the rapporteur when it is really the work of the committee. "give to caesar what is caesar's".
in writing. - we support the guidelines of the stevenson report, which seeks to promote the cultivation of vegetable proteins, which are essential for feeding livestock (soya, but also peas, beans, chickpeas, lupins, and to a lesser extent, legumes, cereals, grasses, etc.) in the european union. it appears that we are now very dependent on imports (more than 77%) even though plant protein production is growing worldwide and we could do much better. this dependence poses serious strategic problems for us, but also public health problems, because it is difficult to trace the product under these conditions, which can lead us, for example, to buy non-genetically modified soybeans. but why is european production in this field so limited? the blair house agreements had a further disastrous effect, in that they encouraged the use of animal meal, which in turn gave rise to mad cow disease. it is imperative that these agreements be revised or bypassed. unfortunately, the commission does not seem to be ready for this. once again, we are left wondering on which side it is playing and whether the community system is not yet weakening us.
in writing. - that we should develop the production of vegetable proteins for feeding cattle, rather than feeding cattle animal flour, with the consequences we know, why not? but the report is concerned only with the trade war with the united states, on which the european livestock feed is now largely dependent. the real needs of the world's population are not even being addressed. the food production system is fundamentally unfair, since it is designed to satisfy only the needs of countries and social groups with high purchasing power. in order to sell the high value-added food which brings the most profit to those with the strongest purchasing power, what could feed the poorest is wasted. for example, several kilos of fishmeal are needed to produce more expensive fish in fish farms. it is a revolting system because it contributes to the plundering of the resources of poor countries and to starving part of the world's population. it is in the name of this same profit logic that europe subsidizes the set-aside of land in order to avoid a fall in prices. we did not want to endorse the whole system by voting for one option.
in writing. - while the eu is highly dependent on a few suppliers for its plant protein supply, the commission proposes to continue to rely on imports, preferring a market opportunity to the coherence of its various policies. in doing so, it ignores the difficult experience farmers have already had in this type of situation and deprives agriculture of new prospects. the development of oleoprotein crops would help to meet the need to develop diversified and sustainable agriculture, consumer demand for traced products and their rejection of gmos. it would also open up new prospects for farmers by developing non-food markets, including biofuels. finally, these crops play an important role in the agricultural and environmental spheres. we must not sell this sector of agriculture. on the contrary, let us give it the means to achieve its ambitions by establishing conditions of profitability comparable to those of cereals, by promoting the diversity of species, and more particularly of those not covered by the blair house agreement. but these efforts will be in vain if our negotiators do not commit themselves to defend our agricultural production with conviction on the international stage.

the council. - mr president, i should like to begin by congratulating the house on the form of debate we have just tried in practice with 'catch the eye'. for a former member of parliament, all these debates with scheduled speaking time have been a pain; but now it is a relief and a delightful experience to have real debates with spontaneous speeches, where one answers to another instead of reading ready-made manuscripts. as regards afghanistan, i would first like to remind you that a year ago afghanistan was a country in ruins, with a population that suffered first under an occupying power and under successive warlords, then under an extreme islamic revolution that forced a de-modernization of society and introduced medieval methods. eventually, the country became a home for fundamentalist terrorists. it is all the more remarkable and gratifying that today, nine months after the start of the bonn process, we can report on a country where the situation is gradually returning to normal. however, there is still a long way to go before we can speak of a stable afghanistan again. the security situation in the country remains inadequate. in july, vice president haji qadir was killed in the street. fighting between local warlords continues and gross violations of human rights continue. the conclusion of the bonn agreement in december 2001 between afghan groups under the auspices of the un marked the beginning of the positive developments we are now seeing in afghanistan. the bonn agreement sets out a process for the restoration of democracy. as a first step, an interim government was established and ruled the country for six months until an emergency assembly of elders, the loya jirga, convened in june and appointed a transitional government headed by karzai to run the country for two years until elections are held. the implementation of this loya jirga and the formation of the transitional government were significant achievements. the loya jirga process and the regional and district elections showed that afghans throughout the country have the will and the courage to participate in the democratization process. afghan women played a prominent role. there have been attempts at mediation in the conflicts in afghanistan before. the success of the bonn process is due in part to its traditional structures in the country, which are based on the need to ensure a broad representation of the various ethnic and religious groups. it is precisely ensuring representativeness and the protection of minorities that will be the key to the long-term stability of the country. afghan ownership is another code word. although the un has acted as a major catalyst in the process now unfolding, its role has been played out with full respect for and support for afghan ownership. the re-establishment of an afghan state capable of ensuring the unity, peace and stability of the country and of standing as a guarantor of respect for human rights is absolutely essential. the development is slow, the transitional government has continued to struggle to control large parts of the country, making it easy for local warlords and bandits to gain access. central to the efforts to promote security is the creation of an afghan army and police force that enjoys the confidence of the people and operates with respect for human rights. in this context, the eu has expressed its great satisfaction with the establishment of the afghan national defence council. equally important is the capacity of the state to deliver development - including access to health care. a large number of afghan refugees have returned and those returnees need international support to ensure their lasting reintegration. on the question of the return of refugees, i am pleased to note that according to the unhcr, the situation in afghanistan has now improved to the point where it allows the vast majority of afghans to return voluntarily without risk of persecution. i agree with the unhcr that return should be supported by appropriate international assistance and that individual afghans should be offered 'realistic repatriation packages'. seville gave high priority to the adoption of elements for an accelerated return to afghanistan. the danish presidency will work with the commission and the member states to live up to the seville declaration. i myself had a meeting with ruud lubbers not long ago. there are still forces that are seeking to derail developments in afghanistan. there are still various ethnic groups who, with the support of circles in the neighbouring countries, do not feel that their views are adequately represented. there are various warlords who have long been accustomed to a high degree of self-determination in the areas they control and who oppose the establishment of a central power. there are also differing views on how quickly and how far afghanistan can move towards a modern islamic state with close contacts with the west. the hope is that the establishment of a democratic process will create opportunities to resolve these conflicts through political negotiations rather than through a return to the futile acts of war of the past. the relatively positive development is also due to the international community's engagement in afghanistan. the united states played a critical role in the rapid removal of taliban rule through operation enduring freedom. us-led forces remain in the country to fight the last pockets of al-qaeda fighters. in and around kabul, the international security force, isaf, is helping to ensure stability so that the interim government can function. the eu also attaches importance to contributing to the promotion of stability in afghanistan and the region. the country must not become a hotbed of terrorism and drug production again. we want to assist the afghan people in their efforts to secure a peaceful development. the eu member states collectively contribute the bulk of the isaf force and are the largest international donor. the total amount of assistance committed by the commission and the member states in 2002 was more than eur 550 million. the council of ministers recently adopted conclusions on the situation in afghanistan, on 22 july. it was stated that the eu would base its dialogue with the transitional government on the key principles agreed by the afghan parties and the international community. the principles are laid down in the bonn agreement, the tokyo final declaration of january and un security council resolution 1419. the principles include the formation of a broad-based, multiethnic and representative government, including women. the eu, through its special representative, mr vendrell, maintains a close political dialogue with the kabul government and other afghan parties. the aim is to help developments to move in the right direction. the dialogue with neighbouring countries is also being pursued to ensure their cooperation. the international engagement in afghanistan will ultimately depend on whether the afghan parties are actually working towards the stated objectives. the eu will therefore seek to promote a process whereby the afghan transitional government, in partnership with the international community, develops verifiable criteria and monitoring systems for the large-scale assistance provided. the eu will promote the delivery of assistance in a way that strengthens the central government and weakens those who are not involved in or directly opposed to the bonn process, while ensuring that the population as a whole receives the aid as a visible peace dividend. the financial situation in afghanistan is characterized by a serious budget deficit and the government is soon unable to pay wages. direct budget support is therefore also necessary to ensure political stability in afghanistan. the international community and the eu can thus strengthen the peace process. whether the steps in the right direction that we are now witnessing in afghanistan can be translated into real long-term improvements in the situation will ultimately depend on the afghan people's own willingness to back up the process that has begun.

- commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to be speaking this evening on a subject which is very close to my heart: that of citizenship of the union. citizenship which, as the treaty says, complements national citizenship without replacing it. citizenship should also be a plus for all those living in our european union. in december 2000, the charter of fundamental rights finally placed the citizen at the centre of the european construction, eight years after the maastricht treaty. it was time, because at european, national and local level, how could we imagine doing politics otherwise than by placing the citizen at the centre of all thinking, all social action and all social projects? although i am well aware that the facts are different, that should not stop us from fighting to change things. quite the contrary. the rapporteur recalled the areas which are supposed to fall within the scope of citizenship of the union. so i don't need to quote them again. but i cannot forget a whole series of social rights which were mentioned by other speakers. the report takes stock of the implementation of these rights. it is a mixed record because while it shows progress, it also highlights the persistence of many shortcomings. we have already mentioned the european elections, which saw a turnout of less than 50%. we must therefore put in place measures to encourage citizens to participate in these elections and, above all, we must rethink the link between the elected and the voter. we must give citizens back the desire to vote and the desire to be involved in the life of the community. the citizen must be an actor and not just a spectator. the recent elections in the various member states of the union support this analysis. what about mobility for education? mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as a former dean of a faculty in lyon where nearly thirty foreign languages are taught, i have noted in mrs gutiérrez-cortines' report many positive elements alongside others which, unfortunately, seem to me more questionable. positive elements: efforts to reduce administrative and other obstacles to student and teacher exchanges, efforts to promote the learning of foreign languages, not just english, efforts to create networks and common information services, efforts to encourage training courses and even sports competitions, all this is excellent. however, i have reservations about the stated aim of this report, namely the creation of a european higher education area. the commission's assessment of the entire university system, both public and private, could lead to the creation of a new european supranational bureaucratic hierarchy, despite the principle of subsidiarity mentioned - somewhat formally - in the first paragraph of the report. the desire to impose uniform criteria in the architecture of degrees, or to harmonize all university courses for students, will necessarily be achieved at the expense of the diversity of particular academic or scientific models, which are a factor of emulation and a guarantee of progress. european civilization has invented diversity in all fields. it is by first mastering a specific knowledge, a science, a technique, a particular experience and a national culture that we are most faithful to the true european traditions.
in writing. - in paragraph 29 of the coelho resolution, the committee welcomes the judgment of the court of first instance of the european communities of 3 may 2002, which recognised a right of direct action by jego-quéré against a european regulation. although the company was not 'directly and individually' concerned, if the action had not been declared admissible it would have had no other means of defending itself in court, so that there would have been 'denial of access to the judge'. we too welcome this appreciation, but we regret that it did not come earlier, for example when we lodged a complaint, clearly justified on the merits, against the change of name of the single currency. unfortunately, the commission, probably feeling that its tranquillity was threatened, immediately asked for the jego-quéré judgment to be quashed, and it was granted a judgment in accordance with its wishes during the judicial holidays. the european institutions have thus succeeded in placing themselves in a position to destabilize member nations permanently, while virtually making their general regulations immune from individual citizens' appeals. it is a perversion of the present system that protects the supranational enterprise, but it will have to be corrected in the future.
in writing. - many of our colleges have a nasty habit of twisting the meaning of words to meet the needs of the federalist cause. after the charter of fundamental rights, which some misunderstand as the preamble to a hypothetical constitution, after governance, an unidentified political object, there is european citizenship, a concept which has no meaning. citizenship is a political, not a technocratic, concept based on a political, not a bureaucratic reality, based on rooting, on belonging to a natural community. citizenship is a status granted only to those who, by birth or merit, share common values. it also presupposes the existence of a political space, the most complete form of which is still the nation. where is the european nation when it lacks what renan called 'a collective will to live'? without a common language, culture and traditions for the peoples of the european union, there is no more european people. as joseph de maistre would later say, no one has ever met a 'european citizen'. your "real-fake" citizenship is not consistent. so this report is pointless.
in writing. - we voted against the van brempt report on 'a european area of lifelong learning' because it is a good example of undue extension of european competences. it starts with article 150 tec, which provides, in an otherwise obscure and questionable way, for the implementation of a european vocational training policy 'in full respect of the responsibility of the member states', and then seeks to extend this competence to the rest of education. it proposes that the commission should draw up (in close cooperation with the member states, anyway) a 'european framework of basic skills' which all pupils should have acquired before leaving compulsory schooling. in such circumstances, the machinery for extending competences is endless. the european parliament reiterates that the current situation in the field of qualifications 'seriously hinders mobility between member states and the establishment of a european labour market' (recital f). however, it was understood that the european labour market was already functioning. in reality, it is clear that, with the objective of full mobility in a fully unified labour market, the nations themselves will soon become the obstacle.
in writing. - although we agree with some of the proposals in this report, and with some of the good intentions expressed, we abstained on the whole. the proposals are not based on the aspirations of the young and the old that they are supposed to train, or even on the needs of society. everything is designed in terms of what the report modestly calls the labour market and its flexibility. behind the noble sentiments, the goal is to provide industrial groups, capitalist enterprises, with a workforce trained according to their needs alone. this is not the same as a policy of providing education and training throughout life for everyone according to his abilities and aspirations.
in writing. - the creation of a european area of lifelong learning has become a priority for the new century and initiatives in this direction can only be encouraged. this priority is twofold: it is based on the awareness of the need for lifelong learning for all and on the inclusion of lifelong learning in the framework of the european area and no longer just of a single state. the report stresses the importance of training people in the light of the different experiences and methods of each of our member states. it is both a way of enriching oneself and an expansion of the job market for everyone. finally, although this report does not place enough emphasis on apprenticeship, it nevertheless reflects this awareness of the need to strengthen vocational training policies at european level and reinforces my conviction of the absolute need to set up, in the coming years, a genuine erasmus of apprenticeship which allows for vocational training in networks, both sharp and open to the multiplicity of the experiences of each people.
in writing. - this report is a concrete manifestation of the irresponsibility of an assembly which is abusing its right of initiative in a scandalous way. this scandalous text attempts, with a rare hypocrisy, to place the university under the exclusive tutelage of brussels. a few recitals clearly show the hidden intentions of this report, namely: to make universities the commission's subservient relays, to transform professors into docile supplements of the european technocracy, to give the commission a right of review of the national university systems, to encourage the massive arrival of professionals and experts duly mandated by brussels in our universities. this report is the natural complement to the jean monnet chairs, which in france have aroused the legitimate anger of many professors, now grouped together in the jean bodin observatory to counter the federalist offensive. it is the same perverse, obscurantist logic at work. and what contempt for the fundamental principles that made the universities great! scientific neutrality is being undermined by this europeanist ideology which the brussels workshops are supposed to propagate. the independence of the professors is violated by the interference of supranational bodies in the functioning and organisation of the universities. you are making universities the trojan horse of european federalism.
in writing. - the right of citizens to information and participation has long been in conflict with the so-called right to secrecy, behind which the public authorities have entrenched themselves. progress in reforms aimed at improving relations between the administration and users has made this practice an exception. the walls of the "bureaus" are gradually breaking down, also in environmental matters. this is of course a welcome development. i therefore support the commission's proposal for a directive of 19 january 2001 to transpose the second pillar of the aarhus convention of 25 june 1998 into community law. this is an innovative proposal, but it is up to the member states to give the public effective opportunities to participate in the decision-making process. however, i would like to make a few reservations about the amendments in the korhola report which go beyond the aarhus convention and confirm the option chosen by the rapporteur himself. the mpf delegation believes that transparency of information and the participation of citizens in decision-making must be encouraged and supervised. however, this should not lead to overly burdensome procedures which would be contrary to the very aims of the proposal. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the information is not used in a way that would be contrary to the interests of the public. the only thing to be done is to transpose into community law the provisions of the aarhus convention, which are quite appropriate, in order to promote its effective application. - mr president, on the subject of floods, it can be said that one knows one's friends in adversity. this old adage could illustrate the european union's attitude towards the victims of the floods which have devastated member states and candidate countries. by reacting swiftly, going to the ground and agreeing to provide financial aid, the union has strengthened its community policy and its civic proximity. it has lived up to the solidarity that is expected of it and for which we work. the commitment to create a fund for assistance to natural disasters in the union is welcome, but the causes of these climatic disturbances must be borne in mind. scientists all over the world are unanimous in telling us that global warming is irrefutably punishing our lifestyles and that greenhouse gas emissions are only exacerbating these disasters. on the other side of the planet, they have to sell their cattle because there's no water, no fodder. in other places, since july, floods have devastated entire areas. it may be recalled, mr president, that in nepal 422 people have died and 173 are missing. in russia, 50 people were killed and 100 are missing. in mexico, torrential rains have killed 21 people and left 15,000 injured. in asia, 250 people have died this year. millions of homes are affected by rising water levels. unfortunately, as we know, these geographical areas do not have the chance that we have here to make these victims benefit from solidarity. the rapid and concrete provision of aid and emergency aid is to be welcomed here, but it is not enough to shout 'let us implement the kyoto protocol', we must go much further. we must integrate the environment into all our projects, into all our policies, so that perhaps we can shine a little light of hope. we have to move forward to try to stop this climate change. the rio summit is not producing much, so we must set an example!
in writing. - the report presented by the commission on its asian strategy makes good use of wishful thinking. but it has the advantage of being very clear on some key issues, in particular the willingness of the eu's governing bodies to pursue the unequal liberalisation of trade and capital movements against all odds, and to give the wto an ever wider field of competence. no lessons have been learned from the financial crises of 1997-98 and the asian disaster, the current stock market crisis and the latin american disaster. the reality must be erased from the liberal dogma in the age of capitalist globalisation. the asem-4 summit in copenhagen will also discuss security. at a time when immigrants are being scapegoated in europe for the social crisis and when washington is deploying its policy of 'permanent war' in asia in the name of counterterrorism, is regaining its military footing in the philippines and is threatening to intervene in iraq, we would like the eu to ensure the rights of immigrants and oppose american interventionism. but in the real world, the european union intervenes in asia as the dominant economic power and the united states as the belligerent power. that is what the european parliament should be debating. beyond the diversity of situations in asia, there are general guidelines which concern the whole eurasian continent. - doc. b5-0465/2002 by mr wuori, mr boumediene-thiery and mr piétrasanta, on behalf of the green group, on the case of mr saad eddin ibrahim; - b5-0471/2002 by mr napoletano and others, on behalf of the group of the party of european socialists, on the sentencing of saad eddin ibrahim in egypt; - b5-0473/2002 by mr hugues martin and mr posselt, on behalf of the group of the european people's party, on the case of saad eddin ibrahim (egypt); - b5-0480/2002 by mr boudjenah and others, on behalf of the gue/ngl group, on human rights in egypt;
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the union attaches particular importance to freedom of expression and fundamental rights. the strict respect of these rights is a sine qua non of our association agreement. the strengthening of the euro-mediterranean partnership cannot therefore be achieved by denying this indispensable and irrevocable clause. since 1981 egypt has been under an emergency law that gives the authorities wide powers, in violation of human rights. more and more freedoms are being locked up and placed under the strictest control of police authorities backed by judicial authorities. today saad eddin ibrahim and his colleagues at the ibn khaldun centre are being convicted on the pretext of embezzlement or misuse of process, but the real reason is that they are defending democratic freedoms, as nawal el saadaoui and other human rights activists did yesterday, while individual freedoms are also being violated, with the conviction of several homosexuals. we therefore call on the egyptian government to end the state of emergency so that every citizen can fully enjoy his rights, that sexual orientation, freedom of religion and freedom of expression can be protected without being criminalised and that freedom of association is guaranteed so that those who defend freedom are no longer persecuted. the egyptian state, like the other states which have signed association agreements, should finally understand that the democratic clause in article 2 is neither a luxury nor an option. let our friends know that it is not a question of interference, or of a spirit of superiority, or of a desire to teach, but of a duty, that of denouncing and condemning everywhere the violations of freedom. human rights are universal and transcend all borders.
commission. – mr president, the trial of dr saad eddin ibrahim and his colleagues has aroused widespread international interest and concern, not least among those who, like many of us here, consider ourselves true friends of egypt and the egyptian people. when dr ibrahim and his co-accused successfully appealed for a retrial last february, we hoped that the best traditions of justice would prevail, not only on the merits of the case, but because of the evident damage to egypt's international reputation caused by the handling of the case by the egyptian authorities. we were therefore profoundly shocked on 29 july when dr ibrahim was again sentenced to seven years' imprisonment with hard labour, a cruel sentence for a man in his frail physical condition. a further four defendants were also sentenced to prison and the remaining 24 have suspended sentences. even if the charges were credible, and we do not find them so, these sentences are completely disproportionate. the following day i personally voiced my dismay and repeated that, despite careful monitoring and a mid-term external audit, the commission has no evidence of financial or other wrongdoings by dr ibrahim or his co-defendants with respect to the two ngo contracts managed by them. we made this clear in an affidavit submitted during the appeal. furthermore, i repeated then and i repeat now that we deplore the use of state security courts and procedures to pursue cases of this nature. even the court of appeal has misgivings on the use of military court order no 4 under which this prosecution was brought. we were disturbed by the decision to retry the defendants after a successful appeal and despite dr ibrahim's failing health. we are troubled by the conduct of the trial and the speed and manner of the court's decision. this unseemly rush to judgment did nothing to improve the court's credibility. the case has been closely followed by the ec and member states and we made our concern clear at the highest levels from the beginning. with respect to the charge of accepting foreign european union funds without authorisation, the commission insists that direct grants to civil society are perfectly proper and are covered by the eu-egypt framework convention on financial and technical cooperation. at the conclusion of the first trial last year, the severe sentences led to an ec statement on 23 may and the presidency declaration two days later, expressing deep concern. then, as now, the european union stressed the importance it attaches to the development of civil society and reiterated that actions to this end are an integral part of barcelona and bilateral programming which egypt has signed up to. with respect to the claimed misuse of eu funds, the commission is, to say the least, surprised that the court has reportedly ruled as irrelevant the views of the commission, the alleged victim, that its normal monitoring procedures, including an external mid-term audit, gave no cause for concern whatsoever, financial or otherwise. we have no access at present to the ngo files, which have been confiscated by the authorities. the european union has always hoped that due legal process and justice would prevail. we have scrupulously avoided any intervention that might prejudice that expectation. the commission's affidavit during the appeal was strictly factual and correct. we are concerned that the court, in its written explanations, is reported to have implied the contrary. the commission and the member states continue to follow the case closely. the cairo-based troika has already visited dr ibrahim in prison and the swedes visited again this weekend. we are in close touch with the family. if, as first press reports indicate, the court's formal explanation of its verdict, which still has to be translated, misrepresents the european union's position, we will not hesitate to rectify it. the legal process is not finished and i understand that the defendants will appeal. the egyptian authorities are well aware of the wider implications of a judgment that is perceived as unjust and politically influenced. only the due process of law in full transparency can prevent further damage to egypt's international standing. the ibrahim case raises issues of real concern, but the overall human rights situation in egypt is complex and not entirely clear. there is some cause for optimism, for example, in relation to women's rights, judicial control of general elections and social legislation. but there are also some signs which give cause for concern, such as the new law on non-governmental organisations, the alleged harassment of homosexuals referred to earlier and the further arrests of members of the islamic opposition. what we have to do is discern the trend and react accordingly. the ibrahim case casts a long, but hopefully temporary, shadow over the egyptian human rights and democracy movement. although the international outcry at the verdict has provoked a strong reaction in cairo, many influential egyptians accept that egypt must adopt the highest judicial and democratic standards if it is to achieve its developmental and political ambitions. we can only agree with that. we will continue to use appropriate measures to express our concern on individual cases. we shall discuss the broader issues concerning human rights and the promotion of democracy within the context of our cooperation programming and the enhanced political dialogue that must characterise the new and privileged relationship between the european union and its mediterranean partners. i confirm directly to the member who raised this question that i shall certainly be discussing the matter when, god willing, i visit egypt myself next month. (applause)
- the house thanks you immensely, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place at 4 p.m. today or immediately after the end of the debate.
- doc. b5-0466/2002 by mr frassoni and others, on behalf of the green group, on human rights violations in nigeria; - b5-0470/2002 by mr gröner and others, on behalf of the pse group, on the death sentence imposed on amina lawal in nigeria; - b5-0474/2002 by mr mccartin and others, on behalf of the group of the european people's party, on the human rights situation in nigeria; - b5-0479/2002 by mr eriksson and others, on behalf of the gue/ngl group, on human rights violations in nigeria; - b5-0486/2002 by mr nicholson of winterbourne and others, on behalf of the eldr group, on the violation of human rights in nigeria.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the african continent, which for too long has been synonymous with tragedy and loss, has recently shown a new face to the international community. the founding of the african union as a successor to the oau and as a reference to the european union is a promise of future for this continent and a tribute to the institutions that unify our continent. beyond a model of political structure and a unified project for the continent, the european union must also defend the rights recognised by international conventions. yet the drama of another age currently being experienced by amina lawal violates all these promises and signatures ratified by her country, nigeria. the vivid distress expressed by ms. lawal, like ms. husseini before her, and by so many other voices ignored, testifies to the caricature of the fracture between political and judicial commitments and practices in some african countries. how can we understand that today a death sentence, death by stoning, can be pronounced? how can we accept that such a barbaric act can be pronounced for the mere fact of giving birth after a divorce? and above all, how can we accept regional legislation in a federal state which denies and flouts a national constitution? it is true that it is the primary responsibility of the federal authorities of nigeria to ensure compliance with and respect for its national legislation and international commitments throughout the territory and jurisdictions of its state. but it is also the moral and political duty of our union, many of whose member states share a common history with this african continent, to oppose criminal deviations, such as certain interpretations of sharia law here, and to support with all our strength and means those who are fighting for the rule of law, rights and true justice for all. to be content with a mere formal declaration for every kafkaesque action against an acp citizen is to make ourselves complicit and to encourage, by this diplomatic inertia, the return to these obscurantisms. that is why i am calling here, with my group, for the establishment of a working group on the question of sharia and women's rights within the framework of our next acp-eu delegation. the stability of the nigerian nation is at stake here and across this most populous country in africa, it is the entire stability of the country that could be shaken. the shockwave of amina lawal's voice has now reached our europe; let's find out how to answer him so there won't be any more.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, once again a woman, mrs amina lawal, has just been sentenced to death by stoning in one of the muslim states of the nigerian federation. her crime is having a child when she was divorced. a few months ago, safiya husseini, condemned to the same fate, was saved thanks to international mobilization. but how many barbaric sentences were passed before this victory and how many will be passed after it? it is time that such ancient judicial decisions, contrary to all human dignity, can no longer be made in nigeria or elsewhere. this strict application of sharia law, which has nothing to do with respect for the muslim religion, has been declared unconstitutional by the nigerian minister of justice, including in the muslim states of the northern federation. the federal republic of nigeria defines itself in its constitution as a secular state. the country is also a signatory to international conventions. while the state of katsina is at fault, there are other responsibilities: those of the nigerian federal authorities who have the duty to guarantee strict respect for the constitution and the protection of human rights for every nigerian citizen regardless of his status, religion or gender. the international community, and europe in particular, must condemn this unacceptable violation of fundamental human rights. europe is opposed to the death penalty. she was committed to the defense of women's rights against all sexual discrimination and against religious intolerance. doing everything to spare amina lawal from death by stoning is also part of his commitment. human rights groups are fighting bravely in nigeria. often threatened, they mobilize despite the lack of resources and little support, except from european associations. we must support their demands. finally, in the context of the cotonou partnership agreements, europe can and must encourage nigeria to respect its international commitments and to promote democracy and women's rights.
mr president, we shall vote for this resolution despite all the criticisms that can be made of it. if a position of the european parliament can prevent a crime against amina lawal, it must be taken. to condemn a woman for giving birth to a child in the name of medieval laws is an abject crime, as are all forms of oppression of women, all mutilations, whether they are perpetrated in the name of religion or not. we are happy to join the protests against the oppression of women and the denial of their human rights in the name of the sharia, but we are equally strongly opposed to it being done in the name of the vatican or the bible. we must denounce the barbarism in nigeria, but we must also denounce it when it is manifested in the united states, the superpower that is the model of civilization today, or even here in the european union, which tolerates that some of its member states perpetuate laws that deny women the elementary right to dispose of their bodies. so while we oppose barbarism when it occurs elsewhere, we must also sweep away at our own doorstep.
- mr president, commissioner, after the success of the international mobilization for the life of safiya husseini in march this year, it is all the more shocking to be faced with another case of the threatened execution of a nigerian woman and mother by stoning. the nigerian government, despite international pressure, is not prepared to honour its international obligations and is putting local religious criminal law before national constitutional law and international human rights law in ten nigerian states. at the same time, we must be aware that nigeria is not an isolated case. for example, according to amnesty international, in iran in 2001 and 2002, at least six women were sentenced to death by stoning for crimes such as adultery and corruption of the earth, some of whom were sentenced to long prison terms. in total, 35 people - men and women - have been executed in different ways in iran this year alone. it is therefore time for the european union to take a stand against this barbaric practice, not just in individual cases but in principle. it must also be possible to seek to impose sanctions on those regimes where such practices are carried out. (applause from the centre)

parliament. throughout, the commission has been deeply concerned by the possible application of harsh penalties in nigeria. this time we, like members, are particularly concerned about the case of amina lawal, who has been condemned to death by stoning, which, as mr bowis said, is in effect a state-sanctioned and organised brutality, although she is at present awaiting appeal. the commission is all communities to accept international norms concerning human rights, gender equality and respect for human life. we are resolutely opposed to the use of the death penalty and fully subscribe to the european union guidelines against the death penalty adopted in 1998. we have had the opportunity on more than one occasion to discuss those guidelines in this parliament. a troika démarche was carried out to restate this position only last year in nigeria. the commission will continue to provide support for human rights and democracy initiatives, through its cooperation programme with nigeria and through other instruments such as the european initiative for democracy and human rights, which has so many eloquent champions in this parliament. this initiative includes nigeria as a focus country, agreement, depending on how the situation evolves. i was interested by the proposal, which was also mentioned by one of the authors of this resolution, to establish a working group on sharia and human rights and women's rights under the cotonou agreement. as parliament may know, we financed a study – the peters report – on the problems of applying the sharia law in nigeria. i am sure parliament mr president, i would first of all like to protest against the expulsion of political refugees in violation of the most basic right to asylum, such as the expulsion of the italian refugee paolo persichetti by the french government. the successive french governments have been able to provide a golden exile for many fallen dictators and protect them from their own people. unlike the report by mr robert j.e. evans, which, despite some positive aspects, is still too timid on this subject, i believe that the right to asylum must be an absolute right which cannot be called into question. but more generally, all the countries of the european union have to deal with the situation of these tens of thousands of people who find themselves on their own soil after having fled, either from dictatorships or forms of oppression such as those exercised against women in certain countries, or simply because they have fled poverty. all national governments are pursuing an inhumane and backward policy in this matter by denying many of these immigrants the right to have proper papers permitting them to stay and work. it is unacceptable that a class of women and men should be deprived of all rights and turned into prey for employers who are fond of low-paid underground work and for 'sleep-dealers'. if the european parliament wants to show that it represents progress, at least on this point, it should take a clear stand. it should influence national policies to ensure that immigrant workers are not only granted legal papers that would allow them to live in dignity and in the open, but also the opportunity to enjoy the same political, trade union and associative rights as those enjoyed by all citizens of the european union.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, once again we are being led to discuss the european union's asylum policy, unfortunately through the prism of 'everything is safe'. we are dealing today with two commission documents which, by their nature, their scope and their objectives, should not be dealt with together, unless we wish to keep them together. this joint handling of two important and sensitive cases gives the impression that asylum seekers are potential terrorists. the commission's report does, however, indicate that it is unlikely that terrorists will use the asylum procedure. what a paradox then! would the member states not rather seek to evade their international commitments by invoking exclusion clauses, clauses which, if interpreted broadly, would ultimately free them from these commitments, which are fundamental in terms of human rights? with all the difficulties that the question of asylum poses, and despite all our differences, let us not forget that we are dealing with victims, not criminals. only an integrated approach and a restrictive application of exclusion clauses can guarantee compliance with the international obligations of european states in the field of asylum. the return, expulsion or extradition policy must offer all guarantees with regard to respect for human rights, including the death penalty incurred by these persons in their country of origin. added to this are the social and domestic conditions of each country. is it right to deport people to countries where civil war is raging, where the threat of death is daily added to economic and social misery, as in algeria or elsewhere? non-deportation is a requirement of the european union in our association agreements. extradition implicitly calls into question the right of individuals to seek asylum when their lives are threatened. in addition, a european solution must be found for asylum seekers who are denied the right to asylum, who are left without rights and who are adding to the ranks of the undocumented, who are the delight of unscrupulous employers who exploit them for their own interests, while these people live in inhuman conditions in our european democracies. these men and women have waited so long to receive a response from the administration! often, deep links have been forged with the host countries; children have been born; the links with the countries of origin have become distant, have become non-existent. to expel them would be to uproot them again. the only solution today would be to regularize them. i would just like to recall these few points in order to ensure universal respect for fundamental rights, but i support the rapporteur.
- mr president, we have nothing against compensation for victims of crime or against the easing of the bureaucratic procedure which often delays the award of compensation. however, it is necessary to extend the concept of crime and the resulting compensation to environmental crimes or crimes in general for which the owners of companies are responsible, who, in order to increase the profit of their shareholders, save money on measures to prevent accidents. the industrial disasters at azf in toulouse, france, lanhelas in portugal, enschede in the netherlands, to name but a few, all had dramatic consequences in terms of human and material losses. and how many deaths have been caused by the misuse of asbestos by companies, even at times when the harmful nature of this substance was perfectly known? as these are often among the richest and most powerful companies, the managers are solvent. in this case, it is not the taxpayers who pay, but the employers who are responsible for the damage. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of the road is not compromised.
