in writing. - if, after the floods which overwhelmed central europe this summer, the earthquakes in turkey, greece and, more recently, italy, it was still necessary to demonstrate the need for a fund for disaster relief, the news of the sinking of the prestige has finally convinced us of this. however, this solidarity fund is a necessary but not sufficient guarantee. the aid to the victims of such disasters must not be left without a fundamental reflection on the causes of these disasters, on our production methods and economic policies. on the contrary, it should encourage a radical re-examination of our profit-saving behaviour! small profits for shipowners registered in panama, recruiting filipinos and flying the flag "gibraltar"! but there are personal and family tragedies, and inestimable losses for the european and international communities, perpetrated by each illegal tanker sinking, destroying the socioeconomic fabric of the coasts for years and killing off ecosystems, marine biodiversity, for centuries! more than a solidarity fund, i am calling for the creation of a european bank for the prevention and restoration of environmental damage, which should be permanent and upstream of ecological trauma. so that this latest prestige disaster will be the final warning shot to these ecocide attacks.
in writing. - i voted for the mobilisation of the eu solidarity fund. this vote is the culmination of the rapid legislative work that has been carried out since commissioner barnier's proposal was presented on 18 september. i should like to thank him for his efforts in this matter. when the political will is strong enough, europe can move forward quickly and well. i only regret that we did not reach the same conclusion after the terrible storms of 1999, which particularly hit france hard. today, we can only rejoice at the mobilisation of this new european instrument of solidarity. the 728 million euros will provide additional relief to families who have suffered from natural disasters this summer. in my region and in several departments in the south of france, violent storms and torrential floods hit about 400 communes on 8 and 9 september, killing 24 people and causing extensive damage. my thoughts today go to these families, the elected representatives of these communes and all those, civil security forces or volunteers, who have given them help and support in the emergency. they know the price of solidarity and i hope they will appreciate the gesture that europe has made today.
in writing. - the commission proposes to make the regulations on additives in animal feedingstuffs more consistent and we support this approach. but on the grounds that it was making a technical adaptation of existing legislation, it took the opportunity to make fundamental changes to the authorization procedure. as regards the regulation of additives, we support the proposals to end the use of antibiotics still authorized as growth promoters by providing for a transitional period and to simplify the authorization procedure for additives already authorized in human food. we also agree that coccidiostats and histomonostats should continue to be considered as additives, pending the development of other ways of protecting animals against these diseases. however, we are waiting for proposals from the commission which will ensure that the same requirements will be applied to imported meat. as regards the authorization procedure, we cannot support the commission's proposal to give the european food safety authority sole competence to examine application files, which until now had been the responsibility of the member states. for this reason we cannot vote in favour of this report.
in writing. - in line with the commitment made in lisbon to a european future characterized by a quantitative and qualitative improvement in employment and greater social cohesion, i will support this report only if amendment no 42, which abolishes the application of a deadline proposed by the commission to guarantee the essential protection of the temporary worker, is voted on. it seems to me that it is essential that the so-called principle of 'non-discrimination', which is that a temporary worker is not treated less favourably than a similar worker of the employing undertaking in terms of working and employment conditions, is applied fully and therefore without 'discrimination'! in short, this principle must be guaranteed from the outset: it cannot be exempted or derogated from in any way, especially since this form of atypical work is, in comparison with all forms of atypical work, the one most prone to offences, despite community legislation on the matter, and to shameless exploitation, that is to say, in fact to a kind of 'rectification' of work. in line with this basic idea, i shall also vote in favour of the amendment requiring member states to prevent the use of temporary workers to break up a strike.
in writing. - the commission proposes a directive to regulate the working conditions of temporary workers in the member states. the choice of this binding measure will impose on the member states a regulation which will not necessarily be adapted to their national specificities and which may therefore penalize this mode of work, whereas the objective was to promote it. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work is a very good one. it would appear that this proposal for a directive is not based on a sufficiently solid basis. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be given the right to decide on the application of the directive. i cannot therefore vote for a text which, far from achieving the objectives it has set itself, runs counter to them.
in writing. - we voted against this joint motion for a resolution because, behind its convoluted wording and its 'self-congratulations', it seeks above all to clear up the responsibility of the russian authorities for the dirty war they are waging in chechnya. if we condemn terrorism in all its forms, it is shocking that the joint motion for a resolution expresses its 'firm condemnation' only of the terrorist attacks in moscow, and not of the state terrorism carried out by the russian army against the civilian population in chechnya. as for the way the neutralization of the chechen terrorists in moscow has unfolded, it shows not only the shame of terrorism but also the total disregard of the russian government for its own citizens. we are in favour of the closest possible links between the peoples of the european union and those of russia, but against the complicity of their leaders, who are preparing for war against iraq while the others are waging it against the chechens.
in writing. - so who can honestly be satisfied with the results of the eu-russia summit? certainly the supporters of liberalism who see in this country only an additional space for the market, competition and privatization, especially in the fields of energy, research and transport. certainly putin, who, legitimized by the post-9/11 us attitude, is flouting freedom of expression and increasing police and military pressure on all the peoples of the russian federation, especially the chechens. we cannot identify ourselves with these results. on the contrary, we stand firmly with the people who are victims of savage capitalism and we fight alongside them for the maintenance of public and social services and for the defence of the right to work and to retire. we support even more strongly the right of the chechen people to self-determination. we condemn the russian military aggression and the hypocritical attitude of the eu and denmark, which, on russian orders, arrested akhmed zakayev, the representative of chechen president maskhadov. finally, we cannot vote for the joint resolution of the european parliament which authorizes and legitimizes military operations in chechnya.
in writing. - we could have voted in favour of this joint resolution, since it recalls a number of well-founded considerations concerning the musharraf military regime in pakistan. however, the convictions do not go far enough. paragraph 2 of the law legitimises the regime following the last elections in october 2002. but these elections were not democratic. they were conducted as a commercial operation. the rich have been able to buy the votes of the poor without the electoral commission being able to stop it. military officials of all ranks have been pressuring local government to help their favorite candidates. the aim of these elections was to encourage politicians to follow the instructions and recommendations of the military, the "new" allies of imperialism in the region. all the decisions taken were dictated by economic considerations: continued privatization, deregulation, the decline of collective agreements and mass unemployment. according to the sustainable development planning institute in islamabad, 6.8 million pakistanis fell below the poverty line in the last three years of the musharraf regime. the imf and the world bank are the real agents of the regime. that is not the subject of this resolution and the condemnation of the musharraf regime does not go far enough. we abstained.
in writing. - we are in favour of the development of life sciences, biotechnology and, more broadly, of all sciences in general. for it is this development which can lay the material foundations for the progress of humanity and the intellectual foundations for its emancipation from all kinds of prejudices, beginning with the obscurantism conveyed by religions and various reactionary ideologies, some of which are very fashionable at the moment and which periodically resurface in this society where men do not control their destiny but are crushed by an unjust, harmful and aberrant mode of social organization. we reject, however, the many direct or indirect complacencies in the report with regard to private enterprises. these companies are not concerned with what is useful to mankind in the development of science, but rather with what can be marketed to a creditworthy clientele and make a profit. we also reject all calls for public funding in the interests of private capital, even when this interest is hidden behind the needs of research. we therefore abstained on this report.
in writing. - we obviously cannot endorse the report by alain lipietz, who expresses his 'bitter disillusionment at the lack of progress towards the effective liberalisation of the european gas and electricity markets'. we call on the citizens to mobilize against such a project. like most of them, we have 'very little awareness' of the benefits of competition policy at eu level, as it is translated into restructuring-licensing and the satisfaction of social needs at a discount. in contrast to such a policy, which is at least as stupid as the stability pact, we are in favour of structural policies, planned at european level, for example in the field of transport and energy. in general, the commission's approach is to make such policies permanently impossible, in particular by reducing state aid which is systematically presented as harmful. unlike the rapporteur, we do not subscribe to 'the commission's continued commitment to go even further in reducing state aid'. we shall therefore vote against his text, which is an unreserved endorsement of neoliberal ideology.
in writing. - in recent years the commission has carried out its task of hunting down state aid with a somewhat blind zeal, seeing faulty aid everywhere. for the first time, the council has recently tried to moderate it, making use of article 88 (3), which allows it, acting unanimously in exceptional circumstances, to exempt certain aids from any prosecution. it is regrettable that he did not have the courage to do so earlier, for example when the commission condemned public employment aid in the french textile sector. the court of justice also struck another brake with the ferring judgment of 22 november 2001, which exempts state aid when it merely compensates for the additional cost of a public service obligation. we hope that this case law will be upheld. it seems to us that the relevant part of the treaty (articles 87 to 89) should now be updated to define more clearly the acceptable public aids, for example for employment, the environment or compensation for public service obligations. moreover, the commission must not be left with exclusive and discretionary powers: national democracies must also have a say.
in writing. - the report by philippe herzog proposes some minor adjustments to the state aid scoreboard and expresses some wishful thinking. like him, we deplore the stagnation of r & d aid, like him, we are in favour of derogating treatments. but this report must be severely criticized on the merits. it treats the absence of any evaluation procedure as one of the points. but this is the key question: rather than being asked to vote on a table of figures, democracy would like the european parliament to be able to decide on the basis of real balance sheets. if this is mentioned only in passing, it is because the rapporteur has already made it irrelevant by declaring his allegiance to neo-liberal dogma. the report closes the discussion before opening it by stating that it supports 'the objectives of reducing aid granted by states or financed from public funds, in whatever form, which distorts or threatens to distort competition'. the report is therefore characterized by detailed arrangements with a pure competition logic, and that is why we voted against it.

mr president, the sea serpent of the status of members of the european parliament is once again before this house, without it being clear what the outcome of the discussion with the council will be. in our view, the main reason for the failure of the negotiations, beyond the technical details, is that the european parliament wants to secure for its members a purely european status with remuneration from the community budget, even though this objective is contrary to the spirit and the letter of the treaties. articles 189 and 190 clearly state that the members present here are each representatives of the people who elected them. that is why we have long ago put forward a proposal which we still believe would be a good compromise. it consists of three parts. firstly, meps should continue to receive their main salary from their country of election, with national taxation, as they do now. it would be absurd - and i am not being too harsh - if a representative of a country could be paid in a way other than by his own country and not be taxed in the same way as his fellow citizens in respect of his main salary. secondly, travel and other expenses should be reimbursed in accordance with their actual amount, within a reasonable ceiling of course. finally, where appropriate, a limited allowance paid by the european parliament per day of attendance could be identified as a complement. it would constitute income - but this time clear and transparent income - which could be subject to community taxation. we have long felt that this proposal offers a good compromise between several objectives. it is rational, it is comprehensible, it is transparent. and finally, for us, it preserves a fundamental principle: the legal and financial link between each member of parliament and the people who elected him.

mr president, the souchet report, which we adopted recently by a very large majority, has already been strongly in favour of maintaining public aid for the modernisation of the fishing fleet. the varela report goes in the same direction and we welcome it. the european parliament must confirm its commitment to maintaining this aid and not endorse the commission's proposals to abolish it under the pretext of preserving the marine environment. aid for modernisation is still needed. they are not the cause of overfishing. no, it's the opposite. it is with modern and properly equipped vessels, engaged in selective and controlled fishing, that we will contribute to the sustainable management of resources and the fight against fraud. it is not these aids that are a factor in overcapacity. they contribute to improving working conditions, hygiene and safety on board. they contribute to the conservation and quality of fishery products. they therefore have a vital function. more generally, having just heard mr fischler's general policy statement, we would like to stress with him that good management of the resource is obviously necessary, but with objectivity, transparency, association of the professionals and with reductions or increases in quotas, depending on the evolution of stocks. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. for whose benefit? how can we avoid this perverse effect ? we would like to know the answers to all these questions.

and the creation of an emergency fund to deal with the problem of overcapacity of the union fleets. it is up to the member states to choose their model of action during this period. i would like to make a plea here for small-scale fishing, which is the kind that provides the maximum number of jobs and allows many families of traditional fishermen to survive. so far, industrial fishing has been the main area of support, and i thank commissioner fischler for the proposals he has made in his policy on this subject. first, when ifop subsidies are used to build larger and larger and more powerful vessels, the states encourage a naturally larger and less selective predation to the detriment of small businesses concerned with maintaining a powerful tool maintained in good condition and in particular with good safety conditions, while being less aggressive to the marine environment. we want more money to be given to businesses, particularly in the structural funds. the latter must be used for better equipment and not for the destruction of the tool. for example, smaller vessels with less power should also be given access to areas reserved for them in relation to its main resources. member states could take similar action to promote access to markets where smaller fishermen, who are less organised than the larger ones, have less influence on management. hence the help that can be given to fisheries and auctions. as regards the representation of fishermen on the advisory committees for the commission, small businesses must be favoured. the capacity of representation of these traditional fishermen should be improved, particularly at the level of the regional fisheries committees, which are the bodies in which the professional organizations can express themselves, as the example of the mediterranean fishermen shows. this would give them a stronger voice in defending their interests. finally, it is always the big ones who can go further, whether in africa, for example in senegal, where species are exploited more, or in other countries whose fisheries resources are fundamental to the local economy. they contribute to the depletion of stocks, which is harmful both for local fishermen and globally. so these are some of the proposals we can make to promote small-scale fishing.

the commission. madam president, we are at a time when the economic prospects are not the best and it has become clear in the european union that there is a need for more effective coordination of economic and employment policies. the commission's proposal to streamline the coordination procedures has attracted the interest of all the institutions, there have been many discussions at various levels, and this makes it clear that this proposal is not merely technical, as it seems at first sight, but that important political objectives are certainly at stake, such as efficiency and transparency in the implementation of the lisbon agenda, but also the role of the european employment strategy, which has now been consolidated after five years of implementation. i would like to thank in particular the rapporteur, mr karas, and the draftsman of the opinion of the committee on employment and social affairs, mr bullmann, for the very good work they have done. i would therefore like to focus on a few key issues. firstly, the report supports the focus on medium-term action. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission will adopt a set of guidelines, for the first time under the new programme, in april 2003, with a three-year horizon until 2006. significant changes to the guidelines should be avoided before this mid-term review in 2006. it has been shown that it is much better to stick to the guidelines and to see that they are implemented than to add new elements all the time. secondly, this medium-term action will also require a new discipline on the part of all the parties involved, the commission, the council, the european parliament and the other interested parties. the commission will of course review the country-specific employment recommendations annually to ensure that they continue to reflect the policy developments in each member state. i would like to remind you that, according to the treaty, there is an obligation for this annual report, which will take the form of monitoring implementation. this leads to the second issue, which is ensuring consistency and complementarity. it is essential that the two procedures have the necessary complementarity in order to have as much cooperation as possible between economic and employment policies. in the past we have had a lot of overlap, but sometimes conflicting approaches between the two strategies. thirdly, the need to focus on implementation. after several years of implementation of the employment strategy, we have identified the main problems in implementation and, in many cases, the gap between the submission of the national employment action plans and their implementation. in particular, i would like to stress that this process of rationalisation should lead to closer cooperation, not only between the different council formations - the ecofin council and the employment council should find a clearer and more effective way of working together - but also between all the institutions of the european union. i believe that parliament and the whole process will certainly benefit from this proposed streamlining of procedures, in particular from greater transparency of information and the main elements linked to the implementation of economic and employment policies being provided in a coordinated manner. i would remind you that in the past, information on the two procedures has often arrived at different times, leading to a great deal of confusion. fourthly, streamlining means a better governance model for these processes, which means more effective consultation with the european parliament and greater involvement of the social partners and civil society. in the evaluation of employment policies, the major issue was the lack of the required involvement of both the social partners and national parliaments. finally, madam president, i should like to say that this proposal respects the autonomy of the procedures, as provided for in the treaty. in short, i would say that the economic guidelines, the economic guidelines, are the framework within which the whole of economic policy operates, but that the employment strategy also retains the necessary autonomy. i am glad that parliament supports this approach. what are the next steps? the whole process coincides with the review of the employment strategy. we will present the first communication in january 2003 and these two documents, the communication on the revision of the employment strategy and the draft joint report which we presented a month ago, will be the two main political documents which will have to be discussed in order to be able to reach the spring council and after that to proceed with the first implementation of the new guidelines procedure. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i think that now we have the opportunity to work together more effectively and more effectively.
- madam president, no coordination, no procedure is effective when the political will is lacking. that's where you start. good objectives were set in lisbon and gothenburg, but there is a huge gap between declarations and deeds. the european union is facing serious economic problems. his growth potential is slowing. its public and private investments are very low. she lacks qualifications. the stability pact and monetary policy do not address these challenges. they refer everything to the member states and coordination, conceived as a discipline of the states, cannot work if, at the same time, the union does not assume and implement common policies. there is no real european economic policy because of the differences between the member states. coordination does not study economic interactions between countries. and there is still no overall thinking about the european economy and its euro zone, seen in the context of globalisation. we don't have supply policy yet, we don't have networks, we don't have human capacity. we are still in a competitive regulatory and fiscal space, where the very notion of a social market economy is not accepted and will not be incorporated, i think, in the future constitution, not to mention that a real aversion to the public economy still prevails. i come now to the institutional procedures. what the commission is proposing is purely technocratic. i'm all for grouping the subjects, establishing a cycle. i agree with the principle of rationalization. however, this will not remove the political obstacles mentioned above, hence my suggestions. firstly, the treaties do not provide a solid basis for the community's economic policy. the first priority is to establish this basis in the convention. secondly, there are no reliable statistical and comparative analytical tools, especially for social cohesion and sustainable development. the union must therefore be given the means of thinking and analysis that are commensurate with its declarations. thirdly, the procedures proposed do not yet have democratic value. the priority is to have a broad public discussion of the situation and options before the commission's package, and an ex post evaluation by civil society and elected officials, not just by the commission. fourthly, i do not believe that the european parliament is still capable of debating properly and of choosing a coherent economic policy. too many positions are marked by national interests and ideological biases. that said, parliament is better placed than the council and the commission to work on the deliberation and evaluation of economic policy. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. it is only then that the commission will draw up its proposals, only then will the decision be taken by the council, but then parliament could have a power of ratification. in conclusion, without a shared political will and a common democratic procedure, national policy coordination will not work.

mr president, the institutional reform proposal which the commission is presenting today to the convention and parliament, and which the journalists have already had in their possession for at least two days in substance, contains an apparent innovation: the commission's responsibility before the council. however, this 'innovation' serves as a pretext in all areas for the increase in the powers of the college, which is considered a priori as the sole holder of the general european interest. but that is a biased view. the commission proposes to consolidate and extend the monopoly of initiative to the whole of what it calls the legislative field. why should 20 commissioners know more about the general european interest than all the governments in the council? we are told that each government is defending its national interest, but it is precisely their debate that allows us to go further. the same is true in the market: each consumer defends his own selfish interest, but nevertheless all their transactions give prices which provide the best general orientation. the commission, with its monopoly of initiative, is therefore in the position of a planner who claims to know prices better than the market. in a world of openness, freedom and democracy, this is unacceptable. this monopoly of initiative, reinforced by the requirement for unanimity in the council to reject commission proposals and by the extension of the majority to accept them, distorts all european decision-making and undoubtedly contributes to the perceived gap between the union and the citizens. we believe that it must be reformed by taking a global view of the institutions. either we open up this monopoly of initiative to other actors such as the european parliament and the national parliaments, which have undeniable democratic legitimacy, or we maintain it, but then, in return, we formalize a right of veto for each national parliament. in any event, it seemed that the debate on the commission's monopoly of initiative had been closed at the convention in recent times before it had even been opened. in writing. - the commission proposal aims, inter alia, to amend regulation (ec) no 2792/1999 by abolishing the aid provided for in the current rules, such as those on the renewal and modernisation of the fleet. while it is obvious that an optimal balance between the fleet and fisheries resources must be achieved, this must not be done at any price and certainly not at the expense of the men and women who live and support fisheries. in other words, a genuine fisheries policy is not just the adoption of rules on fish stocks: it is also an economic activity with a very high social impact. the point is not to forget it. in addition, the abolition of public aid for the modernisation and renewal of the fishing fleet is unacceptable because it does not lead to overcapacity, overfishing or distortion of competition between member states. i believe that the only effective and relevant instrument for managing fisheries resources, provided that it is properly controlled, is that of tacs and quotas. amendments are being tabled to that end. i shall therefore vote in favour of the amendment.
in writing. - while it does not seem to me to be an aberration to take a measure to remove surplus vessels from the fleet in view of the availability of fisheries resources, i am not prepared to accept such a measure which is not currently financed. the establishment of this emergency measure for the demolition of ships does not take account of fifg appropriations; i do not agree with the member states being forced to reprogram appropriations already programmed and allocated for other purposes: the objectives set out in the national programmes concerning fifg appropriations, such as the necessary renovation and modernisation of the fleet, can thus be countered by demolition. a programme for the withdrawal of fleets of surplus vessels at community level could, for example, have been an effective and fair means of identifying any overcapacity existing in certain member states and thus responding precisely to the commission's concern to reduce the community's overcapacity. in short, it would be highly desirable for the commission to consider a solution which gives priority to tacs over irreversible demolition measures which have a more radical socioeconomic impact on the areas concerned. the report is in line with these remarks and i shall vote in favour of it.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i think that no one will be able to deny that the system of legal acts of the european union is monstrously complicated, not transparent, incomprehensible to public opinion and, sometimes, even difficult to understand for ourselves. there is no doubt that there is an explainable and justifiable complexity. it is not easy to have a legal order that matches the legal orders of 15 states today, 25 states tomorrow, which are fundamentally different. the european union must also deal with the classic problems of the hierarchy of standards which arise in each of our member states - the constitution, the law, the implementing regulation, individual decisions - and with problems specific to the union, which are linked to the ever delicate balance between the powers of the union and those of the member states. so there's justifiable complexity and we'll never get to an ultra-simple system. however, there is also a complexity in this case which is not justifiable: we are faced with a chaos of norms, a chaos of procedures and a chaos of languages. the european parliament has been a very active participant in the debate on the future of the european union. it contains provisions on policies, and provisions on institutions. there is also a budgetary decision, such as resources, which is taken within a framework that is virtually constitutional. on the other hand, since there is no clear distinction between the field of general legislative measures and that of regulatory measures, we see implementing measures which are taken in the context of the law and we see measures of general scope which are taken in the context of implementing regulations. finally, we are indeed faced with a linguistic chaos, since everything is done to not name what we do. we make laws, but we're careful not to call them laws. both individual and constitutional measures are called decisions, that is to say, something that falls below the hierarchy. nobody understands anything about it. i would add that the problem of the pillars arises and that, in a paradox i cannot understand, it was decided that it was possible, even necessary, in view of the sensitive nature of certain decisions to be taken, for example decisions on fundamental rights in criminal matters, to use less democratic procedures - without the european parliament - less efficient, and which would be adopted unanimously. they would also be less legally secure without the assistance of the court of justice in taking them. understand who can. why should something which directly concerns fundamental rights not benefit from the guarantees and procedures of legislation established elsewhere? the report proposes to put all this in order and to apply a simple principle: a standard, a procedure, a name, a name. we therefore propose to organise all this in three main blocks: the constitutional block, which will comprise - i believe this is also the view of the convention - two parts: part a dealing with what is constitutional in its own right, namely the values, principles, objectives, institutions and procedures which enable the union to function, and then part b, which will include the main political principles currently contained in the treaty. the question on this block is whether the ratification procedures should be changed. your rapporteur made proposals which have not all been followed up by the constitutional committee, but it is clear that we must evolve if we do not want to reach a general blockade by 25 states of any possibility of evolving this standard. secondly, a legislative bloc. a legislative bloc is simple. we must call for a law, a law, and we propose, of course, to distinguish between organic laws, which would be somewhat solemn laws subject to a special procedure, framework laws which would replace directives, ordinary laws which would replace legislative regulations, and then, on the other hand, between financing laws and budgets which would, of course, deal with the matter. but let's call all of these laws, because they are laws. and above all, let us be very clear that the law is characterized by codecision, and that codecision must become the single decisionmaking procedure for the whole legislative bloc. there are undoubtedly special applications, particularly in financial matters, but we must move in this direction. finally, the third element is the regulatory block, namely the implementing regulations. three simple principles are needed. first of all, we must draw the consequences of the fact that the legislative authority is no longer the council alone, but the council and parliament acting in accordance with the codecision procedure. the powers currently conferred on the council, in particular under article 202, must therefore be exercised by both branches of the legislative authority. on the other hand, we must admit that we cannot regulate at 25 as we have done so far. we need a greater division of labour between a legislative authority which enables and controls, and an executive authority which makes the implementing regulations, and we believe that this should be the commission. this will of course be the case, subject to a call back procedure allowing both branches of the legislature to ensure that the regulations are in conformity with the enabling legislation on which they are based. so that's the gist of it. of course, there is still much more to be said about this report, but we feel that if we were to introduce this great clarification between a constitutional bloc, a legislative bloc governed by codecision and a regulatory bloc which would put an end to these comitological procedures, at least in an advisory capacity as the commission would like, and which would replace comitology with genuine control of the two branches of the legislative authority, then we would have gained in transparency, democracy and efficiency, and perhaps some people in europe would finally begin to understand what we are doing!
mr president, the bourlanges report is both brilliant and technical, two qualities which are normally almost impossible to bring together in a single text. this is a first achievement for which the rapporteur should be congratulated. mr bourlanges then succeeds in a second feat - but i do not commend him for that - which is to seduce without saying the essence of his intentions. the report is based on an implicit assumption, namely that of a pyramidal europe in which the nations occupy the bottom, the same pyramidal europe that is so strongly condemned in the napolitano report when the model risks being applied to the regions and local authorities. the top of the pyramid is occupied by a european constitution, the report of which, with great skill, does not directly say that it subordinates the nations. on the contrary, it even states in paragraph 4 that it is an act of international law signed by the member states. but this sentence does not say the essential thing: the states would thus be giving up their sovereignty in a fundamental way, since the european constitution would dominate national constitutions and, for example, would impose majority decisions on all so-called legislative acts. the report calls for this development to be achieved, but it raises a fundamental problem. what happens when a decision taken by majority vote at european level contradicts a national constitution or a fundamental principle which a people holds dear? the report says nothing about that, because if it did, it would have to admit that it is proposing a surrender of sovereignty without any safety net. this model of europe is unacceptable to us; and besides, in an ever more heterogeneous enlarged europe, it simply could not work. in such a europe, the extension of majority decisions could only work if, in return, a veto right of the national parliaments was clearly recognized, as i have explained in the minority opinion which i have attached to the bourlanges report. more generally, this report uses the pretext of simplification to push through proposals for supranational unification. it is also the well-established method within the convention, which explains to us at all times that unification of the treaties is simpler, the single legal personality is simpler, the merging of the pillars is simpler, the generalization of codecision is simpler, the abolition of unanimity, including for the revision of the treaties, is simpler. it could be summed up in a slogan, which is also unique: the superstate is simpler. and while this solution does indeed seem simpler, we must not overlook its major drawback: it is a major drain on democracy. it is true that the bourlanges report states in paragraph 1 that its proposals are based on the principle of 'democratization'. but if we read his description of it, we can see that it is what president prodi calls, in his speeches and in his draft constitution, supranational democracy. in short, it is a question of taking powers away from the national parliaments and giving them to the european parliament, which is the heart of the co-decision procedure with a majority in the council. unfortunately, mr president, this supranational democracy seems to be largely artificial, because the peoples of today give their national democracy the main legitimacy. it is therefore a ruse to remove the power of the peoples in order to better capture it. finally, we reply to the bourlanges report and to the convention that it is not acceptable to put forward technical simplification considerations in order to avoid the debate on the essential political questions. the main political question today is this: the peoples do indeed want a closer europe, but europe will not be brought closer by simplifying a little the procedures which are by nature distant from the nations and which deprive them of their powers. europe will be brought closer together simply by giving national parliaments the right to intervene directly in the european decision-making process. everything else is just details.

commission. – mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs breyer, for her report which responds to the question put forward by the commission. the question was which foods should be allowed to be irradiated in the european union? the commission put this question to parliament and the council following a consultation of industry and consumer organisations and other interested parties. the consultation received a polarised response. stakeholders were either totally against this technology or in favour of it. there would seem to be no common ground between these two camps. currently, the european union-wide positive list of products authorised for irradiation treatment contains only dried aromatic herbs, spices and vegetable seasonings. for the completion of this list, the commission presented three options for discussion. the first option proposed allowing the irradiation of shrimps and frogs’ legs, as these foods are often imported from subtropical and tropical countries and a certain microbe content can hardly be avoided. the second option proposed to allow the irradiation of a number of foods in addition to shrimps and frogs’ legs, all of which have been, and continue to be, irradiated in the member states in substantial amounts. such foods include dried fruits, cereals, chicken, offal, egg white and gum arabic. the third option proposed that the current positive list should be regarded as complete, which would mean that only dried aromatic herbs, spices and vegetable seasonings could be irradiated in the european union. the report adopted by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy provides the possibility of adding further products to the current positive list if the safety of these products can be proven. the adoption of amendments nos 2 and 3 tabled by the rapporteur and other members of parliament would, however, result in the third option, which is the most restrictive one. the commission will take note of parliament's conclusions but must await the reaction of the council before making any formal proposal. however, i would like, on behalf of my colleague, mr byrne, to take this opportunity to clarify a few points. first, i would like clearly to reiterate that the scientific committee on food has concluded that irradiated foods are safe. this opinion is based on many scientific studies and is shared by the world health organisation and scientific bodies. therefore, additional toxicology studies are not required, as the views of the scientific community are very clear on this issue. there are many misconceptions about this technique. i would stress that not all foods can or will be irradiated. this is a similar situation to cooking and freezing: not all foods are cooked and not all foods are put in the refrigerator. irradiation is just one method of food preservation. for some foods it is better than other techniques, for others it is not. the european union has very strict labelling rules for irradiated foods. even if a compound food contains only small amounts of irradiated ingredients, this fact has to be clearly indicated. we also have the technical tools to enforce correct labelling. the commission has financed the development and standardisation of methods for the detection of irradiated foods. these methods are used by the food control authorities to check foods on the market. the first report of the commission on food irradiation, published recently, shows that the overwhelming majority of foods on the market are correctly labelled. this means that consumers can choose freely between irradiated and non-irradiated products. i would also like to reiterate that current legislation already requests member states to report the results of their checks on irradiation facilities and on food products. if products are detected by the food control authorities which do not comply with legal requirements, they have to be removed from the market. finally, i note that the report stigmatises third countries, in particular the united states and brazil, for using this technique. i consider this to be inappropriate as our own scientific committee considers irradiated foods to be safe.

- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are gathered here today after several months of work, hearings, field visits, exchanges with experts, farmers, men and women, and finally with all those who have lived through this foot-and-mouth disease crisis, suffered from it and, above all, do not want it to happen again. this was the aim of our work: to understand the event, to analyse it in all its forms - economic, social, psychological - to draw lessons from it and to minimise the risks and effects of this type of epizootic in the future. some people would have liked to use the temporary committee as a tool to find the culprit or culprits, which is a normal reaction when one is desperate, outraged by a situation one is experiencing. but that was not the purpose of our committee or the reason why it was set up. can we accept that in this report, which purports to be the result of the most objective reflection possible, we can find very subjective elements, irrational assumptions? i don't think he is. the credibility of our work as members of parliament is at stake and that is why our group has tabled a number of amendments to rebalance the report. apart from these few political deviations, we must admit that our work has been very enriching and fruitful, as the many direct contacts have enabled us to better understand the problems of managing the crisis and its multiple consequences. it should be remembered that the epidemic was traumatic for tens of thousands of people, not least because the memory of foot-and-mouth disease was that of an epidemic, serious as it was, but not so serious as to wipe out entire territories and lead to the death of millions of animals that men had taken such pains to feed and care for. as a result of new methods of animal husbandry and the increased movement of animals, we have not been able to cope with this crisis, to react as we did fifty years ago by isolating the infected farms: their numbers were already too high when the epidemic was identified. so, of course, afterwards, we can always say: "we should have done this or that", but we must not forget that at that time, we were facing a crisis and that the responses had to be found in the urgency with institutions, communities, populations unprepared for such a situation. even experts believe that the crisis could have been of the same tragic scale if it had started in another european country. the sad experience of the united kingdom has made it possible for member states to be more vigilant and better prepared for the epidemic. what do we do now ? what decisions must the european union take? the rapporteur and several of my colleagues have just explained this, as has the commissioner. firstly, prevention is essential, and this prevention requires better information, continuing training for farmers - who have not always been able to identify the disease early enough - traceability of animals, more and more easily mobilisable animal health professionals. vigilance within europe's borders is essential, but we also need to strengthen our surveillance of imports, both at land borders and at sea and airport borders. because we are at the heart of global trade and because people are increasingly travelling, we have to take this international dimension into account. we also need to provide solutions in case of crisis by anticipating responses with more relevant emergency plans, promoting emergency vaccinations where possible, not forgetting that slaughter is the only possible way out when contamination is proven. finally, i would add that research is an area in which we are entitled to expect results, provided we put the resources into it. in conclusion, in the wake of the recent maritime disasters in europe, i would like to point out that our reports, full of good intentions, are of little value if the european union and the member states do not take their full share of responsibility in the rapid implementation of the recommendations we are making here. we are now awaiting the report which the commission is working on at the moment and hope that it will be in line with the conclusions of our temporary committee. finally, i would like to thank and congratulate our rapporteur, the president, and all our colleagues who have taken part in the work, as well as the commission and all the staff involved in this work.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it was essential to learn from the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak in britain in 2001, because it was unprecedented in that country, in particular because of negligence - by both the british government and the commission - in emergency planning; because it has seriously threatened other european countries; because it reminded us how frightening this disease is, how suddenly it spreads, and the economic loss and the psychological trauma that it causes. our committee has done a good job overall. the kreissl-dörfler report emphasizes, in particular, and this is essential, that the enormity and specialization of herds, the concentration of livestock in certain regions, the disappearance of local slaughterhouses, the rapid development of live animal transport are factors which, in the absence of prophylactic vaccination, facilitate the spread of an epidemic like dry brush fires. when we look at future agricultural policy guidelines, we must bear this in mind, in order to ensure that we promote a harmonious distribution of agriculture throughout the territory and refuse to encourage the concentration of livestock farms as the extreme specialization of the regions. for example, it is clear that the abolition of milk quotas, which the european commission seems to be considering with a certain predilection, would very quickly result in the disappearance of dairy herds from areas with natural handicaps (mountain areas, wetlands) and the acceleration of the concentration of livestock on the plain. let us therefore ensure that we maintain a family farm structure on a human scale; it's the best prevention against fmd. our temporary committee was right to recommend emergency vaccination as the first priority in the fight against the epidemic, which can prevent the mass slaughter which has rightly shocked public opinion and traumatised farmers. while hundreds of millions of people are suffering from hunger, it is unacceptable to destroy the meat of millions of healthy animals, as was the case in 2001. with emergency vaccination, a ring is created around an outbreak where animals are vaccinated, animals that can eventually be slaughtered and consumed without the pressure of the emergency. however, i regret that the commission has not been more bold on this point. with the progress of vaccines - vaccines with a wider spectrum, vaccines with a longer duration of action, marker vaccines which allow vaccinated animals to be distinguished from infected animals - it is now possible to leave member states free to authorise or even make compulsory prophylactic vaccination, that is preventive vaccination, as was the practice before 1992, where the risks of epidemics are highest. this possibility should be left to the discretion of the member states, which are best placed to assess the consequences of specific risks for their farms. i also regret that the report does not more clearly challenge the current framework defined by the international office for diseases of animals, whose rules are clearly too rigid, too restrictive, too dogmatic as regards the conditions for the award of the fmd-free zone certificate. clearly, they are giving an outrageous preference to the countries of the new world, which have large areas, where the land is less densely occupied than here and therefore less exposed to the risk of an epidemic spreading. these rules, we absolutely must evolve them. mr president, we are now faced with the constant threat of new outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease, as new strains are constantly appearing, especially in europe, which is surrounded by countries where foot-and-mouth disease is endemic. this is particularly the case with turkey, which is a permanent danger, and also with the rest of the middle east and the maghreb. endemic outbreaks are also common in asia and latin america. the globalisation of trade in live animals can only encourage and accelerate the globalisation of diseases and viruses. the preference for short-distance transport, the rejection of a certain aberrant form of extreme specialisation which multiplies the transport of animals over long distances, the preference for birth and fattening on the same holding and slaughter in the production area are all wise behaviours which constitute the best prevention against the development of new epizootic diseases. we must remember this, mr president, commissioner, when we discuss the future cap, if we do not want to relive the nightmare of 2001.
- mr president, the health crisis is fortunately behind us, but its effects are not resolved. so we have to understand first. unfortunately, we have only hypotheses as to the origin of the contamination and the factors that spread the disease. nevertheless, we can draw a first lesson from this: the importance of a local policy, whether it be the convergence of upstream and downstream sectors or the maintenance of public services at local level in order to avoid transport which seems to have played an important role in this case. it is obvious that such a mass slaughter cannot be repeated. the report also makes proposals which we will support: revision of the alert plans in consultation with all partners, training policy, effective exchange of information between member states, strengthening of the means for research on marker vaccines. prevention programmes will also have to take account of the conservation of genetic resources; the commission has already proposed that the member states should take measures to ensure that the use of the plant protection products in question is not restricted to wild species, game, or small breeds. finally, these programmes will only be effective if adequate compensation is guaranteed.
commission. – mr president, i am very pleased to have the opportunity to respond to this valuable and important debate on this report. a number of issues have been raised by many speakers which i ought to address – even if only briefly at this stage. firstly, on the question of control of imports, many – if not all – of you have addressed this important issue. it is of critical importance to ensure that not only is there legislation in place to deal with this kind of issue but also that the controls are in place to ensure that the legislation is properly implemented. it is the job of the commission to bring forward legislation on the control of imports. it is, however, for the control authorities in the member states to ensure that legislation is fully and properly implemented and not, as mr santini suggested, a function of the commission to ensure that controls are in place. we must ensure that we identify who is responsible for what, so that we can clearly indicate to those who have the responsibility that they must exercise those functions properly. with regard to legislation, since 1972 we have legislation in place at eu level in respect of imports of commercial products. it is illegal to import goods in contravention of that legislation. more recently, we have put in place legislation on personal imports, which will be operational from 1 january 2003. i, like you, call on member states to ensure that their control authorities make sure that these pieces of legislation are properly and fully implemented. this issue is also addressed in the hygiene regulations before parliament at the moment. therefore, cooperation of all parties in this is of critical importance in trying to ensure that another outbreak does not happen in the future. the second did not apply it all, the other did, but then decided that the animals that were vaccinated should be killed. they had permission from the commission to vaccinate and keep the animals alive. however, decided not to use vaccination at all and the other decided to use vaccination but nonetheless – for trade considerations – went ahead and culled the cattle involved, even in circumstances where it could have allowed those animals to remain alive. i am very happy that a number of speakers praised the work of the commission. i am sure that the people who work with me, my collaborators who are in writing. - this directive of the european parliament and of the council, which aims to bring together in a single text all the rules on the organisation of working time which have been drawn up by the eu for many years, reflects, even more clearly, the desire to let employers organise working time as they see fit. we therefore take this opportunity to stress in particular our total opposition to night work when it is not socially necessary, since it is then just another means of increasing profits at the expense of workers' health. as regards the duration of working time, the number of pages devoted to the derogations authorised for a transitional period of five years, from 1 august 2004, shows how much less is the question of arranging the working time of employees than of leaving the hands free to employers to exploit workers as they see fit. one of these scandalous derogations, among many others, states: 'states shall ensure that, under no circumstances, the number of hours of work per week does not exceed an average of fifty-eight hours during the first three years of the transitional period, an average of fifty-six hours during the following two years, and an average of fifty-two hours for any additional period.' we cannot of course approve such a directive.
in writing. - we voted against this report and against the reports on bulgaria and romania, because they are an incentive, or even an obligation, to the governments of these countries to 'restructure' their steel production. under the pretext of 'rationalization', the text calls for a 'reduction in the productive capacity' of these countries. we oppose this utterly stupid and inhuman 'rationalization' which will result in the closure of some of the existing enterprises, the dismissal of their workers and the worsening of unemployment, and whose sole purpose is to make the surviving factories bring in profits for their owners. while we are in favour of the enlargement of the european union to include the countries of eastern europe, we are opposed to this enlargement being used as a pretext for worsening the living conditions of the working classes in these countries.

in writing. - i approve of the report by elisa maria damião and warmly congratulate her on her work. the asbestos tragedy is an example and we must learn from it! we've known for a long time that there was a serious risk. for a long time, for economic reasons, this risk was ignored, and today tens of thousands of victims suffer and die. now we're trying to protect ourselves. but tomorrow, those who didn't want to see it will have to answer to their victims and compensate them. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies, such as the new asbestos, but that it is also able to take account of the new risks posed by certain products, by new forms of production, by genetic manipulation and by the unlimited creation of new magnetic fields (to name just a few well-known examples). in short, if there is no appeal to reason, we must recall the legal, even criminal, responsibility. that is the meaning of my vote on the damião report.
- mr president, if i may, i would like to emphasize the exceptional quality of mr bourlanges' report, which is timely in view of the evolution of the convention. we have been able to speak of a sort of vampirisation of the convention by a virtual igc with the arrival of many foreign ministers. the european parliament, thanks to mr bourlanges' report, is reinvesting the convention in the most fundamental aspects of clarity and a sense of perspective. the clarity of legislation, because if no one is supposed to ignore the law, it is still necessary that the categories of laws be perfectly clear, and the sense of perspective, because it is always important to distinguish constitutional data from policies themselves. the bourlanges report will make a powerful contribution to this. and to be honest, we have the feeling that this is less a report than the matrix of a bourlanges constitution.
in writing. - in the minority opinion annexed to the bourlanges report, i denounced the proposal in paragraph 5 to allow for the revision of the treaty by a majority (which is admittedly overqualified) and not by unanimity. it is a method which, by continuing the trajectory of present-day europe, would completely disconnect the nations from the european decision-making process. one of our luxembourg colleagues, mr jacques poos, former foreign minister of his country and former president of the council of the european union, wrote to jean-louis bourlanges to tell him this. the council also stressed that 'no member state will accept an amendment to its basic law imposed against its will', and added: 'the citizens of such a minority state will turn their backs on a europe with authoritarian tendencies. as several successive constitutional amendments are made, an increasing number of member states could thus be subjected to vassal status. the result can be imagined in terms of joining the community project". the resolution adopted contains a more vague text on this point, but the intention remains. in any case, the spirit of this proposal remains more broadly in the idea of the report (and the convention) to generalize codecision by qualified majority in the council, without the counterweight of any national veto.
in writing. - one could almost complain about the rapporteur trying to put some order into what he himself calls a 'chaos', that is to say the jumble of contradictory or inapplicable rules, regulations and directives resulting from the bargaining that took place between national states throughout what is wrongly called the construction of europe. but the chaos he laments is not just in the texts. he's in the real world. this reality is the total contradiction between the process under way, evolving according to the balance of power between rival private interests defended by the member states, and a real unification creating a europe without borders with a rationally organised economy at the level of the continent. the attempt to reconcile european unification with competing capitalist interests reduces the ratio to the square of the circle.
in writing. - in view of the talent mr bourlanges usually displays, one might have expected something else from him than this uninteresting report which, above all, is not particularly original. the hierarchy of standards it proposes (constitutional block, organic laws, ordinary laws) is never more than a faithful copy of that provided for by the french constitution of the fifth republic. moreover, since the hierarchy of standards necessarily implies a hierarchy of functions and bodies, the rapporteur is here presenting, no more and no less, a new community architecture which reproduces at european level the state-national constitutional model. like any such exercise, however, institutional mimicry has its limits. is it really appropriate to want to transpose the constitutional model common to the member states at community level in this way? the answer is, of course, no. what the rapporteur forgets when he replaces the current regulation with european law, by demanding, of course, the extension of the codecision procedure, or when he talks about reforming the procedure for revising the treaties, is that even if the union has a political system identical to that of the states, it will still lack the essential thing: democratic legitimacy.
in writing. - this report, without giving any opinion on the merits - the advantages for consumers of the ionization process, which it does not dispute - points out certain abuses and dangers in this field. we are voting for this report only because it calls for caution, which we believe is in the interests of consumers. the real problem is not so much the ionisation process itself as the use made of it. although it already has applications which are beneficial to producers and consumers (food preservation, pest control, etc.), the agri-food and retail sectors, concerned only with increasing their profits, can turn the process against users. the report illustrates this danger: the consumer is not warned by adequate labelling that the product, despite its appearance due to ionisation, nevertheless deteriorates, which has already caused poisonings (cases of fatal exposure of workers to ionising products have been reported in some enterprises). again, while an innovative process could bring progress for the people, the 'market' makes irresponsibility rhyme with danger, and the pursuit of capitalist profit with contempt for the life and health of human beings.
in writing. - the foot-and-mouth disease epidemic that hit europe in 2001 was a disaster of great proportions, and not just in britain where livestock had to be slaughtered en masse. in addition to the dramatic impact on livestock farmers, the impact of this massacre and the emergency health measures taken has extended far beyond the agricultural context. the report highlights a number of factors that have aggravated the situation: livestock and the agri-food sector, meat subject to the imperatives of importer-exporters and the race to dominate world markets; non-transposition of european health directives into national legislation; veterinary checks at borders, which sometimes fail when major interests are at stake; continuous reduction in the number of veterinarians. but, while stressing aggravating factors and the 'deficiencies' of the authorities (which some amendments try to hide), this report backs down from calling into question the overall financial logic of 'rent-raising', the logic of the capitalist race for profit. it is precisely this that justifies the decision of the authorities to ban prophylactic vaccination at european level, even resorting to mass slaughter in the event of an epidemic, in order not to lose their position in world trade. so we supported some of the recommendations in the report but abstained.
in writing. - i am generally satisfied with the text adopted. the aim is to involve all the actors concerned (public authorities, the agricultural sector, citizens) and to involve them in the thinking upstream, particularly with regard to the development of alert systems. alert systems which, once set up by the commission, should show increased monitoring and vigilance of their operation. information on risks and on relevant measures must be circulated and understood. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. otherwise, the penalties shall be proportionate to the offences detected. while farmers have a significant responsibility in the system, too often the increase in the number of livestock is perceived as a key risk factor for epidemics. international trade is another factor to consider. i am therefore pleased that my colleagues have welcomed my proposal to introduce a ban on the import of goods for free warehouses or for ship-refuelling from countries which are not authorised to export to the eu. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the meat is not transported to the slaughterhouse. in writing. - i am pleased that the kreissl-dörfler report was adopted by a large majority, including the important part on the need to strengthen considerably the controls on imports of animals and animal products from the sensitive countries and neighbouring countries which are the source of the epidemic that struck europe in 2001. however, no controls on imported products can ever be as exhaustive, as precise, as rigorous as those applied by the member states and the trade organizations themselves. the controls on imports will never give the same guarantee of safety as the continuous control and traceability of national production and production located in europe. this is a further incentive to apply community preference effectively and to keep the maximum of agricultural production within the territory of the european union. the community preference, which is at the heart of our treaties, must be the preferred means of meeting the new requirements of european consumers in the field of food safety in the future. this is all the more reason to defend it vigorously at the wto and to make it clear that we have the right to make imported products bear the cost of the controls we have to apply to them.

- the next item is the report (a5-0442/2002) by mr nisticò, on behalf of the parliament's delegation to the conciliation committee, on the joint text approved by the conciliation committee for a directive of the european parliament and of the council laying down standards of quality and safety for the collection, testing, processing, storage and distribution of human blood and blood components and amending directive 2001/83/ec (pe-cons 3652/2002 - 5-0469/2002 - 2002/0323 ((cod)).
- madam president, it is on behalf of my group, the gue/ngl, but also on my own behalf, as a long-time blood donor and blood donor myself, that i am pleased to be able to speak tonight on this particularly important, and indeed vital, matter. the blood donation, as many know, has a unique human dimension, which affects us all. i shall start by mentioning some very telling figures. they concern only france, and i apologize for that, but i imagine that they are largely transposable in most of the member states of the union. in france, it takes 8,000 donors a day to save 60,000 lives and to perform 800,000 transfusions each year. a car accident may require 10 to 30 people to compete for survival, and yet only 5 percent of people donate blood. so it is reasonable to ask why there are so few blood donors. i know that the european commission has understood - and i thank it for this - a key element of the problem in defining the objective of its december 2000 proposal. the aim is to build public confidence in the safety of blood and blood products and thus achieve self-sufficiency within the european union. i shall not end this evening on the scandals of contaminated blood, which have rightly shaken that trust and, moreover, have shocked some politicians for having sinned through lack of vigilance, if not incompetence. without forgetting or forgiving, i'd rather focus on three questions. what can we do now to restore that trust ? how do we get people to give more blood and to give it in larger numbers? and thirdly, is the solution not to pay blood donors, as some european countries already do? to that last question, i will say at once that the answer, for me, is 'no'. a clear and unambiguous no. blood and blood products are not commodities. i would also like to point out that there are some people here and there, and even in this parliament, who are crying out for ethical principles on issues relating to human genetics, and who have no qualms about defending the option of paying for blood and therefore for the body. i won't say more at this moment, it will save me from getting angry. but i must also point to the heinous trafficking that takes place in countries where people have no other option to survive than to sell blood or other organs. we must therefore remain firm on this issue, avoiding any drift, any scandal and any attack on human dignity and the ethical principles that we hold dear and that we share. blood donation should therefore remain based on the principles of free consent, anonymity and gratuitousness. i don't think this is something that should even be discussed. of course, there is a difference between the payment of blood itself and the reimbursement of the costs incurred to donate blood - snacks, refreshments, reimbursement of actual transportation costs, as well as the time taken out of work to donate blood. the proposal we have received is in the right direction. it has fortunately been strengthened and clarified by the european parliament. i would like to take this opportunity to warmly congratulate professor nisticò on the quality of his work. finally, it is important to emphasize a few key points: the standards of blood quality and safety, the strengthening of the requirements for the eligibility of blood and plasma donors, the control of blood donations in the european community. finally, as regards the points which were the subject of the dispute, i can accept the results obtained at the end of the conciliation procedure as regards the guarantee of traceability and the quality of the personnel directly involved in the collection, control, processing and storage. for all these reasons, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i can vote in favour of this report and call for a vote in favour. it is our responsibility to participate in raising public awareness of this gesture that saves the lives of tens of thousands of people a year, a gesture that could be more frequent in the future to properly respond to our needs in a humane and ethical way.
- this debate is over. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.
