commission. – mr president, firstly i would like to say how grateful i am to members of parliament for raising these important issues. let me also say that i am sure all of you may well accept this as a valuable contribution to debates in parliament but sometimes general questions are followed up by extremely detailed questions that can best be responded to in correspondence. however, i will do my best to answer such questions as you have raised. i have taken notes and if i am not able to deal with technical issues of a specific nature, i will respond to the questioner in writing. the issues that have been raised centre around the question of why the inspections were suspended and when these inspections will be resumed. as i indicated in my earlier contribution, these inspections were suspended either because there was a ban on the importation of products from that country or because in the two countries in question there was 100% testing in respect of all products coming from those countries. it is expected that the controls that are put in place in member states effectively carry out the job that they are supposed to do because it is understood that these inspections have to be 100%. therefore it is important that they reveal any residues in any of the foods that are designated for testing. when the tests show positive, i want to confirm, as i indicated earlier, that these products are destroyed. a number of you raised the question whether there were doubts about standards and whether there was any pressure being put on the commission and on dg sanco in particular by other dgs in relation to the carrying out of tests or the changing of procedures, either by suspending fvo inspections in third countries or by not doing so. i confirm to the house considerations of that kind never impinge on a decision in relation to food safety. i have made that point here in this parliament on many occasions and i am happy to repeat it now. inevitably you meet representatives from the developing countries that we are talking about and often others, sometimes members of parliament, who make the suggestion that perhaps the european union is putting in place precautionary barriers in place of tariff barriers. this is an important issue and has to be taken into account, but i have always responded by saying that the protection of public health, the protection of consumers and the maintenance of the standards that consumers expect in relation to the importation of food must come first. i have to assure members of parliament who raised this question that the decisions that are taken in relation to these kinds of issues – testing for residues – are strictly based on the scientific analysis and judgement of the technical and scientific staff in dg sanco, who give their advice as to the appropriate way forward in respect of these issues. no other political or trade consideration is ever taken into account. that simply does not happen. on the question of when the inspections will be resumed, that will happen in the spring, but there is not much point in sending inspectors to third countries – or the ones i have been describing – to carry out tests to determine what we know already, to confirm the continuation of either a ban or 100% testing. the only conclusion that is being suggested by those who raised this question is that, if these tests and inspections continue and if it is found that there are still residues or that 100% testing is an inefficient and inadequate response, we should there and then decide to put in place a ban on the importation of foods from those developing countries. that is a very serious decision to take. we have to determine whether it is a proportionate response to a risk that may exist to the consumers of the european union, bearing in mind not just trade considerations but the kinds of consideration i am sure questioners have in mind here today. i know that you have concerns about the welfare of and benefits to developing countries also. this is not an inconsiderable issue. in deciding what is an appropriate response, we have to take into account all of these considerations and make sure that we come to proportionate responses. one of the most difficult aspects of my job in dealing with food safety is to come up with solutions that are proportionate. very often, when you are too hard, people will point that out. sometimes when they believe that you are too weak, the other side will point that out. it is not always possible to keep everybody happy on all occasions. but i am satisfied, bearing in mind the rigour with which inspectors from the food and veterinary office carry out their work and the reports they make, which are made available to the public on the internet for all of us to read, as well as the work that is undertaken by the control authorities in the member states to ensure that where 100% testing is required, that is done. that appears to me to be the proportionate response to the risk that may have been identified. all the time we keep this under review. in the event that a problem arises, to the extent that it arose in china, it was felt that the only appropriate response in those circumstances was a ban. as a consequence, a ban was placed on the importation of chickens, crustaceans, honey and one or two other products. that was the appropriate response in those circumstances. if we come to the conclusion that is the appropriate response in respect of other countries which seek to trade with the european union and send food here, as distinct from the continuation from a 100% control programme, that will happen. but we have not reached that view in respect of the two countries i have identified. the more detailed and technical questions that have been raised by many of you i have taken note of. i will ensure that each of you receives a response in writing in due course.
- thank you, chief. the debate is closed.

- the report (a5-0438/2002) by mr florenz, on behalf of the european parliament delegation to the conciliation committee, on the joint draft directives of the european parliament and of the council on waste electrical and electronic equipment (weee) approved by the conciliation committee (pe-cons 3663/2002 - 5-0486/2002 - 2000/0158 (cod)); 2. the restriction of the use of certain dangerous substances in electrical and electronic equipment (pe-cons 3662/2002 - c5-0487/2002 - 2000/0159 (cod)).
- mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr president of the commission, the copenhagen summit is undoubtedly a historic milestone in the construction of europe. i thank the danish presidency for its active contribution. it is to be welcomed that at this stage nothing has finally compromised the conclusion of your work. this enlargement can and must be a chance for europe in terms of stability, peace, unification of the continent, rapprochement of peoples, intermingling, opportunities for co-development, and in terms of increased influence on the world stage. but can we say, as you did last saturday, mr president-in-office, that we now have a common vision of an integrated europe? i'd be more careful. i think we are not even with the peoples of the applicant countries. after these long and difficult negotiations, some wounds are still very much alive. i believe that sooner or later we risk paying the dividends of the conception, which i consider far too liberal in substance and sometimes perceived as arrogant in form, of our negotiations with these countries. for example, has the unfortunate effect of the discriminatory measure on direct agricultural aid on the entire population of the countries concerned by 2013 been measured? this choice, in my view, has strongly reinforced the latent feeling that the fifteen would regard the countries of central europe as second-class members. the drastic safeguard clauses imposed on our partners have also given rise to the impression that there is an unequal relationship between the iron pot and the earthen pot. we should also stress the rigid application of the acquis communautaire to them, despite the fragility of their economies and the exorbitant social cost of a sudden transition to a market economy. the european council in brussels on 14 and 15 december adopted a resolution on the situation in the middle east. in the course of this process, the union has been seen on more than one occasion as the arrogant posture of the rich and powerful vis-à-vis the poor relative who has no choice but to bow down or isolate himself. it is no coincidence that the polish foreign minister was able to speak, just before copenhagen, of diktat, or his colleague in charge of agriculture of capitulation. watch out for the boomerang effect of internalized humiliation! let us not forget that the ratification referendums are due to take place in the first months of 2003. i think we should do something about our partners: send a signal of respect and openness, and make it clear that we do not consider the acquis to be set in stone, when reality reveals its limits or contradictions in a particular area. the fifteen regarded the stability pact as part of the acquis until mr prodi, in a way, relativised its relevance. citizens of the candidate countries are not the only ones to be seized by doubt or anxiety; the commission has also proposed that the member states should be given the same rights as the member states. as soon as citizens do not really feel involved in a project, as soon as they feel that they are dependent on inaccessible decision-making centres, from which various standards, laws and orders, often with serious consequences, are pouring in, they perceive a priori, rightly or wrongly, more the risks than the chances of any new adventure. the enlargement process has been carried out without the citizens. the polls show that four out of ten eu citizens can name only one candidate country and of those who do, almost a third mention turkey. here too, initiatives are needed. we must encourage all possible meetings between eastern and western europeans on issues that challenge and mobilize them. the news is full of societal issues, ranging from maritime security to migration, which affect the enlarged europe. the same applies to the need to secure employment and training and to defend services of general interest, the need for political choices to take precedence over market requirements, the role of the union on the world stage and the role of social partners in the decision-making process. as we move towards the adoption of a new treaty, which is moreover constitutional, the idea of an enlarged europe and its purpose must be debated in our societies, otherwise we would not be immune from a major incident which could shake the project of civilization which we all want to succeed. finally, mr president, it has been said - not here - that this great enlargement is a revenge for yalta. i think that this is the wrong way to go. but nothing healthy or lasting is built on revenge. this cold war approach is, in my view, completely outdated. these are all the tragedies of the 20th century which the unification of europe must enable us to overcome today. it is possible, provided we do not look back with nostalgia to the blessed era of the "mitteleuropa", the habsburg legacy. we must now look to the future with confidence if we are to lead a united europe into the 21st century.

the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the european parliament is rightly involved in the mountain regions. as you know, the commission is also giving these matters a great deal of attention. this is what the conference on 'community policy and the mountains' organized in october this year on the initiative of my colleagues michel barnier and franz fischler showed. my colleagues mrs wallström and mr barnier, who is in brussels to take part in a meeting of the convention's bureau, have asked me to inform you of some of the work in progress and outstanding issues concerning the commission's activities in the mountain regions of the european union. the ec treaty does not mention the concept of mountain areas as such. in the context of the policy of economic and social cohesion, article 158, which is also the legal basis, states that the community shall in particular aim at reducing the disparities in the level of development of the various regions and the backwardness of the most disadvantaged regions or islands, including rural areas. it might be argued that the inclusion of the term 'mountain areas' in the treaty would better reflect the concerns of those involved in these areas. 95% of mountain areas are covered by objective 1 or objective 2 of the european structural funds. the compensatory payments for lessfavoured areas under the agricultural policy also benefit mountain regions in many cases. the commission has commissioned a study to better assess the problems and strengths of mountain regions. this study has three objectives: the commission has also proposed that the mountain regions of the enlarged union be delimited, a database of these areas be established, and that the situation of mountain areas and existing community and national policies be objectively analysed and evaluated. the first objective is to define mountain areas for the 27 member states and candidate countries covered by the study. this definition is based on topographical criteria and in some cases climatic criteria are added. at the beginning of december 2002, the contractor of this study submitted 16 possible definitions to the commission; they are currently undergoing a thorough investigation. the definition to be used will be decided at the end of december. on the basis of this territorial delimitation, statistical data can then be collected. the surveys and analyses are expected to be completed and the final report submitted in september 2003. i have already said, with regard to the future consideration of mountain areas in the framework of regional policy and the common agricultural policy, that regional policy and agricultural and rural development policy are two policies which take mountain areas directly into account. in the case of regional policy, this is done through the regional programmes under objective 1 and objective 2 and the interreg community initiative, and in particular the alpine programme. the agricultural policy mainly provides support through the compensation for lessfavoured areas. the future of these policies is currently being considered. the commission's proposals on the future of regional policy will be presented at the end of 2003 as part of the third cohesion report. it would therefore be premature to decide now on the way in which mountain areas can be taken into account in the framework of regional policy in the forthcoming programming period 2007-13. the commission proposal, which is part of the mid-term review of the common agricultural policy, focuses on strengthening agri-environmental measures, which are often of benefit to mountain regions. as regards the measures for mountain areas under other community policies, i would like to go into more detail on competition policy and the provision of services. as you know, the european union's policy on state aid is based on article 87 (1) of the treaty, which states that state aid is in principle incompatible with the common market. however, this article also lists the cases in which state aid may be authorised. these exceptions include regional aid, which is 'aid to promote the economic development of areas where the standard of living is abnormally low or where there is serious underemployment', i.e. areas where the per capita gross national product is less than 75% of the community average. certain other territories are also eligible for this exemption. the commission also attaches great importance to the provision of services, as its communication of january 2001 shows. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission can only provide a stimulus in this area. in its communication, the commission clarifies that the aim and purpose of public services is to provide basic services throughout the territory, i.e. to provide access to essential services, including in remote or inaccessible areas. the new article 16 of the treaty also expressly recognises the important role of services of general economic interest in promoting economic, social and territorial cohesion. the importance of these provisions was also underlined by the heads of state or government at the lisbon summit in march 2000. the last point i would like to make is the alpine convention. although the alpine convention only directly concerns four member states, the commission was involved in launching this initiative. it was not until the end of the summer of 2002 that a sufficient number of contracting parties to the convention had ratified the various protocols to make it operational. the commission, for its part, is examining the possibilities open to it for more active participation in the convention. the commission has already submitted to the council its proposal for the signing of the transport protocol. i must tell you, however, that this project has not yet been taken forward by the council. it should also be stressed that these protocols must also be supported by the member states at the level of the council, which is responsible for signing and ratifying them on behalf of the community. as you know, several states party to the alpine convention have not yet ratified the protocols. we hope, however, that the situation will develop positively in the coming months, in line with the efforts made by some member states at the end of this summer to revive the alpine convention. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission continues to pay close attention to mountain regions. the current and future work, in particular the study by the directorate-general for regional policy, the results of the mid-term review of the current programmes and the conclusions of the third report on economic and social cohesion will give us a clearer picture of the situation and indicate possible ways forward.
- mr president, commissioner, thank you for this statement which shows us that the mountain may no longer be the great forgotten one of european politics. unfortunately, we have not yet made many comments or recommendations on the mountain. these areas deserve special attention. the mountain regions are rich in natural resources. these are mostly exceptional areas, which must therefore be managed in a specific way, through a comprehensive policy of sustainable mountain development. these are difficult territories because of their geography and climate. these are areas where agriculture plays a key role - but not just any agriculture: an agriculture which must be extensive, concerned with the preservation of species of fauna and flora and water resources, the protection of forests and habitats as defined by the european union. but this agriculture is not done without men; hence the need to protect these mountain areas from desertification and to do everything possible to maintain human presence. the provisions for young farmers must therefore be strengthened and updated. the commission has put in place a number of programmes which we are all familiar with: leader, interreg... it would probably be necessary to simplify the aid, because these are specific areas, to make it more flexible so that it is better adapted to the terrain and takes account of the specific features of the land, the need to protect the environment and the existence of many specific methods of managing these areas, for example, pastoralism. the same is true of tourism. we must promote sustainable tourism, which values the richness of the mountain, but refuses to turn the mountain into a concrete recreation area - - mr president, the mountain claims to be a place of economic, social and cultural life, but it is seeking recognition and, first of all, recognition of its handicaps. the classification of mountain areas cannot be based on altitude alone. the difficulty of access, the harshness of the climate and the slope are all factors which must also be taken into account. the mountain is also seeking recognition for the quality of its produce. it does indeed enjoy a quality image, but this can only be enhanced if the consumer can identify its products. the commission has already taken steps in this direction and we must support them. the dynamisation of the mountain economy must take account of the fact that it is in a fragile environment which must be both preserved and developed. the balance is therefore difficult to find, which must be served by coherent legislation. that is not the case at present. i am thinking in particular of legislation on the standardization of livestock farms or herders' huts which is impossible to implement in certain areas. conservation programmes, such as life or natura 2000, also have negative consequences for economic activities. the mountain areas will remain open only if every effort is made to offer future prospects to those who have chosen to live there, especially young people. effective mountain policies are therefore needed; the measures will be adapted to each mountain range and based on concerted management between elected officials, public services and professionals. these policies will have to help to offset the extra costs of production, to open up the market, to diversify activities, to maintain public services, to develop specialised training and to provide access to new technologies. agriculture, pastoralism and logging play a vital role in the mountains. they are not only the generators of quality products, they are also the only tools that allow the sites to be maintained and secured. however, in some mountain ranges, pastoralism is being challenged by the reintroduction of predatory species and poor management of their population development. diverse landscapes, high-quality products, green lungs, rare species, the mountain is and must remain plural. we must not make it a sanctuary or a desert.
